Sports.title: Infantino installs loyalist to oversee Caribbean as he splits Fifa management
Sports.content:
Gianni Infantino has separated Fifa’s management of the Caribbean countries from the rest of Concacaf in a move widely regarded by his opponents as an attempt to split the alliance to remove him from office.

Concacaf covers North and Central America as well as the Caribbean and was previously managed as one bloc. But the Guardian has learned that the former Switzerland midfielder Gelson Fernandes, an Infantino loyalist, has been appointed as the director of member associations for the Caribbean, in addition to his position looking after Fifa’s African members.

Fernandes, who played for Manchester City, Leicester and eight other clubs, joined Fifa in 2022 as director of member associations for Africa and was promoted two years later to become deputy chief members associations officer globally.

The 40-year-old works closely with Fifa’s chief members associations officer, Elkhan Mammadov, a close ally of Infantino described by many national associations as the president’s key enforcer.

Fernandes has replaced Jair Bertoni as Fifa’s liaison with the 21 Caribbean-based members, with the national associations and Concacaf informed of the change last week without consultation.

In a statement Fifa confirmed the appointment, which it said was designed to support Infantino’s vision of making the sport truly global.

“Fifa can confirm that Gelson Fernandes has taken on responsibility for the Caribbean region, in addition to his current role as regional director Africa,” it said. “With his extensive experience at Fifa and strong knowledge of football development programmes, Gelson will lead the regional team and will work closely with the member associations across the Caribbean to further support the development of football in their respective countries, following the Fifa president’s vision: making football truly global.”

Concacaf is attempting with Uefa and the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) to oust Infantino. Sources at several member associations in Europe and North America regard the change as an attempt to split the Concacaf vote before March’s presidential election, with one characterising it as “an administrative war” against its president, Victor Montagliani.

The Canadian is viewed by many in Uefa as the most credible candidate to beat Infantino, although Montagliani has yet to decide whether to stand and is committed to seeking re-election as Concacaf’s president.

Infantino has stepped up his re-election campaign in the aftermath of the World Cup sell-off scandal, ignoring a written request from Montagliani to stay away from a meeting of the Caribbean Football Union (CFU) in the Dominican Republic last month.

As revealed by the Guardian, Infantino used the CFU meeting to announce approval for numerous Fifa-funded development projects for the region worth millions of dollars in what some observers described as an attempt to lobby for votes.

Mexico has split from Concacaf by announcing its support for Infantino, and losing the backing of the Caribbean would be a significant setback for those pushing to remove Infantino.

There have been some early signs that Infantino’s tactics are paying off, with the president of the Jamaican federation, Michael Ricketts, this week backing the status quo and comparing Uefa to spoiled children.

“Infantino might have made a mistake, but the intentions were to help Caribbean countries or help smaller countries,” Rickets told the Jamaica Observer. “Can you imagine Jamaica getting $40m to invest in football? Can you imagine the difference that would make in four or five years?

“I am not supporting Uefa because I think that they always want to be in opposition and always want to oppose. It doesn’t matter who is president, they are going to have issues. It doesn’t matter how well the president does, they are going to have issues and I think that Uefa is behaving like a set of spoilt kids.”

Uefa’s 55 members are believed to be united but the strength of the AFC alliance is unclear, with Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates having defied the confederation by endorsing Infantino.

Infantino last weekend reaffirmed his intention to seek re-election for a fourth term. The deadline for other candidates seeking to stand is 18 November.

Sports.title: Rosario ‘grabbed my bottom’ during Manchester City’s win at Porto, claims Haaland
Sports.content:
Erling Haaland has claimed Pablo Rosario “grabbed my bottom” during Manchester City’s 2-0 win at Porto on Tuesday. The incident occurred in the 92nd minute, with Haaland having scored City’s goals. The forward and midfielder grappled, went to ground and were booked after being separated.

“I was really keen on a hat-trick and it seemed like he was very eager to stop me from getting it,” Haaland told Norway’s TV 2. “It was a little interesting, that – you’ll be seeing a picture where he’s grabbing my bottom. It’ll be interesting to see that picture.”

The flashpoint followed one as half-time neared in a niggly encounter. After Marc Guéhi and Gabriel Veiga had a coming together that left the latter with a head injury, tempers frayed. When the teams walked off for the interval a bust-up occurred involving players and staff near the tunnel.

Images showed Rúben Dias placing a hand on what appeared to be Francesco Farioli, the Porto head coach. Uefa will wait for the match report of the referee, Szymon Marciniak, and its delegate, Stéphanie Ford, before deciding whether to bring any action against the defender or City.

Haaland’s 47th-minute opener was a header and the No 9 revealed he had been working on the skill recently with his dad, Alf Inge, a former City player.

“Two days ago I was practising headers with my dad in the garden,” he said. “Over the years, I’ve worked a lot on my heading. I’ve improved it massively and it’s become a strength of my game. I think a lot of it comes down to experience.”

Haaland concurred with his manager, Enzo Maresca, that he may need a break soon. “It’s not easy to get any rest in this business,” the 26-year-old said.

“Like during the international break, we play four games in 10 or 11 days, so it’s not easy. But you have to try to squeeze in a few days here and there and give your mind a bit of a break.”

Sports.title: Carrick up for ‘magical’ Champions League but derby timing ‘not ideal’
Sports.content:
Michael Carrick is excited to lead Manchester United on their return to the “magical” Champions League but admitted playing on Thursday night was “not ideal” with the derby on Sunday.

United welcome Sabah to Old Trafford after a two-year Champions League absence. The Azerbaijani club are making their debut among Europe’s elite, having been in existence for less than a decade.

“It’s a magical competition,” Carrick, who won the competition in 2008 with United, said. “It’s where we all want to be. When you’re out of it, you realise how special it is, and when you’re in it, you want to make the most of it. I think we’ve all seen some special, special nights and felt some special things in this competition over the years.

“It’s where we want to be, it’s what we want to get back to, and it’s the best competition to challenge yourself and to push against the best. We’re delighted to be here, but we’re not here to just enjoy the occasion. We’re here to do business and go as far as we possibly can.

“To win the Champions League for me was the ultimate and was the best feeling I’ve had. Be nice some day to feel that again.”

United have made a mixed start to their Premier League campaign, picking up four points from three games, and this will be a testing period for a club that played just 40 games last season. If United reach the quarter-finals of the Carabao Cup, they will not have a free midweek until mid-January.

View image in fullscreen Michael Carrick won the Champions League in 2008 against Chelsea in Moscow. Photograph: Ash Donelon/Manchester United/Getty Images

Manchester City visit Old Trafford on Sunday and will have an extra two days to recover from their game at Porto on Tuesday. “I’m not concerned,” Carrick said of the turnaround.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

“I wouldn’t say it’s ideal in some ways, but it’s not something that we’ve given too much thought about. We’re not in control of that. We’ve got to deal with the cards that we’re dealt and that’s what it is, so we’ll make the most of it.”

United’s only senior left-back, Luke Shaw, did not train on Wednesday after being given a further day of rest. “We’ll see by tomorrow how he is, but it’s not an ongoing thing or a plan,” Carrick said.

Sports.title: ‘A dream come true’: behind the scenes with Wolves Women as they enter new era
Sports.content:
Suddenly the bustling classroom at the back of the Guru Nanak Satsang Sikh Gurdwara falls almost silent and all eyes are on Dan McNamara. The Wolves head coach, experiencing a wrestling lesson, is engaged in a tense tussle. He twists, panting and heaving, eventually ends up on top of his opponent, and the room erupts. Compared with some of the challenges McNamara and Wolves have grappled with during his eight and a half years coaching the team, this exercise was child’s play.

Wolves, promoted to Women’s Super League Two in May, are visiting the gurdwara – which became Wolverhampton’s first in 1966 – as part of an afternoon city tour which has also included a trip to the historic The Halls music venue and a walk in the centre, as some of their new signings acquaint themselves with the area before the club’s first season as a fully professional women’s team, and their first WSL2 home match, against Sheffield United, on Sunday.

View image in fullscreen The Wolves head coach, Dan McNamara, in his new office at the Sir Jack Haywood training ground. Photograph: Fabio De Paola/The Guardian

Victory against Plymouth in the third-tier promotion playoff was the culmination of years of hard graft in the amateur game, and McNamara pauses for reflection as he chats from his office overlooking the Sir Jack Hayward training ground in Compton.

“Initially, I think my ‘office’ was me sitting in the driver’s seat of an old Ford Focus,” he says. “I first walked on to an Astroturf with about seven bibs, three footballs and 58 players and probably thought: ‘What the hell have I done?’ Now I’m in my own office. We’ve got a fantastic setup here, we’ve got our own spaces for the women, changing facilities, which have been added over the summer. It’s night and day.

View image in fullscreen The Wolves captain, Anna Morphet, leads players during a session at the Sir Jack Haywood training ground. Photograph: Fabio De Paola/The Guardian

“Everybody grows up and dreams of being a professional footballer. I was no different. My claim to fame was I was in the same youth team as Wayne Rooney for a few years at Everton – our tactics were: ‘Pass the ball to Wayne and he will score.’ And [when I left Everton] I probably fell out of love with the game for a little bit. To be here now working professionally in football is a dream come true.

“People always talk about what success looks like. And I think: ‘Leave the place in a better place than what you got it.’ I don’t think anyone could argue that we’re going to leave this place in a better place than when we first picked it up. It’s not been me; the girls have gone on the pitch and they’ve achieved it. But to have inputted a small bit into making dreams come true gets me quite emotional.”

View image in fullscreen The Wolves squad are put through their paces at the Sir Jack Haywood training ground. Photograph: Fabio De Paola/The Guardian

Promotion was a long time coming for Wolves, who won tier three’s northern division in 2022 but – with only one team promoted then – lost the playoff decider against the southern champions, Southampton. McNamara missed that because he was overseas with the Royal Air Force, and watched from the Falkland Islands. Since 2024, he has coached Wolves full-time as part of the RAF’s elite athlete scheme – “they have extended me for an additional year to continue at WSL2; hopefully I can do them proud and represent the air force in a good way over the next 12 months,” he says – and his team lost two league games across the next two seasons.

In 2025, they finished second but were heartbroken to find the club had not applied for a licence for promotion. A year later, with a new executive chair in Nathan Shi, the club’s approach to the women’s team has changed, and McNamara’s team have cabins at the training ground as private changing areas, a meeting/analysis room and places to relax together. Some of the squad engage in a tense round of the card game Dobble after having breakfast together, before heading out for training. Further new training pitches will follow soon.

View image in fullscreen The England youth international goalkeeper Emily Orman has arrived on loan from London City Lionesses. Photograph: Fabio De Paola/The Guardian

This summer the club also hired a new head of women’s and girls football, Russ Fraser, who worked in the WSL at Reading, West Ham, Leicester and Liverpool over the past decade, before a spell with Al-Qadsiah in Saudi Arabia. Many of last season’s squad left their day jobs and turned professional but there has also been a big recruitment drive. Signings include former WSL players such as Mel Lawley, Jasmine Matthews, Yana Daniëls and Mel Filis.

“We don’t want to just be a team that goes up and then straight back down, so the work was almost immediately after the playoff,” McNamara says. “It’s been non-stop since. We were quite careful at what we went after. We wanted to bring in the right technical players, but also players that represent this great club and the city. And that’s hard work, ethics, having the right morals on the pitch, being quite energetic.”

Another new signing the England youth goalkeeper Emily Orman, on loan from London City Lionesses, enjoyed taking part in the wrestling demonstration. “I’ve never wrestled before,” she says. “That was really tough. I got a real bead on doing that!” It is not the squad’s only team-building experience. They also went bouldering in the Lake District, and the midfielder Tammi George – who first joined Wolves aged 13, before a spell at Sunday’s opponents – says: “That brought the group together so much because people were put through difficult situations and needed an arm around them at times. Everybody really saw the benefit.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen The Wolves squad take a walking tour through the city. Photograph: Fabio De Paola/The Guardian

On the city walk the players learn about everything from the AD910 battle of Tettenhall to the origins of the Prince Albert statue, and are informed of the iconic sets played by bands such as Queen and Nirvana at The Halls. There is also an important stop at Molineux, first so the players can help out at a session run by the club’s foundation during the school holidays for youngsters, through Premier League Kicks, in partnership with West Midlands police. The squad play pool and help with arts and crafts before touring the club’s museum, where the women’s football writer and Wolves fan Tony Leighton has written the latest part of an exhibition charting the women’s team’s rise.

View image in fullscreen The Wolves players Mel Lawley (left) and Chloe Williams play table football with attendees during a summer youth club organised by the Wolves Foundation at Molineux. Photograph: Fabio De Paola/The Guardian

The former BBC WM presenter Jenny Wilkes has been the chair of Wolves Women since 1999 and is full of pride. She knows how much the efforts of volunteers have helped the club. “I remember Rachael Heyhoe Flint, who had been such an amazing support for us in the days when it literally was one woman and a dog watching the game and she was one woman who brought her dog and walked her dog around the pitch,” she says. “We’re come a long way since then.

“It’s incredible, being fully professional, which we never thought we’d manage to do. In the long history of the club, we have played in the top flight before but it was when the top flight wasn’t professional. Now to see professional footballers at Wolves Women for the first time really is incredible.”

View image in fullscreen The squad take part in wrestling at Wolverhampton Wrestling Club. Photograph: Fabio De Paola/The Guardian

The captain, Anna Morphet, who handed in her notice for her day job as a physio a week after Wolves’ promotion, says: “We used to collect the kit out the back of Macca’s car boot. Those 90 minutes [against Plymouth] were the opportunity to change our lives. The work that’s gone on over the summer and in pre-season has been immense and I think now it’s about believing that we are ready for this level.”

Wolves opened with a defeat, albeit a respectable one, 2-0 at one of the favourites for promotion, Newcastle. Fraser says: “Wherever we finish in the league, I want other teams to go: ‘Wow, Wolves were so much better than I thought they were,’ because I think a lot of teams will probably think: ‘Oh, Wolves have just come up, they’ll go straight back down.’ I think we’re better than that. I think we’ve got a good group here.”

Sports.title: Men’s Ballon d’Or 2026 power rankings: will there be an English winner for the first time in 25 years?
Sports.content:
1) Harry Kane (England/Bayern Munich)

Even adjusting for the goal-drunken Bundesliga, his 61 goals in 51 matches for Bayern last season undersells his all-around impact, considering his playmaking and hold-up skills. Kane was gameplanned out of England’s later games at the World Cup, but he was unstoppable through the last 16 to close out the finest year of his career to date. If not now, when?

2) Rodri (Spain/Manchester City – now at Barcelona)

He boasts a comparable case to when he won this prize in 2024 – Rodri remains the epicenter of an incredibly effective Spanish collective. This time around, there’s no Premier League glory to bolster his hopes, as City’s late challenge fizzled out with the club “only” winning domestic cups in his final season at the Etihad. Back to his best en route to Spain’s second World Cup title, though only one of the four previous World Cup champions had the corresponding Ballon d’Or winner (Lionel Messi, 2023).

3) Kylian Mbappé (France/Real Madrid)

Mbappé and José Mourinho have launched an aggressive campaign for the Frenchman to win his first Ballon d’Or. He was even more difficult to slow in his second Spanish season, with 40 goals in 42 matches across La Liga and the Champions League; the less said about his pressing, the better. Few players captivated and dominated like Mbappé at the World Cup, as he won the Golden Boot. But a lack of team accomplishments could set back his candidacy, made even more glaring given Madrid’s chronic success.

4) Lamine Yamal (Spain/Barcelona)

Another member of the World Cup champions, although injuries limited his impact in North America – the master of suspense was not as involved as he’d have liked. Then again, he managed greater consistency in his third season as a regular for Barcelona, with 41 goal contributions in all competitions across 45 appearances. He only just turned 19 in July.

5) Lionel Messi (Argentina/Inter Miami)

Messi could well have ranked higher had Argentina won the World Cup this summer, as the 39-year-old was the heart and soul of their campaign. Alas, a putrid final showing (by his teammates, more than Messi) dulls the sheen on his hopes for a ninth Ballon d’Or, and he is also hit by the fact that he doesn’t play for one of Europe’s elite clubs, even though Inter Miami won the MLS title. His remarkable 17th appearance on a Ballon d’Or shortlist is well deserved.

6) Michael Olise (France/Bayern Munich)

Who knew Bayern’s most thrilling attack in recent memory would be spearheaded by signings from Tottenham and Crystal Palace? An elite secondary attacker, and one who has come to relish operating as the string-puller in transition and at the edge of the final third. Spain masterfully closed his passing lines and took him out of the semi-final, but a pair of assists in the third-place match put him top in that category at the World Cup. A career year, or evidence he’s set a new standard for himself?

7) Erling Haaland (Norway/Manchester City)

Even as City stumbled down the stretch, this was another season to pad his growing legacy as one of the game’s great strikers of any era. He made the most of Norway’s return to the World Cup, finishing as the tournament’s joint-third top goalscorer (seven) despite exiting in the quarter-final.

8) Jude Bellingham (England/Real Madrid)

Birmingham City’s decision to retire his number when his career had barely started has aged well. A man for the big moments, he forged a rare tandem with Kane at the World Cup, alternating headline hero shifts en route to another semi-final heartbreaker. His goals and assists plummeted in his third season with Madrid, though most of his teammates saw diminishing returns in a forgettable campaign.

9) Ousmane Dembélé (France/Paris Saint-Germain)

Lacking some of the bombast that typifies his rivals, Dembélé remains a silky threat for club and country. His stats for PSG dipped from last year’s award-winning campaign, from 35 goals in 53 games to 20 in 40. His partnership with Mbappé and Olise for France was as dangerous as the international game has seen. If nothing else, Dembélé has made certain that he is no one-year wonder.

10) Khvicha Kvaratskhelia (Georgia/Paris Saint-Germain)

On a per-minute basis, few players are more effective in the biggest games. Unfortunately, his club’s domestic dominance means he can take more shifts off than most of his gilded peers, logging a measly 1,479 Ligue 1 minutes in 28 appearances. Georgia’s absence from this summer’s World Cup also limits the evidence available to bolster his case. Nonetheless, his barnstorming exploits in the Champions League knockouts saw the 25-year-old hit rare form.

11) Declan Rice (England/Arsenal)

The most vital cog in Mikel Arteta’s meticulous machine, and a key all-around impact in England’s run to the World Cup semi-final, even if he at times understandably looked tired after a long domestic campaign.

12) Bruno Fernandes (Portugal/Manchester United)

One of a few Portuguese players whose cases for this prize were scuppered by this summer’s underwhelming showing under the stubborn Roberto Martínez. Truly sensational to restore the Red Devils to prouder days.

13) Pau Cubarsí (Spain/Barcelona)

Looked every part the lead center-back that his club and country need to play in a possession-dominant way. Then again, these prizes seldom skew towards defenders.

14) Fabián Ruiz (Spain/Paris Saint-Germain)

Success in the Champions League and World Cup has seen this fine facilitator get his due at age 30.

15) Vitinha (Portugal/Paris Saint-Germain)

Involved in PSG’s best stuff no matter the competition, with six of his seven club goals coming in the Champions League last season. Unable to shed the stench of Portugal’s World Cup, but he is the world’s finest deep-lying playmaker all the same.

16) Luis Díaz (Colombia/Bayern Munich)

Took to Germany with glee, bagging 26 goals and 19 assists in 51 appearances to dwarf his output at Liverpool. Struggled for most of the World Cup, however, as Colombia crashed out sooner than expected.

17) Gabriel (Brazil/Arsenal)

Always close to any fracas, Gabriel was steady as ever as Arsenal enjoyed a long-awaited Premier League title. Some great summer showings at the World Cup, especially against Japan, but struggled – like the rest of his team – against Norway.

18) Nuno Mendes (Portugal/Paris Saint-Germain)

Few opponents have found how to best neutralize Mendes, save for hoping that PSG give him another domestic day off between Champions League games.

19) Lautaro Martínez (Argentina/Inter)

Another dependable goalscoring campaign in Italy, and excelled in a super-sub role during Argentina’s knockout run. One of this era’s great strikers, and already off to a hot start this season.

20) William Saliba (France/Arsenal)

Especially steady in the Premier League and Champions League, helping Arsenal to their most successful year in decades. His injury hurt France’s chances against Spain in the World Cup semi-final, perhaps bolstering his reputation in absentia.

And the rest of the field …

21) Achraf Hakimi (Morocco/Paris Saint-Germain)

22) Vinícius Júnior (Brazil/Real Madrid)

23) Dayot Upamecano (France/Bayern Munich)

24) Marc Cucurella (Spain/Chelsea – now at Real Madrid)

25) João Neves (Portugal/Paris Saint-Germain)

26) Willian Pacho (Ecuador/Paris Saint-Germain)

27) Ferran Torres (Spain/Barcelona – now at Paris Saint-Germain)

28) Marquinhos (Brazil/Paris Saint-Germain)

29) Julián Quiñones (Mexico/Al Qadsiah)

30) Sadio Mané (Senegal/Al Nassr)

Sports.title: Football Daily | Troy Parrott enjoys a big week after taking the scenic route to success
Sports.content:
THE REAL DEAL?

There are, you suspect, quite a few folk with links to the London postcode of N17 who would be thoroughly grateful if Troy Parrott could stop popping up to score winning goals for a bit. The Republic of Ireland striker has barely unpacked his bags at Real Betis, yet he’s already ruined the afternoon of his former manager at Tottenham, pouncing to sink José Mourinho’s Real Madrid. Four days later? He made headlines again on his Bigger Cup debut at Lille. Two games, two goals, two match-winners. Not entirely shabby for a lad who was once given the classic Mourinho treatment and declared “not ready”. Mourinho, as ever, remains a central character in this particular soap opera. It was the Special One who handed a teenage Parrott his Premier League debut in December 2019, throwing him on during a 5-0 win over Burnley. It was also Mourinho who promptly decided the youngster needed a fair bit longer in the oven.

When Harry Kane and Son Heung-min were both sidelined in March 2020, Tottenham fans dared to dream that Parrott might get a go. Instead, Mourinho simply declared that the youngster was not prepared for the cut and thrust of regular top-flight football. A brief cameo against Norwich followed before the pandemic halted the season – and, for all intents and purposes, Parrott’s Spurs career. What followed was the classic, harrowing English loan circuit: Millwall, Ipswich, MK Dons and Preston. Ouch. None of them quite took. The Spurs academy hope was beginning to look less like the next Kane and more like another promising youngster destined to become a pub quiz answer. Enter the Netherlands. A formative spell at Excelsior steadying the ship was followed by a proper explosion at AZ, where he smashed in 51 goals across 97 games – giving Robin van Persie nightmares along the way.

That – and a high-profile international hat-trick last year – was more than enough to persuade Betis to fork out £17m for him this summer. His full debut was, it is fair to say, forgettable – a 5-2 hammering by Levante – that prompted Manuel Pellegrini to sigh forlornly about his new forward’s mistakes. But the beauty of Parrott these days is his refusal to sulk. Coming off the bench in the 68th minute against Madrid, he reacted quickest to a Thibaut Courtois parry, shoving the ball into the net from close range. No stepovers, no 30-yard curlers, just pure instinct. “That’s a striker’s job,” Parrott squawked. “In a game, I might do this 10 times, and it might not happen. So, it’s a mentality thing to just keep on going in there, hoping it comes. Today, it did.”

It also happened to come against Mourinho. The same Mourinho who had decided Parrott was not quite ready was now watching the 24-year-old end his perfect start to his second spell at Madrid. Football does enjoy a punchline. And Parrott had another one ready for Lille, pouncing on some poor defending by Nathan Ngoy to fire a low effort into the far corner in a thrilling 3-2 win. Four appearances, two goals, two winners, Madrid slain, and a Bigger Cup debut goal logged. Meanwhile, Tottenham sit in the Premier League’s bottom three still waiting for their first league goal. There is, naturally, a danger in getting carried away. Two goals do not suddenly mean Spurs made the biggest transfer blunder since selling Gareth Bale. Parrott is 24 now, not the teenager Mourinho was dealing with, and his development has been anything but straightforward. But that is what makes his current run so enjoyable: he has had to take the scenic route.

LIVE ON BIG WEBSITE

Join Rob Smyth from 8pm BST for hot Bigger Cup coverage of Napoli 1-1 Arsenal, while Daniel Harris will have a clockwatch on the rest of Wednesday’s action.

QUOTE OF THE DAY

“I appeal to all Ugandans to remain patient and allow the Omusuuga and the committee to perform their duties in accordance with our cultural traditions for enthroning a new Omukama. Let us focus entirely on mourning my cousin, His Majesty King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV” – South East Dons keeper, George Desmond Kamurasi, calls for calm amid speculation that he may succeed his cousin and become the next king of the Tooro Kingdom. It’ll be quite the step up from the Southern Counties East League Premier Division.

View image in fullscreen George Desmond Kamurasi in his non-ceremonial gear, earlier. Photograph: SE Dons

double quotation mark Re: Ken Muir’s letter (yesterday’s Football Daily letters) and mention of Arbroath’s famous 36-0 victory over Bon Accord in 1885. On the same day, in the same competition and just 18 miles away, Dundee Harp defeated Aberdeen Rovers 35-0. Arbroath and Harp were rivals and after the final whistle, officials from Harp sent a telegram to Arbroath simply containing the result of their match and then retired to a pub to celebrate their world record. Later that evening, a reply was received which read ‘Arbroath 36-0 Bon Accord’. Both sides thought the other was winding them up. The results were not a surprise. Rovers and Bon Accord were both playing only their third official fixtures. Bon Accord arrived for their match with nine players and no goalkeeper, so played an outfield player in goal and two spectators made up their XI. The Aberdeen Weekly News reported that Arbroath’s keeper ‘neither touched the ball with hand or foot … but remained under the friendly shelter of an umbrella the whole time’. Arbroath also had seven goals disallowed. Unsurprisingly, the qualification rules for the Scottish Cup were changed for the following season” – Jamie Gaukroger.

double quotation mark Call me one of those bluffers and chancers with ‘fantastic theories and philosophies’ if you will but, after sitting through the chaotic mess that was Real Madrid v Inter in Bigger Cup, two things spring to mind. Firstly, if Madrid has had an obvious gap of no central midfielder who can control the momentum and flow of the game for over two seasons, since Toni Kroos and Luka Modric, why ignore it yet again but spend £115m on yet another left-sided attacker? Secondly, even if you don’t have one, never mind two of those types of players, once you go 2-0 up in the 23rd minute against a team at home, can’t you just kick the ball five-10 yards to a teammate consistently, keep possession and tire the opposition out? As the late, great Johan Cruyff used to say: ‘As long as we’ve got the ball, they’re never going to score’” – Noble Francis.

double quotation mark OK, Mike Wilner (Monday’s letters), I’ll bite. ‘What isn’t what it is?’ Football Daily is not a humorous teatime newsletter. ‘What has a club not won what it won?’ Senegal did not win Afcon. ‘When does a team not lose what it’s lost?’ USA USA USA ... did not lose Folarin Balogun against Belgium in the GWC. Is there a plausible weeklong riff here? Oh, yes. Yes there is. There most certainly is” – Chi.

If you have any, please send letters to the.boss@theguardian.com. Today’s letter o’ the day winner is … Jamie Gaukroger, who gets a copy of The Mbappé Project by Philippe Auclair. Copies are available in the Guardian Bookshop if you are not the lucky scribe. Terms and conditions for our competitions, when we run them, are here.

Sports.title: Aryna Sabalenka is DETHRONED as world No1 with Elena Rybakina swiping the top spot ahead of potential US Open final showdown
Sports.content:
Aryna Sabalenka is DETHRONED as world No1 with Elena Rybakina swiping the top spot ahead of potential US Open final showdown

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Aryna Sabalenka has lost her status as women's world No1 after major rival Elena Rybakina booked her spot in the US Open semi-finals by defeating Olympic champion Zheng Qinwen.

The Belarusian had spent 99 consecutive weeks at the summit of the women's game and 106 weeks in total, but knew her position was dangerously under threat heading into the tournament in New York.

To keep hold of her position, Sabalenka would have had to defend all of her ranking points won at Flushing Meadows as the reigning champion, and seen Rybakina go out to Zheng.

Having only reached the fourth round last year, Rybakina had fewer points to defend, combined with a consistent year that has seen the Kazakh star win the Australian Open in January.

Rybakina has never before been world No1, and admitted that it was 'tough to find words' after reaching the milestone.

'It's been a very difficult match, with a lot of nerves, and it wasn't maybe the highest level,' she told on-court interviewer Andrea Petkovic, 'I'm glad I pushed through.

Elena Rybakina will start next week as the reigning world No1 for the first time in her career

Aryna Sabalenka has spent 99 weeks as world No1 but still has the US Open trophy in sight

'It's been an early match, and in my head I was complaining about sun, shadow - it was definitely a battle inside me, and I'm glad I pushed all the negative thoughts away and I'm happy to be in the semi-finals here.

'I didn't start that well, and I was negative, and it wasn't easy (transitioning from night to day matches), (but) I was just telling myself, keep on fighting, work on some things.'

On her ranking, she added: 'it's just a number right now, and of course I'm in the semis. My goal is to win the tournaments I play.

'It's an amazing achievement, but you know how quickly everything can change in ranking points, in matches. I just need to focus (on my next match).'

At the moment that Rybakina played her final point against Zheng to confirm that she would break new ground at the top of the sport, Sabalenka was on the practice court a stone's throw away from the Billie Jean King National Tennis Center's showcourt.

Sabalenka paused her drills to wander over to a nearby television screen by the courts, to watch the final stages of the match.

Had Rybakina fallen to Zheng, who has come through the tournament as a qualifier after tumbling down the rankings due to a spell sidelined by injury, Sabalenka might not have been the only one to benefit.

Home favourites Coco Gauff and Jessica Pegula could have also captured the No1 ranking, if either American was the one to lift the trophy after Saturday's final.

For Sabalenka, she will look ahead to the end of the year and the start of 2027, where Rybakina has a lot of points to defend as WTA Finals champion and the winner in Melbourne.

But in the present, she admitted on Tuesday that she would gladly swap her ranking for the chance to pull off a 'three-peat' by winning in New York.

'I'll be more than happy,' she grinned when asked if she would accept the hypothetical exchange.

'Yes, three-peat. Sounds great.'

Sports.title: Tottenham suffer huge blow as Mykhailo Mudryk is ruled out for up to two months with ankle injury - four days after playing for first time in almost two years after drugs ban
Sports.content:
Mykhailo Mudryk is expected to be out for up to two months after injuring an ankle in training just days after his first Premier League appearance in almost two years.

Tottenham’s new winger, on loan for the season from Chelsea, made his debut as a 74th minute substitute in a goalless draw at Nottingham Forest on Saturday.

It was his first taste of competitive football since his return from a doping ban which hit in November 2024.

Spurs boss Roberto De Zerbi said it would take time for the Ukraine international winger to get up to speed but his progress has been halted by a setback in training.

It is a blow for De Zerbi who left Richarlison out of his Premier League squad because the Brazilian asked to leave in the summer.

Teenager winger Mikey Moore was released on loan to Cologne when Mudryk signed on deadline day.

Mykhailo Mudryk faces up to two months out after suffering an ankle injury during training

Mudryk made his first competitive appearance for almost two years when he came on as a substitute against Nottingham Forest on Saturday

Xavi Simons and Wilson Odobert are recovering from serious knee injuries and neither is expected back this year.

Dejan Kulusevski is closing in on a return after more than a year out with a knee injury. Sweden boss Graham Potter said Kulusevski was ‘very close’.

James Maddison, also on his way back from a serious knee injury, has not started a game since before Kulusevski and picked up a shoulder injury coming off the bench against Brentford on the opening day of the season.

De Zerbi’s options to start up front against Everton are likely to come from Dominic Solanke, Omar Marmoush, Mathys Tel, Savinho and Mohamed Kudus.

Sports.title: Man City star Erling Haaland opens up on heated scenes during Porto Champions League clash - and claims his opponent 'grabbed my bottom'
Sports.content:
Man City star Erling Haaland opens up on heated scenes during Porto Champions League clash - and claims his opponent 'grabbed my bottom'

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Erling Haaland has opened up on the heated scenes that occurred towards the end of Man City's Champions League victory over Porto on Tuesday.

Haaland, who scored twice in the 2-0 win, was cautioned after tussling with Pablo Rosario late in the game and claims that the midfielder wanted to stop him by any means necessary.

‘I was really keen on a hat-trick and it seemed like he [Rosario] was very eager to stop me from getting it,’ Haaland told TV 2. ‘It was a little interesting, that. You'll be seeing a picture where he's grabbing my bottom... it’ll be interesting to see that picture.’

That was not the only flashpoint of the match, with both sets of players having to be dragged away from each other in the tunnel at half time.

City reserve goalkeeper Marcus Bettinelli is understood to have been pushed by Porto officials after the home team were incensed by refereeing decisions.

UEFA’s disciplinary committee are assessing reports by the match delegate and referee Szymon Marciniak to ascertain whether any action is necessary. The punishment for any guilty party is likely to amount to a fine.

Erling Haaland has opened up on his tussle with Pablo Rosario during Man City's Champions League victory over Porto on Tuesday

Haaland scored twice during the 2-0 triumph, including a header shortly after half-time

Haaland also spoke about his recent flurry of headed goals and said they have come from perfecting the art with his father in the garden.

The City striker managed to score six headers last season but now has three in his last three matches – including the first of a brace in Porto.

HAALAND BY NUMBERS His incredible goalscoring record in club football: Left foot - 221 goals Right foot - 43 goals Head - 37 goals Other - 1 goal TOTAL: 302 goals

Haaland pinpointed his aerial ability as something to improve after sealing a move to the Etihad Stadium in 2022 and believes it has now added another string to his bow.

And the dedication has extended to impromptu sessions with Alfie Haaland at home in Cheshire, seemingly recreating scenes of his childhood.

‘Over the years, I’ve worked a lot on my heading,’ Haaland said. ‘I’ve improved it massively and it’s become a strength of my game. I think a lot of it comes down to experience.'

Haaland has 37 career headed goals in club football, just over 10 per cent of his overall haul and added: ‘Actually, two days ago I was practising headers with my dad in the garden.'

Sports.title: What insiders are saying about Joe Root's England: The major change he's made to the setup and how they're already learning from the pitfalls of Bazball after another dominant day against Pakistan
Sports.content:
What insiders are saying about Joe Root's England: The major change he's made to the setup and how they're already learning from the pitfalls of Bazball after another dominant day against Pakistan

Ben Stokes hated the word ‘ruthless’ because he felt it was only ever used after the event, but Joe Root’s England clearly have no such qualms.

Needing victory to wrap up a 3–0 whitewash and send them into their winter programme of six Tests in South Africa, Bangladesh and Australia in good heart, they dismantled Pakistan’s flimsy batting yet again, before a century stand between Emilio Gay and Harry Brook eased them into the lead as the shadows fell across Edgbaston.

Root himself fell lbw for the 10th time in 13 innings, a raucous maiden Test wicket for the 21-year-old debutant fast bowler Razaullah.

But it was a rare blot on a day when England – who closed on 156 for four, a lead of 23 – confirmed their superiority over a demoralised and deflated Pakistan.

Two years ago, England reacted to the possibility of a 3–0 win over Sri Lanka and a first perfect Test summer for 20 years by handing a debut to the unknown Leicestershire left-arm seamer Josh Hull. It was too clever by half, the worst kind of Bazball affectation. England lost by eight wickets, and Hull is yet to win a second cap.

Later that year, they went two up in New Zealand, then celebrated too hard after victory in Wellington. In the final Test at Hamilton, they were a rabble, losing by 423 runs – an unserious conclusion to a weighty series win.

Ollie Robinson claims Abdullah Shafique, one of his four wickets during another dismal Pakistan batting display

But Root’s team have been determined to avoid another pratfall. They returned to training on Sunday, three days before the start of this Test, prompting one insider to remark: ‘That would never have happened with a 2–0 lead under the old regime.’

And in his pre-match press conference Root himself deadbatted any suggestion that selectorial thoughts were already drifting towards Johannesburg on December 17. His entire focus, he said, was on the here and now, on reacquainting his players with the feeling of victory. The opposition have been poor, and the cricket not always thrilling, but it sure beats the alternative.

Root has been helped by a seam attack that is operating – three-quarters of it, at least – at the peak of its powers. Ollie Robinson began the procession once more, and finished with three for 15, taking his series figures to 19 wickets at 6.84. Josh Tongue picked up four, leaving him with 17 at 12, and Jofra Archer three, to move to 11 at 18.

Only Gus Atkinson failed to chip in, his analysis of none for 31 from five inconsistent overs taking his series aggregate to a single wicket at 156. Deprived of the new ball, he is struggling to reinvent himself as a change bowler, even if he hasn’t always enjoyed much luck.

The Pakistan innings was as sorry an enterprise as we have come to expect, and every bit as chaotic as the off-field shenanigans that preceded it.

Saim Ayub, one of four players drafted into the side from a group of seven summoned in the aftermath of the defeat at Lord’s, was trapped for a 10-ball duck by Robinson, giving him 100 Test wickets at an average below 20 – a feat achieved for England in the last 60 years only by Ian Botham and Derek Underwood. And it was the signal for Pakistan to unravel in hapless fashion on a blameless surface.

Saud Shakeel is bowled by Josh Tongue after top scoring for Pakistan with 43

Azan Awais and Shan Masood were both caught at midwicket aiming dreadful shots at Archer, while Abdullah Shafique nibbled Robinson low to Dan Lawrence in the cordon.

The day before, Babar Azam had left his press conference in a hurry as the questions rained down about the Pakistan Cricket Board’s dramatic intervention, and he didn’t linger long here either, trapped on the crease for seven by a nipbacker from Tongue which hit the top of off stump.

He has now scored 21 runs in three innings since returning from the hand injury that ruled him out at Headingley, and looks a lost soul, whether the inquisition is coming from the pacemen or the press.

His dismissal also meant the top five had all fallen for single figures – unprecedented for the first innings of a Test match, yet entirely predictable for a team devoid of confidence and identity.

As in the second innings at Lord’s, Saud Shakeel fought a lone hand, until he was bowled for 43 by a delivery from Tongue so good – nipping back through the gate to take out off stump – that the batsman allowed himself a nod of appreciation. Otherwise, most resistance came from Mohammad Abbas and Mohammad Ali, whose last-wicket stand of 26 was the highest of the innings.

All out for 133, Pakistan have now been dismissed for fewer than 200 for a national-record five innings in a row – and in the equivalent of just seven sessions.

Emilio Gay chops on to end a promising innings after a second half-century of the Test summer

As if in a hurry to take the lead, Ben Duckett continued his poor series when he edged a loose drive off Mohammad Ali to second slip for 11, before Jordan Cox was pinned for four by an inducker from Mohammad Abbas.

And Pakistan were eyeing an improbable comeback when Razaullah trapped Root on the crease with his fourth ball as a Test cricketer and celebrated his team’s best moment of a farcical tour with gusto.

But Gay, playing with care and attention– and possibly for his Test place – put on a restorative 104 with Brook before dragging a wide one from Razaullah on to his stumps. A Test-best 60 made some kind of statement before the winter tours, but he walked off knowing it might have been better.

Still, with Brook bringing up his own half-century, England were in control. Don’t tell Stokes, but it all felt suspiciously ruthless.

Sports.title: The three things Arsenal need to do this season to finally win the Champions League - from the players Mikel Arteta must learn to trust to the January transfer window plan and a returning hero
Sports.content:
The three things Arsenal need to do this season to finally win the Champions League - from the players Mikel Arteta must learn to trust to the January transfer window plan and a returning hero

The Hilton Budapest had been primed, a function room already booked in advance for Arsenal’s staff and players after last season’s Champions League final.

But instead of a raucous party to mark a first European Cup in the club’s 140-year history, a few reflective, sorrows-drowning drinks followed before an early flight back to London for the Premier League title parade through the streets of north London.

The disappointment exuding from Mikel Arteta in the post-match press conference following the defeat on penalties by Paris Saint-Germain was marked. Ending a 22-year wait for a Premier League title had gone out the window, his words verged on anger.

‘Pain, that's it, when you are so close in the competition and you are a few penalty kicks away from winning the biggest football club competition, that's the way which you feel,’ he said.

After ending that long, agonising wait to be crowned champions of England, conquering Europe is Arteta's final frontier. The Spaniard has never tasted success in a European competition as a player or manager, and often uses the Champions League as a reference point in how legacies are defined.

Arsenal are well primed to make that final step. They were, after all, only a few kicks from glory in May, and have strengthened further this summer with additions such as Bruno Guimaraes, Christos Tzolis and Ezri Konsa. But how do they get over that final hurdle?

Mikel Arteta's side were a penalty shootout away from finally lifting their first European Cup against Paris Saint-Germain in Budapest in May

Gabriel's decisive miss from the spot was an agonising end to a season that could have been historic

1. Trust the depth

Arsenal’s squad depth gives Arteta the luxury of rotating without necessarily weakening the starting XI.

Ben White has made a case to continue at right back even when Jurrien Timber returns from injury, his telepathic connection with Bukayo Saka and Martin Odegaard forming a triumvirate which opponents have difficulty stopping on the right flank.

In the middle, Myles Lewis-Skelly has performed well in place of the injured Bruno Guimaraes. The new £75million Brazilian is expected to walk into the line-up on Wednesday against Napoli but after his recent displays, Lewis-Skelly will be on the Brazilian’s heels if there’s any dip in form. It’s a great situation to have for Arteta. But he still needs to utilise it.

Last season, he arguably gave far too many minutes to Declan Rice when he was already tiring, for example. The England midfielder, who went on to play a key role at the World Cup, made 55 appearances in all competitions, with 49 starts and 4,454 minutes, or 91 per cent of Arsenal's minutes when he was available for selection. No Arsenal outfielder played more. Rice himself during the World Cup admitted he had been playing through neural pain in his hamstring since December.

Arsenal had four outfield players above 4,200 minutes - Rice, Martin Zubimendi (4,298), William Saliba (4,254) and Gabriel (4,210). This level of excessive workload must be better shared if Arsenal are to go all the way to the final again, and potentially lift the elusive trophy.

Zubimendi and Rice's back-up, Christian Norgaard, were not trusted to give the Spaniard a rest, but now Lewis-Skelly or Guimaraes can offer that. Konsa can cover while Saliba and Cristhian Mosquera are injured, and Piero Hincapie can slot seamlessly in if Gabriel needs a spell out.

Even Arteta hinted at this in Budapest after the defeat by PSG, saying: ‘You have to get into the competition with all the squad available in the best moment, each player. And we've had more players, many more players than last season but not all of them in that condition for different reasons. And that's something we have to improve as well.’ At least he’s aware. Now he needs to trust those on the bench to get him through.

Declan Rice has spoken of the neural pain he suffered from this summer, and surely cannot keep on playing as many minutes as he did last season

In Myles Lewis-Skelly and Bruno Guimaraes, Arteta has two high-class options he can call on to give Rice a rest

2. Go again in January

Viktor Gyokeres has fallen down the pecking order with Kai Havertz fully fit.

It was always the plan last season, but an injury to Havertz on the opening day at Old Trafford last season resulted in Gyokeres becoming the Gunners’ first-choice striker in the previous campaign, where he struck 21 goals across all competitions after joining for £56million.

The Swede, though, has only made one substitute appearance in three league matches, coming off the bench for 12 minutes against Chelsea on Sunday and showing signs of rust.

After Havertz and Gyokeres, though, Arteta’s options thin out dramatically. Midfielder Mikel Merino could once again be thrown up front to fill the gap, though this would not be ideal. Having failed in their chase for either Vinicius Junior, Julian Alvarez or Lautaro Martinez, Arsenal are very light in the striker position.

It begs the question: can the club lure the likes of Bournemouth’s Eli Junior Kroupi in the January window? He’s a player Arteta admires, has a special place in fans' hearts after scoring the goal that helped seal the title in May and could provide the firepower needed to get Arsenal over the line in Europe too.

Eli Junior Kroupi scored home and away for Bournemouth against Arsenal last season - could he be the missing piece in Arteta's puzzle?

3. Timber's limbering up

The importance of Timber can’t be overstated. In the Budapest defeat, the Dutchman was only half-fit, and came on for an out-of-place Mosquera only after the Spaniard had given away a penalty for a lunge on PSG's Khvicha Kvaratskhelia.

Timber is defensively solid, rarely bypassed by opposition players and commits forward with overlaps, too, in the final third. When fully firing, he is arguably the best right back in the league, and was voted as such in the PFA Team of the Year last season.

The 25-year-old trained on Tuesday morning and is in the squad for Wednesday’s fixture against Napoli.

Timber’s return has been a long, arduous journey from a groin injury which had affected him since March. It ruled him out of the Netherlands’ World Cup squad before returning to light training sessions at the start of Arsenal’s pre-season in July.

If the Gunners can have Timber fully fit for the latter stages of the competition, that is a huge plus.

Sports.title: Michael Carrick admits Man United's derby disadvantage is 'not ideal' with City handed two extra days to prepare - as he outlines Champions League ambitions with Luke Shaw a doubt for opener
Sports.content:
Michael Carrick admits that having two days less than Manchester City to prepare for Sunday’s Old Trafford derby isn’t ‘ideal’ for Manchester United.

While City opened their Champions League campaign with a win in Porto on Tuesday night, United face Sabah of Azerbaijan at Old Trafford in a one-off Thursday slot.

It has given Enzo Maresca more time to work with his squad before the 199th Manchester derby this weekend, and Carrick has no choice but to accept the situation.

‘I'm not concerned,’ said the United head coach. ‘Listen, I wouldn't say it's ideal in some ways, but it's not something that we've given too much thought about.

‘We're not in control of that. We've got to deal with the cards that we're dealt and that's what it is, so we'll make the most of it.’

Carrick is waiting to make a decision over Luke Shaw’s availability for the next two games after the veteran defender missed training at Carrington on Wednesday.

While City opened their Champions League campaign with a win in Porto on Tuesday night, United face Sabah of Azerbaijan at Old Trafford in a one-off Thursday slot

Carrick is waiting to make a decision over Luke Shaw’s availability for the next two games after the veteran defender missed training at Carrington on Wednesday

The club said it was a designated day off, but Carrick admitted it was a decision taken after Shaw played in United’s 2-2 draw at Everton on Sunday.

His absence raised concerns that United’s decision not to sign left-back cover for the 31-year-old England defender before the transfer window closed last week could backfire on them.

‘We just gave Luke an extra recovery day,’ added Carrick. ‘We'll see by tomorrow how he is, but it's not an ongoing thing or a plan or anything like that. It was just off the back of the game the other day.

‘So, as normal, each individual has different little things that we manage, and Luke was one of them today.’

United decided against signing cover for Shaw in the transfer window despite showing interest in Newcastle’s Lewis Hall and rejecting an opportunity to sign Rayan Ait-Nouri on loan from Manchester City on deadline day.

The 31-year-old veteran defender started every Premier League game for United last season, but it was widely accepted that he could not go another season without injury. Shaw was replaced by Noussair Mazraoui in added time during Sunday’s 2-2 draw at Everton after setting up a goal for Benjamin Sesko, but it was assumed the change was tactical.

United are relying on a number of back-up options if Shaw is unavailable, with Patrick Dorgu able to play at left back after being used in a more advanced role under Carrick.

Both right-backs, Mazraoui and Diogo Dalot, are capable of playing on the opposite flank, and academy product Harry Amass has stayed at the club when it was anticipated he would leave. New £70million midfield Carlos Baleba – currently out until October – could also be used as an auxiliary left-back.

United’s clash with Sabah marks their first appearance in the Champions League for 1,003 days stretching back to December 2023.

Carrick, who played when United last lifted the trophy in Moscow in 2008, insists the club are back where they belong but must be humble considering their recent history in Europe.

Carrick, who played when United last lifted the trophy in Moscow in 2008, insists the club are back where they belong but must be humble considering their recent history in Europe

‘It's a magical competition,’ he said. ‘It's where we all want to be. When you're out of it, you realise how special it is, and when you're in it you want to make the most of it.

‘I think we've all seen some special nights and felt some special things in this competition over the years. It's the best competition to challenge yourself and to push against the best. We're delighted to be here, but we're not here to just enjoy the occasion. We're here to do the business and go as far as we possibly can.

‘Winning the Champions League is the best feeling I've been lucky enough to have as a footballer. For me, it was the ultimate and it would be nice to feel that again some day.

‘It's not something that you can take for granted, what it takes to be there and what it takes to stay there. We've missed out on it for a number of years, and now we're back so I think it means a lot.

‘We've done an awful lot of good work to be here in a short space of time. We want the expectation, that's a privileged position to be in. But I think we've got to be humble enough and realistic enough to know where we're coming from and where we want to get to.’

On facing Sabah, a club that didn’t even exist until 2017, Carrick said: ‘They're a very well-coached team. They've obviously won a lot of football matches over the last 12 months, and so they're playing with a lot of confidence. We’re fully aware of what we're up against and the challenge that we face.’

Sports.title: Newcastle Confidential: Revealed - the key detail in Lewis Hall's new deal, Toon line up contract extensions for long-serving duo, Will Osula injury update, how close NUFC got to signing £85m star and club cash in with two new sponsors
Sports.content:
Newcastle Confidential: Revealed - the key detail in Lewis Hall's new deal, Toon line up contract extensions for long-serving duo, Will Osula injury update, how close NUFC got to signing £85m star and club cash in with two new sponsors

Lewis Hall’s new contract does NOT include a release clause, Confidential can reveal – and that could be bad news for Manchester United.

Hall, 22, was Man United’s top target at left back this summer but he was a player Newcastle had no intention of selling. Omar Berrada, chief executive at Old Trafford, was told by opposite number David Hopkinson that Hall would be going nowhere, and the Red Devils did not attempt to test that resolve thereafter.

Contract talks accelerated last week and an agreement has now been reached, with improved terms and a two-year extension. Lawyers have this week been going over the finer details of the five-year deal – as is the way with all modern contracts – and an announcement is due.

Crucially, there is no release clause in the package, amid suggestion from Manchester that the club will return for Hall next summer.

Their interest is likely to be revisited, but the new contract protects the player’s value and rewards him for his development since joining Newcastle from Chelsea for £35million in 2023, making 102 appearances and scoring three goals.

Hall is set to be included in Thomas Tuchel’s first England squad of the season when he names his players for four Nations League matches next Friday.

Lewis Hall’s new contract does NOT include a release clause, Confidential can reveal - and that could be bad news for Manchester United

The 22-year-old's form for Newcastle has earned him four caps for England, and he is set to be named in Thomas Tuchel's Three Lions squad next week

New deals lined up for Murphy and Willock

Sticking with contracts, talks over extensions for Jacob Murphy and Joe Willock will take place after they stayed at the club beyond the transfer window.

The pair are now in the final year of their current deals but club chiefs will look at extending those terms by 12 months.

Newcastle turned down a £15m offer from Nottingham Forest for Murphy, while Besiktas explored a £17m move for Willock.

New boss Matthias Jaissle sees the value in both players and communicated his wish for them to stay put.

Joe Willock and Jacob Murphy are two of the longest-serving players in Newcastle's squad, having joined in 2021 and 2017 respectively

Osula making good progress

William Osula is out of his protective boot and is now fully mobile as he targets a return to action, which could even be this side of the international break.

Reports in Denmark last week suggested his foot injury – first revealed by Confidential two weeks ago – was far more serious than anticipated and claimed the striker was set for an extended spell on the sidelines. We can allay those fears by revealing there has been no fracture and there is no need for surgery.

Indeed, Osula is now able to work on rebuilding his fitness at the training ground and staff are pushing to have him involved before next weekend’s visit of Hull City, the final fixture ahead of the three-week break. The more likely target, say sources, is the first game after the international matches at Coventry City on October 12.

However, news that the 23-year-old has not suffered a serious injury will be welcomed by supporters and head coach Matthias Jaissle, who has only had the Dane available to him for 56 minutes of this campaign so far.

Meanwhile, staff were today assessing the severity of the hamstring injury that forced off Amar Dedic at Millwall on Tuesday night. The early indications are that the problem is not serious.

Newcastle staff staff are pushing to have Will Osula involved before next weekend’s visit of newly promoted upstarts Hull City, the final fixture ahead of the three-week break

New man's central demand

Matias Fernandez-Pardo has told Newcastle he wants to start matches as a No 9 – and that is where they intend to play him.

The 21-year-old finished the campaign as a centre forward at Lille, but up until March, he had spent most of his time on the left wing. The season before, he started only once as a striker in Ligue 1.

However, that is the position Fernandez-Pardo spoke about during talks to sign him last month. Now he is in the building, the plan to use him there remains unaltered.

Interestingly, Newcastle’s data analysts returned only two players with the same profile as Anthony Gordon, in terms of their output in both the left wing and central striker roles. One was Fernandez-Pardo, the other was Said El Mala of Cologne. El Mala, 20, did not move this summer, but he remains on Newcastle’s watchlist.

Meanwhile, Pardo’s wish to play as a No 9 will see him compete with Osula for the starting jersey, with Yoane Wissa likely to be used more as a No 10.

Matias Fernandez-Pardo has made clear to the club that he wants to play as a No9

One that got away?

Here is a belated one on transfers – three years later! – but Newcastle spoke with Ayyoub Bouaddi when he was 15 years old.

I only heard this in recent days and thought it was worth sharing after seeing the 18-year-old Moroccan make such an impressive start at Manchester City, whom he joined for £85.6m from Lille last month.

The midfielder and his family, I’m told, had conversations with club staff with a view to building a relationship.

However, they were not the only club to do so, and Bouaddi had his pick of several major European sides this summer after a stellar World Cup.

Newcastle made contact with Man City's new midfield gem Ayyoub Bouaddi three years ago, when he was in Lille's academy

Show me the money!

Finally, Newcastle will confirm a new multi-million-pound partnership with Coca-Cola this week.

The global drinks brand will replace Sela as sponsor of the St James’ STACK fan zone.

Newcastle have also signed a new multi-year deal to extend their partnership with betting and entertainment brand, BetMGM.

Negotiated by chief executive Hopkinson, the deals represent another step in the club’s drive to increase commercial revenues. More partnership announcements are expected in the coming months.

Sports.title: Rory McIlroy opens up on 'bad habits' and vows to change before Donald Trump visit
Sports.content:
Rory McIlroy opens up on 'bad habits' and vows to change before Donald Trump visit

Rory McIlroy has been brutally honest about the state of his game at the moment and pledged to make some big chances before his Irish Open defence

View 3 Images Rory McIlroy is getting ready for his Irish Open title defence (Image: Richard Heathcote, Getty Images)

Rory McIlroy has made it clear there are many "bad habits" he must iron out before his Irish Open defence. Since he retained the Masters, McIlroy has admitted there are inconsistencies in his game, particularly with his swing.

‌



This weekend, he has the opportunity to correct all of those and show his best form at his home tournament, which will be attended by US president Donald Trump.

‌



Last year, McIlroy won the competition in stunning fashion. He holed a 25-foot putt for an eagle in the 72nd hole to force a play-off with Swedish ace Joakim Lagergren, before eventually sealing the victory in the third hole.

‌



JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! All the best sports news and much more on our dedicated Facebook page

McIlroy has not won a tournament since retaining the Masters this year, with his best display coming in last month's BMW Championship, where he placed third.

Discussing the recent struggles he has experienced with his swing, the Northern Irishman said: "I played Memphis (FedEx St Jude Championship) and played very poorly, and was looking at my swing on video and just didn't like where it was. I submitted to making a few changes - not changes that are unfamiliar to me, changes that I have had to do before.

‌



"Everyone has their tendencies and bad habits in the golf swing and I just got into a bad habit in mine. It is still something I am working through and conscious of, but I do think if I can really dig into it in the next few months, I feel like I will start the 2027 year where I want it to be.

View 3 Images McIlroy was brutally honest about his performance after his disappointment in Memphis (Image: Icon Sportswire, Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)

"I think everyone's golf course is a work-in-progress - mine is no different. There is always things that you want to try to improve upon."

‌



McIlroy finished 66th in Memphis after carding eight over par, a massive 25 strokes adrift of eventual champion Scottie Scheffler. Following the tournament, he confessed to feeling "lost" with his swing, sparking worry amongst supporters of the game.

At the time, he said: "Obviously didn't come in here with a ton of reps, almost felt like the more the week went on, the more I felt lost with my golf swing a little bit.

View 3 Images McIlroy opened up about the improvements he has made to his swing (Image: Richard Heathcote, Getty Images)

Article continues below

"I figured it out a little bit the last few holes today, I think. Yeah, swing wasn't in sync and obviously didn't do a ton of practice coming in here.

"I guess nice to shake the rust off a little bit, but I'm going to have to work pretty hard between now and next Thursday to feel like I have any sort of golf game to compete next week."

Sports.title: Premier League panel's Liverpool verdict is laughable and makes mockery of VAR
Sports.content:
Premier League panel's Liverpool verdict is laughable and makes mockery of VAR

A Premier League panel has ruled that Nottingham Forest's penalty against Liverpool last month shouldn't have been awarded - but nor should it have been overturned

View 2 Images Liverpool were furious with Samuel Barrott's decision (Image: Dan Mullan/Getty Images)

Making a mockery of VAR is not that difficult these days. Even in these so-called modern times which continue to embrace ancient but now traditional mistakes.

‌



But this hasn't stopped the Premier League panel from rubbing the nose of a VAR system it continues to tolerate right in the dirt. The latest ruling has decreed Nottingham Forest should not have been awarded a penalty at Liverpool following Alisson's challenge on Neco Williams.

‌



Yet the League's 'Key Match Incidents' (KMI) panel insisted the decision did not reach the threshold for a VAR intervention. So, Michael Oliver was correct not to send referee Sam Barrott to the pitch-side monitor.

‌



The decision helped Forest go 2-1 ahead before a late equaliser saw Liverpool salvage a point. The KMI Panel voted that Barrott should not have given the penalty, but supported the VAR outcome.

‌



It said: "The contact from Alisson was inevitable as a consequence of his momentum in attempting to save the ball. The contact made was not reckless and below the threshold for a penalty.

"However, the non intervention by the VAR was unanimously supported, on the basis that it was not a clear and obvious error."

Confused yet? Well, here might be a simple explanation to the umpteenth incident in top-flight football to leave a farcical and lasting stain on its current reputation.

‌



The verdict is laughable, because it is essentially admitting not one mistake has been made but two - yet those making them continue to be right. Go figure.

Barrott got it wrong in awarding a penalty in the first place. Then Oliver compounded the mistake by making one of his own, having decided not to send Barrott to the monitor to correct his original blunder.

Should the Premier League scrap VAR? Have your say in the comments section.

‌



View 2 Images Alisson was deemed to have fouled Neco Williams (Image: Simon Stacpoole/Offside/Offside via Getty Images)

Which begs the question - if VAR cannot be used to review or correct potential mistakes, what is the point of it in the first place? The simple answer is, there isn't one.

The introduction of the 'clear and obvious' threshold, which appears ironic in itself, has become the biggest cancer of the VAR era. VAR is supposed to exist to enable officials to make correct decisions.

‌



But according to all of the above, cannot be used when referees make mistakes which are deemed to be too minor. Like costing Liverpool three points at Anfield, right?

The incident involving Alisson and Williams is the kind of scenario VAR was invented for to resolve. Instead, it has made itself, those officials involved, and the English game, look laughable.

Sports.title: Xabi Alonso brutally confirms Chelsea star is not in his plans with exit still possible
Sports.content:
Xabi Alonso brutally confirms Chelsea star is not in his plans with exit still possible

Chelsea have recalled teenager Kendry Paez from his loan spell but Xabi Alonso admits the winger is not part of his plans as they continue to eye a possible exit solution

View 2 Images Kendry Paez has still never made an appearance for Chelsea

Chelsea boss Xabi Alonso admits he's ready to snub Kendry Paez until the January transfer window opens with the Ecuadorian seemingly not in his plans.

‌



Paez is back at Stamford Bridge after his loan spell at River Plate was cut short last month. The club did attempt to get him off their books before transfer deadline day, but missed out on finding him a new suitor.

‌



Paez has not played for Chelsea since completing a move from Independiente del Valle for £17.3million last summer. He was signed as a 16-year-old but ultimately never moved to England until he was 18, as per the agreement between the two sides.

‌



Despite now being back at the club's Cobham training base Alonso insists he's not being introduced into the first-team environment, with the club's focus instead on finding a way to improve his standards, reports the Athletic.

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

‌



When asked on Tuesday if he is considering using Paez before January, Alonso replied: “No, no. He is not part of the plans. At the moment, he is not part of the first team squad.”

The teenager was previously been sent on loan to Strasbourg, Chelsea's sister club, for the first half of last season. The closure of the window means that no English side can no sign Paez but options around the world remain. Mexico, Brazil and Greece are just some of the leagues that could take the player from Chelsea should they push to get the Ecuadorian off their books.

Alonso already has a host of options available to him, which means Paez was always going to find it difficult to get minutes in west London.

‌



View 2 Images The winger had his loan spell at River Plate cut short

The Spaniard, who lost for the first time on Sunday as Chelsea were beaten at Arsenal, has quickly implemented his 3-4-3 formation, which placed unique demands on the wide players in the team. At the weekend Jorrel Hato and Pedro Neto were used as wing-backs with Morgan Rogers and Cole Palmer supporting the centre forward.

Later in the game Alonso called on Estevao whilst among the unused subs were Jamie Gittens and summer signing Geovany Quenda, who could also play on the wings, underlining the depth available for the Blues.

Sports.title: 'Brutal, searing and punishing heat' - Babb on playing for Ireland at USA '94
Sports.content:
While none of the home nations qualified for the 1994 World Cup, the Republic of Ireland did.

It was a second successive appearance at the tournament for the Boys in Green, who were again led by 1966 World Cup winner Jack Charlton.

At Italia '90, the weather had been hot - but at USA '94, it was a different kettle of fish altogether.

The iconic image of Charlton launching an open bottle of water in the direction of Andy Townsend and Tommy Coyne always provides a reminder of that.

Image: Jack Charlton led the Republic of Ireland at Italia '90 and USA '94

He clashed with FIFA over their policy that bottles could not be thrown to the players on the pitch, so took to throwing the contents instead before FIFA later relented and allowed water bags to be thrown.

"They trust me to do what is right for them and I will continue to do it," Charlton said. "We have been right in pursuing this matter and FIFA's change of heart proves that."

Charlton was rarely seen without his white baseball cap that summer. Steve Staunton famously even wore one during the national anthem before the second group game against Mexico.

One of the players in the Ireland squad that summer was Phil Babb. The defender, then 23, had just completed his second full Premier League season at Coventry.

He made his international debut in a 0-0 friendly draw with Russia in March 1994, then played in the next four friendlies leading up to the tournament.

Image: Phil Babb played in all four of the Republic of Ireland's games at the 1994 World Cup

Nothing was set in stone, but he knew he would at least have a decent chance of being included in Charlton's 22-man squad, so started to physically prepare himself.

"A coach at Coventry asked me if I wanted to do anything specific - we ended up doing 12-minute sessions in a sauna!" Babb recalls, with a smile.

"We were doing burpees, press-ups, just trying to acclimatise to that intense heat. We did about six sessions - but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone now!

"I was a fit lad and had played pretty much all the Premier League games Coventry had played that season. I adapted to the heat pretty well, but I know some of the older lads really struggled."

Babb started alongside Paul McGrath in the heart of defence for Ireland's tournament opener at Giants Stadium in New Jersey.

Image: Ray Houghton's stunning strike earned a shock 1-0 win over Italy

That Saturday, they shocked an Italy side that featured Paolo Maldini, Franco Baresi and Roberto Baggio. John Aldridge's stunner sealed a memorable 1-0 win.

It was an achievement made all the more impressive by the fact the Azzurri went on to finish as runners-up - but also given the fact it was played in temperatures exceeding 30C.

"When we walked out onto the field, about two hours before kick-off, you could tell it was going to be absolutely roasting," he recalls.

"You could tell that straight away and we didn't stay out long. I just checked the grass to see which studs I wanted, then I went straight back in. I know some of the lads were walking around and taking the atmosphere in, but I thought: 'This is too hot'.

"I didn't go out for a warm-up with the rest of the lads, either. I stayed in the changing room. It was built for NFL, so they had a 40m sprint track. I warmed up in there and waited until we went out. It was brutal, it was searing, it was punishing.

"It affected everyone's game. You were saturated after just 10 minutes walking onto a pitch, so you had to conserve energy at the right times.

"Recovery was very basic and there was very little ball work because of the demands of the actual games and the fluids you lose. When you're that dehydrated, it's quite difficult. You want a drink, but you don't feel hungry and that is a key part of the recuperation."

Image: Babb, whose Ireland were knocked out by Dennis Bergkamp's Netherlands, joined Liverpool later that summer

Thirty-two years on from that tournament, football has evolved exponentially.

Sports science has taken on a key role in the game and, this summer, is likely to play into the way teams approach games tactically due to the heat. A slower tempo is expected in many.

Charlton was not prepared to facilitate the same in 1994, though.

"We only played one way, so if you tried to go off-piste, Jack would certainly let you know!" adds Babb.

"We had one style of play, with a lone striker. If it wasn't Tommy Coyne, it might have been Niall Quinn up there and we'd be putting long balls up to him, with either willing runners out wide or the midfield bombing on.

"That was the Irish way back then. Tommy ran tirelessly, to the point where he actually collapsed with heat exhaustion on the plane home.

"I think Jack's sports science was a barrel of Guinness in his room and he'd call the lads in and have a pint! I'm sure there's a high calorific content in that, so maybe he was ahead of his time!"
