World.title: Gambia: Gambian President Declares Power Emergency Amid Protests
World.content:
President Adama Barrow has declared the country's prolonged electricity crisis a national emergency and promised to increase power generation as protests over rolling blackouts intensify ahead of the December presidential election.

Barrow urged citizens to remain calm over prolonged power cuts. He said that the country is not alone in facing an electricity crisis that has affected several parts of West Africa.

Demonstrators in Banjul and surrounding areas burned tyres, erected roadblocks and called for Barrow to resign after some communities experienced outages lasting up to 48 hours during the hot season.

Police used tear gas to disperse protesters gathering near Barrow's residence and the headquarters of the National Water and Electricity Corporation.

Barrow has promised a 24-megawatt generation machine by the end of October. He announced plans for a further 50-megawatt solar power plant. The electricity provider has blamed soaring temperatures, climate change and wider geopolitical disruptions for the crisis.

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - September 9, 2026
World.content:
press review

Kenya Launches Crackdown on Foreign Informal Traders

Kenyan officials have started to crack down on foreign nationals running small businesses in the informal economy. This comes after President William Ruto backed measures reserving activities such as hawking and petty retail primarily for Kenyan citizens. Ruto said that foreign investors should focus on bringing capital, creating jobs and supporting local production rather than competing with citizens in businesses requiring little capital. Kenyans have reacted with mixed feelings to the move, with some welcoming it as a way of protecting jobs amid high unemployment. Others fear it could fuel xenophobia and discourage foreign investment. Political economist Sheila Owigo Olang questioned whether removing foreign traders would create more opportunities for Kenyans, describing the policy as potentially populist ahead of elections. The government has insisted that foreign nationals who comply with immigration, work permit and licensing requirements remain legally protected. Questions remain over who will ultimately be affected and how the policy will be enforced.

Gambia Declares Power Crisis a National Emergency

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Gambian President Adama Barrow has declared the country's prolonged electricity crisis a national emergency and promised to increase power generation as protests over rolling blackouts intensify ahead of the December presidential election. Demonstrators in Banjul and surrounding areas burned tyres, erected roadblocks and called for Barrow to resign after some communities experienced outages lasting up to 48 hours during the hot season. Police used tear gas to disperse protesters gathering near Barrow's residence and the headquarters of the National Water and Electricity Corporation. Barrow has promised a 24-megawatt generation machine by the end of October. He announced plans for a further 50-megawatt solar power plant. The electricity provider has blamed soaring temperatures, climate change and wider geopolitical disruptions for the crisis.

Funding Cuts Push Sudan's Health System to the Brink

Sudan's already fragile health system is nearing collapse as international funding cuts force healthcare facilities to close amid the country's devastating civil war, said Médecins Sans Frontières. More than 33 million people now require medical assistance following the conflict between the Sudanese army and the Rapid Support Forces. The loss of USAID funding and reductions in European aid have left many humanitarian organisations unable to sustain their operations. MSF reported a sharp increase in patient admissions at facilities it supports and said the closure of dozens of healthcare centres is placing enormous pressure on the hospitals that remain open. In some displacement camps, maternity and surgical services have shut down, forcing patients to travel long distances for treatment. The crisis is compounded by attacks on healthcare facilities, widespread hunger and continuing violence, prompting MSF to urge world leaders gathering at the UN General Assembly to increase support.

WFP Says Food Aid Key to Fighting DR Congo Ebola Outbreak

The World Food Programme has warned that food assistance must form a central part of the response to the rapidly spreading Ebola outbreak in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, where conflict, displacement and severe hunger are making it harder to contain the disease. The outbreak, declared in May and caused by the rare Bundibugyo species, has become the fastest on record, with more than 5,500 cases and 2,642 deaths reported in its first 100 days. WFP said that people struggling to feed their families cannot easily comply with the health measures needed to prevent transmission, particularly in remote areas far from treatment centres. More than 500,000 people in the affected Ituri province are facing severe food insecurity, while poor infrastructure and ongoing conflict complicate efforts to deliver assistance. The WFP is calling for more international funding to expand both food assistance and Ebola treatment services, noting that adequate nutrition in addition to medical treatment can greatly increase a patient's chances of survival.

Nurses' Strike Deepens Pressure on Kenya's Health System

Kenya's prolonged nurses' strike is placing increasing pressure on the country's public health system, with essential services disrupted as nurses demand the implementation of long-standing labour agreements. Hundreds of nurses have demonstrated in Nairobi, calling on the national and county governments to address salary arrears, allowances, staffing shortages, promotions and career progression. At the heart of the dispute is the 2017 Collective Bargaining Agreement, which the Kenya National Union of Nurses and Midwives says remains largely unimplemented despite provisions for nursing service allowances and improved working conditions. The union has said negotiations alone are no longer sufficient and insists that signed agreements must be honoured before members return to work. The government and county authorities continue engaging with the union, including on the permanent employment of UHC workers. Nurses argue that years of unfulfilled promises and poor working conditions have damaged morale and undermined their ability to provide safe and effective patient care.

Close 

Zimbabwean Vendors Vow to Defy Harare Street Clearance Order



Zimbabwean authorities have intensified efforts to remove illegal vendors from Harare's Central Business District. They declared that uncontrolled street trading is no longer acceptable and ordered traders to use designated markets and vending bays. Local Government Minister Daniel Garwe said illegal vending was contributing to congestion, blocked pavements, litter, poor sanitation and public health risks, including the potential spread of water-borne diseases such as cholera. The government insists that the crackdown is not a war against informal traders. It argued that significant investment has already been made in designated vending infrastructure that remains underused. The move has, however, been met with strong resistance from vendors, who say informal trading is their only means of survival in an economy with limited formal employment opportunities. The order is a seven-day ultimatum to vacate the streets, and vendors have vowed to resist. Traders' representatives have urged the government to implement reforms guided by the National Informal Economy Formalization Strategy of Zimbabwe, rather than just chasing traders off the streets.

World.title: South Africa: Fake Toys Raise Safety and Job Concerns - South African News Briefs - September 9, 2026
World.content:
press review

Fake Toys Raise Safety and Job Concerns

Concerns are mounting over counterfeit toys flooding the South African market, reports EWN. Fake products are now estimated to account for 25% of sales. Farrel Frank, managing director of the South African Toys and Games Association, warned that counterfeit toys can pose serious health and safety risks and cost jobs. He said the growth of online sales platforms has contributed to the problem. Some major platforms are working with the industry to remove suspicious listings. Consumers are also being urged to remain vigilant after a recent complaint involving a toy with a strong chemical smell that allegedly caused burning and tingling when it touched a consumer’s face.

More Witnesses to Testify in Anele Tembe Inquest

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

More witnesses are set to testify in the inquest into the death of Anele Tembe, who fell from the 10th floor of a Cape Town hotel in April 2021, reports SABC News. Lawyers representing Tembe's family questioned witnesses about whether her fiancé, the late rapper Kiernan "AKA" Forbes, had asked for her family to be informed of her death. Two police officers told the court they had no knowledge of whether the family had been contacted. One officer said Forbes did not ask police to contact them. The inquest has also heard from a nearby resident who reported hearing an argument between a man and a woman shortly before Tembe’s death.

Tshuma Extradition Hinges on Plea Deal

Extradition proceedings against UK fugitive Ndodana Tshuma could depend on whether the Johannesburg Magistrates Court accepts a plea agreement between him and the State, reports EWN. Tshuma, who is accused of murdering his wife and two young daughters in the UK before fleeing to South Africa, pleaded guilty to firearm and immigration-related charges following his arrest in Johannesburg. Details of the proposed plea deal and sentence have not been disclosed. The magistrate must still decide whether the agreement is just and appropriate. A custodial sentence could further complicate his extradition to the UK, where he is expected to face the murder allegations.

World.title: Nigeria: Nigerian Army Redeploys Top Generals, Appoints New Person to Lead Boko Haram War
World.content:
A Wednesday statement by army spokesperson Appolonia Anele said the deployments were approved by the Chief of Army Staff, Waidi Shaibu, a lieutenant general.

The leadership of the Nigerian Army has redeployed several top generals, including the person leading the war against Boko Haram terrorists in the North-east

A Wednesday statement by army spokesperson Appolonia Anele said the deployments were approved by the Chief of Army Staff, Waidi Shaibu, a lieutenant general.

A major-general, IA Ajose, will now head Operation HADIN KAI (OPHK), the army's main operation against Boko Haram and other terror groups in the North-east. Mr Ajose replaces another major general, AE Abubakar, who was redeployed to the Nigerian Army Heritage and Future Centre (NAHFC) as Dean, Faculty of Operational Research.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Read the full statement by the army below.

NIGERIAN ARMY REPOSITIONS SENIOR LEADERSHIP TO STRENGTHEN OPERATIONAL EFFECTIVENESS, NATIONAL SECURITY

The Chief of Army Staff (COAS), Lieutenant General Waidi Shaibu, has approved the strategic redeployment of senior officers to key command, operational and staff appointments across the Nigerian Army (NA), as part of ongoing efforts to enhance operational effectiveness, strengthen leadership and align the Service's command structure with Nigeria's evolving security environment. The exercise prioritises critical operational theatres and strategic appointments to ensure the right leadership, experience and expertise are positioned to deliver decisive effects.

In the new postings, Major General IA Ajose moves from Army Headquarters (AHQ), Department of Army Operations, to Theatre Command Joint Task Force (JTF) North East, Operation HADIN KAI (OPHK), as Theatre Commander, while Major General AE Abubakar has been redeployed from OPHK, to the Nigerian Army Heritage and Future Centre (NAHFC) as Dean, Faculty of Operational Research. Major General AM Alechenu moves from Defence Headquarters (DHQ) Garrison to the Nigerian Army Heritage and Future Centre, while Major General RT Utsaha moves from AHQ Department of Army Standards and Evaluation to DHQ Garrison as Commander.

Similarly, Major General AM Umar moves from AHQ Department of Civil-Military Affairs (DCMA) to Army War College Nigeria (AWCN) as Commandant, while Major General UM Alkali moves from AWCN to AHQ DCMA. Major General GS Muhammed moves from the Office of the National Security Adviser (ONSA) to the Nigerian Army Finance Corporation (NAFIC) as Director General, while Major General JE Osifo moves from NAFIC to the Military Pension Board (MPB) as Chairman and Major General IE Ekpenyong has been redeployed to DHQ Department of Defence Logistics as Director Engineering Services.

At the operational level, Brigadier General AA Bello moves from 6 Division Garrison/Sector 3 JTF South-South, Operation DELTA SAFE, to DHQ Department of Defence Operations. Brigadier General MS Adamu has been redeployed from Nigerian Army Women Command to the newly established 8 Brigade as Commander, while Brigadier General MS Sule moves from Special Task Force Operation ENDURING PEACE to 27 Task Force Brigade as Commander.

Close 

Similarly, Brigadier General I Sule, has been redeployed from the Directorate of Recruitment Management to 6 Division Garrison as Commander while Brigadier General E Azenda, moves from Land Forces Simulation Centre to 2 Division Garrison as Commander and Brigadier General AS Bugaje, moves from 2 Division Garrison to the Land Forces Simulation Centre as Director Administration.

The COAS has charged the newly appointed officers to justify the confidence reposed in them through exemplary leadership, operational innovation, professionalism and unwavering commitment to duty and relentless focused on the constitutional mandate of defending Nigeria's sovereignty, protecting its territorial integrity and supporting civil authority in maintaining peace and security.

The NA remains resolute in sustaining a dynamic leadership and force-employment framework that enhances operational outcomes, strengthens joint and inter-agency coordination and improves the capacity of the Service to respond decisively to contemporary and emerging threats in furtherance of Nigeria's national security objectives.

APPOLONIA ANELE

Colonel

Acting Director Army Public Relations

World.title: Mali: Malian Women Resist Renewed Support for Female Genital Mutilation
World.content:
analysis

An online campaign defending cutting, which is still legal in Mali, recasts the practice as a means of protecting girls.

A coordinated social media campaign defending female genital mutilation (FGM) emerged in Mali this August, reigniting societal debates not just about women's bodily integrity, but also about tradition and national sovereignty.

Days after a national non-governmental organisation displayed posters in Bamako denouncing the practice, anonymous online accounts began posting images that reversed the 'no more' campaign's message. Men of various backgrounds are portrayed smiling or with thumbs up, surrounded by the national colours and the message: 'In Mali, yes to excision! Let's protect girls and build their future.'



The slogan turns the protection argument on its head in a country where cutting out parts of young girls' genitals, often without anaesthesia and at the risk of deadly complications, remains commonplace. A 2023 study estimated that FGM caused roughly 44 000 excess deaths a year across 15 African countries, including Mali. This makes it a leading cause of death for girls and young women where it is practised.

For those who survive, the consequences are dire and both immediate and long-term. They include severe pain and bleeding, infection and emotional shock at the time of cutting. Throughout life, they manifest through chronic pain, urinary and menstrual complications, a greater risk of difficult childbirth, and lasting psychological trauma.

Local women's rights advocates have opposed the practice for decades. Soon after Mali's 1960 independence, midwife and lawmaker Aoua Kéita and fellow activists pushed for reforms to advance women's rights in the 1962 Marriage Code. They achieved a ban on forced marriage and a minimum age for matrimony. But they failed to secure a prohibition on excision and polygamy.

Powerful conservatives went on to defeat draft laws in 2009 on advancing women's rights in the household, and in 2019 on violence against women. Mali's 2024 Penal Code condemns violence generally, but stops short of naming FGM.

This legal gap has been costly for Malian women and girls. Mali's latest Demographic and Health Survey reveals that 89% of those aged 15 to 49 have been cut - one of the highest rates globally. Among girls aged 0 to 14 - the age range when cutting usually occurs - the prevalence is lower, at 70%, and down from 74% in 2018. This suggests the practice may be slowly receding.

But the decline is modest, and potentially reversible. Many in Mali, both women and men, still support FGM, believing it is a religious obligation or a tradition worth keeping. Both claims are disputed, but the lack of consensus threatens thousands of infant girls every year.

FGM supporters minimise its physical harms, presenting it as necessary to control women's sexuality - a long-standing feature of patriarchal control. Societal norms across much of Mali's southern and central regions have long glorified suffering as a badge of honour for women, essentially normalising women's pain. The stigma of bad morality that community expectations could attach to an uncut woman is presented as the greater harm she needs protection from.

'Yes' campaigners also try to portray opposition to FGM as a foreign agenda. This erases Mali's long history of home-grown opposition, from Kéita to today's human rights defenders. But it resonates with broader sovereignty narratives that recast women's rights as a foreign import and traditional gender norms as a societal strength.

But this logic replaces one domination with another. It allows men, families and communities to police women's bodies and maim girls too young to consent and call it resisting imperialism. It denies half the population sovereignty over their own bodies in the name of national sovereignty.

It is hard to determine who is behind the 'yes' campaign supporting FGM. Journalists and Malian feminist organisations have traced much of it to accounts sharing artificial intelligence-generated posters, apparently designed to manufacture the appearance of a mass movement. This makes it difficult to assess the campaign's true scope.

While most men whose portraits are used in the campaign have defended it, some have cited unauthorised use of their image or retracted their support under public pressure.

By mirroring the communication style of the 'no' advocacy, FGM supporters have sought to normalise their position, creating a false equivalence between 'yes' and 'no'. Once the two are placed on an equal footing, inaction can be presented as balance rather than a choice to condone violence. Apparent neutrality works in favour of the status quo.

But in the course of Mali's 'refoundation' - a process aimed at resetting societal norms and values, and the basis for political governance - women will not accept a more rigidly gendered social contract without a fight. The pro-excision campaign has met a strong response from women's rights advocates, health professionals and other public voices challenging the notion that defending FGM equals defending Malian values.

Women - and some men - have also been mobilised beyond national borders. In Côte d'Ivoire and Togo, the 'yes' campaign triggered its own swift backlash. Malian and West African diaspora have organised anti-FGM protests in Paris, Montreal and beyond, indicating that FGM can no longer count on silence.

On 26 August, Mali's National Human Rights Commission called on the authorities to criminalise FGM. Other countries where the practice is entrenched - including Burkina Faso, Senegal, Guinea, Niger, Egypt and Sudan - have passed such laws. It has not ended the practice, but it has made it riskier for perpetrators and handed women's rights groups a legal basis to challenge it.

Close 

But legislating may not be the end of the story. In 2024, traditional and religious leaders attempted to have The Gambia's Parliament repeal the 2015 Women's (Amendment) Act criminalising FGM. The case is still pending before the Supreme Court.

Beyond parliaments and courtrooms, significant shifts in community norms are needed to protect women's bodily integrity. Religious leaders should clarify that FGM is neither required nor consensually accepted in Islam. They should work with women's rights organisations, who have long been committed to ending the practice, and health professionals who can best explain its consequences.

International partners should support that effort without becoming its face, a move that risks feeding the campaign's own claim that reform is foreign-imposed.

Ornella Moderan, Regional Director for West Africa, the Sahel, the Lake Chad Basin and Central Africa, ISS

World.title: Billy Baldwin admits he refused to kiss co-star after weeks of tension on set

Billy Baldwin went into detail about the actress he refused to kiss on camera.

During a recent interview on the "Lisa Guerrero Unleashed" podcast, the 63-year-old actor shared he felt so much "tension" between himself and Sharon Stone on the set of "Silver," that he refused to kiss her.

"There was like a couple of, like a whole month, where she wouldn't say hello. She wouldn't say goodbye. She wouldn't say good morning. She wouldn't say good night," he said.

He described her being "off book" and performing for the camera when doing her close-up shots, but then sitting "on an apple box with her glasses on with her script open" during his close-ups, saying, "she wouldn't even look at me."

LISA KUDROW EXPOSES THE DARK SIDE OF 'FRIENDS' SET WITH TROUBLING WRITER ROOM CLAIMS

Baldwin explained that after dealing with Stone on set, he approached director Phillip Noyce and producer Robert Evans, telling them, "I can't do the last love scene."

At this point in the filming process, they had already filmed three love scenes out of four, but those were filmed at the beginning of the production "when everything was jiving."

Noyce and Evans told Baldwin he was hired for a role, "You got a love scene and you got to do this."

"I said, 'All right, listen. I can do the scene,'" Baldwin noted. "I said, 'But I just please please don't make me kiss her. Please don't make me kiss her.'

He then claimed that the iconic love scene between him and Stone in the film was a result of his request not to kiss her.

After all was said and done, Baldwin told the podcast host that he would "love to bury the hatchet" with Stone, adding that he "would love to see Sharon Stone and shake her hand and give her a hug."

During the interview, Baldwin also slammed Stone's previous claims that Evans pressured her to sleep with Baldwin while making the movie so that he would have a "better" performance.

"He wasn’t talking about Sharon not being able to act," he said. "He was saying, ‘I keep getting reports that there’s incredibly bad tension. We know what it’s all about. All this pent-up sexual energy tension. Just do it and get it over with.'"

She first made these claims in her 2021 memoir, "The Beauty of Living Twice." In the memoir she wrote that "they expected me to bring home another giant smash hit" and were trying to "blame me for their mistakes."

"If I could sleep with Billy then we'd have chemistry on screen, and if I would just have sex with him, then that would save the movie, and the real problem in the movie was me because I was so uptight, and so not like a real actress who could just f--- him and get things back on track," she wrote. "The real problem was I was such a tight a--."

World.title: Ted Cruz battles 'The View' on Clarence Thomas and affirmative action, as host says 'Welcome to being Black'
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, defended Supreme Court Justice Clarence Thomas' affirmative action stance on Wednesday as he faced questioning from the co-hosts of "The View" about his new book.

"Clarence Thomas, he stated that affirmative action diminishes achievements because it allowed people to believe he had not earned his place at Yale and I think we can all agree that affirmative action was put in place to provide opportunities to qualified Black students, like Thomas, because those institutions historically would not give them the opportunities to go," co-host Sunny Hostin said during the interview about Cruz's new book, "The Incomparable Clarence Thomas."

"So what I don’t understand how you handle in the book is, why is the lesson from his experience that we should eliminate the remedy rather than eliminate the racism that made the remedy necessary? I don’t understand that," Hostin asked Cruz.

Thomas sided with the 6-3 majority ruling in 2023 on affirmative action, saying the court's decision "sees the universities’ admissions policies for what they are: rudderless, race-based preferences designed to ensure a particular racial mix in their entering classes."

JUSTICE THOMAS RECALLS WHY HE WASN'T FRIENDS WITH ALITO IN LAW SCHOOL: 'CLARENCE, YOU WERE SCARY'

Hostin said, "I mean, I genuinely don't understand the framing in the book about that."

Cruz said that affirmative action "encompasses a lot of things" before describing Thomas' viewpoint.

"If you're talking about removing barriers, if you're talking about expanding access, then I'm for that, he's for that, everyone is for that. If you're talking about quotas and discriminating based on race, then Justice Thomas has been the clearest defender of the principle that the Constitution prohibits the government discriminating based on race," he began, before Hostin questioned why the justice felt his Yale degree was "diminished because people felt that it was a result of affirmative action."

'LOOK AT ME!' JUSTICE FIRES BACK AT CRITICS WHO DARE QUESTION HIS BLACKNESS

Cruz responded, "So there was a reason for that. When he came out of Yale Law School, he had done very well in law school. He applied. Not a single law firm would hire him. Every law firm he interviewed said, ‘No.'"

"Welcome to being Black," co-host Whoopi Goldberg interjected.

Goldberg pointed to Thomas being a constitutional scholar before asking Cruz, "How does he not remember that we weren't part of the Constitution? Right? We were not. So there's a reason people didn't start off, we weren't all equal."

TED CRUZ SHUTS DOWN TRUMP SUPREME COURT TALK WITH A FIERY 'NOT JUST NO, BUT HELL NO'

Cruz argued that Thomas talked about that at length, saying, "Look, the Civil War and Reconstruction, the 13th, 14th, and 15th Amendments. The 13th Amendment ended slavery. The 14th Amendment protected equal protection. And the 15th Amendment protected the right to vote, specifically for African Americans."

"So why are we still talking about it if it protects all of this? That's the thing I guess," Goldberg said before ending the interview as the show ran out of time.

Cruz's office did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

Earlier in the show, Goldberg admonished "The View" audience after they groaned upon announcing Cruz would be a guest later in the show.

"Look, this is a place where Barbara Walters made sure that anybody who wanted to come and have a good conversation could come," she said, shutting down the booing. "So we want people to come, and we want to engage them. We don’t agree with them always. We don’t jell with them always, but we are respectful, and I know you will be too."

World.title: Sophie Cunningham has a bikini boat day during the WNBA break, Sydney Sweeney's ad is a talker & replacing LSU
World.content:
'Nightcaps' is a daily column that catches you up on the biggest sports, news and culture stories you may have missed while pretending to do work at your desk. It runs Monday–Friday on OutKick.com.

To the WNBA, NBA, NHL, MLB and FIFA ... rest easy, your watch has now ended.

The KING is back. The NFL season is upon us. Is it a little weird to be kicking off the new year on a Wednesday? Sure. No argument there.

But will we care at 8:20 tonight when AJ Brown gives us our first anytime touchdown cash of the betting season? Nope.

We will not.

AJ BROWN SAYS THERE'S BEEN SILENCE BETWEEN HIM AND EX-TEAMMATE JALEN HURTS SINCE HIS MOVE TO NEW ENGLAND

Welcome back, NFL. Goodness, we've missed you.

And, of course, welcome to a Hump Day Nightcaps — the one where Sophie Cunningham enjoys a day on the boat before taking in some opening night football action from Seattle.

What else? I've got a 49ers wife saying goodbye to summer before her husband kicks things off in Australia, a rundown of the Rams' INSANE travel schedule this week, and if the SEC were to expel LSU from the conference, who would YOU pick as a replacement?

It'll never happen (right?), but it's still a thinker. And in this class, we like to challenge ourselves!

Grab you some grilled chicken for National Grilled Chicken Day — throw it out and fry some WINGS like a man — and then settle in for a Hump Day 'Cap!

Sophie Cunningham enjoys some R&R while Team USA plays in Berlin

Look, I love the NFL. It's No. 1 for me, followed by college football and MLB. So, I'll never complain about a Wednesday night kickoff.

That being said ...

It is odd that the schedule-makers decided this was the best matchup possible. Did they watch the Super Bowl earlier this year? It stunk. It was never, ever close. Why on earth did they think we'd want to follow it up with ... the exact same matchup?

The Vrabel stuff from the offseason was a juicy storyline in March, but that's faded away (for now). I guess you could argue that AJ Brown makes it more interesting. But other than that? It's pretty much the same teams, minus Ken Walker.

Oh well. It's a nitpick, I know. I'm just happy football is back.

I'm also happy that Sophie Cunningham is getting some nice rest while the WNBA takes a month off for the FIBA World Cup over in Germany.

She deserves it.

She leads off today's class:

Who's excited for some NFL betting?!

That's how you spend the finals day(s) of summer ... one last boat trip before the leaves start to fall and the WNBA playoffs kick into gear.

Sophie gets it. I know the girls are overseas right now playing in the world cup, but I'd rather be here, in the U-S-of-A, on a boat. Point to Sophie Cunningham!

PS: I had a reader bring this up a few days ago, and had to doublecheck it to be sure. Anyone here want to take a guess at when the FIBA championship game is?

This Sunday ... at 2 p.m.

The FIRST NFL Sunday of the year! Right at peak hours for RedZone. Amazing. They don't even stand a chance back here in the states.

OK, let's move it along because I have to fire up the Hard Rock app and see if I can get this NFL betting season started with a bang.

Or, you know, I guess I could try and use Novig for all my sports betting needs this season ...

Rams schedule, LSU replacement and NFL WAGs gear up for the season

Goodness gracious. I saw that ad making the rounds over on Elon's Twitter this morning, and thought it was AI. Seriously. I know Sydney Sweeney doesn't shy away from anything, but even I thought there was no way that was real.

It is real, and it's a TALKER.

"The campaign was about embracing a fun idea," Sweeney in a statement, according to Variety. "The concept is simple: cut through the noise and put the focus entirely on sports. The campaign brings that idea to life with confidence, humor and a playful edge."

Yep. The focus of that ad is certainly all on the sports! No argument here, Sydney.

OK, let's rapid-fire this Hump Day class into a big NFL night. First up? We've got Pats-Seahawks tonight, but did you know we have another game tomorrow?

Rams-49ers ... in Melbourne! It's on Netflix, which is dumb, but that's the world we now live in. It's also, technically, taking place on Friday since Australia is a billion hours ahead of us.

The Niners left the states for this game last week. The Rams? They left YESTERDAY:

"The Rams will spend more than 30 hours on an airplane, travel over 15,000 miles, cross 7 time zones, and play a football game, yet technically be back in Los Angeles less than 72 hours after leaving."

That's insane. Australia is 14 hours ahead of us, which means tomorrow night's game will actually be taking place on Friday at 10:35 a.m. in Melbourne.

And the Rams are going to have been there for a cup of coffee before strapping in and hitting the field.

No idea if it's gonna work, but I'm excited to see if it does!

Next? You know what's probably not gonna work? Kicking LSU out of the SEC. I just don't see it happening. I know the SEC has a big meeting this week about it, but come on. Let's be real for a second. That ain't happening.

If it DID, though, who would you want to replace the Tigers?

First of all ... "hobo on a ham sandwich" and "I've got rocks in my driveway that are smarter than that" are two absolute bangers from John Kennedy.

There is nobody better at their craft right now. He's the GOAT.

Secondly ... I think I'd go with: Miami, Va. Tech, FSU, or my wild card, Tulane. That's right.

Tulane!

Don't forget, Tulane was a founding member of the SEC and competed in the conference until 1966. The Green Wave have three SEC titles to their name. They're already in Louisiana, so you stay in the state.

They were also in the playoffs last year!

Not ridiculous, right?

... Right?!

OK, that's it for today. Good Hump Day, everyone. Welcome back, NFL.

And welcome back to 49ers LB Fred Warner's wife, Sydney! She's celebrating the return of football from a beach in Hawaii as the offseason officially comes to a close.

See you tomorrow.

World.title: Sharon Stone says she 'nearly died' after 'Basic Instinct' opened the door to Hollywood's dark side

Sharon Stone is opening up about how she survived Hollywood's dark side after starring in her hit movie "Basic Instinct."

The actress became an international star after she played Catherine Tramell, a seductive crime novelist and alleged serial killer, in the 1992 erotic thriller. However, Stone recently shared that portraying Tramell took a psychological toll on her and drew dangerous people into her orbit.

During an appearance on the "Mayim Bialik's Breakdown" podcast this week, Stone spoke about times when she's gotten too close to dark characters she's played and "scared the living s--- out of myself." Bialik asked her for an example, and she replied, "When I did ‘Basic Instinct,’ and I had to really look at darkness, and yet I was very still young and inexperienced."

'TEACHER'S PET' STAR MAMIE VAN DOREN SAYS SHE FELT 'USED' AS YOUNG ACTRESS NAVIGATING HOLLYWOOD'S DARK SIDE

She continued, "I didn't understand about holding the core, the core self, the golden self, and then wrapping the character around it with the power of the self driving it. But just bringing it all in there and looking at it all, I opened some dark doors, right?"

"And some of those dark doors really scared the living s--- out of me, because I saw some real, real darkness," Stone remembered. "And what happened then is that real dark people identified and came into my life thinking, 'Oh, you really are like me. You're like me.'"

"And so darkness came into my life. Dark people, dark things, dangerous things came into my life because they thought, 'You're like me.' And then people believed some of the dark things that were said about me because they thought, 'Oh, you couldn't do that if you weren't like that because you've mirrored me to me.'"

While speaking with Bialik and her co-host, Jonathan Cohen, Stone said the experience taught her to be more discerning about what and whom she allowed into her life.

"Really the one thing you got to remember is just because the devil's a very interesting person at the cocktail party doesn't mean you should invite that person, give them a seat. Don't give that person a seat," she said.

The Emmy Award winner explained how she learned to protect herself from people drawn to darkness, emphasizing the importance of maintaining her "core self."

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

"Don't ever give up the core," she said. "You can't be porous."

"You just can't be porous because if any of it gets in, all of a sudden the dark people, they want to be around you," Stone continued. "They want to come to you. They think, 'Oh, you're like me.' And when they find out that you're not like them, they get upset. They get very upset."

Stone recalled that at one point, she felt that the darkness almost consumed her. She credited her survival to the strength of her "core self" and anchoring herself in a higher spiritual frequency.

"When the darkness came, I nearly died," she said. "But the light saved me. The light is what saved me. And the universal consciousness of light that vibrated at my frequency is what saved me."

'BLIND SIDE' STAR QUINTON AARON SAYS HE 'SAW JESUS' WHILE IN A COMA AFTER NEAR-FATAL STROKE

"Fortunately, enough of me held to the light and that just the crack where it got in was dangerous," Stone added.

During her podcast appearance, Stone also revealed that she received a life-or-death spiritual message following her near-fatal stroke.

In September 2001, the "Casino" star suffered a massive, life-threatening stroke at the age of 43. Stone spent nine days in the hospital after a ruptured artery that caused a brain bleed, requiring emergency surgery to repair the vessel.

While speaking with Bialik and Cohen, Stone claimed she encountered five glowing entities of light in a surreal vision during the early days of her recovery.

"When I was first home from the hospital, I couldn’t sleep at night, and I was sleeping in the day," Stone remembered. "When I was laying on the couch, sleeping and awake, these orbs sort of presented themselves to me. These five orbs presented themselves to me and they sort of talked to me, but in a digital language."

She admitted that she had never previously spoken about the experience because she found it almost impossible to explain. Stone said that she believed the encounter carried a premonition that she would soon lose custody of her then one-year-old son Roan.

"I just kept saying to them, ‘I don’t know if I’m supposed to stay here or if I’m supposed to die,’" Stone recalled of her conversation with the orbs. "And they said, ‘You’re supposed to stay.’ And I said, ‘I can only stay if two of you will stay with my son. Because I don’t want him to be alone, and I think he’s gonna get taken from me.’"

"Sure enough, he was taken from me," she continued. "And I said, ‘We have to have an agreement. The two of you will stay with him and protect him.’ And they agreed. And they said, ‘But your destiny requires that we stay with you.’"

Stone and her ex-husband Phil Bronstein adopted Roan in 2000. A year later, Bronstein filed for divorce, citing irreconcilable differences. The former couple shared custody of Roan after finalizing the divorce in 2004, though Bronstein became Roan’s primary caretaker. Stone later adopted sons Laird and Quinn, now both 20, as a single mother.

The actress has previously said she could not fully discuss the original custody decision because of a confidentiality agreement, but she has claimed her "Basic Instinct" image was used against her in court, saying a judge asked Roan whether he knew his mother made "sex movies."

After Bialik asked how long her experience with the orbs lasted, Stone replied, "Several days."

"Wow," Bialik said.

World.title: Skillet frontman John Cooper talks about the risks of talking politics and why he wants to 'stay in his lane'
World.content:
We live at a time when it seems like everything is politicized and everyone is jonesing to make their opinion heard. That's all well and good, but probably not what you want to hear when you show up to a concert, as John Cooper, frontman of the rock band Skillet, pointed out during an appearance on OutKick's "Tomi Lahren is Fearless."

When you shell out some serious coin, do you really want to be lectured by a seventy-something musician who's rolling in money about the evils of Donald Trump?

Me neither, and count Cooper as one of the few entertainers who understands that.

STAY "FEARLESS" ON THE GO! TAKE TOMI LAHREN WITH YOU. DOWNLOAD THE TLIF PODCAST NOW!

Lahren asked the rocker about his openness when it comes to talking about faith and politics, and if there are risks involved in doing so.

"Yeah, definitely. I would say there's not as much of a risk if you're on the left because you will get praised by all of the powers that be," Cooper said. "Now, of course, you're still risking something — there's going to be some fans that don't like it, so I don't want to say they're not risking anything. That's actually not fair, but you will get opportunities from some of the institutional powers."

SKILLET'S JOHN COOPER SAYS WOKE ACTIVISTS HAVE 'BIG HEARTS' BUT ARE 'HURTING THEMSELVES'

But while he has no problem talking politics, he gets where people are coming from when they want entertainers to zip it on the political talk.

"I agree with people when they're like, I don't want to see some actor come up and yell at me about Iran or whatever they're on about; I don't even know if they even know what they're talking about, you know?"

It would seem Lahren knew precisely the type of person he was referring to.

"Yeah. Like the (Bruce) Springsteen of the world," she said.

The two agreed that Springsteen's penchant in recent years for going on mid-concert political diatribes is wearing a little thin.

"It just gets a little bit exhausting," Cooper said. He then pointed to a lyric in Staind frontman Aaron Lewis' 2021 song "Am I The Only One," in which he talks about how he "quits singin' along/Every time they play a Springsteen song?"

However, as Cooper noted, Springsteen's politics don't change the fact that he's an incredible songwriter. It just shows that artists have a choice when it comes to getting political or focusing on the music.

"The Boss is amazing," Cooper said. "One of the greatest songwriters, certainly, of (his) generation, and I still listen to him. But I'm like, 'I don't want people to feel that way about me.' I know some people do, but I'm trying to stay in my lane as best as I can."

World.title: Missouri court opens contempt probe into Republican official over redistricting fight
World.content:
The no-holds-barred fight over congressional maps in Missouri has reached a new level of intensity with the state’s high court opening a contempt probe into Secretary of State Denny Hoskins.

The Missouri Supreme Court late Tuesday issued an order asking Hoskins, a Republican, to explain “why he should not be held in contempt” for violating a ruling last week that said the state cannot use a newly drawn GOP map.

Despite the ruling, Hoskins continued to push to use the new map.

The court also ordered Hoskins to appear in person when the judges hold a hearing in the case Thursday.

Hoskins indicated in a post on X that he would not back down.

“I look forward to my day in court,” he said.

The state court order came after a flurry of court activity Tuesday.

First, the U.S. Supreme Court rejected a last-ditch appeal from Hoskins seeking to use the new map, which seeks to eliminate a Democratic-held congressional seat in the state.

Soon after, a federal judge in Missouri issued a new ruling saying the state is required to use the new map, setting up a dispute between federal and state courts. Litigation in that case continues and could soon reach the nation’s highest court again.

The 2025 Republican redistricting plan, part of a wave of redistricting encouraged by President Donald Trump, sought to eliminate one of the state’s two Democratic-held seats, currently held by Rep. Emanuel Cleaver.

Should the Missouri Supreme Court ruling remain in effect, a map drawn in 2022, with six Republican-held seats and two Democratic-held seats, would be in place for the general election.

The Republican-led Legislature redrew the map for the November elections, seeking to eliminate one of those Democratic seats.

The legal fight was kick-started when a group called People Not Politicians, led by activist Richard von Glahn, gathered signatures in support of a state referendum that would veto the Legislature’s map and put it on hold for the 2026 election while people voted on it.

But Hoskins refused to put the measure on the ballot, arguing that redistricting plans are not subject to being overturned by voters. The Missouri Supreme Court, which has a majority of Republican appointees, disagreed, saying there was nothing in state law that exempted redistricting maps from being vetoed by voters via the referendum process.

The state court’s contempt order came in response to a filing made by the referendum proponents’ lawyers.

World.title: Trump administration fires prosecutor in dropped case against politically-linked Indian billionaire
World.content:
WASHINGTON — A federal prosecutor who had been assigned to the now-defunct case against a politically linked Indian billionaire has been fired by the Trump administration, two people familiar with the firing tell NBC News.

The prosecutor, who had been with the Justice Department’s Fraud Section in Washington, was one of two who previously asked to withdraw from the Gautam Adani case two days after Principal Associate Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter moved in May to dismiss the case against Adani.

Adani was charged in November 2024 in connection with an alleged scheme to defraud U.S. investors and pay off Indian government officials to win a bid to develop the country’s largest solar power plant. He called the accusations baseless.

Adani pledged to invest billions of dollars in the U.S., and Democratic lawmakers raised questions of a quid pro quo with the Trump administration to avoid prosecution. The federal judge hearing the case ordered Adani to explain whether any deal was made in connection with the government’s significant reversal. He denied it, and so did the Justice Department.

U.S. District Judge Nicholas Garaufis of the Eastern District of New York eventually agreed to toss the case against Adani, though he blasted the Trump administration’s “highly unusual” conduct.

The prosecutor’s firing came a month later, the people said. The Trump administration has fired numerous federal employees without explanation, beyond citing Trump’s executive powers in letters, which Justice Department alumni have come to refer to as “Article II letters,” referring to a clause of the U.S. Constitution.

The prosecutor did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Last week, Garaufis let stand some counts against some of Adani’s co-defendants, saying the Trump administration had “not provided sufficient factual information to support the stated reasons” for dismissing the charges.

Gautam Adani, chairman of Adani Group, at the company's headquarters in Ahmedabad, India, in 2024. Sumit Dayal / Bloomberg via Getty Images file

Adani had pledged to invest billions of dollars in the United States but said in a sworn statement filed in July that he was “not aware of any agreement involving any person or entity exchanging anything for the dismissal of the indictment.”

An email from May from U.S. Attorney Joseph Nocella referenced a slide deck presentation from Adani’s defense team that included a proposal to invest $10 billion in the United States, and Nocella wrote that the proposal was “categorically rejected” by the office.

The Justice Department has defended the decision to forgo its case against Adani, with McCotter saying the case was “indefensible” and that he “would have sought dismissal of the securities charges regardless of any mentions of investments, regardless of whether the civil case (or any other matter) was settled or otherwise resolved.”

An attorney for Adani couldn’t be reached for comment about the prosecutor’s firing.

World.title: Lindsay Clancy’s attorney details her mental state after mistrial
World.content:
Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts mother accused of strangling her three young children to death in 2023, is “not very good” and remains “suicidal” after her high-profile murder trial, her defense attorney Kevin Reddington told NBC News on Wednesday in a wide-ranging interview.

On Friday, Judge William Sullivan declared a mistrial at Plymouth Superior Court after the jury deliberating whether Clancy was criminally responsible in the strangulation deaths of her three children said they were deadlocked three times. Reddington sought a last-minute emergency stay to send the jurors back to deliberations, but a justice at Massachusetts’ Supreme Judicial Court swiftly denied it.

“She’s strong. She has incredible family support,” Reddington said of Clancy. “But she is suicidal. I mean, she’s on 24/7, one-on-one suicide watch. I worry about her every day.”

Despite the dramatic end to the trial that leaves Clancy’s legal case in limbo, Reddington says his client does not hold any anger toward prosecutors, jurors or even witnesses who testified against her.

“She was hurt by the way they would talk about her and the way they would attack her. She was hurt, but she never once expressed anger towards anybody in the system,’ he said. “She doesn’t have it in her DNA to be angry with anyone.”

Instead, he added, she talks about her children and often repeats one phrase constantly: “I want my babies.”

The sentiment is a stark contrast to the prosecution’s case throughout the trial, which argued Clancy was aware of her actions and planned the killings ahead of time. Reddington argued that she was compelled to act on auditory hallucinations that told her to carry out the murders, a symptom of the postpartum psychosis he said she was experiencing.

Both parties admit she killed the children: Cora, 5; Dawson, 3; and Callan, 8 months old.

“That was not the Lindsay that is now living amongst us,” Reddington said Wednesday. “The person that committed this atrocious act was as a result of postpartum psychosis combined with the medications that she was provided.”

Postpartum psychosis is a rare but serious condition that can affect new mothers. More severe than postpartum depression, it can cause hallucinations and other intense psychological symptoms.

To prove their argument that Clancy was not actually experiencing psychosis at the time of the killings, prosecutors repeatedly pointed to the fact that she never told anyone she was hearing voices before that night and that she hasn’t heard any since — something said to be exceedingly rare for someone experiencing psychosis.

Reddington, however, said Wednesday that Clancy told her struggles to “anyone who would listen,” including her then-husband, Patrick Clancy, and her mother. He conceded Wednesday, though, that “she should have” told more people about the voices.

The lawyer also challenged the notion that Clancy lied about how she was feeling and that she repeated a list of symptoms to doctors that she found online.

“If she was so smart, and Googling things like psychosis, why would she not have had exactly the symptomology that you can Google about psychosis, about postpartum psychosis, [including] the voices?” he said. “What are you supposed to say? How are you supposed to say it?”

He added: “If she was faking, she would have hit it on every single cylinder. She was telling the truth. She did the best that she could. She was failed by these doctors.”

The broadcast trial and the conversation around postpartum psychosis captured the nation, going viral on social media as online sleuths pushed conspiracy theories and broke down testimony, with many insisting that Clancy did not carry out the murders but that Patrick Clancy did instead and framed her.

On Tuesday, Patrick Clancy’s lawyers responded to those allegations and slammed the true-crime creators behind the theories.

The statement called the theories and online storylines a “campaign of misinformation” that was “publishing what they know to be outright falsehoods that Patrick was somehow involved in the death of his young children and other vile claims.”

Patrick Clancy’s lawyer added that “every appropriate measure will be pursued to hold them accountable, including legally” and that “law enforcement has been notified.”

Reddington told NBC News that Clancy is aware of how the case has taken off on social media and how many people online have hurled allegations at her former husband. She also disagrees with the theories.

“She knows, and it’s readily apparent that Patrick has been set upon, and his life has been turned upside down into a nightmare that he doesn’t deserve. Period. Full stop,” Reddington said.

A lone holdout

After 38 hours of deliberations, the jury on Friday said it could not reach a unanimous decision, remaining deadlocked 11-1. Jurors had the option to convict Clancy of first-degree murder, second-degree murder, manslaughter, or to acquit her due to lack of criminal responsibility.

If she were found not guilty by insanity, she would have been sentenced to time in a state mental health facility.

Three jurors, including the foreperson, told NBC Boston on Tuesday that the majority favored finding Clancy not guilty by lack of criminal responsibility, while one holdout wanted to convict. But that juror expressed reasonable doubt, they said, and still wouldn’t agree with the remainder of the jury.

Reddington, however, defended the juror’s right to his opinion Wednesday, saying it “doesn’t matter” what was going through his head.

“He’s got every right to do that, and I would defend that right, but not to refuse to apply the law,” Reddington said. “This is where you draw the line.”

Now, prosecutors must decide whether to retry Clancy. The next hearing in the case is scheduled for Sept. 29.

Despite telling reporters multiple times last week that he was ready to retry Clancy’s case as soon as this week, Reddington said that is not the outcome he wants and that he will file a motion to dismiss charges. He also said he would be open to plea discussions, but would not take a deal that lands his client in jail for even a day.

Reddington on Tuesday called on President Donald Trump to offer his client a pardon, even though Clancy was tried on state charges and the president can only pardon federal charges.

He explained Wednesday that he made the suggestion because Trump “felt compelled to comment on the case” and thought that maybe Trump could reach out to colleagues in the Justice Department to influence Plymouth County District Attorney Timothy Cruz to drop the charges. Or, he theorized, Trump might even reach out to Cruz directly on the issue.

Despite such strong attention toward the case, Reddington said, he felt that there was some fundamental misunderstanding about Clancy’s situation.

“They feel that if you determine that Lindsay was and is not guilty of this crime because of lack of criminal responsibility, that in some fashion you are ignoring the loss of these three children,” he explained. “That is as far from the truth as possible.”

Reddington added that Clancy, who is in a wheelchair and has been on suicide watch since the night of the murders, is “living in hell.”

“I look back over the years, and the people that I’ve represented — been able to help, not so much help — but yes, this is the one that really has moved me,” Reddington said, agreeing it was one of the hardest of his career.

World.title: John Malkovich cancels Tel Aviv show after promoter fabricates statement from him on Israel
World.content:
Oscar-nominated actor John Malkovich cancelled an upcoming stage performance in Tel Aviv after learning that The Jerusalem Post unknowingly published a made-up a quote attributed to him about his “closeness and solidarity” with Israeli audiences.

Malkovich, in a statement to The Hollywood Reporter on Tuesday, said a local public relations firm “hired by the Israeli promoter drafted a quote for the article that was attributed to me, though I never made the statements that were quoted, nor was I consulted before they were printed.”

“The fact that they were printed as direct quotes from me is unacceptable and untenable,” his statement read. “For this reason, I have decided I cannot participate in the Tel Aviv performance.”

The offending quote, which NBC News obtained by using The Wayback Machine internet archive, was published by The Jerusalem Post on Saturday.

It said: “I am thrilled to return to Israel and look forward to meeting the warm Israeli audience once again, to whom I feel a strong closeness and solidarity. I hope to find you happy and optimistic! Sending you much love.”

After Malkovich complained, the newspaper updated its story to include an apology from the show’s Israeli producer, Alon Yurik.

“I would like to clarify that the original press release contained a mistake, and an incorrect quote from Malkovich was included due to a misunderstanding,” Yurik stated. “I would like to take this opportunity to apologize for that.”

It also included a slightly different version of the offending quote attributed to Malkovich: “I am excited to return to Israel and would be very happy to meet again with the warm Israeli audience, with whom I feel great closeness and identification.”

Tal Spungin, the newspaper’s managing editor, said in an email to NBC News that the “difference is due to a discrepancy in the translation of the quote.”

“It was initially provided to our Hebrew-language sister publication, Walla, in Hebrew, and was then translated into English for The Jerusalem Post,” Spungin wrote. “The quote was removed from our report after the production company confirmed to us that it was fabricated, and the wording was amended in our follow-up to better reflect the nature of the ‘quote’ as it was provided in Hebrew.”

Malkovich, 72, is the latest high-profile artist who had declined to perform in Israel amid the ongoing conflicts with Palestinians in Gaza and the West Bank. But he did not directly criticize Israel.

Instead, in his statement, Malkovich said he counted himself as “lucky” to have had the opportunity to perform “in countries with governments whose values or culture I do not share” and the chance to travel to places “whose view of the world may not align with mine.”

“My appearance in any country, even my own, does not constitute approval of said country’s policies, nor actions, nor its elected or unelected leaders,” his statement said. “My appearances would also not condone nor mean that I am in supposed ‘solidarity’ with any particular political cause, nor with the killing of innocents, nor with any acts of terrorism, nor any other kind of barbarity.”

Representatives for Malkovich did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Best known for his riveting roles in movies like “Dangerous Liaisons,” “In the Line of Fire” and playing himself in the surreal meta-comedy “Being John Malkovich,” he was supposed to perform “The Music Critic,” a touring comedy featuring classical music and criticism of world-famous composers, next April in Tel Aviv.

Malkovich had previously visited Israel in July 2008 as an honorary guest of the Jerusalem Film Festival.

In April 2013, Malkovich returned to Israel with his musical theater show The Infernal Comedy: Confessions of a Serial Killer.

World.title: Jalen Brunson to host ‘SNL’ season 52 premiere hot off of Knicks championship
World.content:
It’s nothing but net for “Saturday Night Live” later this month as the show announced that New York’s own Jalen Brunson will be the first host for the show’s 52nd season.

New York Knicks guard Jalen Brunson is hot off the summer of his career after leading the team to the NBA Championship in June. It’s the team’s first championship league title in more than 50 years.

The sketch comedy institution announced Brunson would host on Sept. 26 with the girl group Katseye scheduled as the musical guest.

The show announced Brunson as the first of four weeks of hosts, followed by “Fifty Shades of Grey” star Dakota Johnson, “Obsession” breakout actor Inde Navarrette and comedian Shane Gillis.

Brunson’s leadership of the Knicks skyrocketed him into the national spotlight earlier this year as the team made historic comebacks in the NBA playoffs.

The 30-year-old rallied in the fourth quarter against the Cleveland Cavaliers in Game 1 of the Eastern Conference finals to overcome a 22-point deficit. Brunson scored 38 points that game and the team eventually won in overtime against the Cavaliers, setting the Knicks up for a 4-0 sweep of the conference finals.

It was considered one of the greatest postseason recoveries in the NBA until the Knicks did it again just weeks later.

The team was trailing the San Antonio Spurs as much has 29 points during the Game 4 of the NBA Finals. But the team pushed to make up the gap in what is now regarded as the biggest championship game comeback in NBA history.

Many credit Brunson’s mentality and leadership for the Knicks’ first NBA championship since 1973. He told NBC News after the stunning Game 4 rally that the team approaches each game as if they are still at 0-0 in the series.

“Whatever’s being said, positive or negative, you can’t really think about or worry about too much,” Brunson said.

Though he’s known for his stoicism on the court, Brunson has a light-hearted side that makes him a good fit for a comedy show.

He often ribs teammate and best friend Josh Hart on the podcast they host together. Brunson can also be seen trying his best not to crack a smile in their post-game press conferences, where Hart is often seen with food he had delivered to the venue.

It’s unclear whether Hart or any of Brunson’s other teammates — or any of the famous faces who sat courtside for the Knicks championship run, including Timothee Chalamet, Mariska Hargitay or Taylor Swift — may make an appearance on the “SNL” premiere. It would be a slam dunk for a show that’s known to score celebrity cameos.

World.title: Don Jr.'s VC firm rejects Rep. Raskin's accusations of "insider political influence"
World.content:
Donald Trump Jr.'s venture capital firm punched back Tuesday at suspicions cast by a key congressional Democrat about potential "insider political influence," likely foreshadowing the political showdowns in the U.S. House if control of the chamber flips in the November elections.

In a letter shared with CBS News, the legal counsel for the president's eldest son's firm, 1789 Capital, rejected Rep. Jamie Raskin's characterizations of the firm and criticized his "spaghetti-against-the-wall approach." The firm did not provide the materials requested by Raskin.

"1789 Capital welcomes legitimate congressional oversight, but it has no intention of being held hostage to political gamesmanship in which assertions are made publicly and broad demands for confidential business records follow in the hope that those records will supply the factual basis that was missing when the assertions were made," lawyers Alexander J. Merton and William A Burck said in the letter sent to Raskin's office.

1789 Capital response to Rep. Jamie Raskin Page of

Raskin, the top Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee, launched what he called an investigation last month into 1789 Capital, alleging that it bought stakes in some companies shortly before they received federal government funding or favorable policy decisions. News reports have highlighted the apparent Midas touch that 1789 Capital developed when Trump Jr. became a partner shortly after his father's second election to the Oval Office.

The Democrat cited the online prediction market Polymarket, electronic cigarette company Juul, defense technology contractor Anduril Industries and a small rare-earth company called Vulcan.

As part of the investigation, Raskin sought records related to its "almost clairvoyant" business moves and its communications with the Trump administration. But the Democrats don't have subpoena power unless they win majority support in the midterms.

Raskin had sought a list of companies in Trump Jr.'s investment firm's portfolio, due diligence materials for its investments and preservation of any conversations with members of the administration, including messages sent via encrypted apps.

While Trump Jr.'s investment firm shared none of that, its lawyer noted the rare-earth company had been awarded federal business dating to 2024, before the financing round in which 1789 Capital participated. The lawyer called 1789 Capital "one of many institutional investors" in the company.

Raskin made "unsubstantiated and emotional aspersions" about 1789 Capital, "repeatedly conflates separate entities, mischaracterizes transactions, and, in several instances, appears fundamentally at odds with the very sources it cites," the response letter said.

Emily Stellakis, a Raskin staffer, said on Wednesday that "[w]e'd be glad to comment on 1789 Capital's blustering and evasive response as soon as they actually send it to us."

The letter was sent on Tuesday, one day before the Republicans' first-of-its-kind midterm convention in Texas is set to begin. Trump Jr. was scheduled to be in Dallas on Thursday for the event.

President Trump is also set to appear and deliver a keynote address on Wednesday.

House Democrats have sent a litany of letters in recent months demanding information from government officials, Trump family members and firms that have done business with either.

The Trump administration and private companies aren't obligated to respond, but the demands could signal that Democrats are planning to conduct aggressive oversight investigations if they win control of the House in the midterms — which would give them the power to issue subpoenas.

World.title: The U.S. just had its hottest summer on record, NOAA says
World.content:
The United States just experienced its hottest summer on record, officials said, after several months of high temperatures and expanding drought across the country.

According to a new report from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, temperatures nationwide averaged 74.4 degrees Fahrenheit between June and August, which is the period known to climate scientists as "meteorological summer." It was the warmest summer the country has ever seen since temperature and precipitation records began 132 years ago, exceeding the previous record set in 1936 and again in 2021 by 0.4 degrees.

August 2026 alone broke monthly temperature records, the report said. The temperature for the entire month averaged out to 75.6 degrees, although the average daytime high was considerably higher at 88.6 degrees — the warmest recorded average of its kind.

Blistering heat

This summer's temperatures showed significant changes from the patterns observed over the course of the 20th century, overall and in August specifically, the report said. In 2026, average temperatures between June and August were three and a half degrees hotter than summer averages collected throughout the 1900s. August's average was three degrees hotter on its own.

Much of the contiguous U.S. endured "above- to much-above average" temperatures last month, according to the report. The only areas where normal conditions were observed were isolated to pockets of the Midwest and northern Plains.

Meanwhile, record warmth was widespread across the West, Southwest, southern Rockies, southwestern Plains and the southern Florida Peninsula, which experienced punishing heat waves, destructive wildfires and declining water reserves as a result.

California, Nevada, New Mexico and Colorado all experienced their warmest August temperatures on record this year, with California and New Mexico seeing average daily highs soar to record heights. Even nighttime lows were, on average, the highest they've ever been in August across vast sections of the West, including Arizona, California, Colorado, Nevada, New Mexico and Utah.

Several southwestern states endured record-breaking heat for the length of the summer, including Colorado, New Mexico and Utah, while Arizona tied its previous record for the warmest summer.

Precipitation rates fell below average

Although parts of the country faced storms that brought heavy rain, precipitation across the U.S. this summer was still lower than the 20th century average, the report found. Nationwide, the average of 8.11 inches of rain that fell between June and August was 0.21 inches below last century's average. Substantially above-average precipitation in states like Indiana, Kentucky and Ohio was canceled out by historically sparse totals recorded in places like California, which had its driest summer since 2002 and its fifth-driest ever recorded.

The contrast was particularly stark in August, when Indiana and Ohio saw record-high precipitation for the month while Texas and Oklahoma neared their record lows.

August also brought deepening drought to parts of the country, the report said, citing the U.S. Drought Monitor. Nationwide, drought had expanded to cover 59.1% of the U.S. at the start of September, after increasing by more than 10% since the start of August. While still present across many areas of the West that had already been experiencing it, the drought spread further into the middle of the country. However, it weakened somewhat in certain sections of the Southwest, Southeast and mid-Atlantic regions.

World.title: Trump says he had "great conversation" with Putin amid renewed peace push
World.content:
Washington — President Trump on Wednesday said he had a "great conversation" with Russian President Vladimir Putin, repeating his claim that he thinks the Russian leader wants to make a deal to end the war in Ukraine.

The phone call, which the Russians said took place Tuesday, came after top Trump envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff met with Putin in Moscow and with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Kyiv over the weekend.

"We had a great conversation," Mr. Trump said Wednesday on the tarmac at Joint Base Andrews. "He is wanting to make a deal. And if Zelenskyy is wanting to make a deal, that would be very nice."

Mr. Trump has repeatedly said he thinks Putin wants to strike a deal to end the fighting, although the Russians could remove troops and relinquish territory at any point. A reporter asked the president what the holdup is.

"The holdup is two people that hate each other," the president said. "I think more than anything else, it's two people that hate each other."

The White House did not release a summary of the call or confirm that it took place, leaving the Russians to provide the only official account of the conversation.

According to the Russian readout, Mr. Trump told Putin that ending the conflict would immediately open up the possibility for the full restoration of Russia-U.S. relations, and that he's interested in reaching a breakthrough in resolving the conflict during his presidency.

Kushner, the president's son-in-law, told reporters Sunday that Mr. Trump has been following developments from their meetings "very closely" and is trying to "find a pathway to end this war." It was the first time Kushner and Witkoff visited Ukraine since Mr. Trump took office in January 2025. Zelenskyy said the goal of the discussions was a "just, fair peace" that would make sure Russia never had a chance to resume its attacks on Ukraine. The Ukrainian leader said Tuesday that he may meet with Mr. Trump later this month.

Putin and Zelenskyy ordered a pause in fighting while Kushner and Witkoff held their talks in both countries. But Russia resumed its attacks on Kyiv on Tuesday morning, killing at least two people.

The conversations come as Lithuania, which borders Russia-friendly Belarus, trains civilians to stand up to Russian aggression, should it arrive at their doorstep.

Russian President Vladimir Putin greets Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff in Moscow on Saturday, Sept. 5, 2026. Mikhail Metzel/Sputnik/Kremlin Pool Photo via AP

Mr. Trump pledged to end the war in Ukraine by his first day in office, but he has admitted publicly that achieving that goal has been more challenging than anticipated, and said the pledge was "figurative" or an "exaggeration." He is approaching 20 months in office.
