Sheinbaum expresses optimism about Mexico’s potential for economic growth

Sheinbaum noted that the Finance Ministry is forecasting growth in the range of 1.5%-2.5% in 2027.

“Let’s see if we grow more,” she said.

Sheinbaum said that higher-than-anticipated growth next year is “possible” because the economic impact of “a lot” of proposed public and public-private investment projects will be felt next year.

“Our idea is that [the economy] could grow more,” she said.

Sheinbaum also said that her government anticipates “greater stability” and “greater certainty” in the trade relationship between Mexico and its USMCA partners, namely the United States and Canada.

She said that the government also anticipates an increase in private investment next year.

“We’re going to wait and see how 2027 turns out and then we’ll make an assessment for 2028,” Sheinbaum said.

“We’re optimistic about what will happen in 2027 and we’re also very satisfied with the [proposed] economic package,” she said.

By Mexico News Daily chief staff writer Peter Davies (peter.davies@mexiconewsdaily.com)

World.title: The MND Peso Index™ for September: MXN is nearly 6% overvalued against USD
World.content:
THE MND PESO INDEX™

Tracking the exchange rate people actually experience

MND Intelligence · Fifth edition

Welcome to the fifth edition of the MND Peso Index™, part of the MND Intelligence™ suite of data products developed by Mexico News Daily.

The MND Peso Index™ is a monthly purchasing power parity measure that assesses whether the Mexican peso is overvalued or undervalued against the US dollar by comparing the prices of a standardized basket of 20 goods and services in Mexico and Dallas, Texas.

As was the case with our previous edition, our latest MND Peso Index™ assessment is being published in the same month as its underlying price survey, making it more timely.

Our headline finding for September 2026 indicates that the peso was overvalued against the dollar by 5.8%, an increase of 3.4 percentage points compared to the 2.4% overvaluation we determined in early August. This is the highest overvaluation assessment the MND Peso Index™ has yielded, surpassing the 4% overvaluation appraisal in May.

For a detailed explanation of the purpose of the MND Peso Index™, the makeup of the basket and more, please refer to the index article we published in June. You can read even more about the index in our introductory article published in early May.

What did the MND Peso Index™ tell us in September 2026?

In September 2026, the MND Peso Index™ suggests that the USD:MXN exchange rate on the date we collected prices in various Mexican cities and in Dallas, Texas, overvalued the Mexican peso by 5.8%.

The Mexican and Dallas prices were collected on Sept. 2, 2026. The MND Peso Rate — the simple average of the 20 item-level implied exchange rates, rather than the rate produced by dividing the total Mexican basket cost by the total Dallas basket cost — came in at 17.96 pesos per dollar, compared with a Banxico FIX rate of 16.98 pesos per dollar on Sept. 2.

The gap between those two figures indicates that the peso — at a rate of 16.98 to the US dollar — was overvalued by 5.8% in early September.

In the table below, you can see the Mexico and U.S. prices for all 20 goods and services in the basket, the total costs of the two baskets, the implied exchange rate for each item, the MND Peso Rate (i.e., the overall implied rate), the Banxico FIX rate on the date prices were collected and the overvaluation assessment for the peso.

Why did the peso’s ‘overvalued’ assessment increase between August and September?

The peso’s overvaluation assessment increased from 2.4% in early August to 5.8% in early September because the gap between the Banxico FIX rate and the MND Peso Rate widened.

The widening occurred due to the appreciation of the peso between Aug. 6 and September 2 and due to an increase in the MND Peso Rate. The peso appreciated 24 centavos from 17.22 to 16.98 over that period, a strengthening of 1.4%. The MND Peso Rate increased 32 centavos from 17.64 on Aug. 6 to 17.96 on Sept. 2. The difference between the Banxico FIX rate and MND Peso Rate on Sept. 2 was 98 centavos, an increase of 56 centavos compared to the gap between the two rates on Aug. 6.

The peso has recently appreciated due to a range of factors, including US dollar weakness and carry trade demand for Mexico’s currency. The MND Peso rate increased due to eight month-over-month changes in the implied rates for items in the basket of goods and services.

The implied rates increased for six items: A Big Mac, a Big Mac meal, a dozen eggs, Kirkland toilet paper, Listerine mouthwash and a Planet Fitness membership. In the case of the Big Mac and the Big Mac meal, the implied rate rose because prices in Dallas fell. In the case of the eggs, toilet paper and mouthwash, the implied rate increased because prices in Mexico rose. The price of a Planet Fitness membership declined in both Dallas and Mexico. However, the Dallas price fell more than the Mexico price, causing the implied rate to increase.

The implied rate for a cinema ticket declined because the price fell on both sides of the border, but the decrease in Mexico was larger. The eighth month-over-month implied rate change was due to the replacement of a Flexon Hose — which is no longer available on Costco México’s website — with a set of glass containers. The implied rate for the set of glass containers was 21.64, while the implied rate for the hose last month was 24.26.

Overall, the combined upward effect of the six higher implied rates outweighed the downward effect of the two lower rates. Thus the MND Peso Rate increased between early August and and early September.

The MND Peso Index™ has now found the peso to be overvalued in April, May, June, August and September

Through the use of the MND Peso Index™, we have now determined that the peso was overvalued against the US dollar by 2.8% in late April, 4% in late May, 2.9% in late June, 2.4% in early August and 5.8% in early September.

The difference between the lowest overvaluation assessment (that in August) and the highest one (this one) is 3.4 percentage points.

So far in 2026, the peso has appreciated 6.4% against the US dollar. It closed at 18.00 to the greenback on the final day of 2025, according to the Bank of Mexico, while the closing USD:MXN rate on Tuesday, Sept. 8 was 16.91. If the Banxico FIX rate was 16.91 when we collected the prices for the Mexican and Dallas baskets on Sept. 2, the overvaluation assessment for the peso would have been 6.2%.

* Price sources: Mexico prices were collected from the websites and apps of Walmart México, Costco México, AutoZone México, Telmex, Cinépolis, Petco México, McDonald’s, Starbucks, Netflix, Spotify and Microsoft. Dallas prices were collected from their U.S. equivalents. The Banxico FIX rate of 16.98 published on Sept. 2, 2026, was used as the official exchange rate reference.

World.title: New 11-tower hotel and apartment complex proposed for Bahía de Banderas
World.content:
A major new 11-tower housing and hotel development in Bahía de Banderas, Nayarit, has been proposed at a projected cost of 515 million pesos (US $30.5 million).

The proposal from BM/5096 Business Trust was published in the Environment Ministry’s Ecological Gazette on Aug. 20 for review, and the start of construction is contingent upon the development obtaining the necessary Environmental Impact Assessment (MIA).

The project, known as Ocean II, will cover 65,453 square meters of land, including private land, land reclaimed from the sea and a portion of the Federal Maritime-Terrestrial Zone. It is expected to consist of a hotel zone and a residential zone, accessible from Paseo de los Cocoteros Avenue.

A 187-room hotel will occupy the Palapar Lot within the Los Flamingos Master Condominium across five towers, ranging from five to 10 stories high, while six residential towers will contain 275 apartments. There are plans for basement parking for 784 vehicles.

Planned amenities include restaurants, a spa, a gym, a beach club, an event hall, retail spaces, swimming pools and over 25,000 square meters of green space.

The developers noted in their submission to the Environment Ministry that they expect the project to take around seven years to complete, with the first phase of construction slated to begin in March 2027 and completion expected in 2033.

The announcement is for a general area where beachside development has been controversial, as it is a nesting habitat for the olive ridley sea turtle.

In July, the Environment Ministry revoked a federal concession for a luxury development in Punta de Mita after finding unauthorized construction and environmental violations by developer Cantiles de Mita.

President Sheinbaum visited Nayarit over the weekend to deliver her second annual report, announcing the creation of a Master Plan to conserve beaches, guarantee free access and protect the entire state coastline’s biodiversity.

“I want to tell you that we’ve been working with the [state] governor for over a year on a master plan for tourism in Nayarit, because we don’t want the mangroves destroyed or all the beaches privatized,” said Sheinbaum in a speech.

With reports from El Sol de México and Tribuna de la Bahía

World.title: Mexico fails the 2025 PISA evaluation: A perspective from our CEO
World.content:
Just this morning, the 2025 PISA 2025 results were released and as feared, they are very concerning both on a global scale and for Mexico specifically.

As a reminder, PISA assessments test 760,000 15-year-old students in 91 countries in science, mathematics and reading. The results show a continued decline globally in all three areas with reading being the largest long-term weakness. Singapore students scored highest, followed closely by China, Japan and South Korea.

Mexico, which historically has done poorly, did even worse than in previous years. Some of the lowlights of Mexico’s performance:

Mexico performed below the OECD average in every 2025 PISA domain and placed 64th out of 91 participating countries/economies globally.

The last time the testing was done, in 2022, Mexico placed 51st out of 81 participating countries/economies.

Mexico declined in country rankings in math and reading, as well as compared to its previous performance.

Mexico ranks significantly below the OECD mean in math, science and reading.

This was Mexico’s fifth consecutive decline in reading since 2009. (The test is taken every 3 years.)

Half of Mexican 15-year-olds read below the minimum proficiency threshold. This is the threshold that one needs to be able to read in order to learn.

Other than the slight gain in science, the results are a disaster. Not only is Mexico getting worse in math and reading scores, but actually getting relatively much worse than other countries.

I often write about the potential of the Mexican economy, but these testing results are a significant red flag. I have written before about two concerns regarding the Mexican workforce:

1. The education barrier means companies have to make significant investments in workforce development and training to prepare workers. This is both a financial cost and a time loss, and puts Mexican operations at a disadvantage versus other countries.

2. The strengthening peso increases the cost of the Mexican workforce. A relatively lower-skilled, relatively expensive workforce means that many companies will instead invest in automation and robotics versus investing in workers.

World.title: Goods from Mexico now make up almost one-fifth of the US import market
World.content:
Listen to this article

Mexico captured almost one-fifth of the U.S. import market in July, well ahead of second-placed Canada, shipping a record US $60.55 billion worth of goods to its northern neighbor, according to official U.S. data.

Mexico’s share of the $332.92 billion U.S. import market in July was 18.2%, ahead of Canada (10.1%); China (8.1%); Vietnam (7.9%); and Taiwan (7.7%), according to data published last Thursday by the U.S. Census Bureau and the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis.

In other words, nearly one in every five dollars the United States spent on imports in July was spent on products from Mexico.

Compared to a year earlier, Mexico’s share of the U.S. import market increased 2.7 percentage points in July.

The difference between Mexico and Canada’s shares of the U.S. import market in July 2025 was 4.5 percentage points. In July of this year, the difference was 8.1 points. Similarly, the difference between Mexico and China’s shares of the U.S. import market increased significantly, rising to 10.1 points in July from 6.5 points in the same month of last year.

The increase in Mexico’s share of the U.S. import market coincides with a boom in Mexican exports. The boom is largely driven by a sharp increase in the export of computer equipment, including AI servers, and other electronics to the U.S.

While such products are helping to boost Mexico’s overall export revenue and share of the U.S. import market, their Mexican content is generally very low. That means that a significant share of the revenue Mexico receives from the export of tech products has already been spent on imported inputs, especially from Taiwan.

Mexico’s export revenue increased 33% annually in July

In July — for the first time in any month on record — Mexico’s revenue from selling goods to the United States exceeded $60 billion.

The year-over-year increase in revenue was 33.6% in July. The month-over-month increase was 9.6%.

Canada’s revenue from exports to the United States also increased on an annual basis in July, but only by 4%. Canada’s income declined on a month-over-month basis in July, falling 10%. Canada’s revenue from products shipped to the United States in July was $33.49 billion, equivalent to 55.3% of Mexico’s income in the same month.

China’s revenue from goods shipped to the United States in July was $27.07 billion, up 2.6% from the same month of last year.

Mexico’s exports to the United States reached a record level in July at a time when there was significant uncertainty in the bilateral trade relationship. On July 1, the U.S. government announced that it had declined to renew the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA), the free trade pact that superseded NAFTA in 2020.

Despite that decision, the USMCA remains in effect, allowing most Mexican goods to enter the United States tariff-free and giving Mexico a significant comparative advantage over most of its competitors.

Mexico’s exports to the US increased 16% between January and July

The U.S. data also shows that the United States imported goods from Mexico worth $358.7 billion in the first seven months of 2026. That figure represents an increase of 16% compared to the same period of 2025.

Mexico’s share of the $2.08 trillion U.S. import market between January and July was 17.3%, up from 15% in the same period of last year.

Canada’s share of the U.S. import market remained virtually the same on a year-over-year basis, while China’s share fell almost two percentage points.

Canada’s income from goods shipped to the United States between January and July increased 1.8% to $233.66 billion. Its share of the U.S. import market was 11.24% in the first seven months of the year, an increase of just 0.08 percentage points compared to the same period of last year. Canada and the United States are currently engaged in a significant trade dispute.

China’s revenue from goods shipped to the United States between January and July was $156.39 billion, a 19.4% decrease compared to the same period of last year. Its share of the U.S. import market was 7.5%, down from 9.4% in the same period of last year. China and the United States are engaged in a long-running trade war.

Mexico is the top market for US exports

The U.S. data shows that the United States exported goods worth $34.24 billion to Mexico in July, an increase of 18.3% compared to the same month of 2025. In the first seven months of 2026, the United States’ revenue from goods exported to Mexico was $229.81 billion, a 16.8% year-over-year increase.

In July, and in the first seven months of 2026, Mexico was the top market for U.S. exports. In the first seven months of last year, Canada was the top foreign market for U.S. goods, just ahead of Mexico.

In the first seven months of 2026, U.S. exports generated total revenue of $1.43 trillion. Sixteen per cent of that revenue — or around one in every six dollars — was derived from goods sent to Mexico. After Mexico, the largest markets for U.S. exports between January and July were, in order, Canada, the United Kingdom, the Netherlands and China.

Mexico’s trade surplus with US nears $130 billion

Mexico recorded a trade surplus of $26.31 billion with the United States in July. At the end of July, Mexico’s calendar trade surplus with the U.S. was $128.89 billion. At the end of July last year, it was $112.57 billion, 12.7% lower.

The only country that recorded a larger trade surplus with the United States than Mexico in the year to the end of July was Vietnam. The southeast Asian nation sent exports worth $149.61 billion to the United States in the first seven months of the year, while its outlay on imports from the U.S. was $10.75 billion. Vietnam thus recorded a trade surplus of $138.86 billion with the U.S. in the first seven months of the year.

Mexico’s large trade surplus with the United States has angered U.S. President Donald Trump, who takes the view that the U.S. is “losing money” if its imports from a certain country exceed its exports to the same country. On Friday, he threatened in a social media post to “STOP TRADING WITH COUNTRIES WITH WHICH WE HAVE A DEFICIT” if the U.S. Federal Reserve doesn’t lower its benchmark interest rate, which is currently set at 3.50%-3.75%.

Later on Friday, Trump asserted that Mexico has “nothing” the United States needs, apart from “hot tamales” and “tomatoes,” a claim that collides with the reality that the U.S. and Mexican economies are highly integrated and that Mexico ships huge quantities of goods to its northern neighbor on a daily basis. The data on Mexico’s exports to the U.S. in July and in the first seven months of the year — and that on the United States’ exports to Mexico in the same periods — provide clear evidence of that economic interdependence.

World.title: 500 Chihuahua farmers are benefitting from a 20-year-old Tec student’s prize-winning filtration invention
World.content:
A 20-year-old engineering student from a farming family in Chihuahua has won a national award by developing an irrigation filter that could make water go further for drought-stricken farmers.

Luis Ángel Robles Morales, a mechatronics student at Tecnológico de Monterrey’s Chihuahua campus, leads OAKs Filtration, which last week received the 2026 Eugenio Garza Sada Award in the category of student social innovation.

The award — which includes a prize of 1 million pesos (US $59,121) for Robles — was one of three presented Sept. 2 by Tec de Monterrey and FEMSA, the Monterrey-based company that operates OXXO stores and controls Coca-Cola bottling operations in Mexico.

The two entities jointly established the award in 1993 in honor of the late Garza Sada, an industrialist who was among the university’s founders in 1943 and who helped lead a Monterrey business group that later became FEMSA.

Robles’ irrigation filter makes water use more efficient by preventing clogs that lead to wasted water, disrupted harvests and increased maintenance costs.

A persistent problem in drip and sprinkler systems is sand, mud and other particles clogging emitters.

So far, the system has benefited more than 500 farmers in the south-central region of Chihuahua, according to Tec de Monterrey.

Robles comes from a farming family: His grandfather grew corn, chiles and alfalfa, and his father branched off into making filters for irrigation systems.

In Chihuahua, the need for improved irrigation is acute.

From January through August this year, the state received 247.6 millimeters of rain — roughly 9.8 inches and 11.7% less than the same period last year, the newspaper El Diario de Chihuahua reported. By Aug. 15, drought was affecting 28.3% of the state, up from 11.2% in early May.

OAKs Filtration uses a carbon-steel outer casing and a PVC internal filtering element. Robles said the design provides two to three times the filtration area of commercial systems and channels debris toward the filter’s end, allowing it to clean itself through water flow.

In a test described by the digital news platform Expansion ESG, a competing filter clogged after 30 to 60 minutes, while the OAKs filter ran eight uninterrupted hours without pressure loss and was only about one-third full when inspected.

Robles said the price of the OAKs filter system runs from 30,000 to 100,000 pesos (US $1,773 to $5,910), while traditional commercial filters can cost 300,000 to 500,000 pesos (US $17,736 to $29,560).

OAKs was one of three 2026 Garza Sada Award honorees, with a total prize pool of 4.5 million pesos (US $266,000).

The others were pharmaceutical executive and conservationist Eric Hágsater Gartenberg, recognized for humanistic business leadership, and Formando Emprendedores, a nonprofit that provides education and youth-development programs in northern Mexico.

Since its founding in 1993, the award has recognized 81 winners.

Robles said he will devote half of his prize money to the project and half to an international entrepreneurial experience.

With reports from Expansión ESG, EJE Central, El Economista and El Diario de Chihuahua

World.title: Costa Rica Route 1 Through Cambronero Closed Indefinitely After Truck Crash
World.content:
One of Costa Rica’s main highways between the Central Valley and the Pacific remained completely closed today after a tractor-trailer crashed into a temporary bridge on Route 1 at Cambronero. The Ministry of Public Works and Transport (MOPT) said its latest guidance is that the Interamericana Norte will remain closed in both directions until crews remove the truck and its cargo, inspect the modular Bailey bridge and determine what repairs are needed. No reopening time has been announced.

The accident happened at about 10:30 p.m. last night in Santiago de San Ramón. The truck, which had Guatemalan plates, struck the side of the bridge while carrying large rolls of paper or cardboard. Some of the load was scattered around the bridge, complicating efforts to clear the highway.

The driver became trapped inside the cab and had to be freed by emergency crews. He was taken to Carlos Luis Valverde Vega Hospital in San Ramón. Authorities have not reported his current condition. MOPT bridge specialists were sent to Cambronero Tuesday to examine the structure before any traffic is allowed across it. The bridge was already undergoing preventive maintenance this week before Monday night’s crash.

The closure could create big delays for people traveling between San José and destinations in Puntarenas and Guanacaste. Route 1 through Cambronero is one of the main roads connecting the Central Valley with northwestern Costa Rica and carries substantial passenger and freight traffic. MOPT is directing drivers toward two main alternatives.

Route 27 between San José and Caldera is open to cars, buses and heavy trucks. Drivers should keep in mind that it is a toll road and additional traffic caused by the Cambronero closure could increase travel times. Route 3 through Monte del Aguacate is another option for lighter vehicles, but articulated trucks and tractor-trailers should not use it. Authorities have also identified the local Río Jesús-Piedra Blanca road as an option for light vehicles.

Traffic Police officers are stationed around the closed section to prevent vehicles from entering while crews work. The crash also caused problems for other motorists Monday night. A bus carrying about 25 people went off the roadway while attempting to maneuver near the accident scene. Emergency personnel checked the passengers, but none required transportation to a hospital.

The Bailey bridge involved in last night’s crash is a modular structure installed in the Cambronero area in November 2025 as a temporary solution following earlier problems along the highway. For anyone heading from the Central Valley toward the Pacific today, the safest assumption is that Route 1 through Cambronero remains unavailable until MOPT issues a new announcement. Drivers should allow additional travel time and check road conditions before leaving.

World.title: International News: Apple unveils iPhone Duo, Its first foldable iPhone
World.content:
International News: Apple unveils iPhone Duo, Its first foldable iPhone

By Zoila Palma: Apple has unveiled the iPhone Duo, its first foldable iPhone, featuring a new design that combines a compact 5.4-inch outer display with a 7.6-inch inner screen when fully opened.

Apple says the device is its thinnest iPhone ever when unfolded and is designed to provide a larger canvas for gaming, multitasking and viewing content while maintaining a pocket-friendly form factor when closed.

The iPhone Duo is powered by Apple’s new A20 Pro chip and features an advanced thermal management system, a custom-designed vapor chamber and a dual-battery architecture aimed at delivering high performance and all-day battery life.

The new foldable iPhone features a 48MP Fusion Main camera capable of capturing images at up to 48MP resolution, along with an integrated optical-quality 2x Telephoto capability.

Apple says the folding design also enables new ways of using the camera, while the device incorporates Camera Control and a new Siri Camera mode that allows Siri to analyze what users are viewing through the camera and respond to questions or take actions.

Apple said that the phone will be available in Star White and Night Sky, with pre-orders beginning October 16 and availability starting October 23.

World.title: Friends for Conservation and Development detects possible screwworm infestation in Scarlet Macaws
World.content:
Friends for Conservation and Development detects possible screwworm infestation in Scarlet Macaws

By Zoila Palma: Friends for Conservation and Development (FCD) has raised concerns over possible screwworm infestation in two wild species recorded in the Western Maya Mountains landscape.

FCD said its research team captured camera-trap images showing signs consistent with screwworm infestation in a puma (Puma concolor) and a post-fledging scarlet macaw (Ara macao cyanoptera).

According to FCD, the observations have prompted concern about the potential implications of screwworm for Belize’s wildlife.

FCD noted that while the population-level effects of screwworm on wild animals in Belize are not yet fully understood, the images provide an important warning that warrants closer attention.

FCD said the findings highlight the need for continued wildlife monitoring, documentation and research to better understand the prevalence and potential impact of the infestation on wild species.

World.title: 19-year-old Belize City man charged with murder of Kareem Garcia
World.content:
19-year-old Belize City man charged with murder of Kareem Garcia

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police have formally arrested and charged 19-year-old Leon Emmanuel St. Clair of Belize City with the murder of Kareem Garcia, who was gunned down in Cotton Tree Village last week.

Garcia, 23, of Unitedville Village, was killed at around 10:00 a.m. on Monday, August 31, 2026, while he was with coworkers in Cotton Tree.

Police said Garcia was approached by two men travelling on a motorcycle. One of the men reportedly produced a firearm and fired several shots, fatally injuring Garcia.

Garcia was reportedly working with a contractor carrying out road works near the King’s Children’s Home when the shooting occurred.

At a police briefing following the murder, Assistant Superintendent of Police Stacy Smith said investigators had not yet established a motive. Police also confirmed that Garcia was known to them and had a firearm-related matter before the court.

Police have now announced that St. Clair has been formally arrested and charged with Garcia’s murder. The charge remains an allegation until proven in court.

World.title: Magical history tour makes its way through Benque Viejo del Carmen
World.content:
Magical history tour makes its way through Benque Viejo del Carmen

By Zoila Palma: The Belize @45 Magical History Tour continued its journey across the country with a stop in Benque Viejo del Carmen, Cayo District, bringing history, dialogue and critical reflection to students and community members as Belize prepares to celebrate 45 years of independence.

Led by the Institute for Social & Cultural Research (ISCR-NICH) in partnership with historian Dr. Assad Shoman, the tour encourages Belizeans to examine the country’s journey toward independence, the experiences that shaped the nation and the continuing importance of decolonization.

On September 4, Dr. Shoman met with students of Mopan Technical High School, engaging them in discussions about Belize’s history, national identity and the different perspectives that have influenced the country’s development.

The conversation continued later that evening at the Benque House of Culture, where community leaders and residents participated in a public forum to share perspectives and reflect on Belize’s past.

The Magical History Tour will continue its journey with stops in Orange Walk on September 15 and Corozal on September 16.

World.title: Compol urges Belizeans to celebrate St. George’s Caye Day safely and responsibly
World.content:
Compol urges Belizeans to celebrate St. George’s Caye Day safely and responsibly

By Zoila Palma: Commissioner of Police Dr. A. Richard Rosado is urging Belizeans to celebrate Battle of St. George’s Caye Day responsibly, peacefully and safely as the country commemorates the historic occasion on September 10.

Commissioner Rosado extended warm wishes to Belizeans and reflected on the significance of the holiday, saying, “This historic occasion reminds us of the courage, resilience, and unity that have shaped our nation’s identity.”

He encouraged citizens to honor the sacrifices of those who came before them by respecting one another and embracing the spirit of patriotism.

The Commissioner also called on the public to work together with law enforcement to maintain safety throughout the celebrations.

“On behalf of the Belize Police Department, I encourage everyone to enjoy the festivities safely and to work together to keep our communities secure throughout the celebrations,” Rosado said.

As celebrations take place across the country, the Belize Police Department is encouraging the public to exercise caution, respect others and celebrate responsibly.

World.title: International News: Mexico’s Inflation hits 3.26% in August
World.content:
International News: Mexico’s Inflation hits 3.26% in August

By Zoila Palma: Mexico’s annual inflation rate accelerated in August for the first time in five months, according to official data released today, while underlying price pressures continued to ease.

Consumer prices in Latin America’s second-largest economy rose 3.26% in the year through August, up from 3.12% in July but slightly below economists’ forecast of 3.3%.

The increase comes as the Bank of Mexico maintains a cautious approach to further interest-rate cuts. Pantheon Macroeconomics chief Latin America economist Andres Abadia said persistent services inflation and the possibility of temporary shocks, including El Niño and geopolitical disruptions, give policymakers “little reason to resume easing soon.” Bank of Mexico Deputy Governor Jonathan Heath has also said the central bank should not cut rates again in the short term.

On a monthly basis, consumer prices increased 0.20% in August, compared with a 0.03% rise in July and below the 0.25% increase economists had expected.

Mexico’s government has projected that inflation will end 2026 at 3.5%, before slowing to 3.0% by the end of 2027, according to a draft budget proposal submitted to Congress.

Meanwhile, core inflation, which excludes some volatile food and energy prices, showed signs of easing.

World.title: Central Bank to pay almost $27,000 after tribunal rules termination was unfair and unjustified
World.content:
Central Bank to pay almost $27,000 after tribunal rules termination was unfair and unjustified

By Zoila Palma: The Essential Services Arbitration Tribunal has ruled that the termination of Central Bank of Belize employee Dapheen Bowen was unjustified and procedurally unfair, awarding her BZ$26,998.50 in compensation.

The decision followed a dispute brought by the Christian Workers Union (CWU) on Bowen’s behalf after the parties exhausted the grievance procedures under their Collective Bargaining Agreement.

Bowen had worked at the Central Bank for approximately 19 years as a senior clerk in the Economic Data Management Unit before her employment was terminated in June 2025 following disciplinary proceedings related to a personal social media post.

After reviewing evidence and submissions from both sides, the Tribunal found that the Bank failed to comply with disciplinary procedures under Article 7 of the Collective Bargaining Agreement, including the requirement to provide Bowen with written notice of the complaint and an opportunity to respond before disciplinary action was taken.

The Tribunal also found that the disciplinary process did not comply with the suspension and dismissal procedures established under the agreement and failed to meet the requirements of natural justice.

It further determined that the circumstances did not justify invoking the agreement’s exigency exception and concluded that termination was a disproportionate sanction. Although reinstatement was considered, the Tribunal determined that it was not practical because of the breakdown in the employment relationship and the time that had passed since Bowen’s dismissal.

The Tribunal therefore declared Bowen’s termination unfair and unjustified and awarded her BZ$26,998.50, subject to applicable statutory deductions.

The Labour Department subsequently reminded employers that collective bargaining agreements form an integral part of employment relationships and must be followed when handling disciplinary matters.

World.title: Government enacts new Occupational Safety and Health Act
World.content:
Government enacts new Occupational Safety and Health Act

By Zoila Palma: The Government of Belize has enacted the Occupational Safety and Health Act, 2026, introducing a modern legal framework aimed at strengthening the protection of workers and improving safety, health and welfare standards in workplaces across the country.

The legislation, enacted and gazetted on September 9, repeals the longstanding Factories Act and replaces it with standards designed to reflect current workplace conditions and international best practices.

The new Act applies to a broad range of employment settings, including public and private-sector workplaces, construction sites, industrial facilities, domestic work environments and certain remote work arrangements.

It establishes clearer responsibilities for employers and workers and creates the National Occupational Safety and Health Advisory Committee and the Occupational Safety and Health Inspectorate to oversee policy development, standards, inspections, compliance monitoring and public awareness.

Under the legislation, employers will be required to take all reasonably practicable measures to protect workers, including conducting risk assessments, managing workplace hazards, improving accident and occupational disease reporting and implementing preventive measures.

Workers will also receive stronger protections, including safeguards against reprisals for reporting unsafe conditions and the right to refuse dangerous work where they reasonably believe there is an imminent and serious threat to their health or safety.

The Act further establishes requirements for the safe management of hazardous substances, chemicals, biological agents and other occupational risks, while strengthening worker participation through workplace Safety and Health Committees and Safety and Health Representatives.

However, although the legislation has already been enacted and gazetted, its provisions will come into force in phases through commencement orders issued by the responsible Minister, allowing time for the necessary institutional and administrative arrangements to be established.

The Labour Department will lead implementation through the establishment of the Occupational Safety and Health Inspectorate, development of regulations and codes of practice, nationwide public education campaigns, training for inspectors, employers and workers, and the creation of reporting and compliance systems.

The Government described the legislation as one of Belize’s most significant advances in labour protection in decades, saying it provides a foundation for safer, healthier and more productive workplaces while promoting greater cooperation among government, employers and workers.

World.title: Costly prisons
World.content:
In this August 2021 photo George Williams appears to be pondering his future while standing in the doorway of his house in Linstead, St Catherine. Williams who spent over 42 years in prison on murder charges despite being found unfit to plead from 1971, was released in 2020. He sued the State and was awarded $120 million in damages.

WITH the majority of lawsuits against the State filed by inmates seeking millions in compensation based on complaints about lack of bathroom facilities, overcrowding and general prison conditions, the Attorney General’s Chambers has recommended that the Department of Corrections “address the systematic deficiencies and the administrative shortcomings in order to cauterise the influx of these types of cases”.

“We have a lot of cases before the court that highlight these challenges,” director of state proceedings in the Attorney General’s Department Faith Hall said Tuesday on day two of the 14th annual Association of Caribbean Heads of Corrections and Prison Services (ACHCPS) Conference.

The confab is hosted by the Department of Correctional Services (DCS), Jamaica at the AC Hotel Kingston.

According to Hall, there are currently 10 claims before the Constitutional Court awaiting a ruling on these matters.

Addressing the issue of how the DCS can implement policies or amend systems to stem the influx of civil cases, Hall said chief among the Chambers’ recommendations is that the institution should “allow, where reasonable, liberal use of bathroom facilities; discourage the use of buckets for disposal of excrement; create a system of oversight for cleaning parties or manage it more closely or reimagine what is there; create a system of oversight to increase food standards and implement rehabilitation programmes focusing on hygiene and behaviour”.

Another area of concern is inmates’ lack of knowledge about the channels through which they can access legal help from outside the prison walls.

“The thinking is that when an inmate comes in they get an orientation package that informs about their release date, for example,” Hall suggested, adding that information about how to file appeals should also be included.

She said while the prison’s Bail and Appeal Section offers inmates help in filing appeals, it needs to do more in pointing them to the source of legal advice. According to Hall, a lot of the complaints by inmates is that when they go to that division they are discouraged from filing an appeal. She noted, however, that these claims have not been proven.

Hall also urged the DCS to make a strong push to address unsafe conditions within prisons as there is a serious possibility that DCS would be blamed if an inmate is injured by another using contraband.

“The responsibility is a multi-stakeholder one, in terms of preventing these kinds of claims that we are seeing at the Attorney General’s Chambers which are many times difficult for us to defend in court in this current climate where the society has become more aware of their rights and the society has become more litigious. Once it is [that] their rights are infringed — and there are attorneys there who are seeking out these persons — a claim will be filed,” Hall warned.

She noted that while many of the systematic failures which trigger lawsuits do not rest with the DCS alone, “the fact remains that the DCS plays an important role in advocating for the resources needed to carry out the functions given to it”.

Highlighting other claims being brought because of breach of constitutional rights or systematic deficiencies, Hall said these come from individuals “found unfit to plead and mental health patients” in addition to claims hinging on the inhumane and degrading conditions of prisons and unsafe custodial conditions.

She referenced the cases of Noel Chambers, an 81-year-old Jamaican man who died in custody on January 27, 2020, after being imprisoned for 40 years without ever standing trial, and George Williams who was released in 2020 after he spent over 42 years in prison on murder charges despite being found unfit to plead from 1971. She said these were cases of individuals being lost in the system, due to a multiplicity of errors on the part of various State actors, which have caused taxpayers dearly.

“What is important to note is that there were review mechanisms in place specifically to prevent a mentally ill person from being indefinitely detained without judicial oversight. However, regrettably those safeguards were not implemented in Mr Williams’ case,” Hall said.

“The responsibility of bringing him back before the court is not the DCS’s, so to speak. He was being housed by the DCS; there should have been some alert to say this was the situation and this was happening,” she added, pointing out that those shortfalls led to approximately $120 million in damages being awarded to Williams following the ruling by the court.

She said the department has appealed the ruling but only in respect of the quantum.

“The issues in relation to the failings and the breach of his constitutional rights were clear and we really wouldn’t have any defence for that. But we do believe the judge was a little heavy-handed, in terms of the award. But what the decision reinforced is that there are consequences that the State faces when it fails to address deficiencies in the prison’s administration, especially where vulnerable persons with mental illness are concerned,” she said and mooted electronic systems for tracking inmates among the methods to prevent them from being lost in the system.

In the meantime, she said while the ruling in relation to Williams’ payout is being appealed, $35 million of the $120 million was paid over to him in August this year “as a portion of what we think the claim is worth… as a show of good faith”.

The three-day conference, which began on Monday, is being convened under the theme ‘One Caribbean, One Vision’ and brings together senior correctional leaders, policymakers, and technical experts from across the Caribbean to discuss innovations, legal governance, and rehabilitation.

World.title: More school mergers coming
World.content:
Education Minster Senator Dr Dana Morris Dixon and Hydel Cumberland Principal Carlon Pitt unveil the newly merged school’s name, crest, and motto on Monday. (Photo: Garfield Robinson)

Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness has signalled that more underpopulated schools could be consolidated or left off the Government’s reconstruction list, arguing that Jamaica cannot continue maintaining costly education facilities with too few students to fill them.

Speaking during Tuesday’s official launch of the Jamaica Reconstruction and Resilience Oversight Committee (JAMRROC) at Jamaica House in Kingston, Holness stressed the rebuilding of Jamaica after Hurricane Melissa would not simply mean restoring every damaged asset to its previous form.

He said some infrastructure would be rebuilt differently, some would be relocated, and some assets would not be rebuilt at all — a position he linked directly to the Government’s plans to consolidate parts of the education system.

“Please note they will not necessarily be rebuilt in the same place or in the same way, and there are some assets that will not be rebuilt. I think the public should become aware of that… We are in the process of consolidating our education infrastructure. There are… many schools that are underpopulated. And I know there is a great attachment to the schools because they signal the life of the community, but it is highly inefficient,” he said.

Holness argued that maintaining underpopulated schools places an unnecessary burden on taxpayers, as Government still has to cover fixed costs regardless of enrolment.

He said it was inefficient to maintain facilities designed for 1,000 students when only about 300 are using them, with taxpayers effectively footing the bill for space that remains unused because of sentimental attachment to the school.

Holness did not identify specific additional schools for closure or merger, nor did he announce a list of institutions that would be excluded from reconstruction. Instead, he described consolidation as part of a broader rethink of the country’s education infrastructure, against the backdrop of the massive rebuilding exercise triggered by Hurricane Melissa which ravaged sections of the country last year on October 28.

The prime minister’s comments come as Government has already begun restructuring schools where existing facilities and enrolment levels make consolidation a practical option.

On Monday, Education Minister Senator Dr Dana Morris Dixon officially unveiled the newly merged Hydel Cumberland High School in Portmore, St Catherine, bringing the two school communities together at the former Cumberland campus.

The move followed concerns about infrastructure at Hydel and the underutilisation of Cumberland, which had capacity for 1,200 students but was operating with just over 300 when Morris Dixon visited about a year earlier.

Morris Dixon said the merger was intended to make better use of existing resources and form part of a strategic restructuring of the education system.

“One of the things we had thought about was potentially moving the children in little groups to different schools, putting them all around St Catherine. But I think this is the best option. I think this was quite strategic in nature, and that’s how we’re going to continue to do this restructuring of education in Jamaica — be strategic — because now that we have one institution instead of two, it means we can direct more resources to one… that is our plan,” she said.

However on Tuesday, the prime minister acknowledged that schools are not simply buildings and that closing or consolidating one can have consequences for the communities around it.

He said the Government therefore intends to consult before making such decisions, while maintaining that public money must be used responsibly.

World.title: Caribbean Music Awards to host landmark weekend celebration in Trinidad
World.content:
King of Soca Machel Montano (left) shares the stage with dancehall artiste Ayetian during last year’s CMAs in New York.

AFTER three years of celebrating Caribbean excellence in New York City, the Caribbean Music Awards (CMAs) is coming home. For the first time since its inception, the awards ceremony will be staged on Caribbean soil, with Trinidad and Tobago selected to welcome artistes, industry stakeholders and music lovers for what is expected to be a landmark celebration of regional sound and culture.

The move will also usher in a new era for the CMAs as the event will move from a single celebratory evening to an immersive weekend featuring networking, industry discussions, cultural showcases and opportunities for fans to engage more closely with the people behind the music.

For Paige de Leon, regional public relations strategist for the CMAs, the expansion reflects the steady growth of an event that has increasingly established itself as a credible platform for Caribbean talent.

“I think that when you’re building a movement like this, you are going to find that if the quality of the offering and your product is really solid, and there is authenticity in your intention, you are going to see growth,” she said. “The growth is all positive. One of the things that I most appreciate about the Caribbean Music Awards, as a Caribbean woman, is that it is an intuitive entity that seeks to respond to the needs of its audience — the Caribbean Diaspora. That speaks very highly of its founders, and now to the fact that it will be held in Trinidad and Tobago.”

Since its launch, the CMAs has sought to provide a dedicated stage on which the breadth and diversity of Caribbean music can be recognised. Its growing reach was underscored last year when the awards were broadcast on BET, introducing the ceremony and its honourees to an even wider audience. Having strengthened its footing internationally, de Leon said the time had come to ensure that the people who live within the region and continue to fuel its musical movements could experience the ceremony for themselves.

“We’re bringing it to Trinidad because we want to make sure that the people of the Caribbean have the opportunity to experience the ceremonial splendour of their music in this way,” she explained. “We have spent the last three years or so building the event, and last year the CMAs were shown on a major network, BET, and that was a very significant moment for us. Now we want to connect our people with the music. We want the people who fuel this music to have access to this and how it is evolving.”

That connection will stretch beyond the awards stage. The weekend will begin with a Friday-night networking experience, allowing guests to engage with artistes, participants and other members of the entertainment industry. A celebration of the steelpan will also form part of the programme, paying tribute to an instrument born in Trinidad and Tobago that has become an enduring symbol of Caribbean creativity and identity. The weekend will also include a discussion forum bringing together various industry professionals to explore the Caribbean music industry’s place within the global entertainment landscape.

According to de Leon, the forum will provide space for serious conversations about the business, development and international integration of the region’s music.

“There is an intellectual side to the music that we must not forget,” she said. “That will make for a very robust and rounded weekend of activities.”

While several Caribbean destinations could have provided an appropriate backdrop for the historic occasion, de Leon said Trinidad and Tobago emerged as the most natural fit. Beyond its globally recognised Carnival and rich musical traditions, she explained that the twin-island republic possesses the infrastructure and expertise required to successfully stage large-scale entertainment events. Its reputation for celebration is also expected to bring a distinctive energy to the CMAs’ first Caribbean staging.

“We could have picked anywhere in the region to host the awards because, really and truly, the music is everywhere,” de Leon said. “However, we felt Trinidad and Tobago was a natural fit because we have the physical and human-resource infrastructure that routinely churns out shows of this nature. Trinidad is party central, so there will be a lot of activity that will make for a very interesting and vibrant weekend in the capital, Port of Spain. We’re all excited to have a successful weekend.”

The decision to bring the awards into the region also signals that the CMAs is no longer simply an ambitious new undertaking. Though entering only its fourth year, the ceremony is already being positioned as an institution capable of preserving legacies while acknowledging the contemporary artistes carrying Caribbean music into new markets.

“I think, over time, people realised that this wasn’t something that was going to stop and start again or fade away,” de Leon said. “There is a lasting, legacy-type feel to the awards, even though we’re just four years in.”

That commitment to legacy will be reflected in the recognition of Jamaican dancehall trailblazer Patra, whose commanding image and unapologetic expression helped introduce a new representation of Caribbean womanhood to international audiences.

For de Leon, the honour is also deeply personal. “Patra is one of those artistes who has had a really transformational impact on the music. She had such a significant impact on me as a young Caribbean woman when I saw how she handled herself and how authentic she was about her sensuality as a woman and her experiences,” she shared. “She has been a significant influence in spreading Caribbean music across the world. She’s very special to us because of what she changed in how we see ourselves, and we just want to give her her flowers.”

Although Trinidad and Tobago will be the first Caribbean destination to host the ceremony, organisers do not intend for it to be the last. The long-term vision is to rotate the awards throughout the region, allowing the countries that have shaped Caribbean music to participate directly in its celebration while benefiting economically from the event.

“The intention is most certainly to have the awards move around and have all the countries that contribute to the success of music in the region be a part of the celebrations,” de Leon said. “When you have an awards ceremony like this, it means you’re stimulating the economy in the country where that ceremony is being held, and we want that for every country in the Caribbean. We want the CMAs to become an important element of the global tourism product.”

World.title: $5-BILLION GROWTH DRIVE
World.content:
WISYNCO Group Limited is moving to spend up to $5 billion on its operations over the next three years to meet the growing demand for its manufacturing and distribution business lines.

That’s the update provided by Wisynco Group Chairman William Mahfood following the release of the company’s audited financials for the June 2026 financial year (FY). The next round of investments is focused on growing the company’s manufacturing capacity and warehouse space for its expanding proprietary and third-party product portfolio.

“If you were to lay it out on a map, over the next three years you’d see continued investment in capital in terms of buildings and equipment. We’re looking at even more factory and production [capacity] in the next year,” Mahfood told the Jamaica Observer during a recent phone call.

Wisynco spent $3.24 billion in capital expenditure (capex) on its property, plant and equipment for its 2026 FY, which saw $1.26 billion deployed on land and buildings and $1.13 billion for ongoing work.

Between the 2023 and 2025 FY, the company spent $14.65 billion in capex which supported its ability to meet domestic demand for its existing products, diversify into new packaging types and launch its alcohol portfolio, including its Legend beer. The company invested US$35 million ($5.47 billion) on its new brewery and manufacturing facility.

Mahfood revealed that the company recently acquired additional land at Lakes Pen, St Catherine, and is expected to complete a new 70,000 square foot warehouse by the end of the year which is near completion. This is on top of the new 60,000-square-foot distribution centre to be constructed in Lacovia, St Elizabeth.

“We acquired some land for further expansion across the road. So, we’re looking at building a new distribution centre. We’re going to submit the plans in probably six months,” Mahfood explained.

Wisynco’s expansion comes at a time when its revenue grew 14 per cent to $65.35 billion, underpinned by a diverse product mix and introduction of new products such as the manufactured alcohol and Stone’s Ginger Wine portfolios which contributed $397 million during the year.

However, the company also had to book $454 million related to the new special consumption tax on non-alcoholic sweetened beverages which it must book as revenue and deduct as an expense under cost of sales.

“We’re seeing steady growth every month on the new business, so that’s positive. Overall, we’re happy about the turnout. We’re excited about this year,” Mahfood explained on the new alcohol portfolio.

While the company is spending significant sums on marketing and promotions for its Legend and alcohol portfolio, it has not begun to significantly push this product in the export market.

Wisynco’s exports grew 26 per cent to $1.55 billion for the 2026 FY but represented 2.38 per cent of group revenue. Exports represented $628 million or 1.97 per cent of revenue in 2021, demonstrating how fast domestic sales continue to grow.

“Our main focus is still in Europe. We just started in Canada with a new partnership with GraceKennedy,” Mahfood noted while pointing to the USA and Eastern Caribbean as other focus markets.

The company’s operating profit climbed 12 per cent to $5.87 billion as it spent more on advertising, staff and property expenses following its recent expansion initiatives.

However, earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA) improved 16 per cent to $8.62 billion for 2026. The EBITDA metric is used to remove certain non-cash expenses like depreciation which lowers the company’s operating profit and shows the business’ core profit capacity.

Although Wisynco generated $531.26 million in finance income from its cash and investment portfolio, the higher debt balance pushed up its finance costs by 2.5 times to $847.57 million. The company reported $87.16 million in share of profit from its 30 per cent stakes in Ringtail Holdings Limited and JP Snacks Caribbean Limited.

Ringtail, the parent company of Select Brands Limited, reported $8.07 billion in revenue and $711.46 million in net profit since the July 2025 acquisition. JP Snacks reported $2.19 billion in revenue and a net loss of $29.23 million for the reported period.

While Wisynco reported a two per cent rise in profit before tax to $5.64 billion, its net profit fell seven per cent to $4.12 billion due to the increase in deferred taxes. The earnings per share declined from $1.17 to $1.10.

Despite the slightly lower net profit, Mahfood is confident about the new year which will see the company ramping up initiatives to grow its manufacturing and distribution reach. This comes against the backdrop of the western Jamaica rebuild via the National Reconstruction and Resilience Authority, which will see increased spending in the economy.

“As long as we have no more hurricanes, I think this is going to be a very vibrant winter season going into next year. We’re very excited,” the Wisynco chairman noted.

Wisynco’s asset base improved eight per cent to $47.30 billion as its PP&E stood at $18.37 billion, inventory at $8.53 billion, investments at $5.46 billion and cash at $5.34 billion. Wisynco’s sole stage two investment was restructured in December 2025 while the remaining $4.36 billion in investments are carried at stage one.

Total liabilities increased six per cent to $17.09 billion with total debt of $6.52 billion, while equity grew nine per cent to $30.21 billion.

Wisynco closed Tuesday at $20.14, leaving the stock up eight per cent in 2026 with a market capitalisation of $76.58 billion. That translates to a price to earnings ratio of 18.18 times.

Director Francois Chalifour sold 2,655,000 ordinary shares during the 2026 FY while Chairman William Mahfood and CEO Andrew Mahfood had reduced direct stakes in the business. Executive Lelani Hunt sold 412,937 ordinary shares, but Assistant Corporate Secretary Vanessa Young acquired 3,629 ordinary shares.

GraceKennedy Pension Fund Custodian Limited acquired an additional 15,556,346 shares to become the fifth largest shareholder with 48,478,631 ordinary shares or a 1.28 per cent stake. SJIML A/C 3119 and DOMHAD Investments Limited acquired an additional 2,038,856 ordinary shares and 806,949 ordinary shares, respectively. Sagicor Pooled Equity Fund is now the 10th largest shareholder with 26,913,562 ordinary shares or a 0.71 per cent stake.

World.title: GET BACK ONSIDE
World.content:
FIFA President Gianni Infantino (centre) addresses a round table press briefing at the end of the FIFA Executive Summit at the Montego Bay Convention Centre in St James in January 2018. Also pictured are JFF President Michael Ricketts (left) and Concacaf President Victor Montagliani.

JAMAICA Football Federation (JFF) President Michael Ricketts is calling for unity between FIFA President Gianni Infantino and Concacaf President Victor Montagliani as tensions between the two reportedly continue to escalate.

The relationship between both men has come under scrutiny recently amid the fallout over Infantino’s scrapped proposal to sell stakes in FIFA competitions, including the men’s and women’s World Cup.

Montagliani, who is a Canadian and Infantino’s vice-president at FIFA, is being touted as a potential challenger for the presidential elections next year. Infantino, who is Swiss, is seeking a fourth term as head of football’s world governing body, and is the only candidate who has publicly declared his intention to run on Sunday, with nominations closing in November.

UEFA, however, have called on Infantino to step down while reports from Europe suggest its member associations would strongly back Montagliani should he enter the race. Several European football associations have publicly withdrawn their support for Infantino, who has been in office since 2016.

Last month, Concacaf, which governs North America, Central America, and the Caribbean, released a joint statement with UEFA, and the Asian Football Confederation strongly criticising Infantino.

“When trust is broken through deception, when an individual places himself above the collective that entrusted him with authority, that duty has been abandoned,” the statement said.

Montagliani and Infantino reportedly had awkward moments after Infantino’s impromptu visit to the Caribbean Football Union Presidents’ Meeting and Under-14 Challenger Series in Dominican Republic last month, which Ricketts attended. Montagliani had written to Infantino asking him not to attend.

During the tournament, Montagliani said he stood by the statement” and was coy when asked by

Sky News if Infantino should resign.

“That’s his decision, not my decision,” Montagliani told Sky. “My view is we have to follow proper governance processes and I have to respect my colleagues with that. Once we follow that then those decisions can be made my individuals.”

Reports from Europe also say that Concacaf members were “infuriated” by Infantino’s behaviour.

Ricketts, though, told the Jamaica Observer that both presidents were welcomed equally.

“No truth that Infantino was snubbed,” Ricketts said. “We did show him a lot of respect. In fact, both gentlemen — Montagliani and Infantino — were treated with utmost respect. We showed both of them love.”

However, Ricketts is hopeful that two can come together for football’s development.

“What we really want is for both gentlemen, Infantino and Montagliani, to come together and put the differences aside because obviously right now there’s a strained relationship,” he said.

“I would love for them to just put these issues aside, rekindle the love and warmth and the camaraderie and let’s move on with the growth of the football because both gentlemen in their own jurisdiction and their own portfolio responsibilities have done very well for football and I just hate to think that they are not now seeing eye to eye. The most important thing for me right now is for both of them to come together, put the past behind, get over this strained relationship and both of them continue to do what they’ve been doing for football.”

Ricketts says the JFF board will ultimately decide on supporting Infantino in the upcoming election in Morocco next March. Infantino needs the support of at least 106 of FIFA’s 211 member associations to secure re-election.

However, at least 14 FIFA member associations have publicly withdrawn support, including England and Italy.

Ricketts, though, says he won’t be influenced by the views and stance of some of the established nations.

“When Infantino tried to increase the numbers [for the FIFA World Cup], some of the bigger countries say that he was trying to bring in weak Caribbean teams into the World Cup,” he said.

“When he decided that he would increase our subvention, a number of big countries say that the Caribbean countries can’t manage from a fiscal perspective. So I am not even watching some of these countries because like I say, that’s how politics is. People will have different views and different opinions for different reasons.”

Infantino won a contested election in 2016 to replace Sepp Blatter, defeating Sheikh Salman bin Ebrahim Al Khalifa but has since been re-elected unopposed in 2019 and 2023.

World.title: WapiPay enters Jamaica through JN Money partnership
World.content:
WapiPay co-founder Paul Ndichu (second right) makes a point at the press event to formally announce the partnership agreement with JN Money to support payments to Jamaica through WapiPay’s global network. The signing was done at JN Group’s corporate office on September 3. JN Money will serve exclusively as the local payout conduit, using its established remittance infrastructure to deliver funds to recipients in Jamaica. Also photographed are (from left) Cedrica Reid, head of marketing and sales at JN Money; Horace Hines, general manager, JN Money; and Edward Ndichu, co-founder, WapiPay.

JN Money Services has added Africa-focused fintech WapiPay to its international remittance network, giving the cross-border payments company a foothold in Jamaica following regulatory approval to operate locally.

Under the arrangement, WapiPay customers will be able to send funds to Jamaica for collection at JN Money locations or have the money deposited directly into recipients’ local bank accounts.

Founded in Singapore in 2019, WapiPay operates from offices in Nairobi, Kenya; and Kampala, Uganda; and provides cross-border payment services to individuals, merchants and businesses. The company says it has established payment corridors across Africa, Asia, the United Kingdom and the United States.

WapiPay received approval from the Bank of Jamaica earlier this year to enter the local market, with JN Money serving as its local payout partner. The approval has also been independently reported as coming from the central bank.

The move comes as remittance providers continue to expand digital and cross-border payment options in a market that remains an important source of foreign exchange for Jamaica.

Total remittance inflows to Jamaica amounted to US$3.36 billion in 2024, equivalent to about 15.3 per cent of gross domestic product, according to Bank of Jamaica data. The United States remained by far the largest source market, accounting for roughly two-thirds of inflows.

JN Money General Manager Horace Hines said the WapiPay agreement forms part of the company’s efforts to widen the number of channels through which money can be sent to Jamaica.

“We are deliberate about building strategic partnerships that expand the ways customers can send money to Jamaica while making the remittance experience more convenient, accessible and reliable. As customer needs continue to evolve and demand for digital financial services grows, we remain focused on identifying innovative solutions and strengthening our network to better serve Jamaicans and their families, wherever they are in the world,” Hines said in a press statement.

JN Money currently has a presence in 18 countries, including Cayman Islands, Antigua, Guyana, and Turks and Caicos.

The company has also been adding international partners. Its portfolio includes Mastercard Transaction Services, which supports cross-border remittances from the United Kingdom, United States, Canada, and Cayman Islands.

Meanwhile, Jamaica marks WapiPay’s entry point into the Caribbean as it seeks to extend payment links between the region and markets where it already operates.

Josephat Nelson Mados, WapiPay country director for Jamaica, said the companies expect the partnership to improve connections between the Caribbean and markets in Africa, North America, the United Kingdom, and Asia.

He said customers are expected to benefit from competitive pricing, faster processing and greater visibility of fees, foreign exchange rates and transaction status. However, details around comparative pricing or processing-time data weren’t immediately clear.

WapiPay said its platform supports automated payment routing, real-time transaction tracking, reconciliation, settlement tracking, and partner reporting.

World.title: Rough start
World.content:
Grade two students at Holland Primary School in class under a bamboo structure on Monday. (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

THE education ministry on Monday reported a generally smooth reopening of schools across the island for the start of the 2026/27 academic year but principals, mostly in hurricane-ravaged western Jamaica, highlighted a raft of difficulties.

Among the complaints were incomplete repairs as well as classes held in heat-trapping tents that turn into sweltering ovens under the tropical sun.

“Based on preliminary data received from all seven educational regions covering approximately 1,000 schools, only three schools did not open today, meaning that approximately 99.7 per cent of the schools captured in the data were able to open on the first day of the new school year,” the ministry said in a news release.

While the ministry said late furniture delivery was among the most frequently reported challenges on Monday, Jamaica Observer journalists received first-hand reports of the rough start to the academic year in the sections of the island that suffered the brunt of Hurricane Melissa’s fury last October.
