World.title: New Poll Lays Bare Worst Result for HDZ in the Last Two Years
World.content:
September the 8th, 2026 – A brand new poll has showcased the absolute worst result for HDZ in the last two years, with Prime Minister Andrej Plenković personally scoring very poorly.

Public dissatisfaction over the hazardous waste affair in Lika has been reflected on the political scene, as shown by the latest monthly CRO Demoskop survey. Index reports that according to the poll conducted for RTL this month, both HDZ and SDP recorded a significant drop in support, with the ruling party, being HDZ, falling to its lowest level in the past two years.

If parliamentary elections had been held at the beginning of the month, HDZ would still have been the relative winner. Index reports that the CRO Demoskop survey was conducted by the agency Promocija plus from 1 to 3 September using a telephone survey (CATI) on a representative sample of 1,000 respondents. The sample was stratified by counties and settlement size, with control of socio-demographic characteristics. The standard sampling error is ±3.04% at a 95% confidence level.

most and Možemo! outperform hdz and sdp

According to the latest poll, HDZ has the support of 25.3% of voters, a drop from 27% seen in July. This is also the party’s weakest result since April 2024. SDP is in second place with 20.5% support, also recording a decline from 21.5% in July and its lowest rating in the current term. Možemo! ranked third with 12.9% support, a slight increase from 12.2% in July. The biggest rise was recorded by Most, which jumped from 7.7% to 9.5%. It is followed by the party Drito with 1.8% and Domovinski pokret with 1.6%. Both parties have slightly lower support than in July. Most thus recorded a rise of 1.8 percentage points, and Možemo! of 0.7. HDZ is down by 1.7 percentage points, SDP by 1.0, and Drito and DP by 0.5 percentage points each.

Other parties have support below 1.5%. Above one percent are Domino (1.4%), Centar (1.1%), Pravo i pravda (1.1%), IDS (1.0%) and Nezavisna platforma Sjever (1.0%). Below that threshold are HNS (0.9%), Hrvatski suverenisti (0.8%), HSU (0.8%), HSS (0.7%), HSLS (0.4%) and Fokus (0.3%). All other parties together have two percent support, while undecided voters stand at 16.9%.

president milanović receives the most positive rating among politicians, while pm plenković receives the worst

The most positively perceived politicians are as follows:

Zoran Milanović – 23%

Andrej Plenković – 15.6%

Tomislav Tomašević – 4.1%

Marin Miletić – 3.8%

Ivana Kekin – 2.9%

Dalija Orešković – 2.7%

Nikola Grmoja – 2.5%

Ivan Anušić – 2.2%

Sandra Benčić – 1.6%

Biljana Borzan – 1.5%

The most negatively perceived politicians are as follows:

Andrej Plenković – 37.3%

Zoran Milanović – 12.3%

Tomislav Tomašević – 5.6%

Sandra Benčić – 2.5%

Ivan Penava – 2.3%

Milorad Pupovac – 2.1%

Dalija Orešković – 1.8%

Hrvoje Zekanović – 1.6%

Siniša Hajdaš Dončić – 1.4%

Andrija Mikulić – 1.4%

most believe the country is heading in the wrong direction

This September, only 17.5% of citizens believe that Croatia is moving in a good direction, a drop from 20.2% in July. At the same time, the share of those who think the direction is wrong rose from 70% to 74.6%. Undecided stand at 7.9%. Among HDZ voters optimism prevails and 55.4% of them consider the direction good. Voters of opposition parties are considerably more critical.

President Zoran Milanović received an average grade of 3.08 for his work. He received the highest grade from SDP voters (3.97) and the lowest from HDZ voters (2.32). The work of the Croatian Parliament was rated 2.16. It received the highest grade from HDZ voters (3.0) and the lowest from Možemo! platform voters (1.69). The Government received a grade of 2.23 for its work, the lowest grade in the past year. HDZ voters rated the Government’s work at 3.81, while voters of other parties were considerably stricter. Support for the Government’s policy fell to 25.7%, compared with 27.6% in July.

the appalling lika hazardous waste affair is the hot topic

The hazardous waste affair in Lika and other parts of the country was the most important topic of the past month for as many as 40.4% of respondents. This is one of the highest results for a single event since measurements began in 2004. In second place in importance is the fire in Omiš and the surrounding area, which 27.9% of citizens singled out as a key event. These are followed by the heatwave (5.4%), inflation (3.5%), the extraordinary session of Parliament (3.0%) and the rise in fuel prices (2.9%). Among the more important topics are also sporting successes, Thompson’s concert in Vukovar and arrests related to arson.

World.title: Estonian PM to officially offer former EDF commander the post of defense minister
World.content:
Prime Minister Kristen Michal will ask former Estonian Defense Forces commander Martin Herem to become the new defense minister.

According to Michal, Herem's experience and knowledge of what needs to be improved within the Ministry of Defense's area of responsibility make him a strong candidate. He added that Herem will most likely become the new defense minister.

It was previously reported that Prime Minister Michal had privately offered Herem the position of defense minister, but Herem himself has not publicly accepted the offer. It is now known that the Reform Party board will approve Herem's candidacy at its meeting on Tuesday.

According to Michal, Herem is demanding that defense spending remain at 5 percent. "His message to me, as well as to others who have asked him, has been that the Russian threat is real and must be addressed," he added.

According to the prime minister, Herem needs political support to carry out various reforms, including an overhaul of the defense sector. "The problems that exist there need to be resolved," Michal said.

Herem accepts

Herem confirmed to ERR on Wednesday afternoon that he has accepted Michal's offer and will take office as defense minister.

Had Herem turned down the offer, the Reform Party would have approached other candidates. Michal named Marko Mihkelson, Alar Laneman, Kalle Laanet, Eerik-Niiles Kross, Kristo Enn Vaga and Mati Raidma as other possible choices.

Asked whether the dismissal of Ministry of Defense Permanent Secretary Kaimo Kuusk is also an important issue for Herem, Michal said the former commander of the Estonian Defense Forces would be joining the ministry primarily to put the defense sector in order.

"In that sense, Kuusk's message has been honorable: He was the first to raise his hand and say that he takes responsibility. Hopefully, the government can dismiss him tomorrow and begin, so to speak, cleaning up or putting the ministry in order," Michal said.

Hanno Pevkur, who is still serving as defense minister, told ERR that he asked Permanent Secretary Kaimo Kuusk on Wednesday to step down. The government will approve the move on Thursday.

It emerged on Wednesday that Energy and Environment Minister Andres Sutt, a member of the Reform Party, will step down as minister. "Since we're already reshuffling the Cabinet, it makes sense to change ministers now as well," Michal said. The prime minister will look for a new minister both within and outside the party.

SDE leader finds proceedings unbecoming

Social Democratic Party (SDE) head Lauri Läänemets wrote on social media that he does not consider the appointment of a new defense minister, or the way it is being carried out, appropriate for a democratic state governed by the rule of law.

"The removal of Ministry of Defense Permanent Secretary Kaimo Kuusk is being carried out in the Georgian style, based on party interests, something we have previously seen in Viktor Orbán's Hungary or in Poland. A hallmark of democracy is a professional and apolitical civil service that is free from and protected against partisan agendas and political turmoil," he wrote.

"To prevent the politicization and political influencing of the civil service, the law lays down specific rules governing when and under what circumstances an official can be dismissed. The Government of the Republic Act specifically states that the end of a minister's term in office cannot serve as grounds for dismissing a secretary general. A secretary general can and may only be dismissed for objective reasons. A party's desire to bring someone in as defense minister is not an objective reason," Läänemets wrote.

"By demanding that the Ministry of Defense secretary general be dismissed, Martin Herem, and the Reform Party by carrying out that demand, are sending a signal to the civil service that the party and politicians stand above the law and an impartial state apparatus and must be obeyed. This is extremely damaging to the democratic and continuous functioning of the state," Läänemets said.

World.title: Parents sue Estonian school over early start time
World.content:
A dispute over the start time of the school day in Kõrveküla became so heated that a group of parents took the school operator to court.

More than 700 children attend Kõrveküla Basic School just outside Tartu. Although a government regulation says Estonia's general education schools should start at 9 a.m. from the 2026-2027 academic year, Kõrveküla has used an exemption to retain its decades-old 8 a.m. start.

Tartu Municipality, which operates the school, says changing public transportation schedules would be complicated and, more importantly, expensive.

"We are a sparsely populated area where Kõrveküla school is not just a community school and children come here from many different parts of the municipality," Tartu Deputy Municipal Mayor Agu Laas said.

Laas said bus schedules are coordinated with residents' work commutes and cannot be reorganized as quickly as the Ministry of Education and Research envisaged. He said a survey of parents, students and school staff found that roughly one-third wanted a 9 a.m. start, one-third did not and one-third had no preference.

A group of parents disputes that interpretation. This spring, 142 parents signed a petition calling for a later start, while 18 parents filed a case with the administrative court at the beginning of the summer seeking to force the school to begin classes at 9 a.m.

As far as is known, they are the first parents in Estonia to take the issue to court. They argue that scientific evidence shows later school start times benefit children's health.

Ott Oja, head of the Ministry of Education and Research's preschool and basic education department, agrees that research supports later starts.

"We know from decades of study after study that a later start to the school day translates to a significant extent into students getting more sleep," Oja said. "We also know very well that getting more sleep helps prevent a wide range of health problems, both mental and physical."

Parent Tanel Käär said the effects become particularly apparent as children enter adolescence and their sleep patterns change.

"I'm seeing exactly the same thing now with my older daughter," Käär said. "It's harder to wake up in the morning and she isn't sleepy in the evening."

Parent Marianne Tobro-Kerna said insufficient sleep affects not only children's moods but also their ability to learn throughout the day. Her eighth-grade son starts waking up at around 6 a.m. but struggles to get out of bed by 6:30.

"If a child is chronically overtired, that fatigue carries over into the afternoon, not just the morning," she said. "It isn't a matter of getting through the first class and then everything is fine."

Laas, however, said parents also bear responsibility for children's sleep schedules, including whether they go to bed at 10 p.m. or stay on their phones until midnight.

Tobro-Kerna rejected the argument that teenagers can simply go to bed earlier.

"That's not how a teenager's body works," she said. "A teenager's natural circadian rhythm means they need to fall asleep later and sleep longer in the morning."

The municipality and school administration say a 9 a.m. start would create other problems. In sparsely populated areas, many parents bring their children to school before starting work at 8 a.m., while beginning classes later would also push the end of the school day later.

Piret Jõul, Kõrveküla's head of studies, said older students could finish at 5 p.m., after which many would still have music lessons, sports practices or other extracurricular activities.

"I've thought about it myself and a child's day, during which they're actively engaged in things, would end at 9 or 10 p.m.," Jõul said. "I see it as actually doing children a disservice."

The Ministry of Education and Research. Source: Siim Lõvi/ERR

The government adopted the new start-time regulation in July 2025, giving school operators more than a year to prepare. However, the rules allow schools to retain an earlier start for compelling and carefully considered reasons.

Laas said the central issue for Tartu Municipality is the cost of reorganizing public transportation, which he estimated at more than €500,000.

Three of Tartu Municipality's six schools have moved to a 9 a.m. start, while Kõrveküla Basic School, Lähte Coeducational High School and Tabivere Basic School have retained earlier starts. Laas said those three schools depend on the same broader bus network, while the municipality's other schools have their own smaller bus routes.

The situation is far from unique to Tartu Municipality.

At ERR's request, the Estonian School Heads Association surveyed its members and received information from 122 schools. Of those, 54.5 percent did not change their start time this academic year. Only 31 begin at 9 a.m., while the first bell rings at 8:30 a.m. or earlier at 74 schools.

The pattern is also evident in Estonia's larger cities. In Tallinn, 36 of 61 municipal schools begin classes before 9 a.m. In Tartu, 10 of 23 city-run schools do not start at 9 a.m., while just one of Pärnu's 14 municipal schools does so.

The Ministry of Education and Research does not have comprehensive nationwide statistics, but the available figures suggest a large share of Estonian schools have retained earlier start times.

Laas criticized the ministry's approach, arguing municipalities should retain the right to decide when their schools begin and end.

Oja said the exemptions provided by the regulation are not intended to give municipalities unlimited discretion.

"This is an exceptional arrangement. The exception must have an end point," Oja said, adding that if transportation is the reason for an exemption, municipalities must work to resolve that problem.

Laas described the parents pursuing the court case as a vocal minority. The parents, however, say the school's survey was methodologically flawed and undemocratic. They argue its results could just as easily be interpreted as showing that 67 percent did not favor retaining the existing, earlier start time.

"Other schools have somehow found solutions," Käär said. "It's already working somewhere and I think we should learn from those solutions."

Tobro-Kerna said the municipality must find both a solution and the necessary funding because children's sleep and health justify the expense.

Court proceedings on the substance of the case are due to begin in November. However, the municipality has already indicated that Kõrveküla's school day could be moved to a 9 a.m. start next academic year.

World.title: Number of higher education students receiving needs-based support up by a quarter
World.content:
The number of bachelor's students in Estonia receiving need‑based support has risen nearly a quarter in four years, while more students work to cover rising costs.

While the mean monthly student income stands at €1,078, expenses average at almost the same: €1,023, and more than 60 percent of students now work while studying to make ends meet as the new academic year gets underway.

According to a recently completed Praxis study, expenses have grown nearly twice as fast as income for wage earners has, and students' income has increased considerably more slowly than that.

University of Tartu political science student Marian Müürsepp told ERR she knows many students who have even been skipping meals due to a shortage of funds. Others wait for reduced food items to go on sale, or wait until pastries get sold at half price in the evening. "Without my parents' support, I wouldn't be able to study in Tartu at all," she said.

Needs-based study allowances range from €150 to €440 a month, depending on household income. Students can apply if household income is below €756 per family member per month. A student is considered part of their parents' household until age 24, unless they marry or have a child earlier.

Ronja Ansmann, vice president of the Federation of Estonian Student Unions (Üliõpilaskondade liit), said the system's main flaw is how support gets calculated. "If you read the Family Law Act, it states that a student must be supported until the age of 21, which means that in practice the young person is left completely without protection, for three years," Ansmann said, adding that the system "simply isn't functioning at the moment."

However, Margus Haidak, senior adviser at the Ministry of Education and Research's higher education department, said boosting study allowances further would not be the rational thing to do at present. "The last time study allowances were increased, they were doubled. Today, spending on need‑based study allowances is around €15 million a year, and we see the primary priority as ensuring opportunities for tuition‑free study," he said.

Ansmann countered that while allowances were indeed raised in 2023, that was a one off: They had not increased at all from 2013 to 2023, and have not been raised again since.

Students can also apply for student loans of up to €6,000. Eneli Nairis, head of small‑scale financing at Swedbank, said demand has be rising every year since legislative changes in autumn 2022, with over 1,800 customers seen in 2024 — 4 percent of those eligible.

Müürsepp challenged the assumption that students are supposed to be poor. "I think that in the 21st century, getting a higher education should no longer mean that a person constantly has to worry about whether they have enough money for food or rent," she said. "That mentality should not be the norm."

World.title: Experiment: Pärnu County soil so 'alive' it devours pair of underpants in 3 months
World.content:
An unusual experiment at a horse farm near Pärnu revealed that underpants almost entirely degraded in the space of three months.

The purpose of the activity, at the Tori hobusekasvandus horse farm, was not to investigate the degenerative properties of underwear so much as to demonstrate that the soil is "alive."

The experiment's results will form part of an exhibition at the National Agricultural Museum in Tartu County.

On June 16, a pair of cotton underpants were buried to a shallow depth in the soil at the farm, around 30 kilometers from Pärnu. The Estonian Agricultural Museum (Eesti Põllumajandusmuuseum) aimed to assess soil activity.

The 'pants as they appeared on being buried in mid-June. Source: ERR

Twelve weeks later, the undergarments were dug up, revealing decomposition had been extensive – in fact, only the elasticated waistband remained intact, with the same being the case for another pair buried.

"They have decomposed unbelievably — there was almost nothing left of them. The control underpants had one very small piece left, while the actual underpants had only the waistband and a little bit of thread, that's all. We were not expecting that," said Kadri Valner, agricultural museum chief.

This was indication that the soil at the site was of good quality, with plenty of the microorganisms which speed up the decomposition process.

"Already while digging, it was clear that there were a great many earthworms and various microorganisms there," Valner said.

Kadri Valner holding what remained of the underpants. Source: Kristi Raidla/ERR

A similar experiment was conducted at the Jakobson Museum in Kurgja, also in Pärnu County, and at Ülenurme, near Tartu. These will be compared for decomposition rates, and at least one pair will be put on public display.

"If there is anything left at the other locations, we will first dry out the underpants, clean them, and on September 18 we will open an exhibition where they should also be on display," Valner added.

The exhibition "Milleks mulle muld" ("What Do I Need Soil For?") will be on display at the Estonian Agricultural Museum in Ülenurme, just south of Tartu.

World.title: Doctor: Pärnu methanol tragedy the first major touchstone for Covid
World.content:
Raido Paasma, then head of the intensive care unit at Pärnu Hospital and a clinical toxicologist and anesthesiologist, told ETV's "Ringvaade" that although a quarter of a century has passed since the tragedy, he still remembers many of the details.

At the time, Estonia was still a young country, having regained its independence just 10 years earlier, and incomes were limited. People bought alcohol on the black market where it was cheaper than in stores. To maximize their profits, illicit alcohol sellers mixed cheap methanol into vodka to increase the volume.

"People who knew where they could get their illicit vodka went there to buy it. If we look at the date, September 9 is right around the time pensions were paid. People had received their wages and pensions and it was also potato-harvesting season, so they went and stocked up. That's how it happened," Paasma said.

Paasma believes the people who mixed the drinks did not know how much harm they would cause. "To them, it was alcohol. The fact that it had one less H didn't bother them much."

The scale of the methanol poisoning was significant, but Paasma said the proportion of deaths was not exceptionally high compared with previous mass poisonings. "There have also been cases where 70 to 80 percent of those who consumed it died," he said.

Methanol is converted into a toxic metabolite in the body and ethanol is used as an antidote to treat methanol poisoning. During treatment, the concentration of ethanol in the blood must be kept sufficiently high; otherwise, the body begins to break down the methanol. This process produces toxic formic acid.

Drinking methanol does not cause the typical intoxication associated with ethanol. It also tastes different from regular vodka. "A couple of patients told me at the time, 'It was a damn strange drink. I drank it but didn't get drunk at all and it tasted strange too,'" Paasma recalled.

The mass poisoning was a major test for Pärnu Hospital. The hospital did not have sufficient capacity to treat all the patients, so some had to be transferred to other hospitals.

"We distributed the patients because we realized that our capacity to treat them on site was very limited. We could begin initial treatment, but then we needed somewhere with dialysis and greater intensive care capacity than Pärnu had at the time. Estonia's entire healthcare system responded to it and it responded as one. I think it was the first test ahead of the later Covid pandemic."

Paasma estimated that the most difficult period of the crisis lasted about a week and a half. Twenty-five patients died in the hospital, while 43 people were found dead outside the hospital. "When the poisoning has progressed so far that the heart is still working but the brain has already been damaged and the person develops what is known as brain death, unfortunately there is nothing that can be done."

Methanol poisonings still occur in Estonia today, but they are rare. "A month ago, there was a patient who had drunk methanol," Paasma said. "I don't know whether he is still alive. He did not regain consciousness, but his heart was working and he was able to breathe."

Paasma said methanol poisoning nevertheless remains widespread around the world, particularly in Asian countries. He cited three reasons: people seeking cheaper alcohol, poor availability of alcohol and religious restrictions on alcohol.

World.title: Minister: Estonia will have to shelve some investments in tight fiscal situation
World.content:
Budget talks are continuing within the government. On the one hand, the government is seeking to keep the deficit below 4.5 percent, but ministers acknowledge there is little room for spending cuts.

According to Minister of Economic Affairs and Industry Erkki Keldo (Reform Party), the government is drawing up the budget on the assumption that defense spending must remain at no less than 5 percent of GDP, meaning other areas will have to cut costs.

"We have promised to reduce the shortfall, or deficit, to below 4.5 percent. We are trying to do that. It simply means spending has to be reined in. Operating costs, technical costs. We will also have to forgo investments that might be possible in better times — buildings and other construction projects. We cannot afford those when a large share is going toward defense investments," Keldo said.

Making cuts within the Ministry of Interior's area of responsibility is difficult, Interior Minister Igor Taro (Eesti 200) said. Instead, additional funding would be needed to develop capabilities such as counter-drone defenses. Taro did not say Tuesday how much additional funding would be needed.

"I cannot imagine telling society right now that we are simply not going to deal with civil protection at all. We need shelters. Everyone agrees on that. Everyone is asking where those shelters are — where they are in schools, where they are in residential buildings. Or could we say, for example, that we are no longer going to build the national border infrastructure?" Taro said.

Social Democratic Party Vice Chair Riina Sikkut said the minority government needs opposition support to pass the state budget, but the government has not discussed its budget plans with the opposition.

"If everyone had the same information about the forecast and the use of foreign funding, it would be much easier to find support in the Riigikogu because otherwise questions inevitably arise about where a particular figure came from, why a particular choice was made and what the alternatives were," Sikkut said.

The government wants to make the major decisions on the 2027 state budget by the end of next week.

World.title: 3 cities submit bids to host Estonia's multisport arena by deadline
World.content:
Pärnu, Tallinn and Tartu submitted bids by the deadline to host the major arena planned by the Estonian Olympic Committee (EOK).

All three cities seeking to host the multifunctional arena submitted applications to the Estonian Olympic Committee (EOK) by the September 1 deadline.

More specifically, Pärnu, Tallinn and Tartu submitted proposed locations along with additional documentation, allowing the bids to now be compared, EOK multifunctional arena project manager Helen Veermäe told ERR.

"The aim is to ensure that all potential locations are assessed on a comparable basis and, above all, according to their substantive characteristics and potential," she said.

Tallinn proposed the Ülemiste freight terminal area as the location for the arena. Pärnu's preferred site is near the future Rail Baltica terminal, in Veterans Park next to Papiniidu Bridge on the banks of the Pärnu River. The City of Tartu has reserved a plot of land for the arena on Roosi tänav, near the Estonian National Museum.

The selection process will now begin. In May, the EOK and the Ministry of Culture formed an expert committee that will oversee the selection process and ultimately submit a recommendation, together with its reasoning, to the government.

Artist's rendition of the sports arena complex in Pärnu. Source: Pärnu CIty Council / +Arhitektid

As a first step, however, the expert committee will soon select an independent expert to conduct an economic impact analysis, Veermäe said.

"The independent expert selected will prepare a comparative economic impact analysis based on the materials submitted by the cities, gather additional data where necessary and conduct interviews with representatives of the cities and other key stakeholders," she said.

Once the expert committee has approved the expert who will conduct the analysis, the economic impact analysis will take approximately three months to complete. The expert committee will then prepare a summary and submit its recommendation on the most suitable location to the government, Veermäe said.

The government will make the final decision on which city the arena will ultimately be built in. Once that decision has been made, it will also become clear when construction could begin and when the arena could be completed.

The EOK began the arena project's preparatory phase last November. Among other things, representatives have visited Finland to study the business model of a multifunctional arena.

Plans for the arena began to be pursued more seriously after Estonia secured the right to host the 2029 European Basketball Championship. Estonia's largest indoor arena at present is Tallinn's Unibet Arena, which can accommodate up to 7,000 spectators.

A sketch of Arena Tartu proposed for the Roosi tänav 89 site in Tartu. Source: Tartu City Government / Kuu arhitektid

The government is currently discussing next year's state budget and the state budget strategy for the next four years. Economy Minister Erkki Keldo told "Aktuaalne kaamera" on Tuesday that some investments will have to be dropped in order to reduce the budget deficit.

"We will also have to drop investments that might have been possible in better times — buildings and other construction projects. We cannot afford them when such a large share is going toward defense investments," Keldo said. Estonia aims to spend at least 5 percent of its GDP on national defense in the coming years.

World.title: Estonian‑co‑produced film gets 7‑minute standing ovation in Venice
World.content:
The Estonian‑co‑produced feature "Woman Unknown" premiered Sunday at the ongoing Venice Film Festival's main competition, and got a seven‑and‑a‑half‑minute standing ovation.

"Woman Unknown" (Danish: Kvinde ukendt) is directed by Danish filmmaker May el‑Toukhy and is a psychological drama filmed primarily in Latvia. Of the 28 shooting days, 25 took place in Riga, with Estonia's Nafta Films among the co‑producers.

Esko Rips, CEO of Nafta Films and a co‑producer, said the film's selection among the 21 titles in the main competition is important recognition of the Estonian company's three years of work, which was a truly pan-Baltic states affair as it began in Lithuania and culminated in filming in Riga.

"For us, this confirms that operating in all three Baltic states gives us an advantage in producing international films. It allows us to find the best solution for each film in terms of financing, filming locations and creative needs," Rips said.

The Danish-Swedish-Latvian-Estonian co‑production was locally managed by Nafta Films' Latvian team, with co‑producers including Rips and Latvia's Madara Kalniņa.

"Woman Unknown" stands out in this year's competition also because el‑Toukhy is one of just two women directors from among the 21 competing films, ironically enough given women's invisibility and the limits imposed on them by society are central themes of the film itself.

"My film is about the invisibility of women. On the one hand, about objectification, and on the other, about how women are neither seen nor listened to," el‑Toukhy said at a film festival press conference.

"Woman Unknown" is set in Denmark at the end of World War Two. The story centers on Marie, a young nanny and housekeeper preparing to marry her wealthy employer, Christian, an older widower. A dark secret from her past — an intimate relationship with a German soldier during the Nazi occupation of Denmark — threatens her new life.

The film explores society's control over women's choices, their bodies and pasts, showing that the end of the war did not necessarily spell an end to all violence and condemnation.

Mathilde Arcel Fock ("Second victims," "Special Unit: The First Murder") stars in the lead role. The cast also includes Carsten Bjørnlun ("Barracuda Queens," "The Shooter").

The Venice Film Festival runs to Saturday.

World.title: EU wants to edge out China in public contracts
World.content:
Brussels – The European Union on Wednesday proposed new rules to encourage member states to choose domestic companies over Chinese bidders in government contracts.

The reform is part of efforts to favour European firms and boost the 27-country bloc’s key industries against rivals in China and the United States.

The sums involved are huge: public procurement is worth 2.6 trillion euros ($3 trillion) a year in the EU, equivalent to 15 percent of the bloc’s economic output.

Of that total, around 600 billion euros in public contracts are put out to tender across the 27-nation EU each year.

“Public procurement is both a strategic tool and a powerful policy lever at a time when China, India, the United States and other major powers are using it to advance their industrial and economic strategies,” EU industry chief Stephane Sejourne told journalists.

The EU executive unveiled a proposal to reform current government procurement rules — which it says will cut the number of pages of rules “from 900 to 200” — and create a single European platform dedicated to public tenders.

Brussels believes the one-stop shop will make it easier for smaller companies to bid for public tenders as there will be less paperwork.

The reform will allow local authorities to focus on different criteria when assessing providers, like security of supply, sustainability and “European preference” considerations — and not just the price on offer.

Companies often win contracts because they offer a more competitive price, but the EU wants to prioritise the wider benefit of a bid to the European economy.

Sejourne said many local authorities were not making use of the existing provisions which allow them to choose European companies over foreign firms.

“It will therefore be up to local authorities, national governments, municipalities and regions to set those criteria, apply them and choose to buy European or local products,” he added.

As an example, Sejourne said that Brussels could no longer be blamed if local authorities opted for Chinese buses. “We are now giving them the means to favour European buses,” he said.

World.title: Google unveils 13 bn euro AI expansion in Finland
World.content:
Helsinki – Google will invest at least 13 billion euros in data centres and other digital infrastructure to power its AI ambitions in Finland, in what the US tech giant called Wednesday its biggest single investment in Europe.

The $15 billion plan also calls for clean energy projects over the next two years, which Google said was “a testament to Finland’s leadership in responsibly building AI infrastructure”.

It will partner with Finnish companies and four municipalities across the country: Hamina, Kajaani, Muhos and Vaala.

The buildout aims to power several of the tech giant’s services, including its AI chatbot Gemini.

“This investment is historical in Finland,” the country’s Prime Minister Petteri Orpo told AFP after a press conference.

He called it a sign that “we have done the right things in Finland”, citing investments in the power grid, electricity production and the labour force.

“This makes us a front-runner in digitalisation and AI,” Orpo said.

Since buying a former paper mill and transforming it into a data centre in the coastal city of Hamina in 2009, Google has steadily increased its presence in the country.

Antti Jarvinen, the company’s director for Finland, said the Hamina site had already been expanded seven times and currently housed seven data centres.

“Now we are building more in Hamina, expanding that site on a remarkable level, and we are opening up data centre operations in three new locations in the municipalities of Kajaani, Muhos and Vaala,” Jarvinen told AFP.

He said the final numbers on how many new data centres would emerge were expected in the coming months.

The construction phase of the new investments is expected for 2027 and 2028, and Google estimated it would boost Finland’s GDP by 3.6 billion euros annually and “support more than 37,000 jobs”.

Around 16,000 of these jobs will be in the construction sector.

After the construction phase, running the new operations will support around 7,000 direct and indirect jobs annually, Google said.

– Courting investments –

With its cool climate and relatively stable and cheap electricity thanks to nuclear plants as well as extensive wind and hydro power, Finland has seen a boom in data centres in recent years, with dozens already under construction.

Attracting investments in the sector has been a priority for Orpo’s right-wing government as the Nordic country grapples with record-high unemployment and sluggish economic growth.

The boom in data centres is expected to rapidly increase power consumption, with the network operator Fingrid forecasting a 40 percent jump in the coming years.

The massive power drain has sparked concern about environmental risks as well as soaring energy costs for Finnish households.

And Finland’s Security and Intelligence Service (Supo) recently warned that foreign-owned data centres could raise security risks.

Finnish utility Fortum announced Wednesday that it had signed a 22-year deal to supply power to Google, allowing it to “continue operating the Loviisa nuclear power plant until the end of its operating licenses in 2050”.

Without that financing, the plant — which currently supplies about 10 percent of Finland’s electricity — would not have been able to continue operations past 2030, Fortum said.

World.title: Syria no longer under UN nuclear watchdog probe
World.content:
Vienna – The UN nuclear watchdog’s board of governors on Wednesday decided to close a long-time probe against Syria launched under ousted leader Bashar al-Assad after the country’s new authorities led agency exports to key nuclear sites.

Inspectors from the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) last month visited two sites, one in Deir Ezzor and a second in an undisclosed location identified to them by Syrian authorities. IAEA head Rafael Grossi said on Monday that a near-complete nuclear reactor found in Deir Ezzor and built secretly during the rule of al-Assad would have been able to produce material to make nuclear weapons.

The IAEA board “adopted by consensus” a text stating that a 2011 resolution finding Syria in non-compliance with its obligations was “terminated”, noting the current government’s cooperation, two diplomats told AFP.

The resolution, seen by AFP, was submitted by Egypt, Jordan, Morocco and Saudi Arabia and “encourages Syria to continue its cooperation with the agency, including the excavation work at the Deir Ezzor site”.

It also “requests the director general to update the board, as appropriate, on the outcomes of ongoing activities of the agency” in Syria.

– ‘Clandestine’ activities –

Assad was toppled in December 2024 and the current Islamist government came to power.

Grossi said on Monday that it was “obvious that the previous government was pursuing a number of clandestine” activities.

Besides the reactor under construction at the Deir Ezzor site, the IAEA found a fuel fabrication plant where nuclear fuel for the reactor was manufactured, and a location where nuclear fuel as well as uranium scrap and waste were stored.

In a confidential report seen by AFP last week, the IAEA said it found around 73 tonnes of natural uranium metal.

Grossi has praised Damascus’s “courageous decision” to report the undisclosed site.

The UN atomic watchdog had declared in 2011 that the location was “very likely” to host a nuclear reactor, adding that its information suggested it was being built with North Korean assistance.

Last month, Grossi visited the site in Deir Ezzor in the east, which has been shut for 18 years.

In 2018, Israel admitted carrying out a top-secret air raid on the site 11 years earlier.

In 2008, less than a year after the strike, US officials accused Syria of having sought to build a secret nuclear reactor and acknowledged that Israel had destroyed it in the raid.

Robert Kelley, a former director of IAEA inspections and now an associate fellow of the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, told AFP following the IAEA report that there was “no evidence of any weapons programme” in Syria.

Instead the aim before the site was destroyed may have been to produce plutonium for North Korea, possibly to sell to a third party, he added.

World.title: ‘Nothing left’: thousands in Yemen flee deadly Houthi clashes
World.content:
Khokha – Salama Saeed and her son fled for their lives when shelling and gunfire from Yemen’s Houthi rebels engulfed their village, forcing her to leave other children behind.

They are among thousands of people driven from their homes since the Iran-backed rebels launched a broad offensive in areas near the Red Sea last week, their biggest in years.

Choking back tears as she shelters in a rudimentary hut of wood and straw, the mother describes her anguish for her four adult children who were unable to escape, trapped by the fighting.

“I fled on my own, terrified, on one of my sons’ motorcycles. We have nothing left,” said the woman in her fifties from the Muthalath al-Udain area of Hodeida province.

“We were forced to leave because of the Houthis,” she told AFP, adding: “My children are still there — they couldn’t get out. I weep for them every day, waiting for them to escape.”

Yemen’s long-running conflict has flared into life after a four-year truce unravelled in July, as regional tensions rocketed during the Middle East war.

More than 500 people have died in clashes between the Houthis and Saudi-backed government forces since last week, according to sources on both sides.

The Houthis are trying to seize territory along the Red Sea, where they have been attacking Saudi tankers. The route has become key for Saudi oil since Iran blockaded the Strait of Hormuz, a major route for Gulf shipments.

Meanwhile a wave of Houthi attacks on Tuesday set Saudi oil sites ablaze and wounded dozens of people. On Wednesday, the rebels reported more than 40 Saudi reprisal strikes.

– ‘We’re exhausted’ –

The renewed fighting in southwest Yemen has forced nearly 20,000 people to flee their homes, according to the International Organization for Migration.

Saeed and her son found refuge in a camp for the displaced in Khokha on the Red Sea coast, about 30 kilometres (19 miles) from their village.

When AFP visited, she was carrying water in large, plastic jerry cans and hand-washing clothes in a bowl on the dirt floor.

“There’s no aid. We’re exhausted. Who will give us aid? Every time we’re displaced from one place, war comes and forces us to leave again! Where can we go? We’re tired of this situation.”

Many of the camps in the Khokha area have been open since around 2018, when the last major escalation in Hodeida triggered a wave of displacement.

– ‘It’s a catastrophe’ –

Mohammed Khudairi, who is sheltering in the same camp, described “sudden Houthi bombardment — mortar shells, missiles, and drones”.

“It’s a catastrophe, and the attacks are ongoing. We managed to leave, but others remain trapped there,” he said.

The Houthis have been at war since 2015 with a Saudi-led coalition, in a conflict that has killed hundreds of thousands of people and triggered a major humanitarian crisis.

Around 22.3 million people — nearly two-thirds of the population — were in need of humanitarian aid in 2025, including 5.2 million internally displaced, according to UN figures.

Jamal Al-Mashraqi, an official overseeing work in Hodeida province’s displacement camps, said the violence had pushed about 7,500 people to seek refuge in the Hays and Khokha districts alone.

“Those families fled fearing death,” he said, warning that aid was scarce.

“These families are still suffering from a lack of assistance with food, shelter and basic supplies,” he told AFP.

World.title: Iran war drives oil prices to $100 per barrel as Tehran strikes ships
World.content:
Tehran – Iran said it attacked more than a dozen vessels trying to pass through the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday, as fresh fighting with the United States drove oil prices above $100 per barrel.

The attacks came with the six-month war between the United States and Iran deadlocked, as Tehran chokes off the strategic Strait of Hormuz and Washington presses a counter-blockade of Iranian ports.

Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said on Wednesday they attacked two US vessels, eight oil tankers, and 10 “non-compliant vessels” that were trying to pass through the strait, Iranian state media reported.

The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) said on Wednesday “several” vessels in the Gulf of Oman and the Gulf were “subject to disabling fire as part of ongoing military activity in the region”.

The Gulf of Oman lies on the Indian Ocean side of the narrow Hormuz strait, which normally carries around a fifth of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas.

On Wednesday Iran’s Guards for the first time added parts of the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea to a new “prohibited zone” where vessels will be subject to “sanctions”, saying that exact coordinates will be announced.

The Guards also said they struck a US military base in Jordan in response to US forces destroying five Iranian oil tankers a day earlier.

Iran’s foreign ministry condemned the attack on its oil tankers as “an overt threat to regional and international peace and security,” saying that they “increase the dangers of tensions in the region”.

It said the targeting of US military facilities in the region was “self-defence”.

The Islamic republic warned of further strikes targeting tankers off the coast of US allies Kuwait and Bahrain.

The US military for its part had said it was responding to an Iranian attack targeting an American warship, the second such incident in less than a week.

The international oil benchmark, Brent North Sea crude, breached $100 per barrel on Wednesday as markets worried the conflict would lead to fresh disruptions to oil supplies.

– US warning –

The latest round of fighting was triggered after US forces destroyed five Iranian oil tankers on Tuesday, with the US military saying it “directed the crews to abandon ship” before hitting the vessels.

“Iran continues to try to hit US naval ships, and for every time they do that or try to do that, they’re going to lose tankers, and I think you’ll see that again today,” US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters on Tuesday on a visit to Colombia.

Iranian media reported Tuesday that a US missile struck a tanker off the coast of Kharg Island, adding that there were no casualties.

Iran has asserted control of the Strait of Hormuz since US-Israeli strikes began the war in February, with traffic through the waterway virtually paralysed.

Tehran requires vessels to obtain permission and pay transit fees before using the strait.

World.title: Al Marsoumi: Iran’s Hormuz fee drains 1/3 of Iraq’s oil revenue
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — A financial analysis by Iraqi petroleum economist Dr. Nabil Al-Marsoumi has revealed that transit tolls imposed by Tehran on crude tankers navigating the Strait of Hormuz are siphoning off nearly a third of Iraq’s oil earnings.

In an audit published on Wednesday, Al-Marsoumi calculated that Baghdad paid roughly $1.3 billion directly to Iranian authorities during August alone, depleting what had originally been $4.5 billion in gross hydrocarbon exports down to an intermediate balance of $3.2 billion. Once production costs and licensing dues owed to foreign oil operators were deducted, Iraq was left with just $2.5 billion in net treasury inflows for the entire month.

These figures corroborate warnings issued a day earlier by lawmaker Mansour Al-Baiji, deputy head of the Reconstruction and Development parliamentary bloc, who cautioned that passage fees reaching up to $20 per barrel are being paid directly to Iran by Iraq’s State Oil Marketing Organization (SOMO).

Al-Baiji warned that such transfers could expose the state marketer to severe secondary sanctions from Washington, which views any financial facilitation of the Iranian regime as a breach of international restrictions.

The developments unfold amid mounting economic pressure from the United States. U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent recently began reaching out to countries maintaining commercial ties with Tehran, cautioning that American sanctions could soon target foreign state entities and official bodies if they assist Iran in circumventing financial controls.

According to Iraqi press reports, an unwritten message recently reached Baghdad warning that secondary penalties may be imminent if the flow of funds to Iran continues, sparking visible unease across Iraq’s political establishment.

In response to the growing friction, the ruling State Administration Coalition convened its second meeting in less than a month to assess the fallout of potential American measures. However, the coalition adopted a cautious posture, acknowledging the gravity of U.S. sanctions while conspicuously avoiding divisive deadlines—such as the September 30 target for consolidating state control over unauthorized arms—in an apparent bid to navigate the delicate balance between Washington and Tehran.

The maritime dispute follows a declaration earlier this year by Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, who noted that passage through the strategic chokepoint would be permitted only for allied nations such as Iraq, China, Russia, India, and Pakistan, after reports emerged that Tehran had begun levying steep fees approaching $2 million per vessel.

With Iraq requiring over 7.4 trillion dinars every month simply to meet public payroll obligations, losing over $1 billion to maritime transit fees threatens to plunge state finances into a severe liquidity shortfall while jeopardizing its vital relationship with international energy markets.

World.title: Drone strikes tanker carrying Iraqi fuel oil as US-Iran war escalates
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — A Panama-flagged tanker carrying around 2 million barrels of Iraqi fuel oil was hit by a drone in Iraqi territorial seas on Wednesday, pushing the intensifying US-Iran naval war straight into Iraq’s southern energy-export zone.

According to Reuters and Iraqi port authorities, a drone struck the tanker New Andros at 6 a.m. local time.

The impact started a fire on the vessel, which Iraqi rescue boats subsequently doused.

All 22 crew members were declared safe, with no injuries.

The tragedy poses yet another significant challenge to Iraq’s economy, which is still highly reliant on petroleum exports from its southern terminals as well as maritime routes across the Arabian Gulf and Strait of Hormuz.

It comes amid the most intense escalation of assaults on regional commerce since the US-Iran conflict started six months ago.

Iran announced Wednesday that it has targeted ten boats in the Strait of Hormuz after the United States bombed and destroyed five Iranian oil tankers in retaliation to Iranian ballistic missile attacks on a US Navy destroyer.

Several more merchant boats have reportedly been struck or damaged in the northern Arabian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman, indicating the rising potential that commercial shipping, including Iraqi oil exports, may be caught up in the escalating conflict.

Traffic via Hormuz has already dropped significantly.

According to preliminary Kpler data, just six cargo tankers with active monitoring systems passed through the strait on Tuesday, compared to a 10-day average of 12.

Before the conflict, Hormuz handled nearly one-fifth of the world’s oil and LNG supply.

The unrest is also expanding across the Gulf.

The Iran-aligned Houthis staged huge drone and missile strikes on Saudi Arabia this week, attacking southern towns and oil installations and injuring 73 people, according to Saudi officials.

For Iraq, the attack on New Andros highlights the risk of depending on southern marine export routes during the regional crisis.

Baghdad has lately advanced planning for alternate pipelines to Turkey and Syria’s Mediterranean coast in an effort to decrease its vulnerability to delays near Hormuz.

The current escalation has also jolted global energy markets, with Brent oil surpassing $100 a barrel on Wednesday for the first time since July.

World.title: Yemen rebels report fresh Saudi strikes as conflict deepens
World.content:
Sanaa – Yemen’s Houthi rebels reported dozens of Saudi airstrikes on Wednesday as daily attacks continued in a conflict that has reignited during the Middle East war, with hundreds of people killed in fighting near the Red Sea.

More than 40 attacks targeted several regions including the flashpoint areas of Taiz and Hodeida, scene of fierce clashes between the Houthis and Saudi-backed government, the rebels said.

The latest salvos in Yemen’s previously dormant conflict come a day after the Iran-backed Houthis set oil sites ablaze and wounded 73 in their heaviest missile and drone attacks against Saudi Arabia in years.

The Yemen fighting is taking place against the backdrop of the Middle East war, which erupted in late February with US-Israeli strikes on Iran.

On Wednesday, Iran said it attacked 20 American vessels in the Strait of Hormuz and targeted a US military base in Jordan in retaliation for US strikes on Iranian oil tankers.

The Middle East war has sucked in Yemen, the energy-rich Gulf and others across the region while roiling the world economy, as oil prices returned to $100 a barrel on Wednesday.

More than 500 people have died since the Houthis launched a major offensive last week to seize territory around the Bab al-Mandab strait, gateway to the Red Sea shipping route.

The rebels, who have been attacking Saudi oil tankers, are trying to tighten their squeeze on the shipments, analysts say — a lifeline for exports after Iran’s blockade of Hormuz.

– ‘Dangerous escalation’ –

Saudi airstrikes targeted “various areas across the governorates of Marib, Al-Jawf, Taiz and Hodeida over the past few hours”, the rebels’ Almasirah TV said on Wednesday.

There was no official comment from Saudi Arabia.

The Saudi civil defence later issued a warning for the southern governorate of Khamis Mushait, near Yemen, but quickly lifted it.

On Tuesday, Saudi authorities vowed to respond to the Houthi attacks, saying they caused fires and temporary shutdowns at oil sites.

The Houthis triggered the return to hostilities in July, when they let an Iranian plane land in defiance of Saudi control of Yemeni airspace.

The government retaliated by striking the airport, an attack the rebels blamed on its sponsor, Saudi Arabia.

The ongoing exchanges risk returning Yemen to a conflict that left hundreds of thousands of people dead and sparked one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises.

The Houthis, after seizing Yemen’s capital and forcing out the internationally recognised government, fought a Saudi-led coalition from 2015 until a United Nations-brokered ceasefire in 2022.

On Tuesday, the European Union urged the Houthis to end their attacks, calling them a “dangerous escalation”.

“We call on the Houthis to immediately end all attacks inside and outside Yemen, including attacks against commercial shipping in the Red Sea,” said Anouar El Anouni, a spokesman for the bloc’s diplomatic service.

World.title: J&K launches 3-year rehab scheme for drug addicts
World.content:
SRINAGAR: J&K chief secretary Atal Dulloo Wednesday rolled out a three-year scheme to rehabilitate drug addicts under treatment at govt-run or aided de-addiction centres and institutions, prevent relapse, and aid their reintegration into society.

The scheme will initially be introduced in the districts of Jammu, Srinagar, Kathua and Budgam and later extended to others, officials said.

Under the scheme, a structured rehabilitation cycle will be established for drug abusers to ensure a seamless transition from âdetoxification to socio-economic stabilisationâ to reduce relapse rates and prevent premature exit from treatment, Dulloo said.

The first six months will cover intake, assessment, treatment, stabilisation and rehabilitation planning under Phase I.

The next six to 24 months will involve reintegration and livelihood activation under Phase II. The following 24-36 months will revolve around sustained monitoring and social inclusion.

J&K home department will facilitate tracing and support for individuals requiring intervention. The health and medical education department will provide continuing mental health services, counselling, psychiatric care, de-addiction treatment and relapse-prevention support.





The education department will aid educational reintegration, academic continuity, re-enrolment, bridge learning and access to student support services, officials said.

The labour and employment department will facilitate vocational training, skill development, employment placement and entrepreneurship development. The rural development and Panchayati Raj department will support community participation, family engagement, livelihood inclusion, social support networks and local-level rehabilitation and reintegration initiatives.

The social welfare department will serve as the nodal department for implementation of the policy, officials said.

On April 11, 2026, J&K Lieutenant Governor Manoj Sinha launched a 100-day anti-drug campaign under the âNasha Mukt Abhiyaanâ, which involved large-scale awareness programmes by the civil administration and police, destruction of poppy cultivation, random urine testing of drivers and intensified crackdowns on drug networks.

Over 32,500 drug abuse cases have been registered across J&K since 2022, with the highest number of patients reported from Srinagar and Jammu districts, govt data revealed. A 2022 study by Institute of Mental Health and Neurosciences Kashmir estimated about 67,468 people in 10 Kashmir districts as âsubstance-dependentâ.

World.title: NC tells Congress: Full Vande Mataram a constitutional duty
World.content:
SRINAGAR: National Conference fired a political broadside at ally Congress Wednesday, defending full renditions of

at govt functions in J&K as a âconstitutionalâ duty.

Congress objected after all six stanzas of the national song was played at the inauguration of J&Kâs first international film festival in Srinagar attended by CM

and NC president Farooq Abdullah on Sept 7. As at other official functions, Omar stood at attention throughout.

J&K Congress president Tariq Hamid Karra said NC and Congress should respect how the songâs place in Indiaâs national life evolved through both the freedom movement and constitutional journey. âNational symbols, songs and traditions occupy a special place in the heart of every Indian. Their true strength lies in their ability to bind together a nation as diverse as ours,â he said, calling it a concern that alliance partners had chosen to sing the full version.

NC countered, asking Congress to look at CMs of states governed by the party, including Telangana and Karnataka, who have participated in full renditions.

NC chief spokesperson Tanvir Sadiq shared on X a video featuring Karnataka CM DK Shivakumar at an event where the unabridged song was sung. He said govt protocol must be separated from party ideology. âNC has a clear stand. When Parliament has adopted it, playing Vande Mataram becomes a statutory obligation and that is what govt did,â Sadiq said.





CM Omar later shared Sadiqâs statements on X.

A Union home ministry protocol directive in Feb mandated the six-stanza version of the song at all state functions, official events and legislature sessions. In Aug, the President cleared Prevention of Insults to National Honour (Amendment) Act, which puts Vande Mataram on a par with the national anthem, making disrespect/disruption a punishable offence. The amended law did not change the stanzas, but people are now obligated to respect Vande Mataram as a constitutional duty.

NC spokesperson Imran Nabi Dar said: âThis is a constitutional obligation, and every one holding a constitutional office has to accept it, whether it is the CM, an MP or anyone else,â he said, adding the full version is now regularly played at govt functions across J&K.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

Dar acknowledged the objection among Muslims. âThough religiously it is not acceptable to Muslims, it is a constitutional obligation that has to be fulfilled,â he said.

The freedom movement broadly adopted first two stanzas of Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyayâs 1875 poem, while the full song has six containing religious imagery that has drawn objections from Muslims. Congress general secretary GA Mir said freedom fighters had shaped the version used by the movement with inclusivity in mind.

World.title: Goods train derails in J&K’s Kathua, no injury or damages
World.content:
Kathua, J&K (ANI photo)

JAMMU: A goods train derailed at Chann Aroria railway station in J&Kâs Kathua district on Wednesday morning. Officials said no one was hurt and no damage was incurred in the incident.The derailment occurred around 9.30am when the goods train was heading back after unloading cement, and one of its coaches went off the track in the stationâs yard, officials said. A technical team from Kathua rushed to the spot and brought the derailed coach back on track after two hours of efforts.Earlier on July 10, two bogies of a goods train moving from Jammu to Punjab derailed near Lakhanpur in Kathua after debris fell on the tracks following a rain-triggered landslide.

World.title: Ladakh groups claim breakthrough in talks with MHA on legislative powers
World.content:
SRINAGAR: Leh Apex Body and Kargil Democratic Alliance, the two organisations negotiating with the Union govt for administrative autonomy to Ladakh under the Sixth Schedule, claimed a breakthrough Wednesday in talks with the MHAâs subcommittee in Delhi on legislative powers over land, culture and language, forests and natural resources.

In a joint statement, the groups said the meeting furthered the âin-principle understandingâ reached during talks on May 22 and July 3 on Ladakhâs demands, including constitutional safeguards through special provisions under Article 371.

They said MHA stopped short of guaranteeing powers across the board under Lists II and III of the Seventh Schedule, including law and order.

MHA assured compensation to the families of those killed and the protesters injured in the Sept 24, 2025, violence in Leh, the groups claimed.

The Union govt also agreed to withdraw cases against 24 people and review those against another 34 on a case-to-case basis. Cases against 25 people have already been withdrawn.

Ladakh chief secretary Ashish Kundra wrote on X about the âgeneral air of positivityâ at the Delhi meeting without elaborating beyond the agenda. âThe broad contours of a sui generis model of governance under Article 371 were discussed. Deepening democracy is the goal,â he said.





Another round of talks is scheduled for the first week of Oct.

The groups said they were concerned over the formation of new districts, the creation of hill councils for each and what they called âmajor irreversible changes being done before an elected body at the Union Territoryâ.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

Making such changes before the UT body can legislate, they said, âwould essentially deprive the people of Ladakh an opportunity to democratically decide on the structure of administration in Ladakhâ.

Ladakhi representatives have been in talks with MHA since 2023 for safeguards covering land, jobs, culture and environment. MHA set up the committee on Jan 2, 2023, but the process stalled after four people were killed and over 80 injured in alleged police firing on protesters demanding statehood in Leh in Sept last year.

Activist

, a LAB member, was accused of inciting the protesters, arrested and charged under the NSA. The Centre revoked his detention last March and he returned to the negotiating table in May.

World.title: Raghav Chadha’s Delhi voter registration approved after due process: Poll body
World.content:
NEW DELHI: The Delhi poll body on Wednesday said BJP Rajya Sabha MP Raghav Chadhaâs application to be added to the Delhi voter list was approved after due procedure, days after the AAP questioned his inclusion.

"As per record available, Raghav Chadha, MP (Rajya Sabha) applied for inclusion of his name in Form 6 in AC-39 (Rajinder Nagar) on August 26," news agency PTI quoted Delhi chief electoral officer as saying.

"The Form was approved by the Electoral Registration Officer of the AC-39 (Rajinder Nagar) after completion of mandatory notice period of 07 days," it added.

The application, numbered U05039D6N2608261200000, was processed under the Election Commissionâs prescribed procedure.

The AAP, however, rejected the explanation and alleged that Chadhaâs name was added to the electoral roll "through the back door". The party also questioned whether political pressure was involved.

AAP national media-in-charge Anurag Dhanda demanded that Chadhaâs Form 6 be made public and said citizens should be allowed to raise objections against it as they can for any ordinary voter.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

Dhanda claimed that Chadhaâs name did not appear in any Form 6 received in Rajinder Nagar between September 1 and 7.





He also questioned how Chadhaâs name became the 747th entry when the draft roll had 746 voters and the final roll was yet to be published.

The CEO office said eligible persons whose names are not on the electoral roll can seek inclusion by submitting Form 6 with the required documents.

It also referred to the Election Commissionâs May 14 guidelines on the Special Intensive Revision, which state that additions made during the SIR period would receive serial numbers continuing from the last entry in the draft electoral roll.

World.title: Beyond E20? Only flex-fuel vehicles may have the option, indicates adviser
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Indicating that govt is unlikely to increase ethanol blending in petrol beyond the current 20% (E20) for existing vehicles, adviser to PM Tarun Kapoor said Wednesday that allowing higher ethanol blending will have to be an option with flex-fuel vehicles.

Addressing an event of sugar industry body Isma virtually, Kapoor said E20 has been very successful. âNow, our focus is on going into flex-fuel vehicles and allowing blending at a percentage which will be higher than E20, and definitely it will have to be an option for flex-fuel vehicles,â he added.

He noted that several vehicle manufacturers have announced plans to roll out flex-fuel vehicles. These vehicles can run on petrol with higher ethanol blending of up to 85% and even 100% in some cases.

Kapoor said there is a possibility of more such vehicles hitting the road while mentioning some petrol pumps are already making higher blends available and that this needs expansion.

âBut it has to go hand-in-hand with the availability of flex-fuel vehicles,â the top bureaucrat said.

Dismissing criticisms against ethanol blending in petrol, Kapoor said it may be due to âmisinformation or certain other motivated reasonsâ.





He said a lot of studies and experiments have shown that E20 is good and works very well. Kapoor said there may be âa little bit of fuel efficiencyâ, but the decline gets compensated with higher octane. He said the issues which are being faced are generally due to âother reasons, not due to this blendingâ.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

Kapoor also said if India can also get some product which can be used in diesel, then it will be great considering that in a refinery, a large percentage of the product is diesel.

âSo we canât have petrol demand going down, whereas diesel demand is going up. So, we would like to balance that; we need something to add to diesel also. And if experiments are going on on isobutanol, if that succeeds, then that would open another area where biofuels can be required in large quantities, and then that would be great for us,â he added.

World.title: Baba Neem Karoli’s granddaughters claim their ancestral home illegally occupied by trust
World.content:
NEW DELHI: A dispute has erupted over the ancestral home of Hindu saint Baba Neem Karoli Maharaj in Uttar Pradesh, with his six granddaughters alleging that the property is being illegally occupied and controlled by a trust headed by their aunt, PTI reported.

Following the complaint, Firozabad District Magistrate Santosh Kumar Sharma has constituted a three-member committee to investigate the ownership and management of the property, according to PTI.

The committee is headed by additional district magistrate (Judicial) Arvind Kumar Dwivedi and includes Tundla Sub-Divisional Magistrate Divya Singh and District Tourism Officer Vishal Srivastava.

The dispute concerns house number 154 and adjoining structures in Akbarpur village under Tundla tehsil, the birthplace of Baba Neem Karoli, whose original name was Lakshmi Narayan Sharma, according to PTI.

The property, which is being developed as a tourist attraction by the Uttar Pradesh tourism department, includes the saint's meditation room, dining area, guest quarters and bedroom.

The ancestral residence is a duplex built on a plot measuring around 4,000 square feet and is currently managed by the Shri Neem Karoli Maharaj Trust, headed by the saint's daughter Girija Devi Bhatele. His late wife Rambeti was its former president.





According to family sources cited by PTI, the dispute came to the fore during a family event on August 24, when the six daughters of the saint's late son Dharm Narayan Sharma were allegedly denied accommodation in rooms at the ancestral property.

Following the incident, the six granddaughters, Sunita Sharma, Archana Sharma, Vandana Sharma, Bhavna Rawat, Ritu Tiwari and Richa Rawat, submitted a representation to the District Magistrate seeking that the ancestral residence be freed from the Trust's control, PTI reported.

Manoj Rawat, husband of Bhavna Rawat, confirmed to PTI that relevant property documents had been submitted to the inquiry committee after it sought them.

However, Dhananjay Sharma, son of the saint's other late son Anek Singh Sharma, rejected the allegations and said that the property had been handed over to the Trust in accordance with Baba Neem Karoli's wishes.

He expressed concern over the public nature of the dispute and appealed to family members to resolve the matter amicably.

Trust secretary Sanjay Gupta also denied allegations of illegal occupation and rejected claims of an internal dispute within the Trust. He said he had been appointed by Dharm Narayan Sharma and continued to serve the institution.

Gupta told PTI that the Trust had not received any official notice from the district administration so far.

The dispute comes amid renewed public interest in Baba Neem Karoli's life and legacy following the release of Hanuman Ansh, a devotional biographical film based on the saint's life.

Released on August 7, 2026, the low-budget film starring Shobhinaww Satyaa became a sleeper hit following strong word-of-mouth publicity. It reportedly collected more than Rs 150 crore worldwide within a month, bringing renewed attention to the saint's life and his birthplace, PTI reported.

World.title: India considers it a responsibility, not a favour, to provide aid to Sri Lanka as first responder: Rajnath to president Dissanayake
World.content:
Defence minister Rajnath conveyed greetings on behalf of PM Modi and underlined that the citizens of the two countries share deep friendship based on strong historical and civilisational links and people-to-people exchanges.

He emphasised that as a closest friend and neighbour of Sri Lanka, âIndia considered it not a favour, but a responsibility to provide assistance as the first responder and would continue to do so in the future as wellâ.

Sri Lankan president Dissanayake said his country would never allow its territory to be used for activities inimical to Indiaâs security interests. He also expressed his gratitude for the relief assistance provided by India as part of Op Sagar Bandhu during Cyclone Ditwah and the comprehensive rehabilitation package extended by New.

Both leaders virtually inaugurated three Bailey bridges constructed by the Indian defence forces. The two sides also exchanged MoUs on upgradation of L70 guns for the Sri Lankan Air Force, and cooperation between NCC and National Defence Colleges of both the countries.

Rajnath also met Sri Lankan PM Harini Amarasuriya. âWe exchanged views on a range of issues related to development cooperation, education and close cultural and civilisational ties,â he posted on X.





He underlined that as âsister democracies with shared heritageâ, India and Sri Lanka should continue working towards a shared developmental vision for the peace and prosperity of the region. Rajnath also highlighted Sri Lanka's importance in India's Vision MAHASAGAR, saying the island nation holds a special place in the policy and would continue to do so in the future.

Rajnath called for enhanced cooperation between India and Sri Lanka to shape a favourable and secure maritime environment and tackle emerging maritime challenges before they evolve into serious threats to developmental interests and brighter future.

âSecure sea lanes, freedom of navigation, respect for international law and unhindered maritime trade are pivotal for collective security & prosperity of the Indian Ocean Region (IOR),â the defence minister said while addressing a gathering comprising Sri Lankan deputy minister of defence Aruna Jayasekara, commanders of the Sri Lankan three services.

Rajnath said India and Sri Lanka are bound by the shared ocean, and maritime security is not a matter of abstract theory but a reality that shapes their trade, security and destinies.

âBoth nations are central to any strategic discourse on maritime security in the region. Strong India-Sri Lanka maritime cooperation will be mutually beneficial and vital for collective growth and security,â he said.

Referring to the challenges faced by our fishermen, the defence minister underscored that the issue needs to be addressed together. He observed that maritime cooperation should extend beyond the security framework to also cover areas like aquaculture, marine biotechnology, ocean science, protection and preservation of maritime environment and maritime tourism.
