World.title: No travel tax, no budget: Can TIEZA keep its tourism projects alive?
World.content:
The pesky travel tax is easy to hate, but abolishing it could leave multi-year tourism infrastructure projects in limbo, especially with TIEZA not getting anything in the proposed 2027 budget

Even as the government keeps pitching tourism as a growth priority and jobs engine, the agency tasked with building much of its infrastructure is heading into 2027 with billions’ worth of ongoing projects and a proposed budget of exactly zero.

On top of this, if Congress succeeds in abolishing the travel tax, the Tourism Infrastructure and Enterprise Zone Authority (TIEZA) could also lose the revenue stream that normally pays for almost everything it does.

A source familiar with TIEZA’s budget planning told Rappler that the agency initially sought around P5.2 billion in national government funding for 2027. That request covered infrastructure projects alone and did not yet include personnel services or maintenance and other operating expenses.

Budget Secretary Kim Robert de Leon informed TIEZA that the request could not be favorably considered because of the government’s limited fiscal space, the source said. Consequently, the proposed 2027 budget carries zero subsidy for the agency, compared with P248 million for general administration and support in 2026.

The Department of Budget and Management (DBM) echoed this stance during the budget hearing of the Department of Tourism (DOT).

“TIEZA’s proposal for National Government Subsidy in FY2027 is in view of several legislative measures proposing the abolition of the travel tax. However, as these bills remain under deliberation in the Senate and have yet to be enacted into law, the TIEZA’s requested subsidy was not considered in the FY [2027] NEP,” DBM Assistant Director Lulu Vispo said.

A zero budget may come with consequences on the tourism infrastructure pipeline. TIEZA chief operating officer Mark Lapid told lawmakers during the tourism department’s budget hearing that almost all of its projects are multi-year, with around P5.2 billion needed in 2027 alone to keep them moving.

The DBM, however, pointed to P2.355 billion in supposedly available TIEZA funds: P810.25 million in unobligated allotments as of March 31 and another P1.545 billion in unreleased 2025 appropriations.

“TIEZA may continue to utilize its travel tax collections to fund tourism-related infrastructures or projects,” Vispo added on Monday, September 7.

Meanwhile, TIEZA says that money is not sitting idly. Lapid told lawmakers that the roughly P2 billion cited during the hearing could not simply be used to pay for its infrastructure commitments as it was being used to fund the agency’s payroll.

“The P2 billion is for our personnel services in our office operations. So technically, we wouldn’t have any funds for infrastructure from the amount mentioned,” Lapid told lawmakers in Filipino.

The travel tax problem

The problem is that the pesky P1,620 travel tax that travelers love to hate is also what keeps much of TIEZA running.

Congress is now moving to abolish it. The House has already approved House Bill 8464, while Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian said in August that the Senate is targeting abolition within the year.

Under the current setup, 50% of tax collections go to TIEZA, 40% to the Commission on Higher Education, and 10% to the National Commission for Culture and the Arts. TIEZA’s share from those travel taxes makes up roughly 95% of its funding, an agency source told Rappler.

The House bill does anticipate the problem by requiring the national government to replace those funds through the annual budget. The tricky part is timing. TIEZA is being told to prepare for a future in which the travel tax disappears, but it has yet to receive approval for replacement funding.

Photo from a TIEZA presentation shown during the House budget hearing for the DOT.

The tax cut could also have a very human cost inside the agency that needs consideration. A TIEZA presentation showed that around 300 travel tax personnel may be displaced out of its 1,045-strong workforce. Of those, 115 may have difficulty finding new work because of their age, while some 270 families could be affected.

Lapid told lawmakers that TIEZA cannot simply absorb the workers elsewhere because they are spread across international gateways nationwide and the agency does not have enough plantilla positions at its main office. Some could be terminated, while others may receive separation incentives.

Five projects may get a lifeline

During Monday’s budget hearing, the DOT made its case for Congress to restore an allocation for at least P1.3 billion for five TIEZA projects.

The list obtained by Rappler from a source includes:

P328.9 million for improvements of the Banaue Hotel and Youth Hostel complex in Ifugao. World.title: Zambales expands MPA network with 2 new sanctuaries
World.content:
INTERCONNECTED The coral reef ecosystems of the Calanga Reef Marine Protected Area in Iba and the Rabaw-ti-Bato Marine Protected Area in San Narciso have been added to the Zambales Marine Protected Area Network, strengthening province-wide efforts to conserve marine biodiversity, restore fish populations, and protect the coastal communities that depend on the sea.—Photos courtesy of DENR Central Luzon

MANILA, Philippines — Hidden beneath the waters along this province’s coastline are coral reefs that serve as nurseries for marine life, where fish hatch, feed, and mature before venturing into surrounding fishing grounds.

For years, these reefs have been protected by coastal communities in their respective towns. Two of them are now part of a larger, province-wide conservation network.

With the inclusion of the Calanga Reef Marine Protected Area in this capital town and the Rabaw-ti-Bato Marine Protected Area in San Narciso, Zambales has expanded a network of marine sanctuaries. These areas are designed not as isolated pockets of protection, but as interconnected habitats that can help restore fish populations and strengthen the resilience of coastal ecosystems.

Article continues after this 

In a recent statement, the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) said that the two marine protected areas (MPAs) were formally admitted into the Zambales Marine Protected Area Network (Zampan) through a resolution approved by Gov. Hermogenes Ebdane Jr.

READ: In Zambales, coastal volunteers lead defense of marine sanctuary

The resolution recognizes both sites as ecologically significant coral reef ecosystems and integrates them into the province’s coordinated management framework for marine conservation.

“Protecting these areas as part of a larger network strengthens habitat connectivity, improves ecosystem resilience, and supports coordinated management of coastal resources across municipalities,” said Marife Castillo, provincial environment and natural resources officer of the DENR in this province.

She said both reefs function as breeding, spawning, nursery, and feeding grounds for a variety of marine species, making them critical links in sustaining fisheries along the province’s western coastline.

Article continues after this 

Connecting life

Scientists have long argued that marine protected areas become more effective when they function as networks rather than isolated reserves.

Fish larvae carried by ocean currents can replenish reefs many kilometers away, while adult fish often migrate beyond sanctuary boundaries.

Article continues after this 

Protecting multiple reefs that are ecologically connected increases the chances that depleted fish stocks can recover across a broader seascape rather than in a single locality.

That principle has guided Zampan since its creation in 2013 through a memorandum of understanding among the provincial government, DENR, the Department of Agriculture–Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources, the Department of the Interior and Local Government, the Provincial Agriculture Office, and the coastal municipalities of Sta. Cruz, Candelaria, Masinloc, Palauig, Botolan, Cabangan, San Felipe, San Antonio, Subic, Iba, and San Narciso.

Instead of municipalities managing their marine sanctuaries independently, the network allows local governments to coordinate enforcement, monitoring, planning, and habitat protection across municipal boundaries.

Beyond biodiversity

The addition of the two reefs further strengthens that collaboration, particularly as the province faces mounting pressures from overfishing, climate change, and coastal development.

DENR Regional Executive Director Ralph Pablo said healthy marine ecosystems remain the foundation of productive fisheries and resilient coastal communities.

“By expanding Zampan, we are strengthening ecosystem protection while supporting the long-term well-being of the people whose lives and livelihoods depend on our marine resources,” Pablo said.

The expanded network comes as the country works toward its commitment to protect at least 30 percent of its coastal and marine ecosystems by 2030, in line with the global biodiversity framework.

World.title: Tackling illegal wildlife trade, from Cartimar to the internet
World.content:
POACHED The smuggling of live Indonesian wildlife—particularly parrots—into the Philippines has been documented formore than three decades. Photo shows distressed birds with feathers plucked, behavior they engage in due to the toll ofprolonged captivity. —Contributed photo

MANILA, Philippines — In early July, Haribon Foundation met with wildlife and law enforcement officers in Quezon City, Davao, and General Santos City to strengthen the fight against the illegal cross-border trade of Indonesian parrots—a trade that conservationists warn threatens not only endangered birds, but public health as well.

Illegal wildlife trade in the Philippines was once tied to physical markets. Not anymore, shares Dr. Esteven Toledo, in charge of the Wildlife Rescue Center under the Department of Environment and Natural Resources-Biodiversity Management Bureau (DENR-BMB) and CITES (Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna) wildlife enforcement officer.

“Famous illegal wildlife trade hubs like Cartimar—they’re now gone. The greatest challenge now is the illegal wildlife trade on the internet,” Toledo said.

Article continues after this 

He also warned that trafficked animals pose a health risk to people, since they skip the health checks required for legally imported wildlife.

READ: PH LOSING P50B A YEAR TO ILLEGAL WILDLIFE TRADE

“These animals are coming from the wild, and they are not subjected to any health assessment or the usual process of importing or exporting animals. There is a potential risk of spreading zoonotic diseases like Covid-19,” he said.

The meetings brought together officers from the Philippine National Police, the Philippine Coast Guard, the DENR-BMB, and other government partners.

Coordination for deterrence

Discussions covered updates on Haribon’s ongoing work to curb the illegal parrot trade, as well as next steps for tackling it together—for the sake of the birds, and for the people on both sides of the border whose safety is also at stake.

Article continues after this 

For Rjay Serrano, research specialist at Haribon, the meetings reinforced a lesson that has shaped the project from the start: No organization can dismantle the trade without help.

“Tackling the illegal parrot trade isn’t something any single organization can do alone. When different groups collaborate, we see better results. More seizures are done, more wildlife traders are being prosecuted,” said Serrano.

Article continues after this 

“Coordination ensures that law enforcement know what to do from seizure to prosecution, creating a deterrent that makes illegal traders think twice.”

Toledo added that the public has a role to play too.

“We should not patronize illegally collected or traded wildlife. When the buying stops, the poaching and the hunting will stop as well,” he said.

Three-decade smuggling

The July meetings were part of Haribon’s Tackling Cross-Border Bird Trade: Indonesian Parrots in the Philippines project, which worked with various law enforcement and environment officials across key transport and confiscation points in Luzon and Mindanao.

The illegal wildlife trade is considered the second biggest threat to species survival globally. The smuggling of live Indonesian wildlife—particularly parrots—into the Philippines has been documented for more than three decades, costing the country an estimated $1 billion a year.

From 2010 to 2020, more than 67,500 wildlife specimens were confiscated from 523 suspected violators in the Philippines, while 763 birds endemic to Indonesia were seized in 2022 alone.

The project focuses on gathering data on traded species and trade routes, supporting law enforcement, raising awareness, shaping policy recommendations, and strengthening cooperation between the Philippines and Indonesia.

Haribon is the Philippine national partner of BirdLife International, the world’s largest nature conservation partnership. Haribon is working closely with its BirdLife partner in Indonesia, Burung Indonesia, to align efforts on both sides of the border where the trade begins and ends.

World.content:

MANILA, Philippines — Malacañang on Wednesday evening directed government offices and schools in Metro Manila and 13 provinces to adopt alternative work and learning arrangements on Thursday, Sept. 10, due to the continued effects of the southwest monsoon, or “habagat.”

Under Memorandum Circular No. 135 issued by the Office of the President, the areas covered by the order are as follows:

National Capital Region

Pangasinan

Benguet

Bataan

Bulacan

Pampanga

Zambales

Batangas

Cavite

Laguna

Rizal

Article continues after this

World.title: Navy not yet finished investigating death of its trainee
World.content:
MANILA, Philippines — The Philippine Navy on Wednesday said it has not yet finished conducting its own investigation into the death of a 25-year-old Navy Officer candidate last July.

Philippine Navy spokesperson Marissa Martinez issued this statement after the parents of Aldwayne Agnaonao Dulnuan sought the help of the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) to probe his death last July 22 during a training in Zambales.

“The Philippine Navy confirms that investigations of the incident remain ongoing, through its own internal proceedings and the independent probe conducted by the Criminal Investigation and Detection Group (CIDG) of the Philippine National Police,” Martinez said in a statement sent to the Inquirer.

Article continues after this 

READ: Ifugao kin seek NBI probe into Navy trainee’s death in July

Dulnuan’s parents, Stella and Arnold, said that the Philippine Navy committed to them to launch its investigation into the incident, but they noted that they have not received any updates even 49 days after their son died.

In response, Martinez said that the results are not yet available, “since the Navy wants to ensure that the findings are sound and comprehensive and that nothing and no one has been overlooked.”

Martinez also said the Navy respects Aldwayne’s family’s decision to seek another independent investigation into the incident. It then committed to coordinate with the CIDG and other concerned agencies to ensure that proper procedures will lead to the resolution of the case.

READ: Lack of Navy nod stalls probe of cadet’s death

Article continues after this 

Cause of death

Atty. Dwight Dangilan, Aldwayne’s family’s legal counsel, said that they sought the help of the NBI on Wednesday to determine whether there was foul play in his death.

Citing Aldwayne’s death certificate issued by Ulticare Medical Center in Olongapo City, the spokesperson detailed that his cause of death was septic shock with antecedent central nervous system infection and Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome, which is an underlying cause of pulmonary hemorrhage and acute kidney injury.

Article continues after this 

“No autopsy was performed, and the Certificate of Death makes no finding as to the manner of death. Records reviewed to date contain no documented findings of trauma,” Martinez added.

In an interview with the media, Stella narrated how she found out what happened to her son, noting that she received a message that her son was brought to the hospital due to dehydration. She said that she was wondering why her son was already intubated when they visited him at the hospital.

“Kung kinakailangan na hukayin ulit kung ire-require ng NBI, gagawin po namin para lalabas ang katotohanan sa pagkamatay ng anak ko,” she said.

(If his remains need to be exhumed if the NBI requires it, we will do it for the truth behind his death to come out.)

Further, when asked why the family took over a month to ask for help from another agency, Arnold said that they were waiting for updates from the Philippine Navy on its independent probe.

“Wala pang feedback sa amin, sa family, kung ano na ang sitwasyon, ano na ang nangyari. We cannot wait anymore. Maybe they will conduct their investigation but now we want to seek the help of other institutions,” Arnold said in the same interview.

World.title: Passenger ferry caught fire off Coron, Palawan
World.content:
Photo by CGD-Palawan

MANILA, Philippines — A passenger ferry caught fire off Coron, Palawan on Wednesday evening, with more than 100 passengers and crew on board, the Philippine Coast Guard reported.

The Coast Guard District (CGD) – Palawan said it received a report at 6:45 p.m. that MV June Aster, located 1.2 nautical miles (2.2 km) northeast of Barangay Marcilla in Coron, was engulfed in flames.

At least 117 passengers and 17 crew members were reportedly aboard the vessel.

Article continues after this 

As of 11 p.m., at least 42 individuals were rescued and were temporarily brought to Brgy. Turda basketball court amid ongoing rescue operations.

Meanwhile, five were confirmed dead, according to the PCG.

READ: Floating inferno: Dozens dead, missing in ferry fire

According to the CGD – Palawan, its Maritime Environmental Protection unit also prepared oil spill response equipment to conduct precautionary measures for the possible spill of hazardous materials off its waters.

“CGDPAL, through its responding units, continues to manage the situation and coordinate necessary response efforts to ensure the safety of the passengers and crew and to mitigate potential maritime and environmental hazards,” it said.

The cause of the fire is yet to be disclosed by the authorities as of the time of posting. /cb

World.title: LRT-1 extension commitments should move to actual construction
World.content:
MANILA, Philippines — Commitments regarding the Light Rail Transit Line 1 (LRT-1) Cavite extension should move toward actual construction as the new stations have been long-awaited by people who seek faster and more efficient transportation modes, Las Piñas Rep. Mark Anthony Santos said.

In a statement, Santos said that the funding allocated to the LRT-1 Cavite Extension Project for 2027—P1.17 billion—should ensure that people from the southern part of Metro Manila and its adjacent towns would soon benefit from the new stations.

The P1.17 billion is higher than the P799.64 million given to the project in 2026.

Article continues after this 

“This is welcome news for the people of Las Piñas and the entire southern Metro Manila area. Additional funding means we are giving this long-delayed project a stronger push toward completion,” Santos said.

For the LRT-1 extensions, two stations remain unconstructed—one in Las Piñas and another in Cavite. However, hopes that the stations will be built soon came after the Villar Group of Companies agreed to the agency’s terms for the construction of the Las Piñas station.

During the House of Representatives’ committee on appropriations hearing on the proposed 2027 budget of the Department of Transportation (DOTr), Transportation Secretary Giovanni Lopez reported this development, a week after saying that his agency will meet with the Villar Group regarding its donation of six parcels of land where Las Piñas station is expected to be built.

The agreement is expected to be signed by Thursday, September 10.

READ: DOTr: Villar group agrees to terms on LRT-1 Las Piñas station construction

Article continues after this 

These commitments, Santos said, must now turn into actual construction.

“The people of Las Piñas and our neighboring communities have waited long enough. We must now turn these commitments into actual construction and finally deliver the transportation relief our commuters urgently need,” Santos said.

Article continues after this 

READ: DOTr: LRT-1 Cavite extension to move forward if Villars spurn offer

Under the 2027 National Expenditures Program prepared by the executive branch, the DOTr gets a funding boost, receiving P197.3 billion for the country’s rail transport program in 2027—thrice the allocation given in 2026.

Of the P197.3 billion, the Rail Transport Program will get P141.96 billion, which Santos said is a 256.54-percent increase from the P55.34 billion provided under the 2026 General Appropriations Act (GAA).

World.title: Solon to DOH: Budget is available, but stop doctors’ excessive PFs
World.content:
Parañaque Rep. Brian Raymund Yamsuan

MANILA, Philippines — While the House of Representatives is willing to provide the necessary budget to the Department of Health (DOH) for a better implementation of its programs, a lawmaker has urged the agency to find ways to prevent doctors from inflating their professional fees (PF).

In a statement on Wednesday, Parañaque Rep. Brian Raymund Yamsuan said that the DOH should work towards ensuring that the Medical Assistance to Indigent and Financially Incapacitated Patients (MAIFIP) program—the department’s primary medical aid mechanism—will be more transparent.

Yamsuan said this as several lawmakers raised their constituents’ complaints that doctors are supposedly increasing the professional fees (PFs) once they learn that services will be paid through MAIFIP, which leads to higher hospital bills for patients.

Article continues after this 

“Kailangan natin tingnan ang transparency and accountability rin ng mga doctors. Kailangan mag-set up [ang DOH] ng mekanismo para to make sure na yung mga kababayan natin hindi malagay sa alanganin,” Yamsuan said after the House committee on appropriations tackled DOH’s proposed 2027 budget.

(We need to look at the transparency and accountability of doctors. The DOH should set up a mechanism which would ensure that our fellow FIlipinos are not placed in a precarious situation).

Help DOH find funding

Yamsuan said that the Budget Amendments and Review Subcommittee (BARSc)—a sub-panel of the committee on appropriations—will help the DOH find funding for programs.

During the proceedings of the BARSc, members of the committee, along with representatives of different political parties in the House, publicly realign funds sourced from different agencies towards programs that need more prioritization. In 2025, for the discussions on the 2026 budget, the BARSc reallocated P255 billion of infrastructure funds to health, education, and social services.

While they will help DOH, Yamsuan reminded the agency that helping must go both ways.

Article continues after this 

“Kami sa Kongreso (We in Congress), sa BARSc and also at the bicameral conference committee (Bicam), we will help you. We should be constructive now. We should help each other,” Yamsuan, a member of both the BARSc, said.

There have been several concerns about health programs not being adequate come 2027, due to the huge budget cuts experienced by the DOH.

Article continues after this 

During the hearing of the agency’s 2027 budget before the committee on appropriations last September 2, Health Secretary Edwin Mercado said that DOH and its attached agencies originally proposed P837 billion—but were only allocated P353.8 billion under the 2027 National Expenditures Program (NEP).

The NEP is the budget prepared by the executive branch and submitted to Congress for its own deliberations.

READ: DOH warns of compromised programs due to possible 2027 budget cut

Among the DOH programs that may be affected are the Health Facilities Enhancement Program (HFEP), which got only P14 billion compared to their proposal of P29 billion; hospital operations, which suffered an P11 billion budget cut; and the Philippine Health Insurance Corporation (PhilHealth) suffered which got only P73 billion instead of the proposed P379 billion.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s First Government Meeting Puts Skilled Workers in Focus
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s first government meeting in its updated composition after the Kurultai elections focused on a topic that could determine the success of its economic transformation: whether the country will have enough skilled workers to support planned growth.

At the Sept. 8 meeting, Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov called for an accelerated pace of work at a new stage of political and economic modernization. The decision to put workforce training at the center of the government’s first meeting highlights a growing concern: Kazakhstan has jobs, but increasingly needs people with the right skills to fill them.

By 2035, the economy is expected to require 2.9 million specialists, including 1.8 million workers in skilled trades. More than half of vacancies on the electronic labor exchange are already for working professions.

Political scientist Gaziz Abishev said the problem is therefore not a shortage of jobs, but a shortage of qualified workers.

He linked demand for technical specialists to existing industrial production, new projects under the country’s reindustrialization policy, municipal infrastructure modernization and rapidly growing cities.

Abishev cited Bektenov’s warning that Kazakhstan is “forced to attract thousands of specialists from abroad so that work does not stop,” underscoring the growing gap between demand for workers and the availability of qualified specialists.

Aligning training with economic needs

The government is seeking to make vocational education more responsive to these demands.

Education Minister Zhuldyz Suleimenova said Kazakhstan’s technical and vocational education system is being transformed according to labor-market needs. Some 480 colleges train working qualifications, while 57,000 students entered such programs this year.

Training programs are also being updated for a changing economy. New professions have been added to the national classifier, while micro-qualifications and AI-related skills are being introduced.

The Science and Higher Education Ministry estimates that more than half of labor demand is for technical and vocational specialists. Regional labor-market maps have identified more than 2,000 emerging professions and transformations of existing ones, including the use of digital twins and AI in production.

Employers are also becoming more directly involved. Nearly 50,000 students at 76 universities currently participate in dual education with 6,000 enterprises. Samruk Kazyna Sovereign Wealth Fund portfolio companies train more than 10,000 students annually through dual education and internships.

The need is particularly visible in energy and industry. Expansion of Kazakhstan’s three existing oil refineries is expected to increase refining capacity from 18 million to 29.2 million tons a year, while a planned new refinery would add another 10 million tons.

Such expansion will require a substantial increase in qualified workers.

Can training make these jobs more attractive?

The government’s challenge is not only to train workers, but to persuade people to choose these professions.

Abishev said many people remain reluctant to enter industrial and technical sectors because they consider wages insufficient. But he cautioned against viewing higher wages alone as the solution.

“Simple increases in wages without productivity growth lead to lower efficiency, higher costs and, ultimately, inflation,” he wrote on his Telegram channel on Sept. 9.

At the same time, he expects competition for qualified workers to push incomes higher. Experienced professionals in technical and skilled trades will always command higher incomes, he said. A shortage of skilled workers and competition for them will drive wages higher, while those who know their profession well, keep improving and have a strong work ethic will always be valued.

This could also alter the traditional perception of working professions. As AI transforms white-collar employment, technical occupations could become among the more attractive and better-paid positions in an economy still heavily dependent on physical infrastructure and industrial production.

The bigger test

The government is now developing a digital system to forecast labor demand, update qualifications and connect training with employment.

The priority professions list has already expanded from 51 to 174, covering engineering, construction, manufacturing, biotechnology, green and nuclear energy.

The first meeting of the updated government may therefore extend beyond education policy. Kazakhstan is preparing for an economy in which growth will depend not only on investment and new projects, but on whether it has enough people with the skills to build and operate them.

The question is no longer simply whether Kazakhstan can create jobs. It is whether it can prepare enough people to fill them.

World.title: Masdar’s 1 GW Wind Plant Highlights Kazakhstan’s Race to Build More Flexible Power System
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan is moving ahead with a $1.4 billion renewable energy project with Masdar, a leading renewable energy company based in the United Arab Emirates (UAE), as the country seeks to expand wind generation while addressing electricity shortages and building a more flexible power system. The development was discussed Sept. 8 during a meeting between Energy Minister Yerlan Akkenzhenov, Masdar’s Deputy Chairman for Business and Projects Abdullah Zayed and UAE Ambassador to Kazakhstan Mohamed Saeed Mohamed Al-Ariki.

The meeting focused on the implementation of a 1-gigawatt wind power plant with an integrated energy storage system in the Zhambyl Region, as well as prospects for expanding cooperation in renewable energy.

The project, being developed within the strategic partnership between Kazakhstan and Masdar, is expected to attract approximately $1.4 billion in investment. It will include a 1,000-megawatt wind farm and a 300-megawatt battery storage system with a capacity of 600 megawatt-hours. Full commissioning is scheduled for the third quarter of 2029.

From a wind project to a test of Kazakhstan’s energy transition

The Zhambyl project comes as Kazakhstan moves toward a more complex phase of renewable-energy development. Increasing installed capacity is only one part of the transition. The country also needs storage, modern transmission networks and regulatory mechanisms capable of balancing electricity generated from weather-dependent sources.

The storage component of the Masdar project is particularly important in this context. Wind generation can fluctuate with weather conditions, while electricity demand changes throughout the day. A large-scale storage system can help absorb excess generation and make electricity available when renewable output declines or demand rises.

The Energy Ministry has identified energy storage as a strategic priority. Speaking at the Go Net Zero – Central Asia and Caspian business summit, Turar Alimzhan, director of the ministry’s Department of Renewable Energy, said legislation on energy storage systems is currently under consideration, alongside a long-term concept for the development of green energy.

“We are moving toward this goal systematically. The law on energy storage systems is already under consideration, and this is one of our strategic priorities,” he said.

Under Kazakhstan’s electricity-sector development plan through 2035, the country intends to implement at least 8.4 GW of installed renewable-energy capacity. That target means that the next challenge will increasingly be not simply generating renewable electricity, but ensuring that it can be reliably delivered to consumers.

The Masdar project has already moved beyond the planning stage

The current construction phase also marks a significant progression for the Zhambyl project. When The Astana Times spoke with Masdar Chief Operating Officer Abdulaziz Alobaidli ahead of Abu Dhabi Sustainability Week 2026, the project was still undergoing wind-resource assessment. Alobaidli explained that developing a bankable wind project requires detailed on-site measurements rather than relying only on satellite or historical data.

“We have signed the Power Purchase Agreement, and we have moved into the development phase,” he said, noting that wind projects require specific on-site work, including at least one year of ground-based measurements to establish the project’s bankability.

Since then, the project has advanced to construction. On June 29, Kazakhstan and Masdar held a capsule-laying ceremony and officially launched work at the site in the Zhambyl Region. The progression illustrates the lengthy process behind utility-scale renewable investments, from resource assessment and power-purchase agreements to financing, construction and eventual grid integration.

Masdar sees Central Asia as a core growth market

The Zhambyl project is also part of Masdar’s broader expansion across Central Asia. “In Central Asia, we remain one of the largest renewable energy investors, with Uzbekistan, Azerbaijan, and Kazakhstan as core focus markets,” Alobaidli told The Astana Times. “We also continue dialogue with other Central Asian countries, supporting energy policy development and reform to improve bankability and attract investment.”

This regional approach reflects a broader transformation underway across Central Asia, where countries face similar pressures to increase electricity generation, modernize aging infrastructure and reduce the carbon intensity of their economies.

At the Go Net Zero summit, Alimzhan said Kazakhstan, Azerbaijan and Uzbekistan were increasingly coordinating their efforts to develop a new energy model in which renewable generation, energy storage and low-carbon technologies play a central role. The discussions also focused on the development of a green energy corridor linking Central Asia, Azerbaijan and Europe. The initiative has entered a practical implementation phase and is being considered as a potential area for deeper regional energy cooperation.

The grid will determine how far renewables can go

Kazakhstan’s renewable-energy ambitions ultimately depend on infrastructure beyond the power plants themselves. Large volumes of wind and solar generation require transmission networks capable of moving electricity from resource-rich areas to major consumption centers. This is particularly relevant for southern Kazakhstan, where additional generation capacity is being developed partly to address electricity shortages.

The transition therefore requires simultaneous progress in several areas: renewable generation, storage, transmission infrastructure, digitalization and regulation. The regional dimension adds another layer. Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Azerbaijan already have interconnected energy interests, while the proposed Central Asia-Azerbaijan-Europe corridor could eventually create new opportunities for cross-border electricity trade.

Energy security and decarbonization are converging

For Kazakhstan, the renewable-energy transition is not only a climate-policy issue. The country needs to increase electricity supply while maintaining energy security and gradually reducing the carbon intensity of its economy. These objectives make renewable generation increasingly attractive, but they also expose the limitations of a power system designed around more predictable generation sources.

At the Sept. 8 meeting, Akkenzhenov said Kazakhstan was interested in expanding cooperation with international investors and technology partners in renewable energy.

“Partnership with Masdar contributes to the development of renewable energy and Kazakhstan’s progress toward carbon neutrality,” the minister said, adding that the project would support regional energy security, attract modern technologies and create new opportunities for energy infrastructure development.

World.title: Digital Customs Could Boost Kazakhstan’s Transit Potential, But Infrastructure Remains Key, Experts Say
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan is stepping up its partnership with the World Customs Organization (WCO) as part of a broader strategy to strengthen the country’s position as a key Eurasian transit hub. But while digital customs reforms could significantly reduce trade costs and border delays, experts say their long-term economic payoff will ultimately depend on infrastructure, regional coordination and the changing geography of global trade.

The topic came into focus during a series of high-level meetings in Astana between President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov and WCO Secretary General Ian Saunders on Sept. 8.

During the meeting, Tokayev said Kazakhstan is consistently developing a “smart border” model by introducing digital solutions to optimize customs procedures and improve freight transit across Eurasia. Saunders praised Kazakhstan’s progress in customs modernization and its growing role in developing the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route (TITR), also known as the Middle Corridor.

Customs modernization becomes part of a wider logistics strategy

Beyond the diplomatic symbolism, the meetings reflect a longer-term economic objective: transforming Kazakhstan from a transit country into an internationally competitive logistics platform.

Speaking in the meeting, Bektenov emphasized that resilient transcontinental trade has become one of the key drivers of Kazakhstan’s economic development. He noted that the WCO’s 2025–2028 strategic plan, Data-Driven Customs for a Connected World, closely aligns with Kazakhstan’s own digital reform agenda.

A central element of that strategy is the rollout of KEDEN, a unified customs system integrating declarations, transit procedures and border controls, alongside the Smart Cargo platform, which combines transport services, electronic permits and cargo tracking into a single digital ecosystem.

According to official data, 14.6 million tons of transit cargo passed through Kazakhstan during the first seven months of the year. Freight volumes along the Middle Corridor reached approximately 350,000 tons, with around 24,000 vehicles using the route.

Why digital borders matter

Farkhad Kassenov, head of the A+ Analytics research center, political scientist and international relations expert, notes that cooperation with the WCO should be viewed not as an isolated initiative but as one stage of Kazakhstan’s much broader transport and logistics strategy.

“Kazakhstan has been systematically synchronizing customs procedures, tariffs and border regulations with the countries participating in the Middle Corridor. This cooperation with the WCO is one of the stages of that much larger project,” Kassenov told The Astana Times.

The Middle Corridor has gained strategic importance as trade between China and Europe increasingly seeks alternatives to traditional northern routes passing through Russia. At the same time, Kazakhstan is also positioning itself within the developing North–South corridor, despite temporary disruptions caused by conflicts affecting the Middle East and maritime trade. According to Kassenov, removing bureaucratic barriers may prove almost as valuable as building new infrastructure.

“Digitalization can increase the speed of cargo movement by roughly 30% while simultaneously reducing logistics costs. When paperwork is synchronized and businesses use a single digital window, goods spend less time waiting at borders or in dry ports,” he said.

Digital gains cannot replace physical infrastructure

Yet customs reform alone will not solve every bottleneck. Kassenov notes that the Middle Corridor still faces structural constraints that digital systems cannot eliminate, including different railway gauges between China, Kazakhstan and Europe, as well as the natural limitations of crossing the Caspian Sea.

“There are real physical barriers. Different railway gauges require cargo transfers, while navigation across the Caspian is limited during storms and seasonal ice. Digitalization improves efficiency, but it must be accompanied by major investment in transport infrastructure,” he said.

Kazakhstan has already begun expanding ports in Aktau and Kuryk, while negotiations continue with Azerbaijan, Türkiye and China on improving rail connectivity across the corridor.

A changing geopolitical map of trade

The renewed attention to Kazakhstan’s transit role is also being driven by geopolitical shifts beyond Central Asia. According to Kassenov, growing strategic competition between China and the United States has increased Beijing’s interest in secure overland trade routes.

“The Middle Corridor was once viewed as an alternative route. By the end of this decade, it may become one of the principal land connections between East and West,” he said.

That evolution creates opportunities extending beyond transit fees. Kazakhstan is seeking to develop domestic manufacturing, processing industries and exports of higher value-added products, including critical minerals and industrial goods, that can move along the same logistics network.

A customs dilemma inside the EAEU

At the same time, Kazakhstan’s customs policy faces another question that is less visible in discussions about digitalization: whether the existing distribution of import customs duties within the Eurasian Economic Union reflects the current structure of regional trade.

Aidar Kurmashev, head of the Asian Studies Department at the Kazakhstan Institute for Strategic Studies, recently highlighted the issue in his Telegram channel. According to him, under the EAEU system, duties collected on imports from outside the union are distributed among the five member states according to predetermined shares. Kazakhstan’s share is 6.955%, compared with 85.065% for Russia, regardless of where the duties are actually collected.

“After 2022, trade flows changed significantly, the role of Kazakhstan in trade with China and other directions of foreign imports increased, while our share remained 6.955%,” Kurmashev wrote.

He argued that the issue raises a broader question about whether the formula still corresponds to the current structure of trade within the EAEU.

“If Kazakhstan previously benefited from the system, but now has been losing hundreds of billions of tenge for the third consecutive year, perhaps it is time to at least recalculate the economics of the existing mechanism,” Kurmashev said, highlighting that the figures refer specifically to distributed import customs duties and do not include import VAT.

Trade routes are changing faster than institutions

The EAEU perspective illustrates a broader challenge facing Kazakhstan as it tries to reposition itself within changing Eurasian trade networks. The geography of imports and transit has shifted since 2022, while Kazakhstan is simultaneously trying to deepen direct trade links with China, expand the Middle Corridor and strengthen its position as a logistics hub between Asia and Europe.

That makes customs policy increasingly relevant not only as an administrative function but as an element of economic strategy. Digitalization can make the movement of goods faster and more predictable. International standards can improve interoperability. Infrastructure investment can remove physical bottlenecks.

But the economic payoff ultimately depends on whether these elements develop together. As Kassenov put it, the Middle Corridor is moving from being an alternative route from the global lens toward becoming a potentially central Eurasian connection.

World.title: Golden Horde History Challenges Europe-Centered View of Medieval Eurasia, French Historian Says
World.content:
ALMATY – For centuries, the history of the Golden Horde has often been told from the perspective of the societies it encountered. French historian Marie Favereau is trying to turn that perspective around. Her book, now available in Kazakh, examines the Ulus of Jochi not as a peripheral chapter in European or Mongol history, but as a powerful Eurasian state with its own political institutions, commercial networks and multicultural society.

Favereau presented the Kazakh-language edition of her book “The Horde: How the Mongols Changed the World” at the Kazakh National Academy of Sciences in Almaty on Sept. 8. The event was organised by the Academy together with Steppe & World Publishing and the Embassy of France in Kazakhstan.

The publication comes at a time when Kazakhstan is placing renewed emphasis on the study of the Ulus of Jochi and the history of the Golden Horde. But Favereau’s work offers something more than another account of a familiar historical period: it asks readers to reconsider how the history of the steppe has traditionally been interpreted.

Looking at the steppe from within

Favereau’s interest in the Golden Horde began nearly 25 years ago, when she was a student at the Sorbonne in Paris. She recalled that when she proposed studying the Ulus of Jochi, her supervisor warned her that the subject would be difficult because France had few sources on the period. Rather than discouraging her, the response sent her in the opposite direction.

“I thought, I’m going to travel all around the world and I will gather all the archives, all the material, all the objects I can to document, to explain the history of Ulus Jochi,” Favereau said at the presentation.

Her research subsequently took her to archives and collections in Vienna, Venice, Genova, Istanbul, and Crimea, while academic cooperation brought her into contact with historians and researchers in Kazakhstan and Tatarstan.

That experience shaped the central approach of her work: understanding the Golden Horde on its own terms. Favereau said Western academic discussions of empire have traditionally focused on examples such as the Roman, Greek and Ottoman empires, while nomadic political systems have received far less attention.

“I had to write a book, a book that I would have needed as a student about Ulus Jochi, but from inside, from the nomadic perspective,” she said.

For Favereau, this distinction matters because the political and social structures of a steppe empire cannot simply be measured against those of Rome, Paris or Vienna. The Golden Horde was born as part of the Mongol Empire in the 13th century before developing into an independent political power under the descendants of Jochi, the eldest son of Genghis Khan. Its political organization, Favereau argues, was more complex than the image of a state ruled solely by a khan suggests.

The begs, nomadic elites, assemblies and negotiations all played important roles in political decision-making. Favereau also draws attention to the role of elite women in the highest levels of government.

“I really wanted to show in my book the importance of collective power, of assembly, of negotiations, of the place of elite women as the highest leader of the states,” she said.

An empire connected to a wider world

The book also challenges the perception of the Golden Horde as an isolated nomadic power. Its geographical position placed the Ulus of Jochi at the intersection of Central Asia, the northern Russian principalities and European trade routes. Its connections extended to the Black Sea and Mediterranean, while diplomatic correspondence reached Poland, Lithuania, France and England.

“It’s about diplomacy, letters exchanged with Poland and Lithuania, letters exchanged with Europe, letters exchanged with France and England,” Favereau said.

Trade was central to those connections. Italian merchants, the Byzantine world and the Mamluk Sultanate were among the partners involved in networks that moved goods, people, knowledge and cultural practices across Eurasia. Favereau highlights that the Jochids expanded the scale of existing Eurasian trade networks, including those associated with the Silk Road.

“The Jochis made the system bigger, because the scale is not the same,” she said, pointing to the vast territory controlled by the Golden Horde.

That perspective places the Golden Horde within global history rather than treating it exclusively as a regional phenomenon. Its importance, in Favereau’s interpretation, lies partly in the connections it created across political and cultural boundaries.

A multicultural society in the medieval steppe

The same approach applies to religion. Favereau challenges the idea that Islamization in the Golden Horde was merely superficial. She points to the conversion of Berke Khan and his relations with the Mamluk Sultanate, which developed into a broader exchange involving scholars, religion, literature, science and crafts.

At the same time, the Ulus of Jochi retained a tradition of religious diversity, with Christian, Buddhist and Jewish communities living within its territories. For a medieval empire extending across much of Eurasia, such diversity complicates the image of the Golden Horde as simply a military power built through conquest. It also highlights one of the broader arguments of Favereau’s research: nomadic societies should not be understood through stereotypes of political or cultural simplicity.

Why translation matters

The Kazakh edition gives that research a new audience. For Favereau, translation is not simply about making a text accessible. It is part of the scholarly exchange itself.

“Without translation, we are limited to our own circle,” she said.

She described translating historical concepts as a process of interpretation, requiring scholars and translators to consider how ideas developed in one linguistic and cultural environment can be understood in another.

“The translation in Kazakh language goes deeply to my heart,” Favereau said, highlighting that the translation also reflects a broader effort to bring international scholarship into Kazakhstan’s academic and educational space while strengthening dialogue between researchers working on the history of Eurasia.

Building bridges through history

French Consul General Maxime Gehringer said such exchanges have significance beyond the publication of a single book.

“Countries are not built through political dialogue, economic exchange alone. We depend on a better knowledge of one another,” he said.

He described cultural, scientific and academic exchanges as an integral part of the growing strategic partnership between France and Kazakhstan. Gehringer also highlighted Favereau’s long engagement with Central Asia, including her work as director of the French Institute for Central Asian Studies in Bishkek. He said her research contributes to continuing discussions in Kazakhstan and elsewhere in the region by bringing together different sources and perspectives on the history of nomadic societies.

“The authors present nomadic societies in all their complexity,” Gehringer said. “Political organizations, histories, trade and diplomacy are brought together within a vast space connecting Asia and Europe.”

A history beyond modern borders

Favereau’s book ultimately asks readers to reconsider where the history of the Golden Horde belongs. It is certainly part of the history of the Eurasian steppe and of the territories that include present-day Kazakhstan. But its networks extended far beyond modern national borders, linking Central Asia with the Middle East, Russia and Europe.

That makes the history of the Ulus of Jochi relevant not only to understanding Kazakhstan’s past, but also to understanding how political power, commerce, religion and cultural exchange operated across Eurasia centuries before the emergence of today’s states.

For Kazakhstan, having that scholarship available in Kazakh adds another dimension. It allows international interpretations of the Golden Horde to enter the country’s own academic and public discussion in the national language. For Favereau, that dialogue is part of what historical research is meant to achieve.

“Research and science is a trans-generation thing,” she said, reflecting on the scholars who influenced her work and the students who will continue it.

World.title: Can Kazakhstan Take its Capital Markets to Next Level?
World.content:
The sense of progress and economic momentum in Kazakhstan is tangible and impossible to ignore. Speaking to Kazakhstan’s financial leaders, policymakers, and leaders in the leadup to the Astana Finance Days conference, I understand why. The government’s clear growth agenda, combined with bold steps to reform the nation’s capital market, is having a real, positive impact.

Throughout my time in Astana so far, the question has increasingly shifted from whether Kazakhstan can attract international capital, but what the country should do next to become a true global center.

The foundations are already in place. Kazakhstan is the largest economy in Central Asia and has a growing role as the bridge between major European and Asian markets. The country has spent recent years developing the financial infrastructure needed to open its market and connect domestic companies, investors, and global capital. The Astana International Financial Centre, with its English common law framework, and the Astana International Exchange have complemented the domestic market by providing an international platform for investment and cross-border issuance – drawing in over $21 billion in investment since 2018.

Technology is already part of Kazakhstan’s vision for what comes next. Speaking at a Bloomberg event in 2025, NBK Governor Timur Suleimenov highlighted the importance of financial technology as a major force for financial growth and the role of modern infrastructure in supporting the next stage of market development. Opening the market, however, is only the beginning. The next challenge is making it easier to participate in.

Looking around the world, Poland offers a useful lesson in what sustained market development can achieve. Its emergence as Central and Eastern Europe’s leading financial center was not the result of any single reform. Debt market digitization, regulation, international accessibility, trading and settlement infrastructure, liquidity and investor participation reinforced one another over time. In 2018, that cumulative development helped Poland become the first country from Central and Eastern Europe to be upgraded from emerging to developed-market status by FTSE Russell.

No two markets are the same. Kazakhstan is at a different stage in its economic journey and will follow its own path. But there are undoubtedly parallels to be drawn with Poland a decade ago: a market with growing international ambitions, strategically located, but still considerable scope to deepen participation and strengthen the infrastructure supporting its financial market.

Kazakhstan is already moving in this direction. The recent digitization of government services across the country and the presidential decree on digital assets show a clear direction in one asset class. Last week, authorities announced plans for a new capital-market development program aimed at creating a deeper, more liquid and diversified market and improving businesses’ access to long-term financing. Among the measures under consideration is a centralized securities-lending mechanism designed to improve liquidity in the secondary stock market.

The same focus on liquidity is relevant to Kazakhstan’s sovereign debt market. Authorities are seeking to broaden the investor base and increase appetite for Kazakh debt. Recent reforms to the primary dealer system are intended to bolster liquidity and pave the way for government securities to enter global indices, ultimately helping to reduce government borrowing costs.

Further development of the secondary market can reinforce that progress. A market works better when investors are not simply able to buy but assets but can trade them efficiently once they own them. More active secondary markets support effective price discovery and give investors greater confidence that they can enter and exit positions efficiently. Over time, stronger public markets can become more effective mechanisms for allocating capital across the economy.

As Kazakhstan itself has recognized, technology can help deliver this next stage of development. Electronic trading, integrated data and analytics, pricing systems and modern market infrastructure can reduce friction and make it easier for market participants to transact with confidence. Efforts to digitalize securities issuance, modernize settlement processes and connect its markets more closely with global infrastructure are already moving this agenda forward. As markets become more sophisticated and internationally connected, the infrastructure supporting them needs to evolve as well.

We have seen first-hand the impact that this infrastructure development can have in other emerging markets. In Georgia, Bloomberg worked with the National Bank to introduce electronic trading for the country’s repo market. By integrating trading systems with Bloomberg’s data, analytics and market-surveillance capabilities, interbank transactions became more automated and ultimately more efficient. Similar partnerships with central banks and financial institutions around the world show how modern financial infrastructure and technology can complement wider capital-market reforms and support greater participation.

Kazakhstan has already built much of the foundation and opened its doors further to international investors. The strength and international connectivity of the markets will determine how fully Kazakhstan can capitalize on the opportunity. Get that next stage right, and it will be better placed not only to attract global capital, but to put it to work across its economy.

The author is Sallianne Taylor, the Head of Government Relations for Europe and Central Asia at Bloomberg LP.

World.title: The Semipalatinsk Treaty at 20: Enduring Logic of Nuclear-Free Central Asia
World.content:
Twenty years ago on Sept. 8, 2006, representatives of Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan gathered in Semipalatinsk, now Semey, to sign a treaty that would make Central Asia the first nuclear-weapon-free zone in the Northern Hemisphere. It was also the first such zone established in a region where nuclear weapons had actually been tested and deployed.

I remember that day well. I was there as a representative of the James Martin Center for Nonproliferation Studies. Kazakhstan was represented by its then Foreign Minister, Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, who signed the Treaty on behalf of the country. The ceremony itself, held at the Abai State Kazakh Musical Drama Theater, was relatively modest. Its significance was anything but.

The idea of a nuclear-weapon-free Central Asia was hardly inevitable. It was first proposed by Uzbekistan at the UN General Assembly in 1993 and developed over the following years, as the newly independent states were dealing with borders, economic dislocation and an uncertain security environment. The region also carried an extraordinary nuclear legacy: the Semipalatinsk test site, uranium mining, radioactive waste and communities affected by decades of Soviet nuclear activities.

Yet the five Central Asian states made a strategic choice. They decided that their common security would not be built around nuclear weapons. But translating the idea into a legally binding regional commitment was not an easy process as it required persistence and, above all, agreement among all the parties.

The Treaty prohibits the development, production, acquisition, possession, stockpiling or use of nuclear weapons and other nuclear explosive devices. At the same time, it preserves the right to peaceful uses of nuclear energy. Its parties also accepted important obligations relating to IAEA safeguards and the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty.

There is more to the Semipalatinsk Treaty than the absence of nuclear weapons. It was also an early demonstration that the five Central Asian states could develop a common approach to a question of fundamental importance to their security and future. That is perhaps the Treaty’s most interesting legacy today.

Central Asia has changed considerably since 2006. The region is more economically connected, more strategically important and more closely engaged with the major powers than it was two decades ago. At the same time, the international arms control architecture has come under unprecedented pressure. Nuclear rhetoric has returned to the center of global security debates, while confidence in many traditional arms-control arrangements has weakened.

Against this backdrop, it is tempting to regard the Semipalatinsk Treaty as a relic of a more optimistic era. I would argue the opposite.

Its importance lies precisely in the fact that it was created under difficult circumstances and has survived major changes in the regional and global environment. The Treaty entered into force in 2009 after all five states completed ratification. In 2014, all five nuclear-weapon states recognized under the Non-Proliferation Treaty signed its Protocol, committing themselves, among other things, not to use or threaten to use nuclear weapons against the Central Asian parties. Four have since ratified it; U.S. ratification remains outstanding.

There is also a lesson here about Central Asia itself. The Semipalatinsk Treaty was the first regional security agreement to bring all five Central Asian states together, including neutral Turkmenistan. That achievement should not be underestimated.

But anniversaries should not be occasions only for looking backward. The next twenty years will be more important than the last twenty.

The Treaty provides a framework, but a framework is only as effective as the cooperation built around it. Encouragingly, the five states have expressed interest in the institutional development of the CANWFZ and in closer cooperation with other nuclear-weapon-free zones. This points toward a more practical agenda: strengthening cooperation on nuclear security, peaceful uses of nuclear energy, radioactive waste and environmental remediation, emergency preparedness, and the prevention of illicit trafficking of nuclear and radioactive materials. Its value could also grow as the region’s nuclear energy ambitions develop.

This would give the Semipalatinsk Treaty a renewed practical dimension without changing its basic character.

The Treaty also helped establish something larger than a legal prohibition. It became part of Central Asia’s emerging security architecture – one based not on military blocs or strategic rivalry, but on the idea that regional stability could be strengthened through common rules and restraint.

The significance of the Semipalatinsk Treaty, therefore, is not that it solved every security problem facing Central Asia. It did something more durable: it established a common regional commitment at a moment when the future of the region was still uncertain.

Twenty years later, that commitment has become part of Central Asia’s security identity. The challenge now is to ensure that the Treaty remains a living instrument rather than simply a historic achievement. In a world where the value of restraint, dialogue and nonproliferation is once again being tested, Central Asia has a stake – and perhaps a responsibility – in showing that regional cooperation on nuclear security can endure even when the global environment becomes more difficult.

The author is Dauren Aben, the deputy director at the Kazakhstan Institute for Strategic Studies under the President of Kazakhstan.

Disclaimer: The views and opinions expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the position of The Astana Times.

World.title: Almaty and Astana Maintain Economic Lead as Central Asia’s Cities Race to Catch Up
World.content:
ALMATY – Almaty and Astana are likely to retain their position as Central Asia’s leading economic centers, even as Tashkent and Bishkek record rapid growth and invest heavily in their future expansion. Kazakhstan’s two largest cities benefit from an economic scale, financial infrastructure and established business ecosystems that have been built up over decades, reported the Times of Central Asia.

Almaty has long combined Kazakhstan’s commercial and political functions and established itself as Central Asia’s leading business center. After Astana became the country’s capital, the two cities gradually developed more complementary roles. Almaty remained the region’s main business and financial hub, while Astana accumulated political, institutional and corporate weight.

Updated figures show Astana’s economy grew by about 10% in 2025, while Almaty recorded growth of about 5%. Together, the two cities generated nearly $107 billion in economic output last year.

Their position is supported by Kazakhstan’s broader economic weight. The country accounts for more than half of Central Asia’s GDP and nearly two-thirds of the region’s inward FDI stock, according to The Times of Central Asia’s Central Asia Balance Sheet. That larger economic base provides greater fiscal capacity for infrastructure and urban development, which in turn supports business activity.

Kazakhstan also has the region’s most developed capital markets. The Kazakhstan Stock Exchange (KASE) in Almaty and the Astana International Financial Centre (AIFC) and Astana International Exchange (AIX) in Astana provide companies with access to equity and debt financing, institutional investors and financial infrastructure on a scale not currently available elsewhere in Central Asia.

Kazakhstan is also the only Central Asian country with an investment-grade sovereign rating. That status can reduce the country-risk premium and financing costs for companies and projects compared with lower-rated regional markets.

Tashkent and Bishkek are also growing rapidly

Tashkent is the most significant challenger to Kazakhstan’s two leading cities. Uzbekistan’s political and commercial capital had an economy of about $29 billion in 2025, nearly 40% the size of Almaty’s and about three-quarters that of Astana.

Its growth rate, however, has been considerably higher. Tashkent’s real GRP increased by 11.3% in 2025, according to preliminary national figures. Tashkent also benefits from Uzbekistan’s demographic scale. The country’s population is almost twice that of Kazakhstan, giving its capital access to a considerably larger domestic market and labor pool.

That advantage comes with its own demands. A larger and growing population requires continuous investment in employment, housing, transport and other infrastructure. If productivity and investment do not keep pace with demographic growth, population size can become a constraint rather than an economic advantage.

The difference in economic output per resident remains substantial. In 2025, GRP per capita stood at approximately $29,900 in Almaty and $23,700 in Astana, compared with about $9,300 in Tashkent. These figures measure economic output per resident rather than labor productivity, household income or living standards, but they nevertheless illustrate the difference in the economic scale of the cities.

Bishkek is growing from a considerably smaller base. Its economy was only about 30% the size of Tashkent’s in the reporting years used here, although the Kyrgyz capital recorded real GRP growth of 15.8% in 2024.

Its economic advantages are different from those of Tashkent. The Kyrgyz Republic’s 10% standard corporate profit-tax rate is below the standard rates in Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan. The country’s predominantly hydropower-based electricity generation also provides a relatively low-carbon energy base, with further development potential.

At the same time, seasonal electricity shortages remain a constraint. Bishkek’s much smaller population and economy also mean a narrower domestic market and a smaller economic base from which to finance major infrastructure projects.

Can Tashkent catch up?

Tashkent’s ability to narrow the gap with Kazakhstan’s leading cities will depend on more than maintaining high growth rates. The city’s ambitious expansion will require enormous amounts of capital from public funds, domestic and foreign private investment and international borrowing.

Uzbekistan’s economy was about $147 billion in 2025, less than half the size of Kazakhstan’s $306 billion economy. Its sovereign credit remains below investment grade, while its capital markets are still less developed. Remittances also remained significant, accounting for 14.3% of GDP in 2025. Kazakhstan, by comparison, combines a larger economy with investment-grade sovereign credit and substantially greater financial and resource buffers.

These differences do not prevent Tashkent from growing rapidly. They do, however, mean that sustaining large-scale investment over several decades will require continued development of capital markets, labor-market reforms and stronger institutions capable of reducing investment risk and mobilizing capital. Tashkent is therefore narrowing the gap with Astana, but the current data do not indicate that it is on the verge of overtaking it.

The difference in recent growth rates is also smaller than it might initially appear. Tashkent recorded 11.3% real GRP growth in 2025, compared with 10.2% in Astana, giving it an advantage of only 1.1%.

Both cities are also expanding their physical and economic capacity. Construction of New Tashkent began in 2023. Its first phase is designed for 600,000 residents, while the eventual city is planned to accommodate up to 2 million people. By 2034, plans call for 200,000 apartments, together with business, education and transport infrastructure. Residential complexes, business facilities and university campuses are already under construction.

Astana is simultaneously adding substantial capacity of its own. Around 2.2 million square meters of housing were completed in January–July 2026, while new transport and utility infrastructure continues to be developed. The city’s master plan envisages a population of 2.275 million by 2035.

Almaty is a much higher hurdle

The challenge is substantially greater when Tashkent is compared with Almaty. Almaty’s economy is currently more than twice the size of Tashkent’s. Tashkent recorded 11.3% real GRP growth in 2025, compared with 4.9% in Almaty, giving Uzbekistan’s capital a considerably wider growth advantage over Almaty than over Astana. But again, the size of the existing gap matters.

Based on the 2025 economic sizes, Tashkent would need to maintain an average annual real-GRP growth advantage of about 1.75% over Almaty for 50 years simply to reach parity, assuming both economies continued to grow. There is little reason to assume that such a differential could be maintained indefinitely. Growth rates generally slow as economies become larger, while long-term OECD projections also point to slower growth in emerging markets as they converge toward higher-income economies.

Tashkent could therefore continue to grow faster than Almaty while still requiring several decades to close the existing gap.

Almaty, meanwhile, is not standing still. The city’s development programme and 2040 master plan envisage five key economic and urban centers intended to distribute business activity and development more broadly across the city. Revised proposals anticipate population growth to as much as 3.6 million by 2040, alongside additional housing and infrastructure.

Nearby Alatau City, although separately administered, is also being developed as part of the wider Almaty agglomeration. It could add employment, investment and economic activity to the metropolitan area, although its contribution is not included in the Almaty city GRP used in this comparison.

Can Bishkek overtake Tashkent?

Bishkek’s growth is impressive, but its much smaller economic base makes a near-term challenge to Tashkent unlikely. The Kyrgyz capital recorded real GRP growth of 15.8% in 2024. Yet its economy was only around 30% the size of Tashkent’s on the reporting years used here.

Even if Bishkek maintained relatively high growth for an extended period, it would need to sustain a significant advantage for many years before reaching a comparable economic scale. The city is nevertheless expanding. A 2024 administrative-territorial reform more than tripled Bishkek’s territory, from 12,900 to approximately 41,000 hectares, incorporating 24 surrounding settlements.

The city has since approved a development plan through 2030, with water networks and social infrastructure being developed in the newly incorporated areas. Its approved 2050 master plan prepares for a population approaching 2 million. Bishkek’s lower operating costs and hydropower base could help it attract investment in selected sectors. Its smaller domestic market and limited economic base, however, remain significant constraints on its ability to compete with the region’s larger centers.

Central Asia’s economic map is changing

The most likely outcome is not necessarily one city replacing another, but a more competitive and interconnected regional economy. Still, Almaty and Astana enter this competition with substantial accumulated advantages. Their combined economic output, financial infrastructure, corporate networks and access to Kazakhstan’s broader resource and investment base provide a strong foundation for continued regional leadership.

Tashkent can narrow the gap, particularly if it succeeds in sustaining productivity growth and mobilizing the capital required for its ambitious expansion. But current city-level data do not indicate that either Almaty or Astana is close to losing its position.

Central Asia’s economic geography is changing, but the region’s established leaders are expanding alongside the challengers. The competition is therefore less about one city simply overtaking another and more about whether the region’s major urban centers can convert growing economic scale into higher productivity, stronger connectivity and greater international competitiveness.

The article was originally published in the Times of Central Asia.

World.title: Kazakhstan Announces Teams for 2026 FIDE Chess Olympiad in Samarkand
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan has announced its national teams for the 46th FIDE Chess Olympiad, which will take place in Samarkand, Uzbekistan, on Sept. 16-27.

The women’s team will be led by Grandmaster Bibisara Assaubayeva, currently ranked fifth in the FIDE women’s world rankings. She will be joined by Alua Nurman, Meruert Kamalidenova, Elnaz Kaliakhmet and Zarina Nurgaliyeva. Pavel Kotsur will serve as the team’s captain, reported the Kazakhstan Chess Federation.

Three members of the squad – Assaubayeva, Nurman and Kamalidenova – were part of the Kazakhstan team that won the silver medal at the 45th FIDE Chess Olympiad in Budapest in 2024. It was Kazakhstan’s best-ever result in the women’s competition.

The men’s team will consist of Daniyal Sapenov, Denis Makhnev, Zhandos Agmanov, Sauat Nurgaliyev and Aldiyar Ansat. Sapenov will make his debut at the Chess Olympiad, while the remaining players have previous international experience.

The 46th FIDE Chess Olympiad is one of the world’s largest team chess competitions. Players will compete in Open and Women’s sections over 11 rounds under the Swiss system. The event brings together national teams featuring many of the world’s leading players.

Kazakhstan enters the competition following a series of notable performances by its leading chess players.

Assaubayeva has been among the country’s most successful players in recent years. In June, she won the Norway Chess Women 2026 title in Oslo, defeating several leading players, including reigning Women’s World Chess Champion Ju Wenjun.

In July, Assaubayeva reached a career-high fifth place in the FIDE women’s world rankings with a rating of 2,538, entering the global top five for the first time.

Her rise adds to an already strong record. In December 2025, Assaubayeva won her third Women’s World Blitz Championship title and became Kazakhstan’s second female Grandmaster.

Other Kazakh players have also achieved success on the international stage. Kazybek Nogerbek became the 2024 FIDE World Junior Chess Champion, winning the title in Gandhinagar, India.

In August, four Kazakh chess players, all under 18, took a step toward earning higher titles. Seventeen-year-old Alikhan Daulet finished fourth at the Rudar GM Round Robin tournament in Serbia, earning an International Master norm.

Fifteen-year-old Elnaz Kaliakhmet won the second women’s prize at the 2026 Kanizsa Open and Hungarian Championship in Hungary, also earning an International Master norm. Meanwhile, 15-year-old Sauat Nurgaliyev finished second at the 27th Sants Open–Ciutat de Barcelona in Spain, securing his second Grandmaster norm.

At the same tournament in Barcelona, 16-year-old Malika Japparbekova won the second women’s prize and earned a Woman International Master norm.

The women’s team will also seek to build on its recent international experience, with several players having represented the country at major team competitions.

The upcoming Olympiad comes as chess continues to gain prominence in Kazakhstan, both through international results and the development of young players. Kazakhstan has increasingly hosted major international chess competitions, while its players regularly compete for medals at world and continental events. In August, Almaty hosted the inaugural FIDE World University Team Chess Championship bringing tems from the world’s leading universities, including Harvard, Oxford and Cambridge.

The Samarkand Olympiad will provide another opportunity for Kazakhstan’s teams to test themselves against the strongest chess nations and build on the women’s historic silver-medal finish in Budapest.

World.title: ‘Major cause for concern’: expert view on Armenian school students’ low level of knowledge
World.content:
Low knowledge levels among Armenian school students

School students in Armenia lag behind their peers in Georgia, Azerbaijan and Turkey in terms of their level of knowledge. The comparison focuses in particular on 15-year-old students.

The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) conducted its annual study as part of the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA). Experts assessed students’ knowledge of mathematics and science, as well as their ability to analyse what they read.

The study included 760,000 15-year-old students from 91 countries. The results showed that the overall state of education around the world leaves much to be desired. However, experts in Armenia are particularly concerned about the situation in their own country. The education problems have also alarmed people far beyond the field’s specialist community.

Economist Tigran Jrbashyan sees the study’s results as a major cause for concern.
