World.title: Man charged over court data breach asked AI for legal advice, court hears
World.content:
A Sydney man charged over a massive data breach involving a NSW courts website allegedly used generative AI to create "scraper" computer code for bulk downloading before asking ChatGPT for legal advice, a court has heard.

Prosecutors will seek to rely on ChatGPT conversations and forensic expert testimony in the case against Christopher John Duff, 40, which is believed to be one of the first of its kind in Australia.

Mr Duff has pleaded not guilty to four counts of accessing restricted data held in a computer which were laid after the Department of Communities and Justice discovered a data breach in March last year.

Police previously said cybercrime detectives investigated the alleged unauthorised access of 8,769 restricted documents held by the department's online registry website between January and March 2025.

A three-day hearing in Downing Centre Local Court this week stalled after the judge was told of the extraordinary volume of material involved in the matter.

Lawyers have expressed doubt about the hearing being completed, even if a week was allocated.

Police say more than 8,700 restricted documents were accessed in the data breach. (Pixabay: terydanphiri)

Defence counsel Daniel McMahon gave a rough estimate that there were some 10,000 or more pages of proposed exhibit material.

On Wednesday, he told the judge that there may not be a dispute, in general terms, that his client was responsible for some of the alleged conduct.

The case centres on the use of the online registry, which court users can access with a login.

The court heard Mr Duff was assisting a friend involved in complicated bankruptcy proceedings.

According to police prosecutor Sergeant Andrew Maldigri, the crux of the allegation is that Mr Duff used ChatGPT to code and employ scraper python scripts designed to bulk download data.

"It's a piece of code that a user can run against a website to essentially circumvent the usual navigation process," he told Judge Lisa Graham.

"It means a user has used computer coding to obtain data that they weren't authorised to. That's, in a nutshell, what this matter is about."

"If I can use this analogy: it's our case the defendant was throwing out a fishing net in the ocean, drawing it back in, and then hauling up the catch onto the deck to see whether any of the catch that he pulled up from the ocean was what he was after."

Users can only access the online registry with an authorised login. (ABC News)

Mr McMahon described the prosecution's task as "prodigious" and said it would be a difficult case to present.

He said the offence requires proof that the accused knew at the time that any access he was causing was unauthorised, as opposed to being reckless.

"Recklessness is insufficient. They have to prove actual knowledge and nothing less than actual knowledge [of an offence]," Mr McMahon said.

AI evidence marks possible Australian-first

Sergeant Maldigri said the case would raise an issue that he believed was yet to be canvassed in courts in Australia — generative AI being used by the prosecution to prove motive and as evidence of the alleged offending itself.

He cited some examples from legal cases in the US, including proceedings in New York where a man facing fraud charges unsuccessfully objected to the use of AI assistant Claude records in the case.

Prosecutors allege Mr Duff used ChatGPT to seek legal advice prior to being charged. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

The prosecutor said Mr Duff had allegedly sought legal advice from ChatGPT prior to being charged at a point when his login for the website had been shut down, and made enquiries about what police would be doing in the situation.

Mr Duff also sought "coaching" from the platform in relation to what to say if he was approached and ultimately refused to answer questions in a police interview, Mr Maldigri added.

Mr McMahon said the tenor of the ChatGPT conversations, if they were asked by his client, was more suggestive of a post-fact "realisation".

He said the queries included asking whether authorities knew if "it was even a crime yet?" And "was what was done unauthorised?"

The case was adjourned for a fortnight when a new, longer hearing may be scheduled.

Mr Duff was granted bail in April last year on conditions including surrendering his passport and possessing only one "dumb phone" with only call or text functions.

World.title: Anger as lead found at 10 Broken Hill childcare centres
World.content:
The New South Wales Environment Protection Agency (EPA) is facing criticism for not directly informing parents after finding high lead contamination at 10 out of 13 childcare facilities in Broken Hill.

In response to questioning in parliament last month, the EPA shared results of soil testing conducted at childcare centres across the city on multiple occasions between 2015 and 2025.

The agency said it contacted the centres that recorded lead levels above the national guideline of 300 milligrams per kilogram and offered them remediation.

Lead testing being carried out at a Broken Hill childcare centre. (ABC News: Bill Ormonde)

Of the centres with readings above the threshold, only four chose to have remediation work carried out.

The EPA said it was the responsibility of the childcare centres to inform parents.

"The NSW EPA provided site owners of all centres with results and recommended management or remediation actions where required," an EPA spokesperson said.

"For privacy reasons, it is standard procedure for education operators to have direct communication with parents and families."

Calls for investigation

Greens MP and mining spokesperson Cate Faehrmann has criticised the EPA's stance and called for an investigation.

Cate Faehrmann says the impact on regional communities has been ignored. (Supplied: NSW Legislative Council)

"How can our Environment Protection Authority receive information that childcare centres have 10 times the level of lead in the soil that is safe and not do a single thing but tell the [childcare] operator?" she said.

"This warrants a full investigation of how the EPA has been conducting testing in Broken Hill and what information they have and how they've acted on it.

"If we can't trust the agency that is there to monitor and regulate contamination, then who can we trust on this?"

'Read about it in the paper'

According to NSW Health and the Sydney Children's Hospitals Network, exposure to lead can cause learning disabilities, behavioural problems, slow or abnormal growth, poor coordination and hearing problems.

Children under five are particularly vulnerable because their brains are still developing.

Young children are also more likely to put their hands or objects in their mouths, and their bodies absorb more lead than adults.

Cartoon character Lead Ted advises children to wash hands after playing on equipment at a public park in Broken Hill. (ABC Broken Hill: Em Jensen)

NSW chief health officer Kerry Chant said NSW Health should also have been informed.

"We would have wanted to know about this; I would have been extremely concerned about the issue," Dr Chant said.

" We were unaware of the results in the childcare centre. I read about it in the paper. "

However, the EPA said it had kept NSW Health in the loop.

"The NSW EPA shared updates with the Broken Hill Interagency Working Group, which includes NSW Health," the EPA spokesperson said.

Public health issue

Broken Hill Mayor Tom Kennedy said he expected almost all houses in town would be over the 300mg guideline.

"You don't want to have people scared," he said.

"Those childcare facilities have often had lead well above … These facilities are checked all the time, and when they are found to be high, they are remediated.

Tom Kennedy wants the NSW government to invest in measures that prevent the spread of lead dust. (ABC Broken Hill: Kristina Rosengren)

"Let's remember those children that go to those childcare facilities then go home to yards that probably have lead levels well beyond that at the childcare facilities themselves."

Ms Faehrmann said Broken Hill was facing a public health crisis and argued the government would respond differently if the same lead levels were found elsewhere.

"I just cannot imagine another situation where they wouldn't do anything about it," she said.

" We're continuing to cover the extent of them not wanting the seriousness of the situation to be known. "

World.title: Greyhound trainer handed lifetime ban for 'egregious' actions
World.content:
A greyhound trainer has been found "entirely unfit" to participate in the industry, with the governing body in South Australia issuing a lifetime ban and a $5,000 fine for dishonestly negotiating the transfer of an injured dog to another trainer.

Jack Clayton Trengove, who is from a prominent Broken Hill racing family, was already suspended for previous animal welfare-related matters.

In a sentencing decision handed down by Greyhound Racing SA (GRSA), an integrity hearings panel said Mr Trengove discussed the transfer of a greyhound named "Arctic Girl" to a trainer in NSW without disclosing an "unhealed hock fracture" on the dog's hind leg.

"We found that Mr Trengove knew of the fracture and that his failure to disclose it was dishonest," GRSA said in its decision.

"Arctic Girl was transferred to a trainer who was unaware of the true condition of her hock and commenced preparing her to race, thereby placing Arctic Girl at significant risk of catastrophic injury."

Mr Trengove pictured at the Broken Hill Racecourse last year. (Supplied: Broken Hill Racecourse)

The panel said that although the dog did not ultimately suffer such injury, "that outcome was due in significant part to the timely intervention and positive action of GRSA officers".

"This offending represents such an egregious example that stands in stark contrast to the standard and welfare expected within the industry," it said.

"Accordingly, the [panel] have concluded that this offending not only strikes to the core of the values upon which greyhound racing in South Australia operates, it has also concluded that his conduct makes him entirely unfit to continue participating in the industry."

The panel said it accepted the new owner's account that Mr Trengove had told her over Facebook Messenger that Arctic Girl had been off with a sore hock but was "good to go now".

It rejected Mr Trengove's account that he separately disclosed the fracture by telephone to the new owner.

The decision states the greyhound was returned to SA and rehomed.

SA greyhound trainer banned for dog's 'unnecessary suffering' One of SA greyhound racing's most prominent identities has been disqualified after a 12-month inquiry by the sport's controlling body.

Mr Trengove has been suspended since June 2025 when charges relating to animal welfare rule breaches were laid against him, after an investigation stemming from photos taken inside his kennel.

In the latest ruling, the panel also noted several racing-related infringements Mr Trengove had accrued in 2024 which included a failure to present a greyhound for veterinary examination, striking a greyhound and a failure to maintain a treatment record book.

In response to the outcome, Mr Trengove told the ABC he felt he was being targeted.

" I was not given a fair hearing … their process for the hearing panel is run very wrong. "

The panel's decision document, states Mr Trengove did not attend a hearing related to the latest counts on which he had been found guilty, but had attended other hearings related to separate counts.

In 2021, Mr Trengove was described by GRSA as having a "strong future ahead of him" in a since-deleted online blog.

World.title: Three people arrested over fatal Thomastown shooting
World.content:
Police investigating a fatal shooting in Melbourne's north earlier this week have arrested three people, including two teenagers.

Daniel Hussein, 22, was shot in front of friends at HR Uren Reserve in Thomastown at about 7:30pm Sunday.

Paramedics tried to revive Mr Hussein in front of his loved ones and several shocked onlookers, but he died at the scene.

Police have arrested a 19-year-old Donnybrook man, a 20-year-old Donnybrook man and a 19-year-old Lalor woman over the shooting.

They were arrested in Deer Park at about 5:50pm Wednesday and are being interviewed by Homicide Squad detectives.

The investigation into Daniel Hussein's death in Thomastown is ongoing, police say. (ABC News)

Relatives said Mr Hussein, a plumber, was engaged to be married and had recently bought a house.

"He had his whole life ahead of him," his brother said at the scene of the shooting earlier this week.

Mr Hussein's uncle, Abdallah Hussein, said he had never imagined he would have to say goodbye to his nephew.

"I still cannot believe you are gone," he wrote on social media.

" I still cannot understand that I will never see your smile again, never hear your voice, never watch you walk through that door again. "

The shooting occurred near the Lalor Soccer Club, where junior matches had been played several hours earlier.

Victoria Police said investigation was ongoing and urged anyone with information to contact Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000.

World.title: Watchdog's floodplain admission sparks call for immediate embargo
World.content:
The New South Wales government is facing calls to immediately halt the controversial practice of floodplain harvesting after revelations in parliament that the industry watchdog cannot effectively prosecute breaches.

Floodplain harvesting allows landholders to capture and store water flowing across floodplains during rainfall and flood events.

The NSW Natural Resources Access Regulator (NRAR) chief regulatory officer, Grant Barnes, told a parliamentary hearing in August that the agency was facing "some uncertainty as to the application of the law in regard to floodplain harvesting".

During the hearing, it was revealed that between 2020 and 2025, several NRAR prosecutions for alleged water offences in northern NSW were withdrawn or dismissed due to problems with the evidence, with record-keeping and findings that offences had not been proven beyond reasonable doubt.

Cate Faehrmann says the current framework is fundamentally flawed. (ABC News: Rani Hayman)

NSW Greens MP and water spokesperson Cate Faehrmann said the regulatory framework was "so fundamentally flawed that compliance cannot be reliably enforced".

She said floodplain harvesting significantly reduced downstream flows, degraded river health and undermined the ecological, cultural and economic foundations of communities across the basin.

" The government must act immediately to protect downstream communities, uphold the integrity of the Basin Plan, and restore confidence in NSW's water regulation. "

She called on NSW Water Minister Rose Jackson to impose an immediate embargo on floodplain harvesting across NSW.

"If the government cannot regulate floodplain harvesting, it must not permit it."

An 'extraordinary revelation'

Floodplain harvesting accounts for about five per cent of water taken across the Murray-Darling Basin, or about 571 gigalitres a year.

An embargo would prevent the capture of water during future overland flows and reduce water available to irrigators while allowing more water to remain in the river system.

South Australia's River Murray commissioner Emma Carmody described Grant Barnes's statements about enforcement uncertainty as an "extraordinary revelation".

Emma Carmody says the regulator lacks the powers it needs to manage the sector. (Supplied: Emma Carmody)

She said it was "extremely troubling" that nearly a decade after the ABC Four Corners investigation Pumped exposed problems with floodplain harvesting and triggered major reforms to water compliance, the regulator still lacked the powers it needed to manage the sector.

The program triggered the Ken Matthews inquiry, which led to the establishment of NRAR, and a new federal water compliance watchdog followed in 2021.

Failures in court

In 2020, NRAR prosecuted irrigator Peter Harris and farm manager Justin Timmins over the alleged failure to operate water metering equipment properly at two properties near Walgett.

Grant Barnes told a parliamentary hearing that the regulator was facing uncertainty about floodplain harvesting laws. (ABC Rural: Amelia Bernasconi)

Justice Rachel Pain found that NRAR failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt, resulting in all six charges being dismissed.

Mr Barnes told the inquiry the ruling highlighted a problem with the phrasing of the existing water rules, which made it incredibly difficult for NRAR to successfully prosecute operators for faulty or non-compliant water meters.

He also pointed the committee to a second ruling, Emu Rider Pty Ltd v Minister, administering the Water Management Act, handed down in 2025, in which irrigators from the Border Rivers region successfully challenged the floodplain harvesting access licences the minister had issued them.

The Land and Environment Court found the licences held by the trustee for the Griffiths Investment Trust and others were invalid because the minister had never sent landholders the notice required before their water volumes were set.

According to Dr Carmody, the ruling threatened to unravel the NSW government's entire multi-year rollout of the floodplain harvesting framework because an identical process was used to calculate and issue licences across all the northern valleys in NSW.

Water minister's response

Rose Jackson has been asked to impose an embargo on floodplain harvesting across New South Wales. (ABC Western Plains: Kenji Sato)

In response to calls for an embargo, Ms Jackson said the government intended to make changes to the floodplain harvesting framework following what she described as "recent, disappointing legal decisions."

"I have been briefed on the implications of these legal matters for some time and directed the department to take steps to quickly resolve issues identified by the courts," she said.

"We will continue to make whatever changes are necessary to achieve our shared goal of a clear regulatory framework."

Meanwhile, the measurement, monitoring and determination of water take by floodplain harvesting in NSW will be the subject of a federal audit.

"The audit will examine whether commitments made by NSW during water resource plan accreditation are being implemented as committed," said the inspector-general of water compliance in the Murray-Darling Basin, Troy Grant.

Troy Grant says an audit will examine whether water commitments are being implemented correctly. (Supplied: Inspector-General of Water Compliance)

The audit will focus on the Border Rivers, Barwon-Darling and Macquarie-Castlereagh water resource plan areas.

"In many systems, floodplain harvesting is estimated using water models rather than directly measured, leading to reduced confidence in water take data," Mr Grant said.

" What this does indicate to me is there are issues upstream of compliance and enforcement and it is important governments get the policy, administrative arrangements and licensing right. "

Irrigators back lawful floodplain harvesting

Madeleine Hartley says NSW irrigators are the most licensed, the most metered and the most compliant across the basin. (Supplier: NSW Irrigators Council)

NSW Irrigators Council chief executive Madeleine Hartley rejected claims that court decisions have rendered floodplain harvesting difficult to regulate.

"Floodplain harvesting is and has always been lawful and there is already an embargo in place for this type of water take," she said.

She declined to comment on the statement from Greens MP Cate Faehrmann that the court losses may have weakened compliance and enforcement powers, but defended irrigators' adherence to the rules.

"The rules are strict, and our members have spent tens of thousands of dollars to comply with them," she said.

World.title: Parties divided over purple-lid glass bins ahead of Victorian election
World.content:
There is growing pushback against the Victorian government's glass-recycling bin mandate, with some councils rallying against a requirement for the purple-lid bins to be rolled out to all homes by the middle of next year.

First announced in 2020, the scheme was part of an overhaul of the state's waste and recycling system, with the aim of reducing glass contamination in mixed recycling and diverting more material from landfill.

The purple-lidded glass-recycling bins have already been rolled out in more than half of Victoria's local government areas, but others have refused to participate in the scheme.

The Municipal Association of Victoria (MAV) argues local authorities are best placed to decide how waste is collected and recycled in their communities.

"A one-size-fits-all, mandated solution is not the correct way to approach local government waste services," MAV president Jennifer Anderson said.

" Rubbish really is a council service and therefore the council needs to work out in terms of distances, roads and contractors — it's very complex. "

Jennifer Anderson says kerbside glass bins should not be mandatory across the state. (Supplied)

State government data shows 42 out of 79 Victorian councils have already introduced a separate glass-recycling bin to the waste collection schedule.

Hobsons Bay City Council, in Melbourne's south-west, was an early adopter, with collections every four weeks.

The council said the program had provided excellent environmental outcomes, collecting more than 1,400 tonnes of glass in the past financial year.

"Larger pieces are sent to a local factory to be remade into new bottles and jars and smaller pieces are ground down so that they can be used as a sand replacement for road base," a spokesperson said.

"Only 3 per cent of contents are contaminated, which provides an excellent environmental outcome."

Hobsons Bay City Council introduced the additional bin in 2020. (Supplied: Hobsons Bay City Council)

Geelong mayor Stretch Kontelj said his council supported recycling, but he believed the purple bin scheme was not viable for the regional city.

He said the rollout would initially cost the council $8.6 million, with $5.4 million required to maintain the extra collections each year thereafter.

"These costs have to be borne somewhere, and I'm very conscious that households are already dealing with significant cost-of-living pressures, and this would just add to it," he said.

" There are some councils that have introduced the fourth bin. Good luck to them. But it shouldn't be mandatory. "

Stretch Kontelj says the state government has not provided funding to support his council with the recycling transition. (ABC News)

Purple bins not the only solution

Shattered glass in mixed recycling — the waste that goes in the existing yellow-lid bins — causes major problems for recycling companies, according to RMIT Centre for Urban Research senior research fellow Bhavna Middha.

However, Dr Middha said concerns regarding cost, space in household yards and additional trucks on the road meant a separate bin may not be the best option for every council.

Bhavna Middha believes shared community recycling infrastructure could alleviate council concerns. (Supplied)

Ms Anderson from the MAV said councils wanted to support their residents to recycle, but implementing a universal approach would not work.

"Those principles of what we want to achieve are the same. It's just how you go about it, and unintended consequences of legislation that may not fit all 79 councils," she said.

Here's where Australia's 67 million tonnes of waste per year ends up Australia has been in a recycling crisis for nearly two years now, but what happens once we put rubbish in the bin still remains a mystery for many people.

The MAV said roughly 40 councils had determined the purple bin roll-out was not appropriate for their communities, and instead called for the expansion of the state's container deposit scheme to accept a broader range of glass containers.

Dr Middha agreed there was an opportunity to expand the existing program.

"There is that gap there, things like jam bottles, pickle bottles, all of these that are not categorised as beverage containers fall back into the recycling bin," she said.

" If the government and the recycling companies can get creative, it's absolutely expandable. "

The state government has said it will work with councils to finalise rules for household waste and recycling services ahead of the July 2027 deadline for rolling out the purple bins.

The Liberal-National opposition has pledged to remove the mandate and instead enforce a weekly general waste bin collection — instead of fortnightly in some areas — if it is elected to government.

Opposition Leader Jess Wilson has vowed to scrap the purple bin mandate. (ABC News: Sarah Buchecker)

"It is a big concern, again, a state government trying to mandate what a council should do without having discussions," Ms Anderson said in response to the opposition's proposal.

The Victorian Greens said the party fully supported a four-bin waste system, but was calling on the government to work with councils to find the best solution for local contexts.

One Nation MP Rikkie-Lee Tyrrell told the ABC her party did not support any form of bin mandate, believing councils were best placed to make waste disposal decisions for their communities.

Dr Middha said a shared bin program in place in the City of Port Phillip offered a potential solution.

Port Phillip Council has 80 communal hubs to recycle glass and green waste. (Supplied: City of Port Phillip)

"If there are, say, a few houses and apartments in one street, at the end of the street they could have a shared glass bin," she said.

"This kind of shared infrastructure is what we need, rather than burdening households and councils with extra infrastructure."

World.title: Australia's love for coastal living faces $850b reckoning
World.content:
Climate change means Australia's love of the coast is facing a multi-billion-dollar reckoning, research suggests, as rising seas threaten to turn its prized coastal lifestyle into a question of who will foot the bill: property owners or governments.

In the first nationwide assessment of economic losses from sea level rise, researchers from the University of Melbourne, the Australian National University and Global Environmental and Economic Modelling have found that all coastal states and the Northern Territory face hefty damage bills this century.

Australia could face damage costs of more than $850 billion, with more than $274 billion going to property losses and $580 billion spent on land-use damage.

Co-author Tom Kompas said the findings were "alarming", and the economic toll would mount as fossil fuel emissions continued to drive global temperatures higher.

"We keep warming the planet … so you get more sea level rise, you get higher tides, higher king tides, higher maximum tides," the professor of environmental economics and biosecurity at the University of Melbourne said.

"You get more intense, and maybe even more frequent storms and storm surges, and that causes localised flooding."

Sea level rise hits hard across the board

As temperatures rise, melting ice and the thermal expansion of warmer seawater raise sea levels, threatening coastal communities worldwide.

The Australian research found more than 267,000 coastal properties and 2 million hectares of land across the country will face flood damage by 2100 based on global carbon emissions peaking around 2040 and global warming being limited to about 2.7C.

The United Nations has warned that warming will reach at least 1.8C above pre-industrial levels and projects it could reach up to 2.6C by the end of the century under current policies.

The Inverloch surf lifesaving clubhouse in south-east Victoria during abnormal high-tide activity in May last year. (Supplied: Andrew Harrison Photography Inverloch)

The findings also put a price tag of more than a trillion dollars on impacts associated with global warming exceeding 4C. However, that level of warming was predicated on growing fossil fuel use, and scientists have deemed it unlikely to eventuate due to the uptake of clean energy.

Queensland has been identified as having 93,000 properties at risk of damage due to sea level rise, resulting in an expected damage bill of $214 billion for the state.

The Gold Coast is Australia's most exposed urban area, with projected economic losses of $84.4 billion.

Erosion after Cyclone Alfred has left metres-high escarpments at Surfers Paradise. (Supplied: Mark Davies)

Western Australia faces the largest total losses, while in New South Wales, communities in the state's north and Central Coast region face higher property losses than in Greater Sydney.

With Victoria the only jurisdiction where property damage costs exceed those associated with land use, Professor Kompas said the research underscored the significant costs of inundating farmland and recreational areas.

"Much of it is badly, badly damaged with sea level rise and storm surge … damaged reserves, parks, beaches," he said.

"So it's not just individual properties, commercial and residential properties; it's a wide range of assets that are being impacted."

Before: Erosion at Lancelin Sands Hotel, taken May 25 last year. . . After: Erosion at Lancelin Sands Hotel, taken July 6. . . Instructions: Use left and right arrow keys to control image transition Before and after images SLIDE Erosion at Lancelin Sands Hotel, taken May 25 last year. / Erosion at Lancelin Sands Hotel, taken July 6.

Consequences with every centimetre

The economic assessment forms the basis of a Climate Council report, which highlights how coastal floods previously considered severe will become a regular occurrence in the future.

It found that every 10cm of sea level rise will triple the frequency of "once-in-a-century" flood events.

Global sea levels have already risen by over 22cm since 1900, with projections there could be an additional 14cm by 2050.

Narrowneck Beach and other northern Gold Coast shores suffered severe sand loss, exposed rock walls, and high tides crashing against infrastructure three months after Tropical Cyclone Alfred. (ABC News: Nicholas McElroy)

Report author and Climate Councillor Andrew Watkins said the impacts were already being felt.

"We have seen quite a rapid increase in what we call extreme water levels along the coast, and that gives coastal inundation, coastal flooding and coastal erosion as well," the Adjunct Professor at Monash University's School of Earth, Atmosphere and Environment said.

Sea level rise can damage coastal land and infrastructure in multiple ways, including permanent inundation. Scientists often use the "1 to 100 rule" to describe this — meaning seawater will go about a metre inland for each centimetre of sea level rise.

So 10cm of sea level rise can actually move water 10 metres further inland, inundating any land or building in its path.

The Land and Environment Court has granted consent for a 90-metre seawall at The Entrance North, a coastal village in NSW's Central Coast. (Supplied: Horton Coastal Engineering)

Rising seas can also contribute to isolated coastal flooding events when combined with storms.

"When you have that sea level rise, and then you get a storm surge where the storm is pushing the water up against the coast, it makes the water go even higher," Dr Watkins said.

"Then you get waves on top of that, and if it happens at high tide, that's when you get the full combination of impacts."

Storm surges and wind-driven waves linked to Ex-Tropical Cyclone Alfred led to severe erosion along the coastline between south-east Queensland and north-east NSW last year, with the Insurance Council of Australia announcing more than 125,000 claims totalling $1.36 billion.

Higher sea levels will push storm surges further inland. (X: Lisa Garnham)

Associate Professor of Climate Adaptation at Griffith University Johanna Nalau said recovery from that event was still ongoing.

"There has been a lot of work on beach nourishment and then more acute damage, so we talk about power, power networks, transport, water and sewage; those were resolved within weeks to months," she said.

"But the coastal erosion part is still an ongoing effort, and there has been some reporting in the news as well that some of the housing damage that people experience hasn't been resolved yet."

Bracing for the future

Experts are calling for improved efforts to help coastal regions adapt as climate change not only contributes to rising sea levels but is also expected to increase the frequency and intensity of storms.

Storms last year caused significant erosion damage at Fox Beach, Robe, SA. (Supplied: District Council of Robe)

Warnings of a mounting economic toll have also raised questions around who will foot the damage bills going forward, particularly given insurance generally does not cover "actions of the sea".

"Most coastal properties would have some level of insurance, although the insurance sector is also very, very aware of risks that come with climate change," Dr Nalau said.

" So insurance premiums are increasing quite heavily in some coastal areas. "

Dr Watkins said it was becoming "prohibitively expensive" for some councils to pay for adaptation and recovery.

In the 1970s, old car bodies were used to prevent sand dune erosion in front of a sand mining site at Belongil in Byron Bay. (Supplied: NSW Public Works)

"A lot of councils are effectively having to dip into their own coffers to support resilience building, but also to recover from damage that's done when we have these storm events and sea level events along our coastlines," he said.

"We do need to look at this as a national problem and develop plans with the communities and with the local, state, and federal level about the best ways to go forward."

World.title: Company behind pulled sunscreens sued for 'misleading' conduct
World.content:
The manufacturer of the base formula used by 20 sunscreens pulled from sale for failing to meet their SPF claims is being sued for "misleading" and "deceptive" conduct.

High-profile brand Ultra Violette is seeking millions of dollars from Wild Child Laboratories, following the recall of one of its signature SPF50+ sunscreens last year in the wake of testing by consumer group Choice showing an SPF of just four.

But the status of the litigation is uncertain after Wild Child went into voluntary liquidation in August.

In the month before the liquidation, Wild Child sold its assets to a new company that shared the same CEO and director, which continued the company's sunscreen manufacturing business under the name Heliora.

Ultra Violette told the ABC it understood Wild Child's liquidators were reviewing the transaction and the circumstances surrounding it.

Ultra Violette is seeking millions of dollars from Wild Child Laboratories. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

In a statement, Heliora said it "firmly rejects any suggestion that it was established as a means of avoiding Wild Child's liabilities".

"The liquidators have not raised concerns with us about the transaction," the statement said.

"The conduct and scope of any review of Wild Child's affairs is a matter for the liquidators, and they are the appropriate party to answer questions about it."

Liquidator PKF has not responded to questions.

Wild Child Laboratories' liquidation leaves creditors, including multiple sunscreen brands and the Australian Taxation Office, claiming debts totalling about $20 million.

In addition to Ultra Violette's Lean Screen SPF50+ product, 19 other sunscreens which shared the same base formula were recalled due to low SPF test results, all of which were made by Wild Child Laboratories.

Do you know more about this story? Email rachelcarbonell@proton.me or carbonell.rachel@abc.net.au

Wild Child is also being sued by Advanced Skin Technology, owner of the high-end Aspect Skincare brand, which recalled two products.

Wild Child's creditors also include prominent Australian brand Naked Sundays, which is listed as being owed $8.2 million on the liquidator's report.

In documents filed to the Federal Court before it went into liquidation, Wild Child indicated it would defend the claims and said the sunscreen brands were responsible for ensuring the products met their regulatory obligations.

Heliora was registered about a month before the liquidation.

It was set up by Wild Child director and major shareholder Paul Waldren and is headed by former Wild Child chief executive officer, Tom Curnow.

In Heliora's statement, Mr Curnow said the purchase was negotiated with the involvement of a secured lender to Wild Child and a restructuring advisory firm.

Heliora is backed by investors who originally had stakes in Wild Child Laboratories, including Mr Waldren.

"No Wild Child shareholder received any payment or distribution from the transaction," Mr Curnow said in the statement.

"Heliora also assumed agreed liabilities … including obligations to many Wild Child suppliers and creditors.

Questions over lab's sunscreen tests At least eight sunscreens that failed to meet their advertised SPF50 sun protection claims in a recent review had their original tests for certification done by an overseas laboratory whose results are being questioned by industry experts.

"All Wild Child employees were offered employment with Heliora, and their employee entitlements carried forward."

Heliora has taken on Wild Child Laboratories' clients and manufacturing business and is continuing under its TGA manufacturing licence.

"Heliora has submitted the required dossier to the TGA to support the transfer of the [Good Manufacturing Practice] licence and is working through that process with the regulator," the statement said.

Millions of dollars in claims

Documents filed as part of the liquidation show 11 sunscreen companies are claiming a total of more than $19 million.

The debts also include more than $400,000 to the Australian Taxation Office.

In its statement of claim lodged in the Federal Court, Ultra Violette alleges that Wild Child Laboratories made six separate representations that the sunscreen in question had an SPF of 50 or 50+.

Ultra Violette said it commissioned its own SPF tests on the product, which all returned low results.

"Between July and September 2025 Ultra Violette received seven test results from four laboratories which returned average SPF ratings of 2.9, 3.0, 3.6, 4.1, 10.5, 21.5 and 25.18," the statement of claim says.

The claim also refers to additional testing commissioned by Wild Child Laboratories which showed a result of SPF 21.7.

TGA proposes removing sunscreen SPF numbers in regulation changes The proposals include a number of potential changes to SPF testing requirements for sunscreens listed for sale in Australia.

The company has accused Wild Child of misleading and deceptive conduct and breach of contract.

The liquidator's creditor report listed Ultra Violette as being owed $7 million.

In its statement to the ABC, Ultra Violette said the liquidation has had an "immediate impact on our Federal Court proceeding".

"We cannot ordinarily continue proceedings against a company in liquidation without leave of the court," it said.

In response to questions about Ultra Violette's claim, Mr Curnow said "the liquidators are the appropriate party to respond to … those matters".

He added: "Wild Child's insurer has confirmed in writing that the liquidation has not altered or withdrawn indemnity previously confirmed in respect of relevant claims, and that the relevant insurance continues to respond to those claims following the liquidation, subject to its terms and conditions."

Separate suit

Advanced Skin Technology, which recalled two of its Aspect Skincare sunscreens last year, has also alleged misleading and deceptive conduct on the part of Wild Child Laboratories.

Its statement of claim filed in the Federal Court said the manufacturer failed to take reasonable care in the development, manufacture and supply of the sunscreens and in ensuring they were SPF50+.

These two Aspect sunscreens were recalled last year. (Screenshot)

The company is suing for losses for refunds, credits, write-offs, lost sales and profits and staff management time spent on the recall, as well as reputational damage.

It has not put a dollar figure on the damages it is seeking, but the creditors' report from the liquidator lists almost $2.5 million in debts owed to the brand.

Wild Child indicated it would defend the court action from Advanced Skin Technology in a defence lodged with the court in April this year.

Advanced Skin Technology said: "As the matter is ongoing, it would not be appropriate for us to comment on the details at this time."

Sunscreen safety Two in three Australians will be diagnosed with skin cancer in their lifetime and about 2,000 Australians die from skin cancer every year.

Sunscreen is one of five important ways to reduce the risk of skin cancer. The others are wearing protective clothing, wearing sunglasses, wearing a hat and seeking shade.

It's important to apply enough sunscreen. The recommended amount for an adult is seven teaspoons for the whole body. You should cover every bit of exposed skin and reapply every two hours and after being in water.

SPF 20 filters about 95 per cent of UVB rays and SPF 50 filters about 98 per cent of UVB rays. Source: Cancer Council

In its defence filed in the Ultra Violette proceedings in July, Wild Child Laboratories argued the brand was responsible for making sure the SPF of the product met its label claim.

"Ultra Violette undertook responsibility for meeting all the legal obligations required of a sponsor of therapeutic goods in Australia in relation to the Lean Screen SPF50+ sunscreen," it said.

The defence also stated while Wild Child was not liable, the companies it engaged to perform SPF testing on the failed sunscreen were "concurrent wrongdoers".

One of those companies was Princeton Consumer Research (PCR), used by a significant number of Australian sunscreens, which was found to provide unreliable SPF testing data.

The Wild Child defence stated that PCR "engaged in conduct which was misleading and deceptive or likely to mislead and deceive."

The sunscreen formula used by the 20 products that were recalled last year has been discontinued by Wild Child Laboratories.

The TGA said at the time, "preliminary testing indicates that this base formulation is unlikely to have an SPF of greater than 21" and some products may have an SPF as low as four.

A TGA Good Manufacturing Practice audit of Wild Child facilities last year "did not identify any manufacturing issues that could have contributed to the low SPF results".

World.title: Apple unveils its foldable iPhone Duo
World.content:
Updated TechnologyPhones Apple unveils its foldable iPhone Duo Barbara Ortutay Updated September 10, 2026 — 6:10am ,first published 4:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Apple has unveiled its latest generation of iPhones, including a widely anticipated foldable version called Duo. The company’s new chief executive, John Ternus, who took over from Tim Cook on September 1, introduced the latest lineup at the Steve Jobs Theatre on Wednesday (US time). The new Apple iPhone Duo. YouTube/Apple After cycling through other updates to the iPhone, the Apple Watch and AirPods along with artificial intelligence advances, Ternus told the audience that “actually there is one more thing,” in a nod to the trademark phrase from Jobs that Jobs himself borrowed from the 1970s detective show Columbo. Called Duo, the phone has the “largest display ever on an iPhone, yet fits into your pocket,” Ternus said.



The phone opens to a 7.6 inch display that is 80 per cent larger than the newest iPhone 18 Pro. It will let people use an Apple Pencil on the phone, a capability previously reserved to iPad users. Duo, Ternus said, “will redefine the experience of using a foldable phone”. The Duo also lets users split the screen to use two different apps on the device, or two windows the same website for things like comparison shopping. The Apple iPhone Duo is available in star white and night sky. Apple The iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max, Ternus said, bring improvements to the battery, camera, and performance. They will start at $2099 and $2299, respectively. The Duo starts at $3499. Customers can pre-order the phones starting on September 12, and they will be available on September 18, although the Duo will be available on October 23.



The new models feature a long battery life – 45 hours of video playback for the Pro Max – and faster charging. The camera offers what Apple called “cinematic effects” from regular video captured on the phone, as well as new options for manual controls and “smart focus tracking,” which lets users focus on a single moving subject, such as a kid during a soccer game. Apple is also focusing on Siri’s new AI capabilities with the new phones, emphasising privacy and security to stand apart from rivals who are further along in incorporating AI. The Duo “was always going to eclipse Apple’s other announcements at the event,” said Ben Wood, chief analyst at CCS Insight. “The device adds a distinctive new design to the iPhone lineup and marks the company’s entry into the niche foldable smartphone category.” Wood said that while there is certain to be demand for the Duo, which costs less than some analysts had anticipated, foldables still account for less than 5 per cent of the overall smartphone market. Many of Apple’s biggest rivals, such as Samsung, Motorola and Google, have already come out with foldable smartphones. But Apple is not one to rush on new technologies.



“The foldable launch is straight out of Apple’s playbook: Wait for the product to work out its kinks and for the market to offer glimpses of viability, then enter and shape the category,” said Forrester analyst Dipanjan Chatterjee. New Apple CEO John Ternus at the product launch. Bloomberg “The difference is that foldables still represent a minuscule share of the smartphone market. The test of Apple’s ambition will be whether it can expand that niche into a meaningful new segment.” Earlier this year, Apple unveiled artificial intelligence advances, including upgrades to its Siri assistant, emphasising a focus on privacy and day-to-day use as the company tries to catch up with rivals on AI. The keynote address for Ternus at the tech giant’s headquarters in Cupertino, California, will set the tone for his vision of Apple’s future, Chatterjee said.



Related Article Gadgets Foldable iPhones, touch-screen MacBooks: What to expect from Apple’s big launch “John Ternus inherits perhaps the most successful consumer technology juggernaut in modern times. That is both a boon and a burden for him. Tim Cook’s perfected execution, scale, and monetisation set a high bar, and Ternus must extend that run,” Chatterjee said. “But he must sustain that momentum while positioning Apple to disrupt itself in the near future, when the iPhone, or any smartphone for that matter, will cease to be the consumer’s primary conduit to the world.” Last year’s iPhone 17 lineup, which included a new ultra-thin model, has been selling well. That generation saw a new slimmed-down model that adopted the “Air” name that Apple already used for its sleekest iPads and Mac computers. Wood noted that, with all the excitement around the Duo, the official arrival of Ternus as CEO “felt like less of a story” than he’d expected. “This event marks a seamless transition from Tim Cook, and its timing to coincide with the iPhone Duo was undoubtedly planned,” Wood said. “However, despite the media frenzy about this new device, it is the broader strength of Apple’s hardware, software and services that will drive the company forward.”

World.title: ASX set to fall sharply as Wall Street declines; Trump sends oil price warning as Iran war escalates
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to fall sharply as Wall Street declines; Trump sends oil price warning as Iran war escalates Damian Troise and Alex Veiga Updated September 10, 2026 — 6:08am ,first published 5:27am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Stocks fell on Wall Street as the price of crude oil rose back above $US100 a barrel amid further escalation in the US war with Iran, with President Donald Trump saying he believes prices will remain elevated until after the midterm elections in November. The S&P 500 index fell 0.5 per cent. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 405 points, or 0.8 per cent and the Nasdaq composite lost 0.6 per cent. Wall Street has kicked off its week with a mixed session. AP The Australian sharemarket is set to fall, with futures at 5.50am AEST pointing to a loss of 94 points or 1.1 per cent, at the open. The ASX lost 0.1 per cent on Wednesday. The Australian dollar was trading at US72.16¢. Wall Street’s losses were broad, with retailers among the companies leading the market lower. Amazon fell 1.8 per cent and Starbucks fell 1.9 per cent. Nearly every sector within the benchmark S&P 500 lost ground, but oil companies pushed higher. Exxon Mobil rose 2.2 per cent and Chevron rose 1.9 per cent.



Oil prices drove much of the action on Wall Street. The US destroyed five Iranian tankers on Tuesday in a series of attacks between the two nations. The conflict that began in February has essentially shut down traffic in the Strait of Hormuz, where a fifth of the world’s oil supply passed before the war began. Related Article Opinion

Oil As Trump’s Iran war drags on, we’re facing the next oil crunch Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist The price of Brent crude, the international standard, rose 3 per cent to $US100.87 a barrel. It marks the first time the price surpassed $US100 a barrel since July. Trump said that oil prices that have surged because of the Iran war likely won’t come down until after US midterm elections. “Right after the election, oil prices are going to be tumbling downward,” Trump said. “I think it’s going to take a little bit longer than the midterm.”



Trump, in an exchange with reporters before travelling to Dallas for the midterm Republican convention, added that he believes Iran will finally relent after the pivotal elections are held in the US. “I think the war’s going to end immediately after the election because they can’t hold out any longer,” Trump said. The jump in oil prices over the course of the war has fuelled already high inflation. Gasoline prices in the US are up about 32 per cent from a year ago to $US4.22 per gallon. Higher fuel prices cut into household budgets directly when it comes to the cost of driving, but they also indirectly raise prices for goods because of higher shipping costs. The price of diesel, which can have an outsized impact on consumers because it is used in shipping and production, hit an all-time high Friday and has continued to climb since. The average price for a gallon reached $US5.94 overnight and is now 9 cents higher than it was Friday. Inflation was already stubbornly high when the US started its war against Iran because of the ongoing US trade war with much of the world. That trade war is also heating up, especially between the US and its close ally and trade partner Canada.



Wall Street will get more updates this week on inflation, starting with a look at prices at the wholesale level on Thursday with the release of the Producer Price Index for August. It measures prices businesses pay for goods before they reach customers. That report will be followed up Friday with the release of the Consumer Price Index, or CPI, for August, which shows the more direct price impact for households. Related Article Updated

Phones Apple unveils its foldable iPhone Duo The latest reports are expected to show that the rate of inflation remains above 3 per cent. That has been an issue for the Federal Reserve, which is aiming to hold inflation at a target rate of 2 per cent. The central bank has been holding rates steady, but Wall Street is leaning toward a 62 per cent chance that it will raise its benchmark interest rate at its meeting next week, according to data from CME Group. Higher interest rates make borrowing more expensive. The goal of raising interest rates is to slow the economy and cool inflation. Rising Treasury yields in the bond market were also weighing down stocks on Wall Street Wednesday.



The US Treasury Department on Wednesday said it would buy back up to $US6 billion ($8.3 billion) in long-term debt. That follows an announcement in August previewing plans for an unusually large buyback in an effort to contain rising yields, which make it more expensive for US companies to borrow money and also weigh down other investments, such as stocks. Bond yields had been holding steady prior to the announcement, but gained ground shortly after. “The simplest version here is that market interventions have a long history of not working very well,” said Guy LeBas, chief fixed income strategist at Janney Montgomery. The yield on the 10-year Treasury, which tends to impact mortgage rates, rose to 4.85 per cent — its highest point since late October of 2023 — before easing to 4.83 per cent from 4.80 per cent late Tuesday. The yield on the 2-year Treasury, which tends to track expectations for Fed moves on interest rates, rose to 4.41 per cent from 4.39 per cent late Tuesday. Bond yields have an inverse relationship to prices. Yields rise as bond prices fall. Rising yields signal that investors are demanding a higher return from Treasurys.



Elsewhere on Wall Street, shares of Meta Platforms rose 6.6 per cent as the parent company of Instagram and Facebook launched a personal artificial intelligence agent, Muse, for people 18 and over who are looking for help with day-to-day tasks like schedules and shopping. Markets in Europe fell while markets in Asia closed mixed. AP The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.
