World.title: Republican National Convention 2026 LIVE updates: Trump, Vance to speak as US midterms loom
World.content:
This two-day convention has been dreamed up by President Donald Trump to rally his supporters for this year’s midterm elections.

Trump has said he wanted to channel the kind of political extravaganza that each party holds every four years to formally nominate a presidential candidate and showcase their vision for the country. There’s even going to be a huge balloon drop at the end.

People arrive at the Republican convention in Dallas. AP Photo/Alex Brandon

Republicans have never held a midterm convention before, although Democrats did in the 1970s and 1980s. Trump had long floated the idea of holding such an event, and Republicans worked to make his wish a reality.

Midterms are often difficult for the party in power in Washington, and Trump believes the event can energise the party and boost turnout among his voters.

“Pretend, please, that I’m on the ballot,” Trump said recently in South Carolina. “Just come and vote.”

Republicans hope the gathering will help catapult their candidates into November and also showcase the first two years of Trump’s term. Although his poll numbers are sagging, Trump insists that running on his record will give Republicans their best shot at winning.

AP

World.title: Can Australians have their burgers and their forests too?
World.content:
Exclusive EnvironmentSustainabilityAnimals Can Australians have their burgers and their forests too? Nick O'Malley September 10, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Native Australian bushland continues to be cleared at massive scale for cattle grazing, threatening the Great Barrier Reef and climate targets, despite federal efforts to rein in the practice and major supermarkets committing to stripping beef from cleared land from their supply chains. Land clearing for beef production identified in the Great Barrier Reef catchment identified by the ACF. A team of citizen scientists studied satellite imagery covering 10 million hectares of land and identified 30,000 hectares off forest and woodland that had been bulldozed on 150 sites. The Australian Conservation Foundation, which conducted the study using a network of volunteers, has reported 34 of these cases to the National Environmental Protection Agency, which began operations in July. ACF chief executive Adam Bandt called on the government to use the new agency to crackdown on any landclearing found to be illegal. “I think the fundamental problem is corporations are killing koalas and wrecking the reef to make burger patties,” he said. “The corporate food system is broken, and the new laws give us a chance to fix it so that the way we grow food restores nature.”



Australia remains the only wealthy country that still clears native forests for agriculture, and the extent of the clearing is even greater than the amount of land cleared in Indonesia for palm oil, said the lead author of the study, Nathaniel Pelle. Pelle said the study was only a snapshot of clearing conducted, and that the total area cleared was likely to be between 250,000 and 300,000 hectares. The study found 11 instances of clearing within the catchment of the Great Barrier Reef, in some cases along river and creek lines in apparent contravention of environmental laws. Land clearing is viewed as second only to global warming as a threat to the reef, as it causes sediment and nutrient runoff that can choke chorals and promote algae growth and crown of thorn starfish outbreaks. ACF citizen scientists identifed this satellite image from February showing sediment flowing towards the Great Barrier Reef downstream from land clearing for beef production. It found most clearing was conducted in Queensland and NSW, and the vast majority for beef grazing, with bulldozed forests including habitat for threatened species such as koalas, quolls, greater gliders and pink cockatoos.



The largest case of beef-related deforestation exceeded 1700 hectares – or around six times the size of the Sydney CBD – at Wombinoo Station, whose owner, Warren Jonsson, was instructed to replant a section of land in 2017 after unauthorised clearing. Back then he told media that permitting regulations were complicated and expensive, and that if producers did not clear land then there would be no feed to eat. “My cattle don’t like to eat ironbark. People don’t like to eat ironbark,” he said. Jonsson did not respond to a request for comment put to him via Agforce, which represents Queensland beef graziers, though the organisation’s chief executive Niki Ford, said it was not in a position to comment on individual properties without independently verified information about those cases. “Conclusions of this nature should not be drawn from desktop analysis or unsubstantiated data alone, without appropriate verification and consideration of the circumstances on the ground,” she said.



The report also said that the nation’s biggest beef buyers – Coles, Woolworths and McDonald’s – have not yet met targets they set to eliminate deforestation from their Australian beef supply chains by the end of 2025, due to the difficulty of tracing cattle between properties over the full course of their life. Woolworths said it had met the target to eliminate land clearing in its direct supply chain and was working with industry to implement full life-cycle traceability. Coles has also had difficulty tracing cattle over their full life cycle. “We are committed to engaging directly with our suppliers and we will continue to work with producers, industry, government and other stakeholders to advance a consistent approach to traceability and verification and reduce deforestation risk within our in-scope beef supply chain,” a spokesperson said. McDonald’s, which uses Australian beef in an estimated 70 per cent of its outlets around the world, did not respond to a request for comment. By one 2024 estimate Australians eat over 22 kgs of meat, which causes more greenhouse emissions than any other major food product, each per year.



Pelle said the industry already had a mechanism that would allow for this, known as the National Livestock Identification System, which is used to guarantee hormone-free claims and ensure biosecurity between farms. “Clearly it could just as easily be used to verify that cattle have come from farms that are deforestation free,” he said. Industry Association Cattle Australia opposes using the system to protect against land clearing, and rejected the ACF’s findings. “These organisations are putting legal, regulated Australian land management next to illegal palm-oil deforestation, and neither the World Resources Institute nor the European Union agree with them,” chief executive Will Evans said. Related Article Updated

Biodiversity Land clearing rampant as ‘recalcitrant’ NSW lags on reforms



“The EU rates Australia as a low-risk country, and the WRI doesn’t rank us among the world’s major deforestation contributors at all. What training and support do these volunteers undertake? With no peer review and a two-minute tutorial standing in for training, they’ve repeatedly misidentified seasonal change, bushfire events and even established plantations as ‘deforestation.’” He said Cattle Australia’s opposition to using the NLIS to ensure beef did not come from cleared land was “not about resisting transparency,” but that the system had been developed as a biosecurity and food-safety system by producers. “NLIS data is collected for disease response, food safety and market-access assurance,” he said. “Handing retailers or advocacy groups direct access to producer-level data outside the system’s own governance would erode the producer trust the whole system depends on.”

World.title: ‘Could kill us all’: Anthropic insiders say AI has more than 10% chance of ending humanity – soon
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaAI ‘Could kill us all’: Anthropic insiders say AI has more than 10% chance of ending humanity – soon Michael Koziol September 10, 2026 — 5:45am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: Three researchers at Anthropic revealed the artificial intelligence giant is worried AI will lead to the extinction of humanity within a short time frame, in a stunning public admission that prompted fresh calls for urgent AI regulation in the US and elsewhere. The chain of events was sparked by the resignation of Anthropic researcher David Coxon, who also worked at OpenAI, and said in a series of posts on X that neither company was acting responsibly. View post on X “They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives,” he said. “Do not underestimate the power of this technology. These will soon be superhuman systems that can hack anything, revolutionise any field overnight, and acquire real power and resources. “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade … No other human activity poses this level of danger.”



Coxon’s post has now been viewed more than 100 million times. Anthropic is the creator of the AI system Claude. Responding to Coxon’s statement, the alignment science lead at Anthropic, Evan Hubinger, said his former colleague was correct. “We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” Hubinger wrote. View post on X “I personally think it is [more than a] 10 per cent within the next decade. I believe Anthropic is trying its best, but we do not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence and are not clearly on track to.”



Another Anthropic leader, scalable oversight lead Samuel Marks, supported the stunning assessment of AI’s destructive power. “AI developers believe their technology could cause human extinction (or similarly bad outcomes),” he said. “This could happen in the next few years. In general, the more senior the employee, the more concerned they are.” View post on X Marks noted that AIs could not be programmed to behave as their developers would like, and they frequently misbehaved severely. He said he continued to work on safety research at Anthropic because he hoped it would reduce the chance of an extinction-level outcome. Anthropic was contacted for comment



US President Donald Trump has championed AI and its enabling infrastructure, and framed regulation as a burden that would give China – the US’ great strategic rival – the edge in the AI revolution. However, US politicians who have previously called for additional regulation were shocked by the statements and called for urgent action. Three Anthropic insiders said there was a good chance AI would destroy humanity in the near future. AP Photo/Patrick Sison “The very people building this technology admit that it could threaten the future of humanity,” said independent senator Bernie Sanders, who is introducing a bill to pause AI development. Don Beyer, a Democratic congressman from Virginia and a former diplomat, said he hoped the warnings from Anthropic insiders would spur a swift response to issues he had been raising for years.



“Congress needs a sense of urgency on AI that is has not had so far,” he said. “Doing nothing on AI is unacceptable and dangerous.” Related Article Opinion

AI Did AI really ‘go rogue’? Not exactly, but we have plenty to fear Toby Walsh Chief scientist, AI Institute, UNSW Two other Democrats working on AI regulation bills also called for swift action. “The call is coming from inside the house,” said Massachusetts congresswoman Lori Trahan. “Safety researchers are resigning, powerful AI models are breaking out of their labs, and companies are racing ahead anyway. It’s past time for Congress to get off the sidelines and do its job.” Her colleague Greg Casar from Texas, who is working with Sanders on the bill to ban superintelligence, said the situation was now “an emergency”.



Anna Paulina Luna, a Republican congresswoman from Florida, called for a special session of Congress to determine what the future of AI looked like in the US. “There are very real impacts to society as we know it. Partisan politics aside, there are massive implications of a race towards superintelligence,” she said on X. View post on X The point was not to stop AI development but to protect Americans while securing the benefits, Luna said. “This is happening whether or not we want it to.” Some state governors including Florida Republican Ron DeSantis and Illinois Democrat JB Pritzker also voiced concerns about the statements, although DeSantis noted there may be some hysteria in the commentary aimed at investors ahead of upcoming initial public offerings.

World.title: The 30 best movies to stream on ABC iview right now
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Every streaming platform has thousands of films available. To cut through that, here are 30 great movies that span genres, filmmakers, and languages. This week: ABC iview. For other movie choices, check out our guides on Stan*, HBO Max, Netflix, Amazon Prime Video, Disney+ and SBS On Demand. Ali’s Wedding (2016) Stereotypes are no match for irreverent charm and heartfelt desire in this crowd-pleasing Australian update of the romantic-comedy, where a dutiful Muslim son (Osamah Sami) fakes his university career and then adds to the chaos by falling in love. Osamah Sami in Ali's Wedding. Annihilation (2018) The answers aren’t entirely satisfying, but Alex Garland’s adaptation of Jeff VanderMeer’s cosmic horror novel – with Natalie Portman starring as a member of an all-female mission investigating an alien zone – is creepy, horrifying and memorable. The Bank Job (2008)



The Jason Statham movie with the least amount of hand-to-hand combat, this 1970s heist thriller from veteran Kiwi director Roger Donaldson about a vault robbery is grounded, tense, and rife with telling detail. Ben Mendelsohn with Claudia Karvan in Nadia Tass’ The Big Steal. The Big Steal (1990) Boasting Ben Mendelsohn and Claudia Karvan as 18-year-olds, this wry Australian take on the teen comedy from director Nadia Tass is an endearingly sweet automotive caper complete with a hissable villain: Steve Bisley’s conniving used-car salesman. Boy (2010) Featuring Michael Jackson fantasies to match the Thriller-era 1980s setting, Taika Waititi’s breakthrough New Zealand film, where he plays the absent father to an exuberant 11-year-old (James Rolleston), is a terrific and idiosyncratic portrait of childhood hopes and trials. Taika Waititi as Alamein in Boy.



Breaker Morant (1980) Director Bruce Beresford sent a shockwave through Australia’s historic self-belief, with this superb Boer War biographical drama about a trio of Australian soldiers court-martialled for war crimes by their British superiors. An unrelenting depiction of military hypocrisy. Saoirse Ronan in Brooklyn. Brooklyn (2015) The immigrant experience comes to painful, intimate light in this period drama about a young Irish woman (Saoirse Ronan, once again astounding) who discovers who she might be when she’s sent alone to 1950s New York to start anew. Carol (2015) Can two lovers defy a forbidding world? Cate Blanchett’s married housewife and Rooney Mara’s young department store clerk find out in this heartbreaking 1950s covert romance, directed with restrained desire by a masterful Todd Haynes.



The Chant of Jimmie Blacksmith (1978) Few films from the Australian New Wave movement of the late 1970s have endured better than Fred Schepisi’s frontier drama about an Aboriginal man (Tom E. Lewis) driven to violent breaking point by a racist society. Tommy Lewis (right) and Freddy Reynolds in The Chant of Jimmie Blacksmith. Collateral (2004) Heat director Michael Mann returned to Los Angeles for this nocturnal thriller, where a ruthless hitman (Tom Cruise) takes a taxi driver (Jamie Foxx) and his car hostage, resulting in a cat-and-mouse thriller that becomes a spectral meditation on survival. Film Stars Don’t Die in Liverpool (2017) A rightful showcase for Annette Bening, this romantic drama is built on her performance as the former Hollywood star Gloria Grahame, whose fragile final years as a touring stage actor include an unexpected romance.



The Firm (1993) A bracing Sydney Pollack thriller, with Tom Cruise as the young law graduate whose career dreams sour when he discovers that his prestigious new employer, along with Gene Hackman’s wily mentor, is an organised crime front that allows no resignation. Jason Bateman and Rachel McAdams in Game Night. Game Night (2018) Jason Bateman and Rachel McAdams are great fun in this cascading action-comedy about a get-together of friends that turns into a helter-skelter criminal conspiracy. The 1990s movie references are chef’s kiss for a Gen X audience. Head On (1998) A landmark Australian movie, this charged adaptation of the Christos Tsiolkas novel Loaded follows a hedonistic young Melbourne man (Alex Dimitriades) struggling to reconcile his conservative Greek heritage and his gay lifestyle.

World.title: If you loved Furious, this drama about fraudster Elizabeth Holmes should be next on your list
World.content:
★★★★★ CultureTV & radioReview If you loved Furious, this drama about fraudster Elizabeth Holmes should be next on your list Paul Kalina September 10, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Dropout ★★★★★ Unlike the main characters of showrunner Elizabeth Meriwether’s latest show, the just-wrapped, attention-grabbing thriller Furious (Disney+), Elizabeth Holmes was neither a serial killer nor a policewoman with sadomasochistic tendencies, nor a vengeful, alcoholic FBI agent. She’s a rich, WASP businesswoman, but she shares much in common with the types of people Meriwether’s shows trade in. Amanda Seyfried as Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes in The Dropout. Hulu Holmes, the founder of the medical technology startup Theranos, was the poster-girl for Silicon Valley in the late 1990s and early noughties, when digital disruption, entrepreneurism and vast amounts of capital created the perfect storm to upend numerous industries. For its part, Theranos promised to revolutionise American healthcare with a device that could run hundreds of tests from a single drop of blood from the convenience of a local pharmacy. Except the tech, optimistically called the Edison, never worked. Having once boasted a $9 billion fortune and been the darling of corporate America, Holmes is now serving an 11-year prison sentence. Like the characters in Furious and other Meriwether shows, Amanda Seyfried’s Holmes is a complicated and conflicted anti-heroine. One who isn’t always easy to like, a trailblazer fighting adversaries who want to cut her down, a self-sabotaging obsessive blinded by hubris, her upbringing and disregard for others.



Editor's pick Exit interview

Streaming Yes, Furious is a killer Epstein story but ‘it’s not just him’ … Simply labelling Holmes a fraud doesn’t capture the dimensions of the character that Seyfried so vividly brings to the screen. It’s worth watching just a snippet of footage of the real Holmes to see how Seyfried nails some of her traits and idiosyncrasies, the darting eyes, the flat voice that sounds like it’s been possessed by a robot, the Insta-friendly smile. Through her parents (played by Michael Gill and Elizabeth Marvel) and business partner and boyfriend Sunny Bulwani (Naveen Andrews), we perceive Holmes to be an empty, cold and emotionally unavailable woman. It’s a flaw that allows her to treat others ruthlessly and remain nonplussed when the consequences of her flawed invention are laid bare. The Dropout is more than a rise-and-fall biography. It paints a picture of Silicon Valley workplace culture – chill zones, breakout pods, offices that are fun to work in as long as you ignore the nonstop surveillance – and self-belief. An era when self-made entrepreneurs moved fast and broke things, ran roughshod over rules and regulations, and were rewarded with million-dollar paydays and entrées to the old establishments that once dismissed them as cheeky upstarts. It’s a cautionary tale of what happens when tech entrepreneurs and pliant governments are given free rein to build a world in their image (data centres, anyone?), or when profit is seen as the only marker of success. Naveen Andrews as Sunny Balwani and Amanda Seyfried as Elizabeth Holmes in The Dropout.



The Dropout has the pace and feel of a nervy thriller, of a high-stakes chase, as Holmes and Bulwani race to develop their ambitious gizmo and, later, duck and weave as their house of cards collapses. It’s a wild and exhilarating ride where the viewer’s sympathies are constantly challenged and thwarted. Related Article Review What to stream this week: Sharehouse comedy returns better than ever, plus five more picks Gathered around Seyfried and Andrews is a dream ensemble. There’s Alan Ruck as a schmuck businessman who could be a close cousin of his Succession character; Sam Waterston as George Shultz, a former Republican statesman; William H. Macy, unforgettable as an unhinged corporate grifter; Ebon Moss-Bachrach as John Carreyrou, the New York Times reporter who exposed the problems at Theranos, and Stephen Fry playing Theranos’ chief scientist and whistleblower. Available for the first time on free TV, The Dropout is perhaps even more prescient today than when it debuted in 2022. The Dropout streams on SBS On Demand, from Sunday, September 13.

World.title: Need a complicated and broken bloke? This is the actor you call
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Brendan Cowell was sitting in a sauna recently, when a woman said to him, “Oh, we just love you in Colin From Accounts. You’re so funny”. “And I said, ‘Thank you, but that’s not me. It’s my friend,’” Cowell recalls. “And she goes, ‘No, it is you.’ And I said, ‘Actually, it isn’t me.’ She goes, ‘It’s your face and your voice, it’s you.’ And I went, ‘Do you know what? You’re right. I’m sorry. It’s me.’” The woman, of course, was talking about Patrick Brammall – Cowell’s good friend who is now also his co-star in the new Australian psychological thriller Last Seen. You can see it would be an easy mistake to make – they’re both blue-eyed blokes who have been mainstays of the Australian screen for decades – but where Brammall has perfected the easygoing everyman, Cowell is something else altogether. He’s the guy you call when things get complicated. “I get asked to come onto projects where you want to make monstrous men accessible, likable, or possibly understand what pain caused this reprehensible behaviour,” he says. “And I get brought in to humanise, possibly, men that could be just labelled one thing or discarded or seen in a Machiavellian or villainous way. I guess I can bring some humanity to people that behave in certain ways, I don’t know what that says about me, but you can’t judge it.” Maxine Peake and Brendan Cowell play an isolated husband and wife in the thriller Last Seen. He did it in his breakout role in Love My Way and in Plum, in which he played a retired rugby league star with a brain injury. He’s done it again in Last Seen, in which he plays Henry, a deeply religious family man who lives on an isolated property near the south-west coast of Victoria with his wife Jenna (Maxine Peake) and their teenage daughter Sarah (Chloe Jean Lourdes). Henry is distrusting of outsiders, and wants to protect his family. However, that existence is soon disturbed when Sarah makes contact with the outside world. Her distress call is picked up by former police detective Ian Ridley (Brammall), who becomes convinced that Sarah is in fact Maggie, his daughter who disappeared 11 years ago.



Related Article Streaming Flawed, authentic, and uniquely ours: There’s nothing like Colin From Accounts What follows is a cat-and-mouse chase across Victoria – filming took place at Warrnambool, the rugged high country and Docklands studios in Melbourne – as Ian becomes obsessed with tracking down Maggie and Henry is even more determined to protect his family. It’s Cowell and Brammall playing men who are neither wholly good nor bad, just trying their best to do what they feel is the right thing. “He’s got so much love, especially for his family, for the two women in his family,” says Cowell. “So much so that he’s hiding them from society, and has convinced himself that outside of this little valley, are the enemies and the devil and all the sinners, but it’s [only] a matter of time when you’ve got a teenager and when you’ve got a secret. You can’t contain those two things. Your secrets are your sickness.” The series is Apple TV’s first Australian production (the 2022 series Shantaram was primarily backed by US companies), adapted from Ryan David Jahn’s novel The Dispatcher by Australian screenwriter Kris Mrksa, and directed by German Christian Schwochow. And while it might be a classic page turner – filled with vengeful dads, bad dads, family trauma and life-and-death choices – Last Seen also benefits from Schwochow’s outsider’s eye on the landscape and more arthouse approach. Loading Cowell says Schwochow, who directed on The Crown, would ask him about the very Australian language in the show and was also overwhelmed by our wildlife on set. “He’s like, ‘The birds. I can’t hear. I can’t hear from these birds,’” says Cowell, laughing. “And you forget that [how different it must be] … Every scene was the most important movie ever made, and I love that because it’s un-Australian to be that passionate about something and want to make the greatest, most high-stakes piece of art ever.”



Last Seen also marks the first time Cowell and Brammall have worked together since 2015, when Cowell directed Brammall in the film Ruben Guthrie, which Cowell also wrote. Related Article Review What to stream this week: Sharehouse comedy returns better than ever, plus five more picks And while Cowell jokes their constant confusion for one another is “a bit Face/Off Australia 2026”, their casting in Last Seen is perfect, as Brammall is playing against type – you basically don’t expect to see him playing a vengeful dad – whereas Cowell’s natural shiftiness on screen is exactly what you expect of Henry. “I was genuinely blown away by his performance in this because I hadn’t seen him before, that untapped rage,” says Cowell of Brammall. “And it’s so good for the story because my character, you could go, ‘Well, that’s the villain in the trailer’ – and lots of people have texted me, ‘You the bad guy again?’ – yeah, the charismatic bad guy who doesn’t make it to the next series is usually what I play. Brendan Cowell, Chloe Jean Lourdes and Patrick Brammall at the premiere of Last Seen. Getty Images for Apple TV “And what’s brilliant about this is it’s so murky and grey, which is what you want in drama. Many thrillers are good and bad and this is like everybody is implicit. Everybody is doing the wrong thing. Everyone’s hurting people, and Patrick just pushes away his son while chasing down his daughter. I think it’s the best thing I’ve ever seen him do, and his performance really helps me because it keeps flipping.” Why then does Cowell think people see darkness in him?



“I don’t judge my characters, and sometimes that takes you to a dark place because of what you have to try to understand,” he says. “I’ve played characters who’ve done things I don’t want to do, I’m pretty sure I won’t do. But it’s the wolf you feed, isn’t it, in life? “And you know, I went down some dark paths in my life, and I was drinking a lot and stuff, and you think, ‘Oh, you go down there and then go down there [when accessing characters].’ The mind is a warehouse. There’s all sorts of characters in me and I feel like I can find those in me. But I look to the pain and what pain caused the behaviour, and work from there.” Part of the pain for Henry comes from his past. Without giving away any spoilers, it was Henry’s desire to have a child that Cowell found a connection with. Chloe Jean Lourdes plays Sarah, the daughter of Brendan Cowell’s character Henry, in Last Seen. “I’m not a father, and I wanted to be in the past, but it hasn’t worked out,” he says. “And I don’t think that’s a regret or anything because I feel I’m on a spiritual journey in life more than anything, and I’m going where I need to be, but that definitely helped me. “This kind of feeling of wanting something, or wanting to find a way to nurture and to pull something off, you know, when it might not actually be true. So I think I brought a lot of that kind of energy to it, and doubling down, which I think I used to do a lot in life – just keep going, keep going, it’ll work – which is not who I am any more. But I really love that about Henry. He just loves his daughter so much that he will not stop until it’s how he pictures it.” Cowell has been acting since he was in primary school – his first gig was a Cornflakes commercial when he was eight years old – so he had a deep appreciation for his young co-stars, Lourdes and Felix Cameron, the breakout star of Boy Swallows Universe.



Related Series

Streaming Best movies to watch on Netflix, HBO Max, Stan, Binge, Disney+ and Amazon Prime Video “Chloe, I don’t think needs any advice,” he says, laughing. “She is a force. The first Zoom we had, she was like working on layers. Maxine [Peake] and I have done 50 plays, we’ve done all those things, and we looked at each other going, ‘What’s with this sweet face?’ [She’s a] force, and could mix it with us ... “I spoke to Felix a bit about what it’s like at school and stuff like that, and it is a bit different. And I did a lot of TV ads, and I’d turn up to school, and people would be singing the jingles, the whole school and stuff, and it was pretty tough. “But kids are different these days. They’re a little more advanced, and Felix and Chloe probably don’t need my advice. They’re they’re on their way, and he’s good that kid.” Ariadne Sgouros, Leah Purcell and Brendan Cowell in High Country: What Lies Beneath. Now 50, Cowell says he feels more creative and useful than he’s ever been. He has another show premiering this month, season two of Binge’s High Country, opposite Leah Purcell (yes, he’s shifty again), and will feature in the new season of SBS’ genealogy program Who Do You Think You Are? He’s also finished writing another book and life is split between Sydney and London. One of his few regrets, though, is from Last Seen in which they cut a scene in which he took his shirt off. “I did try to stay fit and trim because there was a shirtless wood chopping scene which didn’t end up in the bloody show! I’m like, ‘Thanks Christian.’ I was on the asparagus for six weeks,” he says laughing.

World.title: Apple unveils its foldable iPhone Duo
World.content:
Updated TechnologyPhones Apple unveils its foldable iPhone Duo Barbara Ortutay Updated September 10, 2026 — 6:10am ,first published 4:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Apple has unveiled its latest generation of iPhones, including a widely anticipated foldable version called Duo. The company’s new chief executive, John Ternus, who took over from Tim Cook on September 1, introduced the latest lineup at the Steve Jobs Theatre on Wednesday (US time). The new Apple iPhone Duo. YouTube/Apple After cycling through other updates to the iPhone, the Apple Watch and AirPods along with artificial intelligence advances, Ternus told the audience that “actually there is one more thing,” in a nod to the trademark phrase from Jobs that Jobs himself borrowed from the 1970s detective show Columbo. Called Duo, the phone has the “largest display ever on an iPhone, yet fits into your pocket,” Ternus said.



The phone opens to a 7.6 inch display that is 80 per cent larger than the newest iPhone 18 Pro. It will let people use an Apple Pencil on the phone, a capability previously reserved to iPad users. Duo, Ternus said, “will redefine the experience of using a foldable phone”. The Duo also lets users split the screen to use two different apps on the device, or two windows the same website for things like comparison shopping. The Apple iPhone Duo is available in star white and night sky. Apple The iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max, Ternus said, bring improvements to the battery, camera, and performance. They will start at $2099 and $2299, respectively. The Duo starts at $3499. Customers can pre-order the phones starting on September 12, and they will be available on September 18, although the Duo will be available on October 23.



The new models feature a long battery life – 45 hours of video playback for the Pro Max – and faster charging. The camera offers what Apple called “cinematic effects” from regular video captured on the phone, as well as new options for manual controls and “smart focus tracking,” which lets users focus on a single moving subject, such as a kid during a soccer game. Apple is also focusing on Siri’s new AI capabilities with the new phones, emphasising privacy and security to stand apart from rivals who are further along in incorporating AI. The Duo “was always going to eclipse Apple’s other announcements at the event,” said Ben Wood, chief analyst at CCS Insight. “The device adds a distinctive new design to the iPhone lineup and marks the company’s entry into the niche foldable smartphone category.” Wood said that while there is certain to be demand for the Duo, which costs less than some analysts had anticipated, foldables still account for less than 5 per cent of the overall smartphone market. Many of Apple’s biggest rivals, such as Samsung, Motorola and Google, have already come out with foldable smartphones. But Apple is not one to rush on new technologies.



“The foldable launch is straight out of Apple’s playbook: Wait for the product to work out its kinks and for the market to offer glimpses of viability, then enter and shape the category,” said Forrester analyst Dipanjan Chatterjee. New Apple CEO John Ternus at the product launch. Bloomberg “The difference is that foldables still represent a minuscule share of the smartphone market. The test of Apple’s ambition will be whether it can expand that niche into a meaningful new segment.” Earlier this year, Apple unveiled artificial intelligence advances, including upgrades to its Siri assistant, emphasising a focus on privacy and day-to-day use as the company tries to catch up with rivals on AI. The keynote address for Ternus at the tech giant’s headquarters in Cupertino, California, will set the tone for his vision of Apple’s future, Chatterjee said.



Related Article Gadgets Foldable iPhones, touch-screen MacBooks: What to expect from Apple’s big launch “John Ternus inherits perhaps the most successful consumer technology juggernaut in modern times. That is both a boon and a burden for him. Tim Cook’s perfected execution, scale, and monetisation set a high bar, and Ternus must extend that run,” Chatterjee said. “But he must sustain that momentum while positioning Apple to disrupt itself in the near future, when the iPhone, or any smartphone for that matter, will cease to be the consumer’s primary conduit to the world.” Last year’s iPhone 17 lineup, which included a new ultra-thin model, has been selling well. That generation saw a new slimmed-down model that adopted the “Air” name that Apple already used for its sleekest iPads and Mac computers. Wood noted that, with all the excitement around the Duo, the official arrival of Ternus as CEO “felt like less of a story” than he’d expected. “This event marks a seamless transition from Tim Cook, and its timing to coincide with the iPhone Duo was undoubtedly planned,” Wood said. “However, despite the media frenzy about this new device, it is the broader strength of Apple’s hardware, software and services that will drive the company forward.”

World.title: ASX set to fall sharply as Wall Street declines; Trump sends oil price warning as Iran war escalates
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to fall sharply as Wall Street declines; Trump sends oil price warning as Iran war escalates Damian Troise and Alex Veiga Updated September 10, 2026 — 6:08am ,first published 5:27am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Stocks fell on Wall Street as the price of crude oil rose back above $US100 a barrel amid further escalation in the US war with Iran, with President Donald Trump saying he believes prices will remain elevated until after the midterm elections in November. The S&P 500 index fell 0.5 per cent. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 405 points, or 0.8 per cent and the Nasdaq composite lost 0.6 per cent. Wall Street has kicked off its week with a mixed session. AP The Australian sharemarket is set to fall, with futures at 5.50am AEST pointing to a loss of 94 points or 1.1 per cent, at the open. The ASX lost 0.1 per cent on Wednesday. The Australian dollar was trading at US72.16¢. Wall Street’s losses were broad, with retailers among the companies leading the market lower. Amazon fell 1.8 per cent and Starbucks fell 1.9 per cent. Nearly every sector within the benchmark S&P 500 lost ground, but oil companies pushed higher. Exxon Mobil rose 2.2 per cent and Chevron rose 1.9 per cent.



Oil prices drove much of the action on Wall Street. The US destroyed five Iranian tankers on Tuesday in a series of attacks between the two nations. The conflict that began in February has essentially shut down traffic in the Strait of Hormuz, where a fifth of the world’s oil supply passed before the war began. Related Article Opinion

Oil As Trump’s Iran war drags on, we’re facing the next oil crunch Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist The price of Brent crude, the international standard, rose 3 per cent to $US100.87 a barrel. It marks the first time the price surpassed $US100 a barrel since July. Trump said that oil prices that have surged because of the Iran war likely won’t come down until after US midterm elections. “Right after the election, oil prices are going to be tumbling downward,” Trump said. “I think it’s going to take a little bit longer than the midterm.”



Trump, in an exchange with reporters before travelling to Dallas for the midterm Republican convention, added that he believes Iran will finally relent after the pivotal elections are held in the US. “I think the war’s going to end immediately after the election because they can’t hold out any longer,” Trump said. The jump in oil prices over the course of the war has fuelled already high inflation. Gasoline prices in the US are up about 32 per cent from a year ago to $US4.22 per gallon. Higher fuel prices cut into household budgets directly when it comes to the cost of driving, but they also indirectly raise prices for goods because of higher shipping costs. The price of diesel, which can have an outsized impact on consumers because it is used in shipping and production, hit an all-time high Friday and has continued to climb since. The average price for a gallon reached $US5.94 overnight and is now 9 cents higher than it was Friday. Inflation was already stubbornly high when the US started its war against Iran because of the ongoing US trade war with much of the world. That trade war is also heating up, especially between the US and its close ally and trade partner Canada.



Wall Street will get more updates this week on inflation, starting with a look at prices at the wholesale level on Thursday with the release of the Producer Price Index for August. It measures prices businesses pay for goods before they reach customers. That report will be followed up Friday with the release of the Consumer Price Index, or CPI, for August, which shows the more direct price impact for households. Related Article Updated

Phones Apple unveils its foldable iPhone Duo The latest reports are expected to show that the rate of inflation remains above 3 per cent. That has been an issue for the Federal Reserve, which is aiming to hold inflation at a target rate of 2 per cent. The central bank has been holding rates steady, but Wall Street is leaning toward a 62 per cent chance that it will raise its benchmark interest rate at its meeting next week, according to data from CME Group. Higher interest rates make borrowing more expensive. The goal of raising interest rates is to slow the economy and cool inflation. Rising Treasury yields in the bond market were also weighing down stocks on Wall Street Wednesday.



The US Treasury Department on Wednesday said it would buy back up to $US6 billion ($8.3 billion) in long-term debt. That follows an announcement in August previewing plans for an unusually large buyback in an effort to contain rising yields, which make it more expensive for US companies to borrow money and also weigh down other investments, such as stocks. Bond yields had been holding steady prior to the announcement, but gained ground shortly after. “The simplest version here is that market interventions have a long history of not working very well,” said Guy LeBas, chief fixed income strategist at Janney Montgomery. The yield on the 10-year Treasury, which tends to impact mortgage rates, rose to 4.85 per cent — its highest point since late October of 2023 — before easing to 4.83 per cent from 4.80 per cent late Tuesday. The yield on the 2-year Treasury, which tends to track expectations for Fed moves on interest rates, rose to 4.41 per cent from 4.39 per cent late Tuesday. Bond yields have an inverse relationship to prices. Yields rise as bond prices fall. Rising yields signal that investors are demanding a higher return from Treasurys.



Elsewhere on Wall Street, shares of Meta Platforms rose 6.6 per cent as the parent company of Instagram and Facebook launched a personal artificial intelligence agent, Muse, for people 18 and over who are looking for help with day-to-day tasks like schedules and shopping. Markets in Europe fell while markets in Asia closed mixed. AP The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: Republican National Convention 2026 LIVE updates: Trump, Vance to speak as US midterms loom
World.content:
This two-day convention has been dreamed up by President Donald Trump to rally his supporters for this year’s midterm elections.

Trump has said he wanted to channel the kind of political extravaganza that each party holds every four years to formally nominate a presidential candidate and showcase their vision for the country. There’s even going to be a huge balloon drop at the end.

People arrive at the Republican convention in Dallas. AP Photo/Alex Brandon

Republicans have never held a midterm convention before, although Democrats did in the 1970s and 1980s. Trump had long floated the idea of holding such an event, and Republicans worked to make his wish a reality.

Midterms are often difficult for the party in power in Washington, and Trump believes the event can energise the party and boost turnout among his voters.

“Pretend, please, that I’m on the ballot,” Trump said recently in South Carolina. “Just come and vote.”

Republicans hope the gathering will help catapult their candidates into November and also showcase the first two years of Trump’s term. Although his poll numbers are sagging, Trump insists that running on his record will give Republicans their best shot at winning.

World.title: Can Australians have their burgers and their forests too?
World.content:
Exclusive EnvironmentSustainabilityAnimals Can Australians have their burgers and their forests too? Nick O'Malley September 10, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Native Australian bushland continues to be cleared at massive scale for cattle grazing, threatening the Great Barrier Reef and climate targets, despite federal efforts to rein in the practice and major supermarkets committing to stripping beef from cleared land from their supply chains. Land clearing for beef production identified in the Great Barrier Reef catchment identified by the ACF. A team of citizen scientists studied satellite imagery covering 10 million hectares of land and identified 30,000 hectares off forest and woodland that had been bulldozed on 150 sites. The Australian Conservation Foundation, which conducted the study using a network of volunteers, has reported 34 of these cases to the National Environmental Protection Agency, which began operations in July. ACF chief executive Adam Bandt called on the government to use the new agency to crackdown on any landclearing found to be illegal. “I think the fundamental problem is corporations are killing koalas and wrecking the reef to make burger patties,” he said. “The corporate food system is broken, and the new laws give us a chance to fix it so that the way we grow food restores nature.”



Australia remains the only wealthy country that still clears native forests for agriculture, and the extent of the clearing is even greater than the amount of land cleared in Indonesia for palm oil, said the lead author of the study, Nathaniel Pelle. Pelle said the study was only a snapshot of clearing conducted, and that the total area cleared was likely to be between 250,000 and 300,000 hectares. The study found 11 instances of clearing within the catchment of the Great Barrier Reef, in some cases along river and creek lines in apparent contravention of environmental laws. Land clearing is viewed as second only to global warming as a threat to the reef, as it causes sediment and nutrient runoff that can choke chorals and promote algae growth and crown of thorn starfish outbreaks. ACF citizen scientists identifed this satellite image from February showing sediment flowing towards the Great Barrier Reef downstream from land clearing for beef production. It found most clearing was conducted in Queensland and NSW, and the vast majority for beef grazing, with bulldozed forests including habitat for threatened species such as koalas, quolls, greater gliders and pink cockatoos.



The largest case of beef-related deforestation exceeded 1700 hectares – or around six times the size of the Sydney CBD – at Wombinoo Station, whose owner, Warren Jonsson, was instructed to replant a section of land in 2017 after unauthorised clearing. Back then he told media that permitting regulations were complicated and expensive, and that if producers did not clear land then there would be no feed to eat. “My cattle don’t like to eat ironbark. People don’t like to eat ironbark,” he said. Jonsson did not respond to a request for comment put to him via Agforce, which represents Queensland beef graziers, though the organisation’s chief executive Niki Ford, said it was not in a position to comment on individual properties without independently verified information about those cases. “Conclusions of this nature should not be drawn from desktop analysis or unsubstantiated data alone, without appropriate verification and consideration of the circumstances on the ground,” she said.



The report also said that the nation’s biggest beef buyers – Coles, Woolworths and McDonald’s – have not yet met targets they set to eliminate deforestation from their Australian beef supply chains by the end of 2025, due to the difficulty of tracing cattle between properties over the full course of their life. Woolworths said it had met the target to eliminate land clearing in its direct supply chain and was working with industry to implement full life-cycle traceability. Coles has also had difficulty tracing cattle over their full life cycle. “We are committed to engaging directly with our suppliers and we will continue to work with producers, industry, government and other stakeholders to advance a consistent approach to traceability and verification and reduce deforestation risk within our in-scope beef supply chain,” a spokesperson said. McDonald’s, which uses Australian beef in an estimated 70 per cent of its outlets around the world, did not respond to a request for comment. By one 2024 estimate Australians eat over 22 kgs of meat, which causes more greenhouse emissions than any other major food product, each per year.



Pelle said the industry already had a mechanism that would allow for this, known as the National Livestock Identification System, which is used to guarantee hormone-free claims and ensure biosecurity between farms. “Clearly it could just as easily be used to verify that cattle have come from farms that are deforestation free,” he said. Industry Association Cattle Australia opposes using the system to protect against land clearing, and rejected the ACF’s findings. “These organisations are putting legal, regulated Australian land management next to illegal palm-oil deforestation, and neither the World Resources Institute nor the European Union agree with them,” chief executive Will Evans said. Related Article Updated

Biodiversity Land clearing rampant as ‘recalcitrant’ NSW lags on reforms



“The EU rates Australia as a low-risk country, and the WRI doesn’t rank us among the world’s major deforestation contributors at all. What training and support do these volunteers undertake? With no peer review and a two-minute tutorial standing in for training, they’ve repeatedly misidentified seasonal change, bushfire events and even established plantations as ‘deforestation.’” He said Cattle Australia’s opposition to using the NLIS to ensure beef did not come from cleared land was “not about resisting transparency,” but that the system had been developed as a biosecurity and food-safety system by producers. “NLIS data is collected for disease response, food safety and market-access assurance,” he said. “Handing retailers or advocacy groups direct access to producer-level data outside the system’s own governance would erode the producer trust the whole system depends on.”

World.title: ‘Could kill us all’: Anthropic insiders say AI has more than 10% chance of ending humanity – soon
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaAI ‘Could kill us all’: Anthropic insiders say AI has more than 10% chance of ending humanity – soon Michael Koziol September 10, 2026 — 5:45am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: Three researchers at Anthropic revealed the artificial intelligence giant is worried AI will lead to the extinction of humanity within a short time frame, in a stunning public admission that prompted fresh calls for urgent AI regulation in the US and elsewhere. The chain of events was sparked by the resignation of Anthropic researcher David Coxon, who also worked at OpenAI, and said in a series of posts on X that neither company was acting responsibly. View post on X “They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives,” he said. “Do not underestimate the power of this technology. These will soon be superhuman systems that can hack anything, revolutionise any field overnight, and acquire real power and resources. “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade … No other human activity poses this level of danger.”



Coxon’s post has now been viewed more than 100 million times. Anthropic is the creator of the AI system Claude. Responding to Coxon’s statement, the alignment science lead at Anthropic, Evan Hubinger, said his former colleague was correct. “We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” Hubinger wrote. View post on X “I personally think it is [more than a] 10 per cent within the next decade. I believe Anthropic is trying its best, but we do not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence and are not clearly on track to.”



Another Anthropic leader, scalable oversight lead Samuel Marks, supported the stunning assessment of AI’s destructive power. “AI developers believe their technology could cause human extinction (or similarly bad outcomes),” he said. “This could happen in the next few years. In general, the more senior the employee, the more concerned they are.” View post on X Marks noted that AIs could not be programmed to behave as their developers would like, and they frequently misbehaved severely. He said he continued to work on safety research at Anthropic because he hoped it would reduce the chance of an extinction-level outcome. Anthropic was contacted for comment



US President Donald Trump has championed AI and its enabling infrastructure, and framed regulation as a burden that would give China – the US’ great strategic rival – the edge in the AI revolution. However, US politicians who have previously called for additional regulation were shocked by the statements and called for urgent action. Three Anthropic insiders said there was a good chance AI would destroy humanity in the near future. AP Photo/Patrick Sison “The very people building this technology admit that it could threaten the future of humanity,” said independent senator Bernie Sanders, who is introducing a bill to pause AI development. Don Beyer, a Democratic congressman from Virginia and a former diplomat, said he hoped the warnings from Anthropic insiders would spur a swift response to issues he had been raising for years.



“Congress needs a sense of urgency on AI that is has not had so far,” he said. “Doing nothing on AI is unacceptable and dangerous.” Related Article Opinion

AI Did AI really ‘go rogue’? Not exactly, but we have plenty to fear Toby Walsh Chief scientist, AI Institute, UNSW Two other Democrats working on AI regulation bills also called for swift action. “The call is coming from inside the house,” said Massachusetts congresswoman Lori Trahan. “Safety researchers are resigning, powerful AI models are breaking out of their labs, and companies are racing ahead anyway. It’s past time for Congress to get off the sidelines and do its job.” Her colleague Greg Casar from Texas, who is working with Sanders on the bill to ban superintelligence, said the situation was now “an emergency”.



Anna Paulina Luna, a Republican congresswoman from Florida, called for a special session of Congress to determine what the future of AI looked like in the US. “There are very real impacts to society as we know it. Partisan politics aside, there are massive implications of a race towards superintelligence,” she said on X. View post on X The point was not to stop AI development but to protect Americans while securing the benefits, Luna said. “This is happening whether or not we want it to.” Some state governors including Florida Republican Ron DeSantis and Illinois Democrat JB Pritzker also voiced concerns about the statements, although DeSantis noted there may be some hysteria in the commentary aimed at investors ahead of upcoming initial public offerings.

World.title: The 30 best movies to stream on ABC iview right now
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Every streaming platform has thousands of films available. To cut through that, here are 30 great movies that span genres, filmmakers, and languages. This week: ABC iview. For other movie choices, check out our guides on Stan*, HBO Max, Netflix, Amazon Prime Video, Disney+ and SBS On Demand. Ali’s Wedding (2016) Stereotypes are no match for irreverent charm and heartfelt desire in this crowd-pleasing Australian update of the romantic-comedy, where a dutiful Muslim son (Osamah Sami) fakes his university career and then adds to the chaos by falling in love. Osamah Sami in Ali's Wedding. Annihilation (2018) The answers aren’t entirely satisfying, but Alex Garland’s adaptation of Jeff VanderMeer’s cosmic horror novel – with Natalie Portman starring as a member of an all-female mission investigating an alien zone – is creepy, horrifying and memorable. The Bank Job (2008)



The Jason Statham movie with the least amount of hand-to-hand combat, this 1970s heist thriller from veteran Kiwi director Roger Donaldson about a vault robbery is grounded, tense, and rife with telling detail. Ben Mendelsohn with Claudia Karvan in Nadia Tass’ The Big Steal. The Big Steal (1990) Boasting Ben Mendelsohn and Claudia Karvan as 18-year-olds, this wry Australian take on the teen comedy from director Nadia Tass is an endearingly sweet automotive caper complete with a hissable villain: Steve Bisley’s conniving used-car salesman. Boy (2010) Featuring Michael Jackson fantasies to match the Thriller-era 1980s setting, Taika Waititi’s breakthrough New Zealand film, where he plays the absent father to an exuberant 11-year-old (James Rolleston), is a terrific and idiosyncratic portrait of childhood hopes and trials. Taika Waititi as Alamein in Boy.



Breaker Morant (1980) Director Bruce Beresford sent a shockwave through Australia’s historic self-belief, with this superb Boer War biographical drama about a trio of Australian soldiers court-martialled for war crimes by their British superiors. An unrelenting depiction of military hypocrisy. Saoirse Ronan in Brooklyn. Brooklyn (2015) The immigrant experience comes to painful, intimate light in this period drama about a young Irish woman (Saoirse Ronan, once again astounding) who discovers who she might be when she’s sent alone to 1950s New York to start anew. Carol (2015) Can two lovers defy a forbidding world? Cate Blanchett’s married housewife and Rooney Mara’s young department store clerk find out in this heartbreaking 1950s covert romance, directed with restrained desire by a masterful Todd Haynes.



The Chant of Jimmie Blacksmith (1978) Few films from the Australian New Wave movement of the late 1970s have endured better than Fred Schepisi’s frontier drama about an Aboriginal man (Tom E. Lewis) driven to violent breaking point by a racist society. Tommy Lewis (right) and Freddy Reynolds in The Chant of Jimmie Blacksmith. Collateral (2004) Heat director Michael Mann returned to Los Angeles for this nocturnal thriller, where a ruthless hitman (Tom Cruise) takes a taxi driver (Jamie Foxx) and his car hostage, resulting in a cat-and-mouse thriller that becomes a spectral meditation on survival. Film Stars Don’t Die in Liverpool (2017) A rightful showcase for Annette Bening, this romantic drama is built on her performance as the former Hollywood star Gloria Grahame, whose fragile final years as a touring stage actor include an unexpected romance.



The Firm (1993) A bracing Sydney Pollack thriller, with Tom Cruise as the young law graduate whose career dreams sour when he discovers that his prestigious new employer, along with Gene Hackman’s wily mentor, is an organised crime front that allows no resignation. Jason Bateman and Rachel McAdams in Game Night. Game Night (2018) Jason Bateman and Rachel McAdams are great fun in this cascading action-comedy about a get-together of friends that turns into a helter-skelter criminal conspiracy. The 1990s movie references are chef’s kiss for a Gen X audience. Head On (1998) A landmark Australian movie, this charged adaptation of the Christos Tsiolkas novel Loaded follows a hedonistic young Melbourne man (Alex Dimitriades) struggling to reconcile his conservative Greek heritage and his gay lifestyle.

World.title: If you loved Furious, this drama about fraudster Elizabeth Holmes should be next on your list
World.content:
★★★★★ CultureTV & radioReview If you loved Furious, this drama about fraudster Elizabeth Holmes should be next on your list Paul Kalina September 10, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Dropout ★★★★★ Unlike the main characters of showrunner Elizabeth Meriwether’s latest show, the just-wrapped, attention-grabbing thriller Furious (Disney+), Elizabeth Holmes was neither a serial killer nor a policewoman with sadomasochistic tendencies, nor a vengeful, alcoholic FBI agent. She’s a rich, WASP businesswoman, but she shares much in common with the types of people Meriwether’s shows trade in. Amanda Seyfried as Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes in The Dropout. Hulu Holmes, the founder of the medical technology startup Theranos, was the poster-girl for Silicon Valley in the late 1990s and early noughties, when digital disruption, entrepreneurism and vast amounts of capital created the perfect storm to upend numerous industries. For its part, Theranos promised to revolutionise American healthcare with a device that could run hundreds of tests from a single drop of blood from the convenience of a local pharmacy. Except the tech, optimistically called the Edison, never worked. Having once boasted a $9 billion fortune and been the darling of corporate America, Holmes is now serving an 11-year prison sentence. Like the characters in Furious and other Meriwether shows, Amanda Seyfried’s Holmes is a complicated and conflicted anti-heroine. One who isn’t always easy to like, a trailblazer fighting adversaries who want to cut her down, a self-sabotaging obsessive blinded by hubris, her upbringing and disregard for others.



Editor's pick Exit interview

Streaming Yes, Furious is a killer Epstein story but ‘it’s not just him’ … Simply labelling Holmes a fraud doesn’t capture the dimensions of the character that Seyfried so vividly brings to the screen. It’s worth watching just a snippet of footage of the real Holmes to see how Seyfried nails some of her traits and idiosyncrasies, the darting eyes, the flat voice that sounds like it’s been possessed by a robot, the Insta-friendly smile. Through her parents (played by Michael Gill and Elizabeth Marvel) and business partner and boyfriend Sunny Bulwani (Naveen Andrews), we perceive Holmes to be an empty, cold and emotionally unavailable woman. It’s a flaw that allows her to treat others ruthlessly and remain nonplussed when the consequences of her flawed invention are laid bare. The Dropout is more than a rise-and-fall biography. It paints a picture of Silicon Valley workplace culture – chill zones, breakout pods, offices that are fun to work in as long as you ignore the nonstop surveillance – and self-belief. An era when self-made entrepreneurs moved fast and broke things, ran roughshod over rules and regulations, and were rewarded with million-dollar paydays and entrées to the old establishments that once dismissed them as cheeky upstarts. It’s a cautionary tale of what happens when tech entrepreneurs and pliant governments are given free rein to build a world in their image (data centres, anyone?), or when profit is seen as the only marker of success. Naveen Andrews as Sunny Balwani and Amanda Seyfried as Elizabeth Holmes in The Dropout.



The Dropout has the pace and feel of a nervy thriller, of a high-stakes chase, as Holmes and Bulwani race to develop their ambitious gizmo and, later, duck and weave as their house of cards collapses. It’s a wild and exhilarating ride where the viewer’s sympathies are constantly challenged and thwarted. Related Article Review What to stream this week: Sharehouse comedy returns better than ever, plus five more picks Gathered around Seyfried and Andrews is a dream ensemble. There’s Alan Ruck as a schmuck businessman who could be a close cousin of his Succession character; Sam Waterston as George Shultz, a former Republican statesman; William H. Macy, unforgettable as an unhinged corporate grifter; Ebon Moss-Bachrach as John Carreyrou, the New York Times reporter who exposed the problems at Theranos, and Stephen Fry playing Theranos’ chief scientist and whistleblower. Available for the first time on free TV, The Dropout is perhaps even more prescient today than when it debuted in 2022. The Dropout streams on SBS On Demand, from Sunday, September 13.

World.title: Need a complicated and broken bloke? This is the actor you call
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Brendan Cowell was sitting in a sauna recently, when a woman said to him, “Oh, we just love you in Colin From Accounts. You’re so funny”. “And I said, ‘Thank you, but that’s not me. It’s my friend,’” Cowell recalls. “And she goes, ‘No, it is you.’ And I said, ‘Actually, it isn’t me.’ She goes, ‘It’s your face and your voice, it’s you.’ And I went, ‘Do you know what? You’re right. I’m sorry. It’s me.’” The woman, of course, was talking about Patrick Brammall – Cowell’s good friend who is now also his co-star in the new Australian psychological thriller Last Seen. You can see it would be an easy mistake to make – they’re both blue-eyed blokes who have been mainstays of the Australian screen for decades – but where Brammall has perfected the easygoing everyman, Cowell is something else altogether. He’s the guy you call when things get complicated. “I get asked to come onto projects where you want to make monstrous men accessible, likable, or possibly understand what pain caused this reprehensible behaviour,” he says. “And I get brought in to humanise, possibly, men that could be just labelled one thing or discarded or seen in a Machiavellian or villainous way. I guess I can bring some humanity to people that behave in certain ways, I don’t know what that says about me, but you can’t judge it.” Maxine Peake and Brendan Cowell play an isolated husband and wife in the thriller Last Seen. He did it in his breakout role in Love My Way and in Plum, in which he played a retired rugby league star with a brain injury. He’s done it again in Last Seen, in which he plays Henry, a deeply religious family man who lives on an isolated property near the south-west coast of Victoria with his wife Jenna (Maxine Peake) and their teenage daughter Sarah (Chloe Jean Lourdes). Henry is distrusting of outsiders, and wants to protect his family. However, that existence is soon disturbed when Sarah makes contact with the outside world. Her distress call is picked up by former police detective Ian Ridley (Brammall), who becomes convinced that Sarah is in fact Maggie, his daughter who disappeared 11 years ago.



Related Article Streaming Flawed, authentic, and uniquely ours: There’s nothing like Colin From Accounts What follows is a cat-and-mouse chase across Victoria – filming took place at Warrnambool, the rugged high country and Docklands studios in Melbourne – as Ian becomes obsessed with tracking down Maggie and Henry is even more determined to protect his family. It’s Cowell and Brammall playing men who are neither wholly good nor bad, just trying their best to do what they feel is the right thing. “He’s got so much love, especially for his family, for the two women in his family,” says Cowell. “So much so that he’s hiding them from society, and has convinced himself that outside of this little valley, are the enemies and the devil and all the sinners, but it’s [only] a matter of time when you’ve got a teenager and when you’ve got a secret. You can’t contain those two things. Your secrets are your sickness.” The series is Apple TV’s first Australian production (the 2022 series Shantaram was primarily backed by US companies), adapted from Ryan David Jahn’s novel The Dispatcher by Australian screenwriter Kris Mrksa, and directed by German Christian Schwochow. And while it might be a classic page turner – filled with vengeful dads, bad dads, family trauma and life-and-death choices – Last Seen also benefits from Schwochow’s outsider’s eye on the landscape and more arthouse approach. Loading Cowell says Schwochow, who directed on The Crown, would ask him about the very Australian language in the show and was also overwhelmed by our wildlife on set. “He’s like, ‘The birds. I can’t hear. I can’t hear from these birds,’” says Cowell, laughing. “And you forget that [how different it must be] … Every scene was the most important movie ever made, and I love that because it’s un-Australian to be that passionate about something and want to make the greatest, most high-stakes piece of art ever.”



Last Seen also marks the first time Cowell and Brammall have worked together since 2015, when Cowell directed Brammall in the film Ruben Guthrie, which Cowell also wrote. Related Article Review What to stream this week: Sharehouse comedy returns better than ever, plus five more picks And while Cowell jokes their constant confusion for one another is “a bit Face/Off Australia 2026”, their casting in Last Seen is perfect, as Brammall is playing against type – you basically don’t expect to see him playing a vengeful dad – whereas Cowell’s natural shiftiness on screen is exactly what you expect of Henry. “I was genuinely blown away by his performance in this because I hadn’t seen him before, that untapped rage,” says Cowell of Brammall. “And it’s so good for the story because my character, you could go, ‘Well, that’s the villain in the trailer’ – and lots of people have texted me, ‘You the bad guy again?’ – yeah, the charismatic bad guy who doesn’t make it to the next series is usually what I play. Brendan Cowell, Chloe Jean Lourdes and Patrick Brammall at the premiere of Last Seen. Getty Images for Apple TV “And what’s brilliant about this is it’s so murky and grey, which is what you want in drama. Many thrillers are good and bad and this is like everybody is implicit. Everybody is doing the wrong thing. Everyone’s hurting people, and Patrick just pushes away his son while chasing down his daughter. I think it’s the best thing I’ve ever seen him do, and his performance really helps me because it keeps flipping.” Why then does Cowell think people see darkness in him?



“I don’t judge my characters, and sometimes that takes you to a dark place because of what you have to try to understand,” he says. “I’ve played characters who’ve done things I don’t want to do, I’m pretty sure I won’t do. But it’s the wolf you feed, isn’t it, in life? “And you know, I went down some dark paths in my life, and I was drinking a lot and stuff, and you think, ‘Oh, you go down there and then go down there [when accessing characters].’ The mind is a warehouse. There’s all sorts of characters in me and I feel like I can find those in me. But I look to the pain and what pain caused the behaviour, and work from there.” Part of the pain for Henry comes from his past. Without giving away any spoilers, it was Henry’s desire to have a child that Cowell found a connection with. Chloe Jean Lourdes plays Sarah, the daughter of Brendan Cowell’s character Henry, in Last Seen. “I’m not a father, and I wanted to be in the past, but it hasn’t worked out,” he says. “And I don’t think that’s a regret or anything because I feel I’m on a spiritual journey in life more than anything, and I’m going where I need to be, but that definitely helped me. “This kind of feeling of wanting something, or wanting to find a way to nurture and to pull something off, you know, when it might not actually be true. So I think I brought a lot of that kind of energy to it, and doubling down, which I think I used to do a lot in life – just keep going, keep going, it’ll work – which is not who I am any more. But I really love that about Henry. He just loves his daughter so much that he will not stop until it’s how he pictures it.” Cowell has been acting since he was in primary school – his first gig was a Cornflakes commercial when he was eight years old – so he had a deep appreciation for his young co-stars, Lourdes and Felix Cameron, the breakout star of Boy Swallows Universe.
