World.title: How Ned overcame a decade of pain to return to running
World.content:
The doubts that occasionally flit across Ned Buckell's mind are likely to be familiar to runners whatever standard they're at.

Buckell's story is different to most, though.

A life-threatening infection as a teenager.

A year-and-a-half on crutches.

Another serious infection just when it felt like things were on track, resulting in a hip replacement before he was 21.

And a race number from the 2016 Melbourne Marathon Festival pinned to his wall, reminding him that there is still a destination to reach despite the darkness.

"There's definitely been times when you think to yourself, what am I doing this for?" Buckell tells ABC Sport.

"Why am I still trying to get back running at a reasonably high level?

"I think the biggest thing is because I knew I would do it.

"Those thoughts always creep into my mind like, 'Why am I still going? You're not going to get the most out of it,' but I can get the most out of what I can, and I've always told myself I can.

"That's probably why I haven't given up.

"Even though there've been countless times when you want to, when you keep getting struck down, there are signs, and the universe is telling you to stop.

"You have to just sort of not ignore them, but just push them aside and prove that it's not."

'If it had gone any further, then that would have been the end of me'

Running was Ned Buckell's life. After his injury and illness, it still is. (Supplied: 2045)

Buckell was always going to be a runner.

His dad, John, was a runner and both Ned and his twin brother, Matt, would tag along to cross-country races around Bendigo and run from the age of five.

Theirs was an early introduction to the lung-busting freedom that a pair of trainers and the open trails of the countryside can afford.

"Me, my twin brother and my two older brothers were all always very competitive," Buckell says.

"That turned us into sporty individuals that always want to be better than each other.

"I've always been a runner, but it wasn't until maybe 14 or maybe 13 where I quit footy and was trying to focus on it a bit more.

"I knew me and my brother had some sort of talent, that we could take it to the next level.

"My twin brother has done that, but I haven't. I've just been struck down with this, really."

Sometimes you have to really love running to get up in the freezing cold of winter. (Supplied: 2045)

Buckell's issues all stem back to an infection he got when he was 14 years old, just after he turned to running seriously.

"The night it all happened, I was playing basketball with my mates at his house," Buckell recalls.

"It was a warm September night, the boys were in shorts and T-shirts, and I was in trackies and a hoodie, I was getting these fevers.

"We were all thinking that something's not right, so I rode home with Matt and then the fevers got really bad."

Buckell's parents were away, so it was up to his Nan and Pop to take him to the local GP, who initially diagnosed a twisting hernia, with Buckell struggling to stand due to the pain.

The GP sent Ned to a specialist, who instantly transferred him to the emergency department, where the scale of Buckell's issue became terrifyingly clear.

A staph infection had entered Ned's hip, driving up his temperature to dangerous levels.

"I ended up getting four hip washouts; three in Bendigo, which had no effect, basically, and then they sent me to the Royal Children's Hospital for another one," Buckell says.

The then-14-year-old spent the next three-and-a-half weeks in hospital, fortunate to be alive.

"I was on the cardiac ward because the infection had spread to my heart," Buckell explains.

"If it had gone any further, then that would have been the end of me.

"I never realised how severe it was, probably until now that I've finished my degree."

'Sometimes it's impossible to see that light'

Ned Buckell says the support of his family was essential. (Supplied: 2045)

Ned was discharged from hospital just in time to celebrate his 15th birthday.

It was a bittersweet moment.

The teenager spent the next 18 months on crutches, "torture" for a kid who described himself as "one of the most active that you'd meet".

"There were times that I, you know, I'm very lucky that I've had a supportive family," Ned says, understandably struggling to find the words to recall what had been a horrendous time.

"If I hadn't had that support around me, I definitely wouldn't be here today.

"There were times when you just wanted a way out.

"I knew that I couldn't do that, but watching all my brothers start work, play their sports … I was never jealous, but I was so sad all the time about missing out.

"It was extremely tough. You wouldn't wish that upon anyone, really."

Buckell says he gets goosebumps talking about this period of his life, underlining what a tough topic it is to address even 10 years on.

But despite all the darkness, Ned says that he always kept an optimistic mindset, something which he knows helped him a lot.

"It has been pretty important just to try to find the good in things," Buckell says.

"It's a hard topic for me to talk about, but it's something that I've acknowledged, and I'm just grateful to be where I'm at right now, to be honest.

"I know everyone battles their own shit, and I think the way I've looked at it all is there's always a light at the end of the tunnel.

"And sometimes it's impossible to see that light. And sometimes it's not there.

"But you just have to keep going forward and pushing through.

"It's hard, but I think talking about it does help me try to word things a little bit better."

Running is 'just something I do'

Ned Buckell has had to deal with serious illness and a traumatic injury, but has found peace in running. (Supplied: 2045)

The positivity was tested in 2022 when, having fought his way back to a high level, running 14:42 at the Bendigo 5km Frenzy to break a local under-20 record, his hip started playing up again.

He was diagnosed with avascular necrosis, the death of bone tissue due to a lack of blood flow.

Surgery couldn't fix it, leading to a hip replacement and yet more time watching the rest of the world run away from him.

"I think it comes from within," Buckell says of his perseverance.

"It's something inside of me that hasn't allowed me to give up at all, me knowing that I'm capable of more."

Buckell can sometimes forget that he has a new hip as he runs, finding the same freedom that he had as a child chasing his two older brothers and his twin.

He describes the hip replacement as being "life-changing".

The reminders that things are different come afterwards, when the muscles that had to be so violently contorted to insert the new joint begin to ache.

But that's not enough to stop him.

"I feel like I don't reflect enough on it afterwards," Buckell says of his relationship with running now.

"I did a race the other week, and I won it, and people like my Nan and Pop cried to me on the phone and told me how proud they are, and I forget to realise everything that I've been through.

"I really do have to reflect deeply on how much I've actually endured and overcome. But for me, it's just like something that you do without thinking about it."

Perhaps running is just a part of him?

"It is, yeah," Buckell says.

"And I don't need to over complicate it more than that. It's just something I do, really.

"But I do have to look back and think of how lucky I actually am, to be more offline and running at the level I am because I was told that it was going to be impossible."

Ned Buckell's race number from a decade before has helped spur him on. (Supplied: 2045)

In October, he will prove that impossible is just a word, lining up at the Melbourne Marathon once more, this time in the 5km race.

The race number that he wore the last time he ran the Melbourne streets as a teenager, just before the universe hit pause on his ambitions, is still stuck to the wall of his childhood bedroom.

"I probably won't actually ever realise how big it has impacted me," Buckell says.

"It was kept there as a reminder that I've got work to do to get back to where I want to be.

"And for a while it sort of just stayed there, and it didn't leave. And I was like, yeah, this is my constant reminder that things don't go your way, but I can get back to what I want to do.

"I feel like I've been working so hard for so long, and you just keep getting shit thrown at you, but honestly, I'm confident enough to say that this is sort of the end of it and I can actually test myself now."

Tech.title: Verge staffers react to the iPhone Duo: What we love and don’t love
Tech.content:
Apple has just announced its first foldable iPhone, the iPhone Duo. The new phone has a 5.4-inch outer screen and a 7.6-inch inner screen, two back cameras, Touch ID for authentication, an IP68 rating, and all sorts of slick software tricks to make iOS feel more at home on the new device. Preorders start on October 16th ahead of availability on October 23rd, and it starts at $1,999 for 256GB of storage.

It’s a huge announcement for Apple, and we have many feelings about it. Here’s our gut reactions to the phone. And let us know in the comments what you think!

Photo: Antonio G. Di Benedetto / The Verge

The Duo name is good

I think iPhone Duo is the perfect name for Apple’s foldable. Two screens, Duo. Two back cameras, Duo. (I imagine a future version will get three, but right now we have two.) Duo is a concise three letters, putting it in line with other memorable Apple monikers like Air, Pro, Max, and Neo. Though somewhere at Microsoft, I am sure someone is fuming. —Jay Peters, senior reporter

It’s too expensive

I’ve never wanted a new iPhone more. As an iPad Mini stan, it is the ideal device for me. The size, the form factor, the multitasking possibilities. But I won’t be buying it. It’s just too expensive. [Ed. note: The phone starts at $1,999.] —Jennifer Tuohy, senior reviewer

Photo: Antonio G. Di Benedetto / The Verge

Bye-bye, iPad Mini

The Apple Pencil support makes the Duo an iPad Mini killer and the perfect on-the-go sketchbook for digital artists. —Kevin McShane, editorial director, audio & video

It’s the opposite of what I need and I’m mad that I want it

A folding phone sounds great, and I dig the form factor of the iPhone Duo. As my eyes get worse, I want a bigger phone, but I don’t want to carry a bigger phone. But if I’m real with myself, I don’t need to spend more time looking at my screen, and I don’t want to downgrade my camera system either. I am a bad photographer who has fast-moving kids and puppies, and I’m not willing to give up the telephoto lens on my 17 Pro. Maybe I’ll get some reading glasses. —Nathan Edwards, senior reviews editor

Photo: Antonio G. Di Benedetto / The Verge

Disrupting TikTok?

If Apple takes foldables beyond niche, the new 1.4:1 aspect ratio (a far superior ratio!) might change how content creators operate. Seriously, that is a far more reasonable aspect ratio, especially for portraits, and, strangely, it might be the thing that I’m most excited about with the Duo. —Marina Galperina, senior tech editor

Apple is selling me on the passport shape

I wasn’t a big fan of the short and stout foldable look when I saw Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, but it’s starting to grow on me. The iPhone Duo looks like it’s comfortable to hold in one hand (which could mean no more dropping my phone on my face while lying down), and its thin profile makes it look pleasant to carry around in a purse. —Emma Roth, news writer

Photo: Antonio G. Di Benedetto / The Verge

Love the bigger size, but can’t stop thinking about a crease

I find myself using my iPhone 15 Pro Max or iPad more and more for watching TV shows and movies, so having a portable screen that unfolds to something larger is so enticing to me. But I can’t stop worrying about a visible, distracting crease as I fold and unfold it over months of use. I know my eyes (and brain) will attempt to focus on it no matter how slight it is. Maybe the crease will be completely indistinguishable even after over a year, but a minimum of $2,000 is too much for me to take a chance. —John Higgins, senior reviewer, TVs and audio

Apple and Samsung had the same idea

The Duo is similar to Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8 in more ways than just its passport-ish size and shape. Both phones have prioritized solid core performance but use more basic rear camera setups that distinguish them firmly from the companies’ Pro and Ultra models. They’re a close match in price, too, with the Duo only $100 more. That leaves space in the market for Android manufacturers like Xiaomi to come in with higher-specced foldables that place more of an emphasis on photography, battery life, and pro features, leaving Apple and Samsung to make the mainstream play. —Dominic Preston, news editor

Tech.title: Apple’s new iPhone camera mode promises to prove your photo isn’t AI
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Apple is launching a new way to prove that the picture you took isn’t manipulated by AI. A new feature, called “Reference Image,” will arrive with the iPhone 18 Pro lineup later this month and is supposed to use the device’s new camera sensor to “sign every pixel it sees.”

The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max will only authenticate photos when placed into Reference mode. Once the camera captures signed sensor data, Apple says its Private Cloud Compute will develop it “into an unalterable reference image” that can be viewed in the Photos app. You’ll be able to compare the reference image with other versions of the photo to see if any edits were made.

You can compare the Reference Image to other versions of the photo. Image: Apple

As AI-generated images and videos become more realistic, several new standards have emerged to label images not created by a human, such as SynthID, C2PA, and Meta’s Content Seal. Apple is putting a twist on these methods by building authentication directly into its hardware.

Apple is letting developers access a Reference Image API across iOS, iPadOS, and macOS, which could eventually allow users to inspect these digitally-signed photos in third-party apps. The company says the iPhone 18 Pro lineup won’t come with its Reference Image feature at launch in the European Union, but says users in the region will still be able to “develop and view” them in iOS 27, iPadOS 27, and macOS 27.

Tech.title: iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max: Our first hands-on impressions
Tech.content:
The new phones look quite similar to the previous iPhone 17 Pro lineup, keeping the same general design, aluminum body, and screen sizes. The 18 Pro lineup comes in four colors: black, silver, “glacier” (which is blue), and burgundy, and they now have color-matched glass on the back that blends in more seamlessly with the body.

Another major new feature is the variable-aperture lens for the main camera and new “pro” controls to help give you more options when taking photos. Apple has also added pro controls to the native camera app, at last our national nightmare is over. You can set the aperture to adjust automatically or use one of four selectable stops: f/1.48, f/1.8, f/2.8, and f/4.0. There are also manual controls for shutter speed, white balance, and focus — the latter comes with peaking in the preview to help determine what’s in focus, which is a nice touch. The Dynamic Island is also smaller, and Apple says you can now use it to look at three Live Activities at once. I can confirm, yes, this works.

Tech.title: Hands-on with the new Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4
Tech.content:
After Apple wrapped up its “Surprise and shine” event today, we were able to get a look at the new Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4.

Ceramic is back, baby. Photo: Victoria Song / The Verge

Both of the new watches launch September 18th, with preorders available starting today.

The Apple Watch Series 12 once again starts at $399 for the aluminum case option in space gray, black, light gold, and dark bronze aluminum. The natural or radiant gold titanium version costs $699, and the night blue or pearl white ceramic costs $899. Apple says this year’s watch offers up to 24 hours of “everyday” battery life, and now offers up to 10 hours of battery during outdoor workouts and supports faster charging with up to 12 hours’ worth recharged in just 15 minutes.

The ceramic Series 12 sure does look and feel nice in person. The night blue version is very fetching, but the stark pearl white is also très chic on the wrist. The new dark bronze did look a lot darker in person, however. Like how the dark green Series 7 looked a bit less green and more blackish green, there’s a similar vibe with the bronze.

See what I mean about the bronze color? Photo: Victoria Song / The Verge

The Series 12 runs on a new S11 chip that powers a few new Audio Intelligence Siri AI features, including Sound Recognition, Live Rewind, and Siri Recap. It also got some health upgrades, including new optical and electrical heart sensors with support for continuous background heart rate sensing that takes readings every five seconds. There’s also a new Health Age feature that compares your health metrics to your chronological age, and a Readiness feature that gives you a score for how to handle the day ahead based on your recent activity, training load, vitals, and sleep score. The Readiness feature will be limited to the Series 12 and Ultra 4, however, because it requires the new heart rate sensor array.

You can see the difference between the sensor array on the Ultra 4 and the Ultra 3 (right). Photo: Victoria Song / The Verge

Speaking of the array, this is the first major update on this front in a while. You can definitely see the difference side by side. Notably, the Apple reps on hand pointed out that the new Series 12 and Ultra 4 have a “32-petal design,” whereas the older watches had a two-petal design. This refers to the spoke-like lines coming out of the electrode. It should theoretically enable much more accurate readings. You can also see that the optical sensors themselves are situated much closer together. This is to help minimize light leakage.

The Apple Watch Ultra 4 also includes the new S11 chip and Audio Intelligence features. It starts at $799 and comes in natural and black titanium, along with a premium Apple Watch Hermès version. Apple says the Ultra 4 offers up to 50 hours of battery life.

Tech.title: Hands-on with the foldable iPhone Duo
Tech.content:
The first foldable iPhone is finally here, and following its announcement, we got the chance to try the phone for ourselves. We’ve long been told that Apple would make a foldable iPhone once the tech was good enough — has it been worth the wait?

It definitely feels like something different. The inner screen has a decidedly matte finish that handled even some glare from the windows above the hands-on area well. The folding mechanism is smooth, and even IP68 rated, and the crease is almost impossible to find with my finger. The 5.4-inch outer screen looks petite by modern slab phone standards.

The real show happens when you open and close the phone — rather than just switching one screen off and lighting the other one up, there’s a gradual transition that happens, and it looks as if the contents of the screen come into focus as it moves toward its final position. It’s a pretty nice touch.

I also saw the phone positioned in laptop mode with Netflix on the inner screen, displaying controls on the bottom half before fading them away. There’s also the usual tricks in tent mode, where you’ll get StandBy even if you don’t have the phone plugged in. I’m very curious to see what that does to battery life.

Rumors that a foldable iPhone was in the works have been circulating since at least 2017, with Samsung releasing its first foldable two years after that. Since then, almost every Android manufacturer has entered the market, including Google, Motorola, Huawei, Xiaomi, Oppo, and more.

Previous Next

















1 / 10

Over the last decade, Apple has been variously reported to be developing traditional book-style folding iPhones, smaller flip phone variants, and even larger foldable iPads, before it eventually settled on its final form factor. While early rumors suggested it would be like having two iPhone Airs side by side, the 1.4:1 aspect ratio is squatter, closer to a passport book when closed. That makes the 7.6-inch internal screen wider and better suited for watching videos in landscape than other foldables, but great for reading long scrolling pages or multitasking in portrait.

The dual main camera setup shoots 48-megapixel photos and includes a 2x optical zoom. It’s largely the same as the iPhone 18 Pro but lacks the variable aperture.

is an editor covering deals and gaming hardware. He joined in 2018, and after a two-year stint at Polygon, he rejoined The Verge in May 2025.

Following Apple’s “Surprise and shine” event that saw the announcement of the iPhone Duo and the iPhone 18 Pro, the company increased the price on all of its last-gen iPhones that are still available for purchase.

Tech.title: Apple iPhone Duo launch event: The 5 biggest announcements
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Apple just wrapped up its first iPhone launch event with CEO John Ternus at the helm, and it did not disappoint. We got a look at Apple’s long-rumored foldable iPhone Duo, along with the next generation of AirPods and the Apple Watch.

Here’s a roundup of all the biggest announcements from the event.

Image: Apple

Apple’s “one more thing” at this year’s event was the iPhone Duo — a passport-shaped foldable that lays flat when opened. The device is Apple’s “thinnest iPhone yet,” coming with a 7.6-inch inner display and a 5.4-inch outer screen. It will also support Apple Pencil “later this year” and comes with Touch ID on the side button.

The iPhone Duo maintains the same aspect ratio across both displays, along with some changes to iOS 27 that make it possible to view two apps side by side, pin videos, and use the device in “any orientation.” Some apps, including Netflix, Zoom, and Slack, have already launched updates to take advantage of the iPhone Duo’s features.

In terms of hardware, the iPhone Duo comes with Apple’s upgraded A20 Pro chip, the company’s in-house C2 cellular modem, a 48-megapixel camera, and a nanotexture finish on its display that reduces glare and reflections. The iPhone Duo offers two batteries with up to 31 hours of video playback when using the inner display and up to 44 hours when using the outer display.

The iPhone Duo will start at $1,999 and come in star white and night sky. It will be available starting October 23rd.

Image: Apple

Apple is skipping the base iPhone 18 at this year’s launch event for two Pro-level models that the company says come with its “biggest camera improvement in years.” The new devices feature a 48-megapixel main camera with variable aperture, along with new “Pro controls” that give users more ways to tweak their camera settings.

The iPhone 18 Pro also has an A20 chip that the company says comes with a “huge gain” in performance, as well as a claimed battery life of up to 36 hours of video playback on the iPhone 18 Pro and up to 45 hours on the iPhone 18 Pro Max. There’s a new Dynamic Island as well, which can show up to three live activities at once.

Both phones support Apple’s “most advanced” on-device AI model so far, with the company’s AI-upgraded Siri supporting more than 300,000 apps. The iPhone 18 Pro starts at $1,199, and the Pro Max starts at $1,299 and will have a new 2TB option. They come in black, silver, burgundy, and glacier when they launch on September 18th.

Image: Apple

Apple is bringing active noise cancellation (ANC) to its cheapest AirPods model for the first time. The company says the AirPods 5 are more durable and come with 50 percent more noise reduction than the previous generation. They cost $129 and offer up to four hours of listening with ANC turned on (or up to 20 hours with the charging case).

Additionally, Apple is launching a pricier, $149 AirPods option with on-stem volume control, up to five hours of battery life with ANC, and a wireless charging case. Both models will be available starting September 18th.

Image: Apple

Apple is launching a new “Siri Recap” feature that will use the built-in microphones on the new Watch Series 12 and Watch Ultra 4 to take notes on your daily conversations. You can ask Siri questions about the transcripts and save them to the Siri app. There’s a new “Audio Intelligence” feature that uses on-device AI to detect certain sounds like sirens or a doorbell, too.

Apple’s upgraded Watch Series 12 now measures your heart rate every five seconds using a sensor that has “larger, more power-efficient green LEDs.” The device will also sample heart rate variability as often as every five minutes. You can also access “personalized guidance” from Apple Intelligence inside the company’s redesigned Health app, which now includes a new “Longevity” tab to assess your health across sleep, movement, heart health, and other metrics.

The Watch Series 12 will offer up to 24 hours of battery life, while the Ultra can now last over two days without a charge, according to Apple. The Watch Series 12 will start at $399 or $899 for a ceramic option, while the Watch Ultra 4 starts at $799. The devices will launch on September 18th.

Photo: David Imel / The Verge

Apple’s big iOS 27 update is nearly here, with Siri AI arriving as a beta for devices set to English, allowing the more conversational assistant to take action across your apps. Aside from this feature, iOS 27 also includes a way to adjust the opacity of Liquid Glass, new icon designs, extra-large widgets, and new volume settings for ringtones, alarms, timers, and alerts.

Tech.title: Everything Apple announced at its fall iPhone event, from the foldable iPhone Duo to an always-listening Apple Watch
Tech.content:
Apple on Wednesday unveiled its latest iPhones and Apple Watches at its first fall event under newly appointed CEO John Ternus. The main event was the tech giant’s highly anticipated first foldable phone, the iPhone Duo. Apple also announced its iPhone 18 Pro lineup, along with new AirPods, and more.

We’ve compiled all of the announcements from today’s “Surprise and Sunshine” event.

iPhone Duo

Image Credits:Apple /

Apple’s first foldable, the iPhone Duo, features a 7.6-inch Retina display when unfolded, while its outer display measures 5.4 inches. The company said that the new device was “Inspired by the versatility of iPad.” The inner display features an “under-display” camera that gives users an all-screen feel.

Apple says the iPhone Duo delivers up to 31 hours of video playback on its inner display and up to 44 hours on its outer display.

The phone features a 48-megapixel fusion main camera and a 48-megapixel ultrawide camera with 2x optical zoom. As with other foldable phones, users can take rear-camera selfies and look at previews on the outer display.

The Duo’s hinge is made from Grade 5 aluminum and comprises more than 100 specially engineered components designed to ensure smooth opening and closing.

The iPhone Duo starts at $1,999 with 256GB of storage and is available in two colors. Pre-orders for Apple’s new foldable open October 16, with the device hitting stores on October 23.

iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max

Image Credits:Apple /

The new iPhone 18 Pro lineup retains the same design as its predecessors, but its biggest upgrade comes in the form of enhanced cameras.

The new Pro series camera features a 48-megapixel sensor with a variable aperture controlled by six thin blades. This system is expected to improve low-light photography while also increasing shooting speed. The camera software also introduces new Pro controls, including white balance, shutter speed, aperture, and a histogram. In addition, new “Photographic Styles” offer greater customization with texture and grain controls.

The new camera can record 4K video in Dolby HDR Vision and apply cinematic effects after shooting the footage.

The iPhone 18 Pro starts at $1,199, while the iPhone 18 Pro Max starts at $1,299, which is $100 more than last year’s models. Pre-orders will open Saturday, with both devices officially available on September 18.

Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4

Image Credits:Apple

A new “Sound Recognition” feature can listen for sounds such as sirens, alarms, doorbells, and a baby crying, providing helpful alerts for people who are hard of hearing. The Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 aren’t getting a major hardware makeover, but they are getting some significant software updates.

Apple is taking aim at the growing wave of AI-powered wearables with new “Audio Intelligence” features that can rewind moments and help users remember details from their everyday conversations.

The smartwatches are introducing a “Live Rewind” feature that shows the previous 15 seconds of a conversation as a text snippet, and a “Siri Recap” feature that’s designed to help you remember key moments from daily conversations, like takeaways from a team meeting or a parent-teacher conference.

A new “Sound Recognition” feature can listen for sounds such as sirens, alarms, doorbells, and a baby crying to provide alerts for people who are hard of hearing.

The Apple Watch Series 12 starts at $399, while the Apple Watch Ultra 4 costs $499. Pre-orders open today, with availability in stores beginning September 18.

AirPods 5

Image Credits:Apple

The latest generation of Apple’s wireless earbuds, the AirPods 5, introduces several upgrades, including improved audio quality, stronger active noise cancellation, and expanded Siri and Apple Intelligence features.

Apple says AirPods 5 can reduce background noise by 50% more than the previous generation. They also feature volume control on the stem, which was previously only available on Apple’s more expensive AirPods Pro.

Transparency mode on AirPods 5 has also been improved to allow users to hear nearby voices and ambient sounds more naturally.

The AirPods 5 offer up to five hours of listening with active noise cancellation on a single charge. The charging case brings total listening time to up to 22 hours.

AirPods 5 start at $129, while the version with a Wireless Charging Case costs $149. Pre-orders begin today, with the earbuds set to arrive on September 18.

Revamped Health App

Image Credits:Apple

Apple announced a redesigned Apple Health app that takes advantage of Apple Intelligence to make better sense of your health data.

The updates introduce a new Insights tab with a summary of the most timely health information, along with personalized guidance, assessments, a new “Readiness” score, and a calculation of your “Health Age.” The updates also introduce a new Longevity tab that uses metrics from your Apple Watch and iPhone to assess your overall health across factors such as sleep, movement, heart health, and more.

The revamped Health app rolls out later this year, starting in U.S. English.

Tech.title: There are new shiny iPhones, so Apple is making you pay more for older models
Tech.content:
Apple on Wednesday unveiled its new iPhone 18 and its first foldable iPhone, the iPhone Duo. But amid all the attention on Apple’s newest and most expensive devices, there’s another change: Apple is raising the price of its existing iPhone models by $100.

Starting today, customers will notice a price hike for existing models on Apple’s online store, including starting prices for iPhone 16 at $799, iPhone 17e at $699, iPhone 17 at $899, and iPhone Air at $1,099.

The price increases are even steeper in some international markets. In India, for example, prices have reportedly risen by around 20.5%. The company also discontinued the iPhone 17 Pro and iPhone 17 Pro Max.

The strategy is an unusual one for Apple. Traditionally, the arrival of a new generation of iPhones means older models become cheaper.

However, the price hike wasn’t entirely unexpected. Speculation had been building that Apple could raise prices as it introduced its next-generation iPhones. One of the biggest pressures is a global shortage of memory and storage chips. Demand for those components has surged as AI companies and cloud providers build out increasingly massive data centers.

In a June interview with The Wall Street Journal, former Apple CEO Tim Cook acknowledged that rising component costs could eventually force the company to rethink its pricing strategy. He said Apple could no longer fully absorb the rising costs of memory and storage chips.

About a week after those comments, the company raised prices across its Mac and iPad lineups.

Other reasons Apple may consider increasing iPhone prices are to remain competitive with rising prices from rivals like Samsung and Google. Additionally, Apple might feel that its new Upgrade program, which allows customers to spread the cost of an iPhone through manageable monthly payments, could cushion the impact of a price hike, making it less noticeable to consumers.

Tech.title: The hinge for Apple’s new foldable phone was built with AI
Tech.content:
In Brief

Apple’s long-awaited foldable phone, the Duo, contains a number of surprises, including a critical hinge that was designed and built with the help of AI and 3D printing.

The new phone represents Apple’s first entry into the foldable phone genre — a category of devices that has seen significant consumer enthusiasm, but whose form factors haven’t always lived up to that enthusiasm. As you might expect from a product that, by design, undergoes twice as much wear as a traditional device, most foldables suffer significant degradation and don’t have the durability of other smartphones.

Apple claims that it has integrated innovative protections into the Duo’s design to keep the phone from falling prey to the typical wear and tear associated with foldables. That includes the hinge, according to Johny Srouji, the company’s chief hardware officer.

“During manufacturing, we use AI algorithms to precisely match each individual hinge with its best-fit housing to ensure perfect alignment, and a confocal laser progressively scans the topology of every single unit, and 3D prints up to 25 micro layers of a custom photopolymer to eliminate residual waviness,” Srouji said during Apple’s Surprise and Shine event on Wednesday.

Srouji also shared that Apple gave the foldable phone “a custom nano-texture finish that significantly reduces glare and reflections” as well as a multi-layer lamination strategy designed to increase the device’s durability. Of course, it remains to be seen whether those protections will be enough to keep the Duo in peak physical condition in the long run.

Tech.title: Apple Watch’s new feature listens to your chats and recaps them
Tech.content:
Apple launched a meeting notetaker on Wednesday for the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, one of a series of new audio intelligence features that can listen to sounds through your Apple Watch.

The feature, called Siri Recap, uses ambient listening to take high-level notes of your conversations, according to the company. Apple Intelligence will automatically generate a title, summary, and key points from the conversation, which can then be reviewed in the Siri app.

Apple said that you can choose to keep this feature always on, set up a schedule, or turn off completely.

The notetaker wasn’t the only audio-focused feature introduced for the Watch during the event. Apple’s new audio intelligence features also include Shazam, which can identify songs instantly. This means Apple has finally caught up to Google’s Now Playing feature. The Watch can recognize loud sounds like sirens, alarms, doorbells, or a baby crying and notify users.

Apple also introduced a feature is called Live Rewind, which lets users recap 15 seconds of conversation when they double press the digital crown.

Apple emphasized that the features don’t store recordings and that raw audio is inaccessible. The Siri Recap feature doesn’t identify speakers either. Users can access Live Rewind recaps, which are end-to-end encrypted. Despite these guardrails, an always-listening feature will likely raise privacy concerns because Siri Recap may still capture sensitive information in its summaries.

Besides some of the privacy features, Siri Recap sounds similar to other notetakers like Granola and Circleback, which also have Apple Watch apps.

Tech.title: Harvey hits $15.5B valuation, months after reaching $11B
Tech.content:
In Brief

Harvey, the legal AI startup that VCs can’t get enough of, has raised another $550 million in funding, this time at a $15.5 billion valuation, the company announced on Wednesday.

The round was co-led by Diffusion and Lightspeed Venture Partners and follows the previous $200 million round at an $11 billion valuation announced in March. And that was just a few months after an $8 billion valuation from a round in December.

With this latest infusion of capital, the company has raised more than $1.55 billion total and nearly doubled its valuation in about nine months. Like Databricks, the company didn’t name the round, though it has completed at least eight priced rounds since 2023 (five of them since 2025), Pitchbook estimates. Since a couple of those were considered extension rounds, this one could be considered a Series F.

The fresh cash comes a couple of weeks after Harvey announced its first in-house model, Harvey Tenet, built from open-weight model Kimi K3 and post-trained with legal data with the help of inference provider Fireworks (who also helped Cursor train its homegrown model). In addition to offering a model, Harvey is encouraging its customers to adopt and post-train their own open-weight models. So Harvey is quickly becoming an example of how an entire industry — law — can both heavily use AI and not rely on proprietary frontier AI labs like OpenAI and Anthropic.

Tech.title: Apple’s revamped Health app will calculate your ‘health age’ and readiness score
Tech.content:
Alongside the new Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, Apple on Wednesday introduced a redesigned Apple Health app that takes advantage of Apple Intelligence to make better sense of your health data. The changes deliver a new Insights tab that includes a summary of the most timely information, plus personalized guidance, assessments, a new “readiness” score, and a computation of your “Health Age.”

The latter is a way to understand how your various health metrics compare with your actual age and uses data like your VO2 max, sleep, and more, including biomarkers from your blood.

Image Credits:Apple

The additions also include a new longevity tab, which uses metrics from your Apple watch and iPhone to assess your health across sleep, movement, heart health, and other factors. Your lab results can be incorporated into this guidance, and Apple announced a team-up with Quest for a 50-biomarker panel for $119, giving users quick access to data that can only come from lab tests.

Image Credits:Apple

With Apple Intelligence, Apple’s Health app has been improved to make sense of other health data, too, which comes into play in features like the readiness score and the Insights tab. For instance, the app could suggest that a user incorporate more intervals into their morning run to improve their cardio health. The app will also go deeper in areas like fitness and heart health as well, Apple said

The Health app also allows users to take in-depth assessments of how well their bodies are moving, which can help people who are aging or recovering from an injury. A trainer can even demonstrate certain moves for you to try as you take the assessment, which Apple claims is like having a coach right there with you.

The updated Health app rolls out later this year, starting in U.S. English.

Tech.title: Apple unveils Watch Series 12 and Watch Ultra 4 with an AI upgrade that can recap your day
Tech.content:
Apple on Wednesday unveiled the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 at its iPhone launch event in Cupertino. While the smartwatches aren’t getting a major hardware makeover, they are getting some significant software updates.

Most notably, Apple is taking aim at the growing wave of AI wearables with new “Audio Intelligence” features that let you rewind moments and remember details from daily conversations.

The smartwatches are launching with “Live Rewind,” a feature Apple describes as letting you go back up to 15 seconds. A double press of the Digital Crown shows the previous 15 seconds of a conversation as a text snippet. You can ask Siri about the content of that transcript, or save it to the new Siri app to revisit later.

Image Credits:Apple /

There’s a “Siri Recap” feature that’s designed to help you remember key moments from daily conversations. It uses ambient listening to take high-level notes of your conversations, like takeaways from a team meeting or a parent-teacher conference. When Siri Recap is turned on, after a conversation, Apple Intelligence automatically generates a title and key points in the new Siri app.

A new “Sound Recognition” feature will be able to listen for sounds like sirens, alarms, doorbells, a baby crying, and more for people who are hard of hearing.

Apple says these audio intelligence features do not create or store audio recordings.

Both of the new smartwatches feature a new health-sensing system with an increased electrode surface area for better skin contact during ECG readings. For improved optical sensing, redesigned photodiodes are arranged in a ring to capture light more efficiently. There are also more power-efficient green LEDs that enable accurate heart-rate measurements throughout the day, even during motion.

The new health sensing system delivers higher-frequency continuous heart rate data, which is a key indicator of your overall health. Background heart rate readings are now taken every five seconds all day long, even while you’re on the go. That’s 60 times more frequent than before.

Image Credits:Apple /

The smartwatches are taking a page from smart rings with new readiness scores that analyze your recent activity, vitals, and sleep each morning, distilling it all into a single score that indicates how prepared your body is to take on the day.

There’s also a new “Health Age” feature that lets users see how their key health metrics compare with their actual age, based on data from their watch, including VO2 max, sleep, and more.

The Apple Watch Series 12 starts at $399, while the Apple Watch Ultra 4 costs $499.

Tech.title: Apple has a new way prove your iPhone photos aren’t AI slop
Tech.content:
In a world awash in AI slop, Apple wants you to trust what gets captured on its iPhones.

The company announced Wednesday during its Surprise and Shine event that it is introducing Apple Reference Image, a feature it says can prove whether an image taken with the iPhone 18 Pro is authentic.

“This is vital for photojournalists and photographers,” the company said.

When a photo is taken, the main camera sensor also captures signed sensor data which Apple’s Private Cloud Compute service then turns into an “unalterable image” viewable in the Photos app. The reference image can then be compared with other versions of the photo to determine whether any changes have been made. Apple likens the reference image to a “digital negative.”

While reference images will initially be viewable only in the Photos app, the company is making APIs available to developers so they can integrate the feature into their own apps.

Apple also said it will support the SynthID standard to help people determine whether images were created or altered with AI.

Apple Reference Image is one of several new features and upgrades to the company’s hardware and software that is focused on the camera.

The company said the iPhone 18 Pro includes its biggest camera improvement in years. One upgrade that will surely get the attention of photographers is the variable aperture on the new 48 megapixel fusion main camera. The aperture is what controls how much light enters the lens. This new main camera has a variable aperture, which means users have more control over the amount of light coming in and ultimately what the final image looks like. It should be especially helpful for those who like to take photos at night.

To achieve this, Apple said it developed a system of six laser-cut blades, each thinner than a human hair and made from a specialized polymer composite, a new rotor mechanism to control movements, and a custom-designed lens.

Tech.title: Everything Apple Announced: iPhone Duo, iPhone 18 Pro, Apple Watch, AirPods 5
Tech.content:
It’s a brand new era for Apple. The company is turning over leadership for the first time in 15 years, with former CEO Tim Cook handing off the reins last week to the new CEO, former Apple VP of hardware John Ternus.

At the first Apple product soiree hosted by Ternus, the company made an even bigger change: it announced its first ever folding device, the iPhone Duo.

The company also announced its new line of iPhone 18 Pro phones, some updates to its Apple Watch line, new AirPods, and new software capabilities powered by Siri AI.

As expected, there were no base-model iPhone 18 announcements; those are likely coming early next year. There was also no mention of Vision Pro, iPads, or Macs. Apple touted new desktop Macs in August.

Here’s everything Apple showed off today.

Apple iPhone Duo

Courtesy of Apple

Apple’s first ever folding device is the Duo, a “passport sized” foldable iPhone. It starts at $1,999 for a model with 256 GB of storage.

It’s a product category that Apple has been working toward for a decade. Now, it hopes to do that very Apple thing where it may not be the first company to the new tech party, but it definitely aims to be the snazziest.

The Duo is a landscape style foldable, meaning it has a vertical magnetic hinge that lets you open the device like a book. Closed, it has a 5.3-inch screen on the outside. Open it up, and the landscape display is 7.7 inches. The Duo is also heavy, weighing in at 254 grams, which might be a little too hefty for some users.

The Duo is made with a titanium frame and what Apple calls a “custom polymer” screen for increased durability. It runs on Apple’s proprietary A20 Pro chip (the same chip in the new Pro-model iPhones 18) and the company’s custom C2 modem. The horizontal format also means it's capable of running iPad-like apps, albeit ones that can adjust on the fly when folding the screen or setting the phone up at an angle. The Duo will also be able to work with the Apple Pencil Pro stylus.

On the back of the Duo are two 48-megapixel cameras, one standard, one for ultrawide shots. There are two 12-megapixel selfie cameras, one on the main screen and one on the inside when the screen is opened. The cameras can also capture 4K video.

Tech.title: Apple Doesn’t Want You to Worry About the New Apple Watch’s Listening Features
Tech.content:
The new Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 come not just with better fitness tracking and upgraded noise reduction, but also a whole new way to listen.

Apple announced on Wednesday that the two smartwatches come with four opt-in “audio intelligence” tools that are powered by audio gathered by the watches’ microphones. They include sound and music recognition, a conversation recap feature, and “Live Rewind” so a user can see a transcription of anything that was said in their environment in the previous 15 seconds.

Seemingly wary that the features could make it feel like the walls have ears, Apple is emphasizing that all of them are built to prioritize privacy and security using the extensive infrastructure the company has developed to protect its other Apple Intelligence and Siri services. As more and more of these types of features debut, though, the audio intelligence announcements are a reminder that AI-powered tools are becoming increasingly universal in all areas of computing and life.

“These features do not create or store audio recordings, and raw audio used for processing is completely inaccessible to the operating systems, apps, the user, or Apple,” the company wrote in a report shared with WIRED.

The new Apple Watch features are designed to process as much data locally on devices as possible, so potentially sensitive data doesn’t go to the cloud. Sound Recognition, for example, alerts users about sounds in their environment—including doorbells, sirens, alarms, or, say, a baby crying—without sending any data off the watch. The tools that do send information out to the cloud preprocess the data so it isn’t raw audio files, then use Apple’s Private Cloud Compute infrastructure.

Apple emphasizes that its on-device capabilities for Apple watches have expanded thanks to the company’s new S11 chips. The chips include a special memory-protected space that Apple calls the Secure Exclave. Designed specifically for sensor data, the exclave is an isolated buffer that is inaccessible to the rest of the operating system where Apple Watch can hold and process audio data in a protected space.

A new Shazam feature “listens” for music and will generate a signature of a song that is stored in the Secure Exclave. If the user navigates to Shazam to find out what the music is, the tool will send that signature—not an audio file—to Shazam’s servers for identification. (Shazam is an Apple-owned service.) If the user doesn’t prompt to identify the music, or as soon as they do, the special signature is “immediately” deleted from the watch.

The recap feature, known as Siri Recap, can be set to be on all the time and generate recaps of any substantive conversation, or it can be given a schedule to listen in at certain times during the day. A dedicated AI model determines when speech is occurring without recording or transcribing any data. If it detects a conversation, audio goes into a protected buffer within the Secure Exclave on the Apple Watch, the watch encrypts it, and then transmits it using Apple’s special secure Bluetooth pairing to the Secure Exclave on a user’s iPhone. Then the audio is immediately deleted from the Apple Watch.

The iPhone uses local speech recognition and language models on-device to transcribe the audio and then generate a minimal version of the transcript that removes nonessential elements like extra words and repeated phrases. Then the raw audio is immediately deleted from the iPhone as well. The last step on the iPhone is a safety model that “screens the text to omit potentially harmful terms,” according to Apple. From there, the distillation of the conversation is encrypted, and the iPhone sends it out to Private Cloud Compute.

Tech.title: UK Lawmakers Are Freaking Out Over AI’s Summer of Chaos
Tech.content:
A leading British politician has urged the United Nations to intervene in “the unsafe development of super intelligence” after an Anthropic team leader posted: “We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!”

Whether “marketing hype” or signposting of a genuine extinction threat, “governments must step in,” Labour MP Darren Jones wrote in an open letter also addressed to the UK prime minister and international Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development.

Jones is the latest lawmaker scrambling to find ways to protect the British public from AI threats to safety. Just one day earlier, Labour MP Alex Sobel had introduced a parliamentary bill proposing to ban the “development, deployment, and operation of artificial superintelligence”—systems which can fully replace and outmatch humans at any task. The legislation would also give the government powers to monitor and control the development of the technology at different points in the supply chain, including at chip level.

“We are not alone in this effort,” said Sobel while introducing the bill, pointing to the US government’s temporary export ban on Anthropic’s Fable 5 and Mythos 5 models in June. "If the Trump Administration, who are perceived as historically against AI regulation, can contemplate drawing a line on models that are too powerful and dangerous, it would be strange for us not to ask what our response should be," he argued.

MPs from across political parties put their names on the bill, including Labour MP Jess Asato, who is suing Elon Musk’s xAI after its Grok chatbot was allegedly used to generate fake sexualized images of her. Lawmakers have become increasingly worried about the threat of AI to national security after a string of incidents of AI agents going rogue in recent months. They want to introduce guardrails against worst-case scenarios, such as these systems seizing control of critical infrastructure and running sophisticated influence operations.

Tech.title: I Let an AI Agent Hack All My Gadgets—and I’d Do It Again
Tech.content:
As the author of a newsletter about artificial intelligence, I consider it my duty to experience the bleeding edge of this technology firsthand. This week, that meant embracing some agentic mayhem.

You’re probably aware that frontier AI models have attained advanced cybersecurity capabilities in recent months. They can find zero-day bugs in large codebases and scan computers for vulnerabilities at lightning speed. To make things even more exciting, cybersecurity agents sometimes go rogue, colluding with one another and hacking into outside systems to gain an edge.

To get a closer look, I decided to unleash one in my own home network. Over the course of a few days, I watched as my own rogue agent found vulnerabilities in various household devices, hacked into a PC, and showed me that several vibe-coded projects were—unsurprisingly—riddled with bugs. (My wife knew what I was up to, and rolled her eyes each time I proudly announced the discovery of a new vulnerability.)

But Will, you might be thinking, giving an impish, all-powerful cybersecurity agent access to your home network is batshit. And you would be correct! Nevertheless, I believe that a good way to understand the cybersecurity hellscape in front of us is to pay it a visit.

In the end, my experiment was revealing, but oddly reassuring, too. My little network gremlin showed me how vulnerable my home life would be to AI hacking, but it also told me how to make everything a lot more secure. In the end, I discovered that the best way to deal with AI hacking may well be having your own AI hacker.

Maverick Model

I got the idea for the experiment after discovering Abliteration AI, a startup that offers access to powerful AI models with the usual guardrails removed.

Most mainstream AI models will refuse to respond to certain queries, and they will certainly refuse to find and exploit vulnerabilities in computer systems. But it’s possible to remove these restrictions by finding and modifying certain patterns within an open-weight model’s internal parameters. You can tweak the patterns that lead to refusals through a process known as abliteration.

Removing AI’s guardrails might seem risky, but it’s not uncommon. Academic researchers use these de-aligned models to better understand how AI actually works, while cybersecurity firms use them to probe software and systems for vulnerabilities. Technically speaking, Anthropic’s Mythos and OpenAI’s Astra work similarly: They’re basically conventional models that lack the usual cyber controls, with access limited to trusted customers for the time being. (The companies also offer wider access to models with a medium number of guardrails so that companies can vet their code and systems for problems.)

Abliteration AI offers several fully de-aligned models, the most powerful of which is a version of Z.ai’s latest agentic coding model, GLM 5.3. This puts similar cyber capabilities to Mythos and Astra right in your hands for as little as the cost of a pizza.

Devon, Abliteration AI’s CEO, believes that making de-aligned models widely available is smart defense: It will help good guys counter bad guys by probing systems for vulnerabilities and by mimicking the behavior of hackers, scammers, and, yes, rogue AI agents. (Devon asked that I use his first name only because his day job doesn’t know about his side project.)

“You have all these critical infrastructure companies, from airlines to banks, that are rolling out agents like crazy,” Devon says. “How do you make sure that a nefarious actor can't use some of these agents in a bad way?”

Tech.title: Apple Debuts the iPhone Duo, Its First Folding iPhone
Tech.content:
Apple says the hinge has a “custom variable torque profile” that precisely opens and closes the phone in an “effortlessly smooth” way. When it’s open, Apple says it’s the thinnest iPhone ever. As Samsung does with its “Flex Titanium” technology, Apple uses a carbon fiber metal plate below the display to better control the stress caused by bending the display. That, alongside a nano-texture finish, helps keep the display flat and “minimizes crease visibility.” An Apple-designed scratch-resistance coating sits on top.

Surprisingly, there is no Face ID sensor, likely to save space inside the phone for the folding components. Instead, like some of Apple’s tablets, the iPhone Duo brings back the fingerprint-sensing Touch ID integrated into the side power button. This is also the first iPhone to support the USB-C Apple Pencil later this year, though there’s no way to naturally store the stylus on the edges of the device like the iPad’s magnetic Pencil dock.

Apple says the Duo has the biggest battery ever in an iPhone. Like most book-style folds, it’s a split system where a battery rests on both sides. That will net you up to 31 hours of video playback with the inner display and 44 hours with the outer display—or 24 hours of mixed overall use per charge. It also sports Apple’s new custom C2 modem (with mmWave 5G support in the US) and the A20 Pro, the same chip powering the iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max.

Video: Courtesy of Apple

There are only two cameras on the back—a 48-megapixel primary camera and a 48-megapixel ultrawide. The lack of a telephoto zoom option is a sacrifice even Samsung made on its latest Galaxy Z Fold8. Like most book-like folds, it has two selfie cameras—a 12-megapixel camera on the outer screen and a second “FaceTime camera" on the inner display, though this one is hidden under the display.

There are familiar folding phone features here with the camera, like distracting a kid with a fun cartoon character on the outer screen to get them to look at the camera. Or your subject can preview the photo before you hit capture. The iPhone Duo can stand upright by itself, so you can set it down and it will automatically capture group photos if everyone stands at the ready.

Hardware is just one part of the story, though. The software needs to adapt and take advantage of the larger screen. Apple has been improving how apps adapt to different screen sizes for some time, making it easy for developers to scale apps from the iPhone to the iPad to the Mac, and even visionOS on the Apple Vision Pro. That means you’ll be able to enjoy iPad-like apps when unfolding the iPhone Duo.

Tech.title: Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4: Ceramic, Specs, Release Date
Tech.content:
The health sensor array has been redesigned with more electrodes for more accurate readings, photodiodes organized in a ring to capture light more efficiently, and new LEDs that allow heart rate measurements to be collected every 5 seconds, giving you a continuous stream of heart data throughout the day.

Video: Courtesy of Apple

Perhaps most notably, the Series 12 brings back the ceramic case, available in pearl white and night blue finishes. Apple first offered a ceramic option with the Series 2 in 2016, marketed as a luxury alternative to the company’s long-retired 18-karat gold edition; the ceramic casing was discontinued in 2020. According to Apple, the ceramic casing—made from compressed zirconia and alumina powder and polished with a diamond slurry—is four times more durable than stainless steel. The aluminum models are available in black, light gold, space gray aluminum, radiant gold, natural titanium, and a new dark bronze. All of the aluminum is recycled.

The new hardware arrives alongside watchOS 27, which will also be made available to people who already own compatible Apple Watches when the Series 12 goes on sale. The new OS updates the divisive Liquid Glass redesign on the smartwatch, and adds a more capable Siri AI powered by Apple Intelligence.

Following the industry trend of AI-notetakers, the new Siri Recap can translate and transcribe real-time conversations for users. In a demonstration video today, Apple showed a server at a restaurant reciting menu specials, and the person sitting at the table was able to use their watch’s dial to scroll back through a transcript of the last 15 seconds, then read what the server said on their Apple Watch screen.

There are several features—all of them opt-in, at least for the person wearing the watch—that are powered by the watch’s ability to record the wearer’s surroundings. Read more about them in Lily Hay Newman’s story about the Apple Watch’s newfound listening abilities on WIRED.

Tech.title: You Can Now Destroy Flock Cameras for Cash in GTA V
Tech.content:
People are not happy about Flock Safety’s automated license plate readers and the cops that allegedly misuse them. If you’re one of those ALPR-haters, you can now take out your rage in the video game Grand Theft Auto V by installing Grand Theft Automated License Plate Reader, a mod built by artist Morry Kolman.

The mod installs 235 Flock cameras around the fictional Los Santos, a riff on the real-life city of Los Angeles. Players can smash and shoot down the cameras and get paid $600 for each one they destroy, which Kolman priced based on a teardown of a Flock Falcon Flex Camera by the Iowa-based civil liberties group Eyes Off of Cedar Rapids. The in-game cameras log every time a player destroys and drives by one, and players can render a photo album of their interactions.

In real life, vigilantes have allegedly wrecked Flock cameras in their communities using spray-paint, saws, bullets, and even flaming projectiles. An NPR analysis found that Flock cameras have been vandalized in at least 36 states.

“GTPLR is not an endorsement of the activities that it allows in the game in the same way that GTA is not an endorsement of the activities that are allowed in the game,” says Kolman, referring to the fact that GTA is largely about doing fictional crimes. “But I think there is a public appetite for some kind of cathartic release against these machines.”

In addition to being fun objects to destroy, the GTA cameras also operate as an extension of the police in-game. Passing by one of the 235 cameras while being chased by the cops prolongs the game’s cooldown period. Because of how dense the cameras are in some areas, it can make the game impossible to play.

There’s also a 5 percent chance that the cameras will trigger a random police response even if the player isn’t doing anything wrong, which Kolman says was inspired by news reports about innocent people being held at gunpoint because of ALPR errors.

“There are violent responses and really dangerous situations that are created by these cameras and their inaccuracies,” says Kolman.

Flock did not immediately respond to a request for comment for this story.

GTA V has been around for over a decade, and a rich modding community has built up around it (WIRED covered one back in 2015.) The long-awaited sequel, Grand Theft Auto VI, is slated to come out in November and will be set in a fictional version of Miami called Vice City.

Kolman doesn’t have specific plans to build a version of GTALPR for that, joking, “We'll probably wait to see what the people of Vice City and their local government have already installed around their map.”

In real-life LA, the Los Angeles Police Department suspended its use of Flock cameras this summer following a recommendation from the LAPD’s inspector general. The tide is turning in other places too—governors in both Texas and Florida recently took steps to curtail the use of Flock cameras in their respective states, and across the US, there were 131 Flock contract terminations in August alone, according to the anti-surveillance advocacy group Secure Justice.

For all the fun that fake-smashing surveillance cameras can be, Kolman seriously hopes that players can feel the “insidiousness and inescapability of the surveillance” through GTALPR.

“I know that you could read a thousand articles about why surveillance is bad and why Flock is horrible,” says Kolman. “Or I could make you feel how pervasive these Flock cameras are by having you try to drive around the map of Los Santos.”

Tech.title: A Stealth Startup Thinks It Just Hacked the Memory Shortage
Tech.content:
An ambitious chip startup that has spent more than seven years quietly trying to redesign the architecture for computer memory has just come out of stealth mode and believes its new approach can help ease the global memory-chip shortage—provided it can produce its technology at scale.

Kepler Computing, a San Jose, California–based startup founded in 2018 by a team of physicists and computer scientists, says it has developed a new architecture for high-bandwidth memory (HBM) that directly addresses some of the chip supply bottlenecks that are constraining the computing market.

While chipmakers typically rely on expensive extreme ultraviolet lithography (EUV) to shrink the transistors on a chip, thereby packing more technology into the same amount of space, Kepler claims that its “3D stacking” approach and a proprietary new material allow it to increase density without relying on EUV at all—and it can work with existing semiconductor fabrication plants.

Kepler says it has made similar gains for the high-speed cache memory typically used in CPUs, GPUs, and XPUs. This so-called SRAM sits within the core of a chip die in order to cut down on data transfer times. HBM, by contrast, uses stacks of DRAM, which is a separate memory component of chips.

The company has raised $468 million in funding over the past few years from big-name backers. This includes GlobalFoundries, Intel Capital, AMD Ventures, the British investment fund Baillie Gifford, and Bill Gates, through his private Gates Frontier fund. In July, the US Department of Commerce committed to give Kepler up to $245 million to “develop in the US a new class of high-performance AI memory technology, enabled by innovative 3D and ferroelectric technologies.”

Tech.title: iPhone Handoff Will Let You Use One Number on Two Phones
Tech.content:
Soon iPhone owners will be able to split their phone numbers between devices.

When iOS 27 launches next week, it will include a new feature called iPhone Handoff, which allows you to use the same number on two different phones, Apple said at Wednesday’s Surprise and Shine event. The announcement came alongside the reveals of the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max and the long-rumored, foldable iPhone Duo.

The feature was first mentioned briefly in June on a slide at the Worldwide Developers Conference, but the company didn’t give many details at the time. Reddit users reported seeing the feature on their devices last month, and a MacRumors user shared a video last week showing how the feature works. Apple says the feature will be available with the iOS 27, which will be released on Sept. 14.

“iOS 27 improves connectivity with smarter transitions between cellular and Wi-Fi networks, and introduces iPhone Handoff that lets you use a single phone number across two iPhones,” an Apple speaker said. “The number is instantly active on whichever iPhone you pick up.”

But there is a catch: Apple says the iPhone Handoff feature will only be available initially with T-Mobile and Telecom Germany. Verizon and EE will get support by the end of the year, with “more carriers to follow.”

Once it’s available, you’ll be able to set up the Handoff feature in the Cellular section of the iPhone’s settings, according to the video posted to MacRumors. You’ll be prompted to hold the phones close to each other and pick which one keeps the main eSIM and which one gets the companion eSIM. Only the phone with the main eSIM will be allowed to change the Cellular Settings after that.

Tech.title: The iPhone 18 Pro Max’s Battery Is a Beast, but Save $100 and Stick to Last Year’s Model
Tech.content:
Apple just leveled up its battery on its new premium iPhone. Is it worth the leveled-up price tag?

As expected, Apple unveiled the pricier part of the iPhone 18 lineup at its “Surprise and shine” event on Wednesday. The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max have some serious upgrades, like faster performance from the A20 Pro processor, a new automatically adjustable camera aperture with built-in AI software, and a larger vapor chamber.

But the big “wow” factor is the battery. We saw a big improvement in the iPhone 17 Pro Max, which wins as our best-tested battery. But the iPhone 18 Pro Max is a pretty sweet upgrade for $100 more than its predecessor’s original price.

During the event, Apple said you can get 45 hours of video playback and 30 hours of usage per charge with the new premium version. It’s also expected to have faster wireless charging, and 15 minutes of wired charging should put the phone at 50%. Comparatively, the iPhone 17 Pro Max has 39 hours of video playback. And based on our testing, the phone’s battery life reached 49% in 20 minutes.

The 18 Pro Max seems to pack a powerful punch with its battery. And surprisingly, Apple’s not raising the price too much. The iPhone 18 Pro Max starts at $1,299 for 256GB, which is only $100 more than the iPhone 17 Pro Max for the same storage. But are the battery upgrades worth the price? I don’t think so.

Sure, the iPhone 18 Pro Max has a better battery, but if you’re like me, you just want your phone to hold a battery for a day without rushing to a charger. If you’re not watching videos for days, you may not see much of a difference between the iPhone 17 Pro Max and the new model. Especially if you want a better battery on a budget.

A recent CNET survey highlighted what US adults really want in a phone upgrade. Most (55%) want a cheaper phone, and next to that is better battery life (52%). Truthfully, while the iPhone 18 Pro Max price increase seems small (especially given the RAM shortage), you may be able to get a solid battery for less.

I have the iPhone 17 Pro Max, and I’m not sold on the new model’s $1,299 price tag when its predecessor is bound to be cheaper soon. Shortly after Apple’s event, the iPhone 17 Pro and Pro Max disappeared from Apple’s site. But you still may be able to compare prices at other retailers and mobile carriers. We also noticed Apple quietly increased prices on other iPhone models, so it’s worth shopping around.

Apple’s Upgrade program and other mobile carrier trade-in programs may make the newer model cheaper. But if you’re buying outright or won’t get a deep discount, save yourself the money and get the older model that still holds a charge for the day.

Tech.title: Already Appled Out? Here Are All the Tech Trends We Found at IFA 2026 in Berlin
Tech.content:
IFA Berlin has often been a place to see cutting-edge tech, cool concepts, and interesting prototypes (or should we say weird?). While there certainly have been some of those this year, like iRobot’s Roomba Duo, various humanoid demos, and a flying car concept, 2026 has felt more muted than last year. We’re still seeing the same demos of things like the Saros Rover and the Dreame Cyber X concept. Instead, what I’ve seen is companies really trying to drill down on perfecting the products and product lines that work for them.



Here are the trends I saw at IFA Berlin 2026 that drew my attention and are worth watching for next year.

Dust mites and allergies are the new target for robot vacuums

The Eufy E35 Omni was at IFA, but they didn’t run it. Ajay Kumar/CNET

Robot vacuums have become good maintenance tools for cleaning up dust and pet hair, but if you’re someone with asthma or serious allergies, you likely still need a good HEPA-certified vacuum and air purifier to keep things manageable. Well, that’s the new target of companies like Anker with the Eufy Omni E35 and Ecovacs with the Deebot X12S Omnicyclone. Both are certified by different organizations to prove they work as claimed. The X12S was tested by the SGS Testing & Control Services Singapore and, in testing, removed an average of 97.44% of dust mite allergens and 95.45% of dust mites from carpet. The Omni E35 also claims the ability to remove a slightly higher 99% of dust mites and has Asthma and Allergy Foundation of America certification.



Realistically, the percentage difference isn’t particularly significant. What’s notable here is that companies are actively seeking out certifications that prove their robot vacuums are capable of robust levels of cleaning and sterilization, that it’s suitable for maternal health, newborns and allergy sufferers. This might sound niche, but as someone who has three asthmatic cats and occasionally seasonal allergies, I’m interested to see if it lives up to the testing claims.

This is something we’re likely to see more of as robot vacuums become established not just for cleaning but for sanitizing as well, with models that can deploy steam, UV light, and sprays. In the same way air purifiers became increasingly common over the past decade as an easy way to cleanse your air and reduce allergies, we may see certified, high-quality robot vacuums take on the same role.

Deep cleaning is the new challenge to overcome

If you’ve been following robot vacuums at all, one thing you’ve probably noticed is that they’ve gotten pretty good at vacuuming, but mopping can still be a challenge with older and dried-on stains. An old spill of tomato sauce, red wine or ketchup on tile is still going to require you to use elbow grease to remove it — I speak from experience.

“One side is suction power, on the other side is mopping itself,” said Frank Wu, Roborock’s vice president for Europe, speaking with me at the company’s IFA booth. “At the end of the day, the target is to bring a better cleaning power to every corner of the home.”

Pretty much every company is trying to address this cleaning gap by using different mopping options, ranging from roller mops that self-clean with more downward pressure measured in newtons, as with iRobot and Eufy’s new lineup, which increases the pressure to 14N or 18N, depending on the model. That’s a simple and theoretically easy solution, just give the robot vacuum the elbow grease it’s missing, and iRobot has tried to do that for the vacuuming side of things too by adding a “skirt” that drops down on the Roomba 875 Combo that significantly increases suction strength on the already substantial 35,000 pascals.

The key problem with this strategy, though, is that robot vacuums are size-constrained, and unless you try something like iRobot’s Duo, which incorporates a floor washing unit combined with a mobile docking station, you’re never going to get the power of a real wet and dry mop, let alone an upright or canister vacuum.

Another way companies at IFA have tried to address this is Ecovacs Deebot X12S Omnicyclone, which incorporates high-pressure water sprayers to saturate old stains and help work them out of hard surfaces. Clever idea, but questionable implementation with the X12S. As I watched, I completely missed its ketchup-stain target and instead doused the floor, but it still managed to remove the mess. The 875 Combo uses a hot steam spray from the bottom of the unit to help loosen the stain, but no demos were offered, so I can’t know how it works in practice until we lab test it.

The humanoid robots were a big yawn this year

Ajay Kumar/CNET

I’m sorry to say that humanoid robot demos were just plain boring this year. Yeah, there are dancing robots and robots that can do backflips, like the PrimeBot T1 and Q1, and ones that can sort laundry or pick things like Dreame’s robot butler and SwitchBot’s Onero H1. Yawn. The real issue is that these things still don’t do anything more than what they did last year, and as I wrote in my cover story, the timeline for these robots is a lot further away than we’d hope and a lot more expensive. With a realistic timeline ranging from five to 10 years for partially functional home assistants that can do things like fold laundry and prices that will be closer to $100,000 than $10,000, I expect us to get many more years of IFA humanoid demos without actually getting a humanoid robot that you can buy and use in your home.

Part of why I’m not particularly impressed by any of these humanoid demonstrations is that robot vacuums have gotten so good. We’ve stopped talking about whether they can clean well or avoid objects easily. The newest models we’ve tested at CNET lab do an amazing job of it, and IFA demonstrations reinforced it for me as I watched Dreame’s X60 Ultra Complete Pro perfectly weave through obstacles with remarkable speed and responsiveness that I don’t typically associate with robot vacuums. The downside is that a Dreame representative confirmed to me that currently there are no confirmed plans for the model to come to the US, and with the added complication around the FCC ban and uncertainity around waivers, many of the more interesting new models may be delayed, though most companies have told me that they plan to move ahead with their launch plans.

This also affects humanoids, since a large share of the parts required for these advanced robots is sourced from Chinese supply chains. If the FCC ruling remains in effect without waivers, expect progress on US humanoids to freeze for the next decade as domestic supply chains are painstakingly built, while China races ahead with its already advanced models.

Balcony solar is a great idea whose time has come

For those who aren’t familiar with it, balcony solar is simply putting a plug-in solar panel on a balcony or other outdoor space and using it to store solar power and use it to power your appliances and devices when energy prices are high. It’s really intended for people who live in apartments or other homes where you might be a renter or don’t have the option of putting solar panels on the roof for a full system. Bluetti’s Balco 260 and Balco 500, Jackery’s Solar Vault 3 Series and EcoFlow’s Stream plug-in solar are all examples of this, which I saw at their booths, though it’s hard to really give impressions for a stationary battery that’s not in use.

Some of these weren’t necessarily IFA releases either and have been launched earlier in the year, such as the Solar Vault 3 Series. What I will say is that all of these systems are scalable, meaning you can add additional batteries based on your needs, connect more solar panels and use smart transfer switches or other power management.

Ajay Kumar/CNET
