With New Jersey becoming the 10th US state to legalize the use of balcony solar power (something that’s already quite popular in Germany and the European market), I do expect to start seeing these being used in the US to help defray our ever-increasing energy costs. New Jersey’s law is particularly beneficial since it restricts the ability of property management or HOAs to stop you from using balcony solar, though you’re going to want to dig into the laws for your state before installing it. In most cases, it should work with a standard AC outlet, but if you want to feed power back to the grid, things get a little more complicated and may require an electrician’s installation.

With nearly every major power station company releasing its own version, I expect adoption to start in the US, especially in New Jersey and New York, where people typically don’t have the option to install a solar panel on their roofs but face high energy costs. However, a Bluetti representative at the company’s IFA booth told me that they’ve currently paused their rollout due to uncertainty around — you guessed it — FCC regulations. So while I do think adoption will happen regardless, since, by all indications, Jackery and EcoFlow are moving ahead, US supplies of home batteries and solar panels may be affected.

Dyson had one of the strongest showings this year as a tech company

At IFA 2026, we’re seeing all the upgraded, AI-powered, repairable, camera-equipped tech. And then some. Tara Brown/CNET

Dyson hasn’t really been just about vacuums for a long time, even though it still has that perception when I mention it to people like my parents. Dyson was off-site at IFA this year, but it still drew tons of attention because its releases entered brand-new product categories, including the famous $500 Dyson CameraJet, which integrates a water flosser into an AI-optimized electric toothbrush to clean interdental gaps. It’s Dyson’s first entry into the category, and unlike vacuums and air purifiers, it’s not necessarily a natural fit where there’s a lot of overlapping tech and development that can be carried over.

Dyson’s new HushJet air purifiers are a total redesign. Tara Brown/CNET

However, Dyson didn’t rest on its laurels, with a total of 11 new products, something smart home managing editor David Watsky noted as being a much faster pace than what the company has released in the past. This includes multiple robot vacuum models with cutting-edge capabilities across price points, redesigned HushJet air purifiers, and new beauty products such as its first dryer brush and next-gen hair straightener. With competitors like Roborock, iRobot, Dreame, Narwal, Mova, Shark and others all coming out with a vast array of products and models on a yearly basis, I can’t help but wonder if Dyson is feeling the pressure to keep up in the pace and frequency of its releases.

Definitely a space worth watching if you’re a Dyson fan.

As usual, some of the best products at IFA can’t actually be purchased by Americans

Robot lawnmowers doing a synchronized fan dance isn’t something I knew I needed. Dillon Lopez/CNET

I’m talking about Dreame and Mova specifically here, though there are other examples like Anker and Ecovacs, with the latter having Tineco and Yeedi as sub-brands. Walking through their booths, I was struck by the sheer number of products they cover. You have the robot vacuums, cordless vacuums, wet and dry vacuums, robot lawn mowers, pool robots, window cleaning robots, air purifiers, smart pet tech like feeders and litter boxes, beauty tech like hair dryers and smart mirrors, humidifiers, fans and cooling, home battery backups, automotive, home security, home appliances, smart lighting, and other product categories I’m surely forgetting.

It’s an incredible, overwhelming number of products that make Dreame and Mova jacks-of-all-trades and almost overwhelming to cover. According to the hefty product brochure a Dreame representative handed me, the company had over 40 product releases for IFA, and I’d estimate a similar number for Mova. Many of these are products that won’t be sold in the US, which was the case for nearly the entire lineup of both companies, so that means we don’t cover them very much at CNET.

Ajay Kumar/CNET

But walking into their booth at IFA always reminds me that there’s an entire universe of excellent, quality product options out there that American consumers don’t have access. It’s tragic, and with the current uncertainity about what you can actually sell in the American market and regulations and tariffs that can change overnight, I don’t expect that to change soon.

Every home will have a wet and dry vacuum to go along with their robot

You’d be forgiven for thinking Roborock, Dreame, Narwal, iRobot and others are primarily robot vacuum manufacturers. They certainly all have an extensive lineup of robot cleaners, but one of the biggest product lines we’ve seen grow is wet-and-dry cleaners.

While Roborock didn’t share its sales with me directly, it said the Roborock F25 Ultra, which I tested and enjoyed using to keep my hardwood floors clean from my horribly messy cats, was one of its most successful new releases. I was able to see its Gen 2 model at the Roborock booth, as well as its integration into a unique five-in-one model (which may or may not come to the US) that combines a cordless vacuum and wet-and-dry vacuum into a base station unit.

Ajay Kumar/CNET

“We see a very, very typical scenario that some of the consumer they buy both a robotic vacuum cleaner and wet and dry,” said Wu. “The robots take care of the routine basis of cleaning, while when something urgent happens, something we just need to clean one certain spot, you can use wet and dry to take care of it.”



This applies to traditional cordless vacuums as well, which are only capable of dry cleaning. Wu gave me an example for where a wet and dry model would excel. “If you are having some gravy or dirt on the floor, you just cooked, your baby just dropped some milk or whatever on the floor. That’s not some kind of scenario traditional vacuum could take care of, that’s the scenario for wet and dry.”

Appliances are getting smart enough to run only during off-peak energy hours

One thing that kept coming up as we walked the showroom floor was energy efficiency. Appliance manufacturers have found a new way to cut electricity costs: large appliances that run when grid energy prices are lowest.

The technology itself isn’t new, but we’re starting to see it built consistently across product lines — not just reserved for premium brands such as LG and Samsung.

A camera in Miele’s new dishwasher helps it pick the perfect cycle. David Watsky/CNET

For context, electricity prices fluctuate throughout the day, with “peak” hours typically falling from roughly 4 p.m. to 9 p.m., the late afternoon into evening. Many of the smart appliances we saw at IFA include settings that restrict cycles to off-peak hours only.

Miele’s Diamond G8 dishwasher was one example, letting you program the machine to run exclusively during off-peak hours — though you can still override the energy-saving mode if you need clean dishes right away. The G8 also has an AI-powered camera that identifies the dishes loaded in the rack, runs an optimized cycle, and reduces hot water waste.

China-based appliance brand Midea unveiled its AI Ecomaster system at its sprawling booth this year. The smart, coordinated home network similarly taps into local energy pricing data and triggers washing machine and dishwasher cycles when grid prices drop. For homes with solar power, the Ecomaster can draw from stored solar energy whenever grid prices spike.

Midea’s new voice-controlled air conditioner follows you around the room with a stream of cool. David Watsky/CNET

This technology is currently limited to dishwashers and washing machines, but because large appliances use so much energy, the savings can add up meaningfully over a year.

Editors’ note: Ajay Kumar’s travel costs for the IFA conference were covered by Roborock. The judgments and opinions of CNET are our own

Tech.title: Apple Reference Photo Lets iPhone Photographers Prove What’s Real
Tech.content:
Apple spent much of its “Surprise and shine” fall event breathlessly detailing the new AI capabilities of Apple Intelligence and the new Photographic Styles with the iPhone 18 Pro. The new features offer greater AI-assisted abilities to change the look of a photo. In the midst of all this, the company also introduced a defense against AI-generated and -altered images.

The iPhone 18 Pro adds a new Reference camera mode, which digitally authenticates that an image you took with the phone hasn’t been altered with AI. It creates an unalterable reference photo captured by the phone’s sensor. The phone sends sensor signatures and other identifiers to Private Cloud Compute to authenticate the reference photo.

Reference photos are saved in the Photos app next to the main image that can be edited so you can see the original and edited versions next to one another to compare the two.

Apple also announced support for Google’s SynthID standard for authenticating images. Together, these tools give photographers and journalists ways to verify their work. And fishermen now have verifiable evidence that the fish they caught really was that big.

Tech.title: Apple Announces a Redesigned Health App and Readiness Score
Tech.content:
Alongside the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, AirPods 5 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 and Series 12 with new health sensors called the Health Sensing System, Apple unveiled a revamped Health app with Apple Intelligence at its core during its Surprise and Shine event on Wednesday. It includes lab tests in partnership with Quest Diagnostics, movement assessments and new Insights and Longevity tabs. Plus, a readiness score on the Apple Watch to prepare you for the day ahead.

On the iPhone

The iPhone’s redesigned Health app will be available later this year in US English, though no specific date was announced. Other languages will follow.

The revamped Health app will feature a new Longevity tab that includes a “health age” showing how a user’s metrics compare to their actual, chronological age. This health age will take into account Apple Watch metrics, including resting heart rate, sleep, VO2 max and HRV, as well as any information from blood tests.

Health age will show your biological age versus your chronological age. Apple

Based on data from the iPhone, Apple Watch, AirPods, clinical health records and third-party apps and devices, the Longevity tab will have a visualization that shows users different areas of their health. It will also show what is impacting their long-term health.

The Longevity tab visualization. Apple

There will be another new tab, Insights, that uses Apple Intelligence to provide users with a timely summary of their health across vitals, fitness, heart, readiness, sleep and cycle tracking. This summary will update throughout the day. Under this tab, there will also be a For You section with personalized recommendations and relevant articles that appear based on a user’s health data.

In addition to articles, there will be videos from Apple Health clinical experts offering insights into various aspects of health, such as what LDL cholesterol is and how to improve it, or how to improve balance.

Using vision-based AI models on the iPhone and heart rate data from the Apple Watch, the Health app will also have new movement tests that measure strength, balance, flexibility, movement mechanics and VO2 max. These tests are entirely on device, according to an Apple news release, so no video is ever recorded, stored or shared.

A person using their iPhone’s camera to complete a movement assessment. Apple/CNET Screenshot

Users can learn even more about their bodies by purchasing blood tests for over 50 biomarkers in the app, starting at $119. Testing can then be completed at US Quest Diagnostics locations.

On the Apple Watch

On the Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, there is the new readiness feature, which looks at a user’s sleep score, recent activity, vitals and training load to provide a score from zero to 10 that gives them one of four recommendations — recover, pace yourself, ready or go for it — to help them decide whether they should push themselves or take it easy during the day ahead. This score will update throughout the day, showing users which metrics are driving the chosen number.

How ready is your body for the day you currently have planned? That’s your readiness score. Apple/CNET Screenshot

This comes with the Watch Series 12’s new S11 chip and Health Sensing System, which Apple calls the most accurate heart rate sensing in a wearable. This is based on a study involving over 1,000 people that compared the Apple Watch’s new heart rate sensors with those of leading wearables. The new, larger, power-efficient green LEDs on the optical heart sensor will passively measure heart rate every five seconds.

Heart rate variability (HRV) will also be measured up to 24 times more often and will be available to view in the Heart Rate app. There will be two different HRVs shown: the “recovery HRV” for identifying stress and recovery, and the “overall HRV” for a user’s broader health. Overnight vitals will also show recovery HRV measurements relative to a user’s baseline.

Speaking of overnight vitals, there will be a new view focusing on daytime vitals. To spot changes between the two, users can toggle between overnight and daytime metrics.

Toggle between overnight and daytime vitals to compare the two. Apple/CNET Screenshot

Along with its heart rate sensing, the smartwatch’s pedometer has been redesigned with new machine learning algorithms, so the Apple Watch Series 12, according to Apple, offers the most accurate step tracking of any smartwatch. This is based on a 1,000-step accuracy test conducted by Apple and validated using video step counting. It compared the Series 12 with industry-leading smartwatches available as of July 2026.

Final thoughts

While similar features, including readiness scores and longevity insights, have already been launched by competitors like Oura Ring, Whoop and Fitbit, what makes Apple’s revamped Health app and accompanying features unique is that they come backed by its sensors. According to CNET’s own testing earlier this year, the Apple Watch Series 11 was the most accurate heart rate monitor during workouts.

While we haven’t gotten our hands on the new Series 12, our testing gives us high hopes that Apple’s health features will stand out for their accuracy, despite other companies already offering similar scores and wellness insights.

Tech.title: Apple Introduces New Audio Intelligence Features for Apple Watch
Tech.content:
During its “Surprise and Shine” event on Wednesday, Apple took the wraps off several products, including the latest iPhone 18 Pro lineup, the foldable iPhone Duo and the Apple Watch Series 12 and Watch Ultra 4. The new smartwatches come with updated specs across the board, but some of the software touches that Apple has included really make the new devices stand out.

One of the more interesting new features for Apple Watch is Audio Intelligence, which uses the built-in microphones to do some helpful things. Apple says that this will allow you to make more sense of the world around you from what you hear.

Apple/Screenshot by CNET

There are three standout features here, all of which are novel for a smartwatch. The first focuses on staying aware of ambient sounds you might otherwise miss, which could be incredibly helpful for people with hearing loss. Both the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 can listen for sounds like alarms, sirens, doorbells and more, and send you a notification when it identifies one of them. Since it uses on-device AI, these notifications can still be sent to you even if you don’t have your iPhone with you.

Live Rewind can transcribe an important conversation you just missed. Apple/Screenshot by CNET

Apple’s also introducing a new feature called Live Rewind. With the new Apple Watches, if you get hit with a ton of information — say, a waitress blurting out a series of lunch specials that you can’t quite keep up with — you can ask your Apple Watch instead of reaching back out. All you’ll need to do is double-tap the crown on your compatible Apple Watch, and it will transcribe the last 15 seconds of what was just said to you. From there, you’ll be able to ask Siri about the transcribed content or save it in the Siri app to view later.

Siri Recap will give you high-level notes from your most important conversations you can save for later. Apple/Screenshot by CNET

Lastly, there’s Siri Recap. Apple says the new feature uses ambient listening to take high-level notes from your conversations so you can be more present in everyday life. These notes will generate a “recap” that will serve up key information from the conversations. Apple Intelligence will generate a title for the recap, along with a general summary and key points, so you always know what was said.

If that sounds a little creepy to you, the Siri Recap feature is optional, and you can turn it off any time you want to. You can also set up a schedule so it only works at night or whenever you’d like it to.

None of the Audio Intelligence features actually create or store any audio recordings for your privacy, and the audio itself is inaccessible, including to Apple itself. Moreover, all Live Rewind transcripts and Siri Recap in the Siri app are end-to-end encrypted.

Live Rewind and Siri Recap require Siri AI, which will be released in beta later this year in English, with more languages to follow.

Tech.title: Apple’s New iPhone Duo Folds Like a Passport
Tech.content:
If you’re used to the vertical flip opening of phones like the Motorola Razr, or still fondly remember snapping your vintage not-so-smart cell phone open and shut, think different. The just-announced folding iPhone Duo opens horizontally, like a book, and its size and fold direction make it reminiscent of a paper passport. The much-anticipated phone was revealed Wednesday at at Apple’s live “Surprise and shine” event.

While it wasn’t confirmed until Wednesday, the Apple folding phone was the worst-kept secret in tech, with hundreds of articles reporting that it was on the way. And it joins a crowded field of foldable phones, with key players including Samsung, Google and Motorola, and Chinese brands like Honor, Oppo and Huawei. But as CNET’s Abrar Al-Heeti notes, Apple’s entry into the fray is expected to nudge foldable phone designs forward.

Al-Heeti notes that the iPhone Duo is compact, and Apple says it’s the thinnest iPhone ever when opened. The phone has a 7.6-inch display on the inside, a 5.4-inch outer display, and will come in two colors, star white and night sky.

Tech.title: Apple Watch Series 12: Familiar Design, Different Everywhere Else
Tech.content:
The Apple Watch Series 12 has arrived, and like clockwork, Apple unveiled its latest flagship smartwatch at its September launch event alongside the Apple Watch Ultra 4, new iPhone 18 models and the long-awaited foldable iPhone Duo.

Apple may have kept the familiar Apple Watch design for another year, but it has seemingly changed everything else inside. The most important upgrades are the hardware that powers its new features: a new S11 processor and reengineered health sensors. Combined, they allow for higher heart rate accuracy, deeper recovery insights, and a new AI-powered Audio Intelligence feature that can play back, transcribe and save important conversations.

It also brings new finishes and colorful accessories to freshen up the otherwise identical design. But perhaps the biggest surprise is what didn’t change: the price. While Apple raised prices on its iPhone 18 Pro lineup, the Series 12 still starts at $399, while the Ultra 4 starts at $799.

More processing power for Siri AI

Apple had ground to make up on processing power this year after using the S10 chip for two generations. The new S11 chip makes up for some lost time, with a faster GPU, CPU and neural engine.

One place that extra processing power could come in handy is WatchOS 27, which brings the new Siri AI to the Apple Watch. I’ve already been testing Siri AI in beta on the Ultra 3, and it’s miles ahead of traditional Siri. It can answer more complex and contextual questions, reference information in Apple’s native apps and generally avoid the frustrating “here’s what I found on the web” response that made traditional Siri feel especially limited on the wrist.

But I’ve also noticed some lag. Some of that could be because the software is still in beta, but I’m curious to see whether the new S11 chip speeds up those interactions on the Series 12.

The new processor could also help with battery life. Apple rates the Series 12 for the same 24 hours as the previous generation, but it’s now taking heart rate samples more frequently than before for increased accuracy.

For context, the Series 11 lasted about 28 hours during my real-world testing, so I’ll be looking to see whether those gains translate outside Apple’s controlled testing.

Apple/CNET

Audio Intelligence feature recaps older conversations

One of the most interesting new AI-powered features on the watch is what Apple calls Audio Intelligence. It’s essentially the ability for your watch to listen in on conversations, to either play back what you missed on the fly (like the specials at a restaurant if you zoned out while the waiter was talking), or in a meeting setting where you got the Apple Watch to take high-level notes for you. It’ll create a new document with a summary and key points.

You can set up this feature manually or enable it to turn on at a specific time. Apple also says none of the conversations are stored and that even what is processed in the cloud to surface on your other Apple devices can’t be accessed by the company (or anyone else).

Apple/Screenshot by CNET

Apple gets serious about recovery

Apple is also expanding its health and fitness tracking with a new Readiness app, which takes some of the health data the Apple Watch already collects and turns it into a snapshot of how prepared your body is for the day ahead.

Rather than looking at individual metrics in isolation, the app combines biometric signals associated with sleep, stress and recovery to help you decide whether your body is ready for a hard workout or could be better off taking it easy.

This is similar to the existing Vitals, which shows when overnight health metrics fall outside your typical range, and an addition to Training Load, which tracks how much strain you’re putting on your body.

Revamped health app and other health features

Apple also announced a redesigned health app that will combine AI insights and biometrics to give you daily summaries and personalized health recommendations. This is similar to what other wearables like Fitbit Air, Whoop and Oura give you, but behind a paywall. Apple is giving all the upgraded health insights for free on the app. It also has a more comprehensive VO2 max test that you can take using the cameras on the phone, and the option to include blood test results that you can order directly from the app.

WatchOS 27 will also bring more health features that aren’t exclusive to the Series 12, including workout updates and new perimenopause insights for women. Workout Buddy, Apple’s hype person in your ear during workouts, will also work in Spanish and without an iPhone nearby.

Familiar design, new paint job

If you were hoping for a dramatically different Apple Watch, this isn’t the year. The Series 12 keeps the familiar rectangular, all-screen display like its predecessor, but Apple is giving it a refresh with new colors, case finishes and bands.

The Series 12 comes in black, silver, gold and a new bronze aluminum finish. Apple is also bringing back a ceramic case option for the Series 12, a material we haven’t seen on its flagship watch since the Series 5 in 2019, as well as a new gold titanium Hermes edition and new band options across the board.

Apple Watch Series 12: Price and availability

The Apple Watch Series 12 starts at $399 for the 42mm aluminum Wi-Fi model, and is available for preorder now.

Is the Apple Watch Series 12 worth the upgrade?

The Series 12 may look the same, but it has enough upgrades under the hood to warrant an upgrade, especially if you’re coming from an older model like the Series 8 or below that won’t support some of the AI capabilities like Siri AI.

The biggest issue right now is that a lot of the best features, including Siri AI, the revamped Health app and Audio Intelligence, won’t be available to test until later this year, so I can’t make a recommendation until these key features have been put to the test.
